<meta>This page marks the beginning of the "Canon of Medicine," one of the most influential books in medical history. It follows the structural gap noted on the previous page, introducing the author Avicenna and the translator Gerard of Cremona.</meta>

### The first book of the Canon, which the prince Abu Ali ibn Sina published on medicine: translated in Toledo by Master Gerard of Cremona. The words of Abu Ali Avicenna.

The first book of the Canon, which the prince Abu Ali ibn Sina <note>original: "abuali ab iusce de mediana," referring to Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna</note> published on medicine: translated in Toledo by Master Gerard of Cremona. The words of Abu Ali Avicenna.
**F**irst, let us give thanks to God, as the loftiness of His rank and the greatness of His bounty deserve. To Him belongs mercy and proper piety. And concerning the things which I see in these better years: by the means through which I can satisfy God for what I am able to do. A friend requested me to write a book on medicine containing particular rules, to encompass them such that the explanation remains brief. First, let me state what is to be presented in the declaration of the work's sections that follow in order. It is planned that I should first speak of common and universal things in both parts of medicine, namely the theoretical and the practical. Then I shall speak of universal judgments: the whole of medical writing. In these particular parts, the Canon speaks of the constitutions that affect the blood and the members. It deals with anatomy <note>original: "anottoia," a medieval spelling for anatomy</note> from the beginning of that member and its function. Regarding the anatomy of simple members, I have spoken in this book on generalities. In the anatomy of the members and their connection, I demonstrate in many places the cavities and the form of their construction, alongside general diseases, their causes, and how to recognize them. After completing these general matters, I will proceed to study specific cases in many chapters. First, my general judgment on the definition of medicine, its causes, and signs. Then I return to the judgments of particular cases, first establishing a general rule for healing. Finally, I will discuss how to proceed with healing specifically, so that every medical writing is accounted for, including what is said regarding the use of medical tables.

<column-break/>

This is good for those who are students in this discipline. When you come to this work, it will not seem a long journey except for a short time. Concerning the medical matters that are calculated and what they contain, I first intend to discuss the human body and how it is preserved. I will leave the rest there. It pleases me that after I have preserved the volume of this book, I shall compose a work on the patient’s condition and the piety of naming the sickness hereafter. I will speak of the fullness of the universal whole, just as the book of particulars which I have set forth, God willing. I have categorized the book according to the appropriate sections; it is not good for this book of particulars to be with every student from memory, because the names of these other things will cease to be understood. For it is necessary for a physician to strive for what is above what has been said, which is comprehensible. If someone prolongs the study of the work, fortune will preserve him. I have prepared myself to compose this book, which I have divided into five books:

**B**ECAUSE medicine is the science by which the dispositions of the human body are known—from the perspective of how it is healthy and how it is moved away from health—it follows that health, once possessed, may be preserved, and once lost, may be recovered. ### Chapter Eleven, Part Three: On Complexions

<margin>
Otherwise: concerning the human being's division or parts.
</margin>

**C**omplexion is a quality that results from the mutual action and passion <note>In medieval philosophy, "passion" refers to being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note> of the two qualities found in the elements, whose parts are reduced to a common point so that whichever of them prevails <gloss>that is, they dominate</gloss>, it provides the soul to the majority. For when they act and suffer upon one another, a flow of virtue is reached, and a summary quality is created in the whole of them together, which is the complexion.

<margin>
. i . in the middle .
</margin>

¶ And since the primary virtues <note>original: "virtutes," meaning powers or properties</note> which are in the aforementioned elements are four: heat, cold <note>The OCR "calitasitas" likely refers to "caliditas" (heat) and "frigiditas" (cold).</note>, moisture, and dryness, it is manifest that complexions in the generation and corruption of bodies occur through them. And therefore, according to how bodies are diversified, a rational soul possesses an absolute presence, which no complexion can reach for any thing, except in two ways. One of these is that the complexion be perfectly equalized, so that the quantity of qualities in the thing composed is exactly equal, not one higher than the other; and this complexion exists in the exact middle between the extremes.

<margin>
Note.
</margin>

The other way is that the complexion of its qualities is not an absolute middle, but rather declines toward one of the extremes, either in the medium which is not between heat and cold, or the medium which is not between moisture and dryness, or both. ¶ And because this maximum mediation is refined, it is as if the thing is at rest, even if it is not truly so.

<margin>
Otherwise: complexions in members and divisions.
</margin>

¶ The medical physicists teach that according to this intention of which we speak, it is impossible to find such a quality, much less that it should be the complexion of a human being or a human limb.

<margin>
In this, complexion through the division in the interior is acquired.
</margin>

¶ It is necessary to know that the quality which the physician seeks in his inquiries is not of that absolute equality in which a species exists equally. Rather, by the nature of living things, a diversification from equal complexion returns it to its proper form, whether it be for the whole body or one limb, as it is composed from elements with certain quantities and qualities in a human measure. Thus, it is content with a better proportion of the soul according to its endurance.

¶ To this is added another division, for they consider this "equality" which is considered in the human species as being very close to that equality which exists in common. This is the composition of others with this equality of the limbs, which is the most excellent equality that a human being attains through the use of medicines.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Beware, for they endure... the science and its works... for him who is divided from it... for him who is divided... they seek him... they endure according to singular opinions.
</margin>

However, it acts according to how it is composed for that which is divided from it. One thing is compared to another according to the species, by an external equal division; and it is not in the mind, but either said according to a singular common thing which is divided from it by that which is in the part. Or it is said according to a singular common thing provided for that which is divided from it, arising from that which it is. And the first human being was made according to a refined limb, as is said of the spirits in themselves, which is said to be equal according to the mode of complexion. This is said of one another among the heavy elements, and it holds a great latitude <note>In medieval science, "latitude" refers to a range or span of intensity.</note> which is said to be the least for the species. In which light some things exist in multitude and through a vacuum, obtaining two extremes from which each soul was made equal, and it becomes a human complexion.

The second mode is called the "mediated" mode, which exists between two extremes as a clear complexion in the variety of individuals, which is in the ultimate external equality. This is in the sincerity of equality and in the being in which anyone reaches his own limit. Although this is equality, and this is the equality also which is taken at a point, because this find is not impossible, for him to have his own <unclear>state</unclear>. Human equality does not exist in every way, but in the heat of his limbs, and so in common, and also in the cold; so that from these, his proper measure is better than all others.

<margin>
Otherwise: [of] another.
</margin>

For when they are balanced and made equal, there is a manifest equality in which no limb is divided into one which is different, just as we said before regarding the properties of the limbs. It is impossible for him to be in this time of equality, as he either recedes from it toward heat or moisture, etc. The cooling of the limbs is a proper thing by which a heat is moved from him, or a coldness is demonstrated.

<margin>
Note the first... they are.
</margin>

And it is not that which exists through heat and is increased through moisture; although heat and moisture are the primary or nearby principles, so it is from labor. And there is a reason why one is cold, so that it arrives at the heat of the heart and is tempered. And it is because one is dry or moist, and because of this, his dryness does not reach moisture until it is tempered. Nor is it the contrary of the cold ones, that their heart is dry; but the heart, being composed of two others, is dry, and another of the two is cold.

<meta>The text continues the physiological investigation from the previous page, moving from the specific humoral balances of organs (like the liver and lungs) to the broader question of the complexions belonging to the different ages of man, specifically childhood and youth. It attempts to reconcile conflicting statements attributed to Galen regarding whether children are fundamentally "hot" or "cold."</meta>

<margin>Here he posits the solution to two arguments, first and second, which seem to oppose Galen.</margin>
...all their complexions are hot, similar to a **tertian fever** <term>tertian fever: a fever that recurs every third day, traditionally associated with an excess of yellow bile</term>, and by their will, the whole is choleric. Likewise, Galen says elsewhere that the first things drawn out in children are cold and moist, and their fevers are **quotidian** <term>quotidian: a fever occurring every day, usually linked to phlegm</term>. Again, he says that in man there is wind <note>original: "flatus"</note> and growth, which exists in children only because of the strength of their heat, in which they are mostly moistened for the greatest desire of their bodies; this signifies the diminution of their heat. These points also concern two sections without a response.

<margin>How youth and childhood are the same according to the Master</margin>
Galen says in other places, and he says it repeatedly, that their heat is from the root <note>original: "ex radice," referring to innate or radical heat</note> and is equal. If the heat of children is of a **greater quantity** but a **lesser quality** (that is, in its sharpness), then the heat of young men <note>original: "iuvenum"</note> is of a lesser quantity but a **greater quality** (that is, in its sharpness). But then, as he himself declares, the opinion is that there is only one heat in measure. Either a body has heat in one quantity and quality, in which that moisture is greatly and at once perceived like thin water—whence it penetrates into it—or it is like a stone, which has little. Again, in this way there was an exchange between the heat of water, which is of greater quantity and softness, and the heat of a stone, which is of lesser quantity and sharper quality.

And so you must act concerning the quality which is in young men and children; if there were not a quantity of this matter which carries much of this heat, it would happen by nature that it would be extinguished. In children, however, the heat increases according to a relative degree, because it is not yet held back. In young men, truly, nothing happens that would increase their innate heat, nor anything else that would extinguish it. And he shows that this heat is of a lesser quantity of moisture and quality simultaneously; one should not add to this, lest he think that in moisture a diminution of moisture is yet a diminution of quality that cannot be retained. In those in whom growth could be achieved because the moisture was so great, it was able to do two things: to guard the heat found there and to look toward achieving growth. At the end, however, it can achieve neither of these two things. But in the middle, such a state exists that it can achieve one thing and not the other. It is false, however, to say that it can increase [growth] but cannot retain the innate heat. Because growth follows afterwards through... <unclear>grindice</unclear>, if it was able to guard and retain, just as he says regarding that heat where nature is the author, because it could not sustain growth—surely this is the age of youth. For the growth that was in children lasts, produced because of...

<margin>Galen</margin>
...that moisture itself, and the stated heat, is false. # Fourth Doctrine, first chapter of the fourth doctrine
# To know what a humor is, and its division.

A **humor** <term>humor: one of the four essential fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine health and temperament</term> is a moist, liquid body into which the nourishment itself is transformed. And in truth, a humor has a moisture which is fixed, so that it may become a part of that which is nourished, either alone or by being assimilated with another; or it is made for the purpose of restoration of that which is dissolved from the body.

<column-break/>

The humor can be **good** or it can be **bad**. And because they do not profit the one acting, or rarely so, those who use the humor, it ought to be expelled from its common place. We say, however, that regarding their moistures, some are **proper** and some are **accidental**. The proper ones are those which we shall notably place in the first order.
Following this, there is a second division: they are called **influential** or **superfluous** <note>original: "superfluites," referring to waste products of digestion</note>, or those which are not proper to the members. And because those which are influential are those which are primarily disposed to be made into the members, or to become like the member through the power of nutrition, they are effectively the beginning of the humors.

### Chapter One: On the nature of the members, to know what a member is and its differences.

<margin>Here begins the first generation of the members.</margin>
**Members** are bodies composed from the primary joining of the humors, just as the humors are generated among themselves from the primary joining of the elements. Of the members, some are **simple**, while others are **composite**. The simple ones are those of which any part is divisible into the same thing, having the same name and definition. For example, flesh in its parts is flesh, a nerve <note>original: "iuvus" / "nervus"</note> in its parts is a nerve, and a bone in its parts is a bone, and similar things. For in a part of the whole, the first composite things are those of which any part does not receive the name and definition of the whole, such as the hand and the face. A part of the face is not the face; a part of the hand is not the hand. 

<margin>Note.</margin>
Of the members, however, the members are instruments of the soul, because they are the tools of the soul for complex movements and operations. The first member of similar parts is the **bone**, which was created hard so that it might be the foundation and the support of movements. Next to it is **cartilage**, which is softer than bone, and therefore it can be bent. But it is among all other members... so that we may live... it was made so that the bone might have a better generation from all soft things. For the hardness of the bone is better protected when it is mediated by something soft.

Of all the bones that exist, some are held as a foundation, upon which the body is supported, such as the vertebrae <term>spondiles</term> of the back. The utility of the radiation and the cavity in the member is that it may be light. And the utility of the unity and the internal cavity is that its heart <note>the bone's core</note> may be hard. Just as it appears most clearly, it is always softened by the marrow lest it be broken, so that its movement may endure.

### Chapter 5: On the Anatomy of the Teeth.

There are, therefore, thirty-two teeth. And though they are many, they are of four kinds. There are the dual teeth <term>dual teeth</term><note>original: "duales"; these are the central incisors.</note>, two above and two below. Then there are two "second" incisors <note>original: "plī"; likely referring to the lateral incisors</note> above and the same below. Then there are two canines above and two below for breaking [food]. And the molars for grinding, on each side, four or five, both above and below. And this total sum is either thirty-two or twenty-eight. There are four duals, four second incisors, four canines, then twenty molars, and four wisdom teeth <note>original: "neguegi"; a Latinization of the Arabic term for wisdom teeth, often called 'dentes intellectus'</note>. These wisdom teeth emerge in the middle of a person's life, or when they have reached full growth. This occurs around thirty years of age. Therefore, these last teeth are called the "teeth of sense" <note>original: "dētēs sūsus"; wisdom teeth.</note>. And the teeth have sharp roots received in the holes <note>sockets</note> of the bones of the two mandibles in which they stand. And upon the margin of each hole, a large gum is joined, which holds the teeth and surrounds them where the holes are.

### Chapter 6. On the anatomy of the back.

The bones [of the spine] were created for four purposes. One is to be the protector of the **spinal cord** <term>nucha</term><note>In medieval Latin, 'nucha' specifically refers to the spinal cord, a term adopted from Arabic medical traditions.</note>, because the spinal cord is the primary source of life for the animal. For this reason, we will clearly describe the utility of the spinal cord in this place. Regarding the most significant living things, we record that at the top of the bones originating from the head, the spinal cord is much larger so that it may then rule over the entire body. I report this because it could not travel the distance and length to all the limbs without reaching them; it would be subject to external injuries like a ray of light falling upon it. And the length of the thing also affects its strength to adhere to the limbs. Because of this, it is judged that the spinal cord has different segments for the sake of nourishment, as the spinal cord continues to the lower parts like channels. Because it was created with a logic of division from its two sides to the interior and the opposite side, it needs protection. This protection and custody is achieved because he wanted to guard the remaining noble member placed before it. Therefore, it is as if it remains from the spine. And now, the back was created to be like the **timber** <note>The keel of a ship.</note> which is first placed in the middle of a ship, because the other timbers establish their foundation upon it. Thus the back was created to be hard. And since it must be possible for the body to move in many directions, the back was ordered into **vertebrae** <term>spondiles</term><note>Individual bones of the spine.</note> instead of being one single large bone. You will find that between the vertebrae, sides are made which—

<column-break/>

—would be weakened in movement likewise, unless there were a great power that could bend it, etc.

### Chapter 7. On the anatomy of the vertebrae.

A **vertebra** is a bone in the middle of which is a hole through which the spinal cord passes. The design of the vertebra is straight so that the supports may properly allow the passage on both sides of the hole. Those parts which face upward are called the superior processes <note>original: "sursum aspe[n]te[n]tia"</note>. And those which face downward are called the inferior processes. There are other supports between them, four on one side and two on the other. There are also others called the axis. In this joint is the utility so that the connection between the vertebrae is joined in a neighboring place, or what I call the "cheeks" of their heads. These exist because of the vertebrae, providing defense and filling the gaps so that a ligament may weave these supports together. There are also broad, rough bones placed along the length of the vertebrae. Those which face the voice of the spine <note>likely referring to the spinal canal or the central axis</note> are positioned as if standing erect and extended. They serve to defend the back along its length, coming from the deep muscle in what is called the rear. And because some parts stand by themselves, they have a different utility. In the middle are the cavities where the humps of the heads of the **ribs** <term>costa</term> are marvelously bound. In each "wing" <note>the transverse processes</note> there are two cavities, because in each rib there are two humps. Thus, those which have two heads have a double support. And there is that which exists in the vertebrae of the neck, for protection. The vertebrae, which have the main hole in the middle, have other holes through which the nerves of the spinal cord exit, as well as the veins. Some of these holes are between them, but one is completed in a single vertebra by a protrusion that matches another, so they exit between two vertebrae. This place is common to both because they exit beneath them. Because of this, it aids the upper and lower parts. And since it is in one part, the ratio in each vertebra is a "semi-circle" <note>original: "semikuilus"</note>; the ratio in one is larger and in the other smaller. And they have holes placed on two sides of the vertebra: this is done for protection so that what goes out and returns is not exposed to danger. Nor would they be placed there unless it were in those central locations.

### Chapter 22. On the anatomy of the palm of the hand.

### Chapter 25. On the anatomy of the thigh bone.

The bones of the <term>alhauius</term> <note>The pelvis or hip region.</note> are two bones, on the right and on the left, which are joined in the middle at the top. And these have, like all the superior bones, a structure in three parts and a localized mechanical friction. Each of them is divided into four parts. That which is at the side of the flank <note>The ilium.</note> is called the <term>alhartafi</term> <note>An Arabic-derived term for the hip bone.</note> or the bone of the flank. And that which is toward the interior is called the bone of the **femur** <note>The thigh bone.</note>. And that which is toward the posterior is called the bone of the <term>aucte</term> <note>The ischium.</note>. And the <term>comestidiai</term> <note>The pubic region.</note> which is toward the superior parts is called the prominence of the hip, in which there is a cavity into which the rounded head of the thigh enters. And this bone does not have a noble structure for us, just as it serves the vessels of the male and the reservoirs of the seed <note>The reproductive organs.</note> in the reproductive vessels or the straight testicle.

### Chapter 26. On the collective discourse regarding utility.

<margin>The word "Tigil" signifies all instruments among the Arabs, such as a leg or its foot...</margin>
The utility of the **bone** consists of two supports or <term>rigil</term> <note>From the Arabic "rijl," meaning leg or foot.</note>. One is for shape and standing. And this is for the part. And the other is for movement, whether equal or swift or jumping. Also, they exist for protection and for help. Since the birth of the feet happened for standing and shape, it would be difficult if movement was not innate in them, for many flexions of movement were created toward one of the feet. Since the birth of the hands happened for grasping, it would be a natural thing, but moving would be difficult. The first of the bones of the leg is the hip, because it is the bone of the limb which exists in the body. It is a defense for it, in which is the movement above it. Its superior extremity was made round so that it might enter well into the cavity. And that which is convex toward the side of the flank is thinned toward the internal part or toward the posterior. Thus, its length is established in straightness. And in the distance of its side, any mode of limping might happen, which is why the joint is such. It well defends the great muscles and the nerves or veins. From all these things, the rule of the kingdom <note>The governing power of the body.</note> is upright. The shape of sitting would be good. 

<margin>And the internal part.</margin>
The fullness of the internal part is reduced. Limping occurs in the other way if its middle standing were not straightly enclosed from all sides or were not equal. And in its extremity, there is a joining of two additions for the sake of the binding of the joint. We will now speak of the leg and the parts of the binding.

The lower leg is composed of two bones. One is larger and longer, situated at the front, and is called the "large cane" <note>original: *canna magna*; the tibia</note>. The other is smaller and shorter; it reaches toward the hip, or rather, it is inserted near it, and then extends to the place where the larger bone hangs, and it is called the "small cane" <note>original: *canna minor*; the fibula</note>. The leg has a convexity toward the outer side and a hollow where it is inserted, and it has another convexity toward the inner side, which ensures that the foot has a better stance. The "large cane" is the primary support, while the "small cane" was created to assist the thigh. In water and on land, these structures serve the purposes for which their size was determined. Their shape and the reasons for their addition involve their final purpose in movement. These parts were made larger for the sake of strength. These two bones of the leg are joined together so that if an accident were to happen to one bone, the other might prevent a total loss of motion, unlike the legs of elephants <note>A common medieval misconception was that elephants lacked joints in their legs; here the author compares human flexibility to elephantine rigidity</note>. If one bone is weakened, it results in a loss of power in movement. This arrangement occurs in humans and other animals. In that "small cane," there are nerves and veins which are covered by the surrounding tissues. The purpose of the "small cane" is to serve the foot so that its structure of expansion and rotation may be faster and stronger.

### Chapter XXIX. The Anatomy of the Knee Bone.

The nature of the knee <term>poplitis; the posterior part of the knee or the joint itself</term> provides two aids for walking which come from the end of the thigh bone into two cavities at the head of the leg bone. It is secured by a strong ligament and another ligament connected deep within, as well as two other strong ligaments. A certain part of it was made larger to protect the "eye" of the knee; this is a bone intended for protection <note>The patella or kneecap</note>. Its utility is to restrain the leg so that it can stand firmly upon the toes and be suspended without rupture or dislocation. This labor-bearing bone was examined for its role in the various movements that carry the heart <note>The "heart" here likely refers to the core or weight of the person</note>, and its location was set toward the front. For the most part, when it moves, it inclines toward the interior. This bone does not naturally decline outward, but rather has a slight inward inclination. All its declination is toward the interior, and this occurs during

<column-break/>

the labor of walking and standing upon the toes of the foot, which sustains the body when one stands in that position.

### Chapter XXX. On the Anatomy of the Foot.

The foot is shaped for walking and standing, configured toward the front so that it may provide support. On its inner side, it has a certain slenderness so that the foot's declination is balanced for those standing or walking, due to the elevation of the foot <margin>vires? <note>Marginal note is truncated; likely "strength" or "it seems"</note></margin> which restrains it. This ensures the stance is regulated and that the heel rests firmly upon the ground. From the large and long bone, the foot is well-formed for taking steps and for the movements by which climbing is achieved. It is composed of many bones because there is great utility in them. Just as the hand holds what it grasps, the foot must firmly hold the ground upon which it walks. Because it must move in various ways, it is better that it be made of many pieces rather than one single piece, so that it can adapt its shape. Among these useful bones, there are twenty-six in total. There is the "talus" <note>original: *Alchaab* or *Cahab*, from the Arabic *al-ka'b*</note> for the joint, which completes the connection. And the "heel bone" <note>original: *calcaneus*</note>, which is the foundation for firm standing. And the "navicular bone" <note>original: *nauiculare*</note> for lightness and structure. And the four bones of the "tarsus" <note>original: *rascete*, a medieval term for the bones of the wrist or ankle</note> which join with the others. One of these is a bone shaped like a hexagon, located toward the outer side to provide a good shape. Because the talus bone in humans is more balanced toward the outside and more inclined toward the inside than the talus of any other animal, it performs the most noble office of the foot in movement, just as the heel bone is the most noble in providing stability. The talus is placed in the middle, emerging from two cavities. One part is at the top and the other at the <margin>that is, the rear</margin> neck, with two parts on the outer and inner sides. These two projections fit into the two cavities of the leg bones. The talus exists between these and the heel bone so that the joint is better protected and secured against dislocation. It is placed in the middle and extends toward the inner side...

### Chapter One of the Fifth Summary, concerning the nature of the muscles, tendons, and ligaments.

**Voluntary** movement is not completed except through the power of the nerves that provide the connection... coming from the nerves to the bones... the roots of the movable members

<column-break/>

in movement... the nerves are hard and are called "subtle nerves." Therefore, the **tendons** <note>original: *cordis/corda*; literally "strings," used here for tendons</note> need both bones and nerves so that a connection is formed, and this connection is called a **ligament**. A nerve is joined to it in a third way to make it one. And because the muscle, which is composed of a gathering of nerves, was first subtle, it increases as the nerve increases. Thus, a member receives strength from the muscle. When movement is removed at such a distance, it must be noted that the nerve does not always follow the increase... to the point where the member moves away from it... it is turned and twisted so that it performs its duty. The same must be noted regarding the muscle... where one has a muscle or a nerve... the movement of the members is confirmed, and they exist in their own specific possibilities. The nerves are branched out into the members, and some of them act as a "root" in the members. This composition is manifest. Those things which govern must be attributed to the soul, which provides for them through the ligaments... because the fleshy cavities are filled. And the nerve is in the middle... so that it can perform its nervous function. In summary, the tendon is composed of a nerve and a ligament with fleshy fibers and a covering membrane. And it binds the member. And it is that which is commonly called a "cord" [tendon], which is composed of a ligament and a nerve, and they bind together to pull or release the member; the tendon is dilated or relaxed and elongated into the member.

# Chapter 5 on the anatomy of the eyelids.

**I**n every movement, the eyelid is required. The intention of nature is achieved only when the upper eyelid completes the closure of the eye. This movement is subject to the will, which is so great that when one wishes it to be more open, the muscle is brought into use. Because of the multiplicity of these parts, the movement is healthy and powerful. The muscle acts so that the upper eyelid remains mobile while the lower remains relatively still. By this action, the will carries out its work according to the principles of nature, so that it may elevate the ends... i.e., in a straight direction. The upper eyelid, however, exists with two origins and properties. One muscle pulls it back and revolves it when needed. Thus, the upper eyelid requires two movements: the elevation by which the muscle opens the eye, and the depression by which it closes it. This closure requires a muscle tending toward the lower parts, so that by nature you may exclude or push down the muscle coming from below. If there had been only one muscle, it would have been continuous with either the extremity of the eyelid or the middle. If the muscle were joined to the middle of the eyelid, it would corrupt [damage] the pupil when it raised the muscle toward it. And if you joined the muscle to the extremity of the eyelid, it would pull only from one end and would not achieve an even closure of the eyelid when it was lowered.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

Furthermore, if the closure were in one part, the parts that are first tightened would be strained, while other parts would be weakened, and the closure would not be equal. This would result in the eyelid of a man suffering a distortion <note>original: *torturā*; a twisting or malformation</note>.
<margin>
Anatomical note.
</margin>
Because of this, there were two muscles created which arise from the two sides and temper the eyelid toward the lower parts together. It was sufficient that the muscles reached the middle of the eyelid. However, the upper parts of the eyelid would dilate and join together when it was pulled back to be opened. For this reason, nature arranged that they descend in a straight line between two continuous parts, and they dilate and join the cartilage-like substance. This is also the origin of the hairs of the eyelid [eyelashes].

# Chapter 6 on the anatomy of the jaws.

**T**he jaw has seven muscles that move the jaw, and they follow the movement of the lower mandible. The reason for this is explained in the *Book of Vision*. For a member has no movement other than that which follows the muscles of that member. When a member moves with another, it is because the muscle belongs to both. There is also a muscle common to each of the jaws, called the **say** <note>original: *say*; likely a Latinization of the Arabic *sa’id*, referring here to the buccinator or masseter area</note>. Each of these has four parts. They compress the cheeks, for they draw in water and air. Its origin is at the fork of the jaw, and its ends reach the extremities of the lips and the lower parts of the mouth. This origin specifically connects to the **furucla** <term>furcula; the "little fork" or notch of the jaw</term> at the two cheekbones and hangs from there. That which goes to the outside joins with the bone that is nearby, and it penetrates and rounds the part that arises toward the outer part of the lower extremity of the left lip. When this whole muscle contracts, it narrows the mouth and pulls it inward, just as a purse-string <note>original: *burla*; a pouch or purse</note> closes. It makes the mouth move from the side... and it joins in the lower
<margin>
Finally, above.
</margin>
hollow of that muscle, and here the lip is covered by similar parts. That which is between the bones of the neck reaches the boundaries of the ear; i.e., it is continuous with the end of the jaw. It moves the jaw with a manifest movement which the

Regarding the inferior mandible <term>lower jaw</term> and the superior <term>upper jaw</term>. Movement was once attributed to the superior mandible in certain animals. However, we know that the movement of the lower jaw is better. There are those who mistakenly say the upper jaw moves in noble members [like humans], but it is not efficient or healthy. It is certain that the superior mandible is fixed, and the muscle is made firm so that the inferior mandible <term>mandibula</term> possesses more movements for nature's needs. These movements are for opening the mouth, for the motion of closing, and for chewing and grinding. Opening the mandible makes it descend to the lower parts, and closing it elevates it. The soft parts allow it to turn or decline toward two sides. It is manifest, therefore, that the motion of closing is made firm by muscles which descend from the superior parts and have their origin in the superior temples. To seize and move, there are two muscles for closing, which are called the muscles of the jaw.

There are two muscles of mastication <term>mastication: the act of chewing</term> on each side. One muscle is angular, since it is also part of the jawbone <note>original: *iugulus*; here referring to the zygomatic arch or the jaw's connection</note> which exists on the face; these two provide a broad side, one descending to the mandible <term>mandible: the lower jawbone</term> and forming it, and the other ascending to the anterior part. Furthermore, they are moved from the depths in a straight and common way by the angle which exists above. These muscles are directed toward the bones <note>original: *ī ōle d̄ō*; likely *in osse dicto*, 'in the said bone'</note> and have a part in equal motion. If they are drawn to incline, the declination is moved through these parts, and thus mastication is completed.

# Chapter 5.
# On the anatomy of the muscles of the head.

**R**egarding the movement of the head, it is noted that with the cervical vertebrae <term>vertebrae: the individual bones of the spine, here called *spondylibus*</term>, the movement is composed of the extension of the head and the tilting of the neck at the same time. Each of these two movements is both primary and common, whether moving forward or tilting to the right or to the left. And between these, they are moved in a diverse form as they are washed <note>The Latin *lotis* is unclear here; it may refer to the "cleansing" or "separation" of the muscles during dissection</note>. The muscles that curve the head downward are two muscles that can be seen descending toward the valley, which they clean with their fibers and are separated from the upper tables of the bone. From the lower parts, they are elevated; and they are found where the arches of the muscles exist. There are two of them: one is a branching prominence and has two heads. When one of these moves, the head is curved downward, but when the other moves, the head is raised upward. It is clear that the muscles which curve the head and neck together are purely from the protective layer of the esophagus <note>original: *meri*; referring to the throat/esophagus region</note> which goes to the part of the vertebrae and joins with those muscles. When the part which is near the esophagus is moved, the head alone is curved. And in the part belonging to the two vertebrae, it is curved toward the front of the neck. If there are muscles that curve only the head forward, there are four pairs there, which provide life. And the junction of these pairs exists in a long line. And from these, three are those that reach the summit. And their direction and length is half of what is seen. And in those that reach the "wings" <note>original: *alas*; likely the transverse processes of the vertebrae</note>, the direction is from the middle. And of these, they are purely those that reach the two transverse wings of the vertebrae; above those that reach the summit, there is a small muscle from the wing that goes to the summit itself. And that which is created is for the tilting of the head, so that when it is curved, it may be elevated; the disposition of these is seen in this way. And from these, there is a pair which penetrates from the upper part of the head.

<column-break/>

There, in the second [vertebra], it goes with precision <note>original: *iusticia*; in medieval anatomy, this often means "due proportion" or "proper alignment"</note> toward its part from the common wing of the vertebrae. The first two pairs of the head move by themselves and not by will, but with a small tilting they curve the head. And whenever there is a tilting, it corrects the twisting. And when it curves forward with manifest precision, and when it is alone, the head is inclined to its side. And by extending the other side, the head will be moved forward without tilting. All those that curve the head with the neck are thin, deep pairs, and one pair is adjacent. When they are together, their angle is at the base of the posterior bone of the brain <note>the occipital bone</note> and from that which remains, they descend to the neck. But in the long pairs, one descends over the two sides of the vertebrae and another does not decline to the wings. Such a path goes through the middle between the two sides of the vertebrae and the two extremities of the wings. Regarding those that tilt the head to the two sides, there are two pairs changed by the junction of the head. One of these pairs is located above where the head and the vertebrae are joined; one is on the right and the other on the left. And a pair is joined at the back of the "jaw-hip" <note>original: *cox̄ē auillaē*; likely the atlas or axis vertebrae connecting to the skull</note> between the first vertebra and the head; one proceeds from the right and the other from the left. And whenever one of these is pulled, the head will be tilted to its side with precision. And when two on one side work together, the head will tilt toward them without precision <note>i.e., a direct side-tilt rather than a diagonal movement</note>. For if the leaders are moved, they will unite in the movement of the head toward the front. And if all four are moved together, the head will stand upright. And of these four muscles, another muscle is smaller. There is a looseness in them in the thickness of the structure. And because other muscles descend there, they are thinner than the others due to their great size. Furthermore, for the joints of the head, two things were necessary, for which two connections were opportune. One is firmness, which is provided by the joined structure; and so that the movements might be obeyed, there is a multitude of many movements. And this is provided by the flexibility of the joints at their axis. But because the looseness of the joints would hinder the completeness of firmness, many muscles surround and accompany them. Two things were acquired in the meantime. One is that God, who is above all, might be the better judge.

### Chapter 14. On the anatomy of the muscles of the tongue.

<margin>Muscles of the vault <note>original: *musculi laquearis*</note></margin>
The muscles moving the tongue are 8, or nearly 9. Two are lateral, arising from the styloid processes... and two are longitudinal, arising from the upper part of the *lauda* bone <term>lauda bone: the hyoid bone at the base of the tongue, shaped like the letter lambda</term>, which meet in the middle of the tongue. And two, which move and retract it to the palate <note>original: *mātūllū*</note>, arise from the two sides of the *lauda* bone, extending the tongue both longitudinally and laterally. And there are two muscles that turn the tongue upward or prick it, which are the *hyoglossus* <note>original: *yloiclas*</note> muscles which we have mentioned. These muscles are spread out in width because they extend from the entire bone of the mandible. Furthermore, they named a single muscle <note>original: *māclā solitanā*</note> which connects the tongue and the *lauda* bone together. And these are the ones that move the mandible and the tongue outward and move it longitudinally. In this way, it does not move itself in a different way, but moves itself during the act of chewing <note>original: *mācitatiā*</note>.

### Chapter 15. On the anatomy of the muscles of the neck.

There are two pairs of muscles that move the neck: one pair on the right, and another on the left. However, since one of them alone would flex the neck toward its own side, it would be bent. But since the two that are on one side flex together, the neck is bent straight toward that side. If, however, they all work together in a straight line, the action will be equal and the neck will stand firm without any deviation.

### Chapter One of the Second Section: The Fifth Discourse, which is a General Summary regarding the Nerves.

<margin><image-desc>A square symbol divided into four quadrants with a dot in each, topped with a cross.</image-desc></margin>
**Regarding** the benefits of the nerves: some are essential to their being, while others are beneficial by accident <note>In medieval philosophy, "accidental" refers to a secondary property that is not part of the essential nature of a thing</note>. That which is essential is that through their mediation, a benefit is provided to all other members: namely, sensation and motion. That which is by accident is that they help so that the flesh may be wrapped around them and their pathways may be formed. And from these, the body perceives that which is harmful.
<margin>Gregory... first rector</margin>
Furthermore, those members which receive sensation—even those lacking it themselves, such as the liver, spleen, and lung—do not have sensation in their own substance. However, they are covered by a sensitive membrane <note>original: "pitiē" / "pūmallo"; likely the pleura or peritoneum</note> that wraps around them. These membranes, when they are pricked or suffer from an abscess, convey the sensation through the nerves that reach them. The heaviness or pain that occurs in them arises from the root of the nerves, resulting from congestion or blockage.
<margin>1st Book</margin>
The source from which the nerves arise is the brain. And that toward which they reach is the extremity. This is the end of the sensory nerves. Since, however, there are fine muscular fibers <note>original: "uilli nuscti"; villi or threads of muscle</note>, they do not all reach the extremities in the same way. Since the brain is the source of the nerves, there are two modes: for just as the heart is the source of the arteries, the brain is the source of the nerves, mediated by the spinal cord <term>nucha: the medieval term for the spinal cord</term> which arises from it. It is seen that the spinal cord serves as a channel for the benefit of sensation and motion in the head and face. Other members have their benefits through these nerves. And Galen <note>original: "hal."; a common abbreviation for Galen or sometimes Haly Abbas</note> has already shown the great care taken regarding the nerves descending to the viscera. The Creator was careful in their protection, protecting them differently than other nerves. And that <unclear>lacuna</unclear> because for that reason <unclear>lacuna</unclear> from the beginning <unclear>lacuna</unclear> they were worked <unclear>lacuna</unclear> in the long vein, affirming with strong muscles that they might rule them, so that through the muscle and the cartilage, which is in the middle of its thread, the nerve might be protected. And this is found in those places where they come toward the epiglottis

<column-break/>

and stay there until they come to the roots of the ribs. And likewise when they pass through the region of the chest. It was done so that another nerve might proceed through those places in which it is useful to provide help in sensing, penetrating through the path and the directness to the part to which it is directed. For directness to that which it aims for is a shortcut to carry the benefit, and in that place the animal spirit <term>spūsio: "spiritus"; the subtle substance believed to carry nerve impulses</term> which flows from the source is stronger. And those nerves which are sensory, because of their hardness, are naturally suited to stretch long distances and provide caution. ### Chapter II. On the Anatomy of the Emerging Nerves.

->From the brain, seven pairs arise<-

**Here** the nerves begin. The first pair of nerves comes from the front of the two ventricles <note>the cavities within the brain</note> of the brain, at the two protrusions in the shape of mamillary extremities, by which the sense of smell is formed <note>the olfactory nerves</note>. These are those where the one from the left goes to the right, and the one from the right goes to the left. Then they meet in a crossing <note>the optic chiasm</note> before they come out. For that reason, the one that is born on the right reaches the right pupil, and the one born on the left reaches the left pupil, which are dilated to the eyes where they receive what is called the vitreous humor. The cause of this—which Galen did not disagree with—is found through dissection: that they meet in a reflection. And he said that in this crossing there exists a great benefit. One reason is so that the spirit <note>the "visual spirit"</note> which goes to one pupil and to the other should not be hindered when an injury occurs. And because of this, when one of the two pupils is closed, the vision in the other eye becomes stronger and clearer than it would be if both were looking at the same time. And for this reason, the dilation of the opening of the uvea <note>the iris/pupil area</note> is increased when the other eye is closed. And this is because the spirit travels more quickly.

### On the nature and the form of the arteries.

There are two pulsing vessels and **arteries** which were before the preceding one; two of them are joined, of which two are hidden. Because the one that assists in pulsation and strong movement was intended to be concealed in a receptacle to be guarded and rolled up. The origin of the **arteries** is from the **left ventricle** of the two ventricles of the **heart** <note>original: "cordis"</note>. The right ventricle is near the **liver** <note>original: "hepati"</note>. Therefore, it was necessary for it to be placed centrally, occupied in attending to its instrumental function.

### Chapter on the anatomy of the venous artery.

<margin>Vein</margin>

Regarding the anatomy of the **venous artery** <note>original: "artie uenale"; the medieval term for the pulmonary vein, which carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart</note>: one goes to the **lung** <note>original: "pulmone"</note>. There are **veins** that spread toward the upper parts of things, and those that reach the **diaphragm** <term>the muscular partition between the chest and abdomen</term>, and those that penetrate more deeply into the body, and the branches that reach the kidneys and the testicles. There are also those that descend to the stomach and the veins which are among the bones. When the artery is located near the non-pulsating vein <note>original: "uena n̄ pūlsatilī"; medieval physicians distinguished between pulsating arteries and non-pulsating veins</note>, it "rides" upon the back of the non-pulsating vein so that the flow <note>original: "luis", likely *fluxus*</note> of the spirit may be protected for the noble organs. In the visible members, the artery is placed under the non-pulsating vein so that it may be better protected and more straight, and the non-pulsating vein is placed above it. Arteries, however, were not made to be entirely separate from veins except for two reasons: one is so that the veins may provide a protective covering for the arteries, and the other is so that the veins may be moved by the pulse of the arteries in those members where they travel.

### The fourth article is completed in this manner.
### Book 5 contains 5 chapters. The first chapter is on the veins.

**All** veins that are non-pulsating have their origin only from the **liver** <term>original: "ep̄e" for *hepar*; in medieval medicine, the liver was considered the source of all veins and the center of blood production</term>. And from the liver itself, two veins arise: one from the "gate" <note>original: "porta"</note> of the liver itself, which is of great utility and lies toward the liver to provide nourishment, and it is called the **portal vein**. The other arises from the hollow part <note>original: "gistola", likely referring to the *vena cava*</note> to serve the nourishment of the limbs from the liver.

<margin>Chapter 2. On the anatomy</margin>
### of the saphenous vein <note>Though usually the leg vein, here the author uses "saphenis" in the context of the portal system</note> which is called the Portal.

**It is** known concerning the vein called the **Portal** that the extremities of the portal vein are joined under the liver. It is divided into five parts and sends out branches: one reaches the convexity of the liver and its extremities, from which the vein returns to the **gallbladder** <note>original: "fel"</note>. And one small branch is like a ray of the sun which goes to the base of the organ itself. The third part, which exits from the cavity of the liver, is divided into parts, of which two are smaller and six are larger. One of the two smaller ones enters the intestine called the **duodenum** <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> to receive nourishment from it. And from it, branches are divided which are spread into the **mesentery** <term>original: "eucharis"; the membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall</term>. And a portion is divided into the lower parts toward the **peritoneum** <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>. One of the six remaining branches returns to the broad part of the stomach, to its surface

<column-break/>

where it is clearly seen to provide nourishment. For the first nourishment of the eyes <note>likely "oculai" as a transcription error for "occulta", hidden</note> is carried out in the **chyle** <term>original: "yv̄" for *chylus*; the milky fluid of digested food</term>, and the stomach is nourished by contact with it. And the second part goes to the spleen to nourish it.
<margin>li. o or white</margin>
Watery parts which are separated for the nourishment of the spleen reach the four branches of the **mesentery** <note>original: "eucharis"</note>, and through that portion which reaches the spleen, it is nourished. From the part reaching the spleen, a large branch returns with the chyle to nourish the **left side** <note>original: "lac n̄ō sinistrū"</note>. And when it reaches the spleen, it ascends in the middle, and some parts recede from it. And from the other part, the vein spreads in the upper middle of the stomach to nourish it, and another part goes into the spleen to nourish it. And another part exits until it reaches the convexity of the stomach, where it is divided into two parts: one part is spread into the upper stomach, and the other to the "mouth" of the stomach <note>the cardia</note> at the top of the vein; there is danger there because if it is ruptured, it assists the stomach in discharging waste. A part of it descending is divided into two parts: one of its branches is divided in the lower half of the spleen to nourish it, and the other goes to the **omentum** <term>original: "rētailū" for *reticulum*; the fatty membrane covering the intestines</term> and spreads into the chyle to nourish it. And the third part goes to the left side and in all the veins that are in the omentum; it remains there and spreads to suck up the remaining nourishment in the stomach. And the fourth part is divided like hairs <note>capillaries</note>, some of which are opposite the right convexity of the stomach, reaching the **jejunum** <note>the middle part of the small intestine</note> and the spleen to spread there. The fifth branch spreads into the **colon** <note>the large intestine</note> to take nourishment from it. And the sixth is like this: it spreads into the cavity of the **jejunum**, and those that remain go into the **caecum** <term>original: "monoculo"; literally the 'one-eyed' intestine</term> and are used to draw nourishment.

Coming from the cavity of the **liver** <term>Latin: *epar* or *hepar*</term> toward its belly: it rises above the liver with great speed and divides into two parts; one part, however, descends toward the root. But from the section outside the **diaphragm** <term>the muscular wall separating the chest from the abdomen</term>, it sends a vein into the diaphragm which spreads out and provides it with nourishment. Then it sends many <margin>branches</margin> across the covering of the heart <term>the pericardium</term> which divide like hairs and nourish it. Afterward, it divides into two parts: one large part reaches the heart and penetrates into it at the right **auricle** <term>atrium</term> of the heart. This is because that vein is the largest of the heart’s vessels. And this vein appears larger than the others because other veins attach themselves to the heart to assist it. But the nourishment of the heart comes from that vein.

They think, therefore, that its arrival in the brain might be more <margin>sensory</margin> <note>original: "sensuas"</note> than if the brain were unhealthy. And here toward the heart <margin>external muscle</margin> three small channels enter, which are made from the exterior toward the interior. Then, as they say, the heart receives nourishment from them, and it nourishes itself when it dilates. And this channel is said to be sweeter than all other channels. This vein, opposite the heart on its exterior side, sends out veins, one of which goes from it to the **lung** at the narrower part near the left side, and in the vessel of the brain <note>perhaps referring to a passage toward the head</note> it goes toward the lung and turns back. And because it has two such arterial functions, it is called the **arterial vein** <term>known today as the pulmonary artery; medieval doctors called it a vein because it carried blood, but "arterial" because of its thick walls</term>.

The first benefit of this is that the fluid which sweats out from it in the furthest small channels of the lung is pure and small; that fluid which previously exited into the heart is the digestion which is poured into the arterial vein. This benefit is created so that much fluid may be digested in it. Second, it returns from these parts into the cavity of the heart, going out for its own nourishment. And this is the second vein, called the **vena cava** <term>the large vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart</term>, which comes from the liver to the right auricle, the boundary of the heart. If it stands in its path, it turns toward the left. Then it goes through the chest and surrounds the ribs, spreading into the sinuses and into those parts made of the hand and other members. ### Division VI: where there is one summary regarding one total, that is, on the powers of the soul, in six chapters.

### Chapter One of the summary, that is, on the power of vivification <note>the power that gives life</note> specifically, which is spoken of in its kinds according to the universal reasoning of the operations of the powers.

Some powers are known from others because they exist as the beginning of operations; for some operation leads into a certain power. Therefore, we have placed in one chapter the powers from which the operations arise among physicians. Which therefore is the genus of universal powers... and the genus of animal powers. And it seems to **Galen** <note>original: *Galieno*; Claudius Galenus, the influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> that each of the powers has a principal limb in which it exists, from which the operation proceeds. And it seems to them that the seat of the **animal power** <note>original: *virtus animalis*; the power responsible for sensation and movement</note> is the **brain** <note>original: *cerebrum*</note> and from it the operations proceed. And this power has two kinds: one kind is for guarding the senses... and the other for the nutritive matter which leads to the end of nutrition. And this kind of operation has its principal source in the **liver** <note>original: *epar*</note>. Another kind is the generative power, to preserve the species, which is common to the seed. From this, the form is created for creatures as commanded. And the seat and operation of this principal source is the **stomach**. The **vital power** <note>original: *vitalis*; the power of life itself</note> is that which <gloss>mentally</gloss> carries sense and motion and renders the body fit to receive those impressions which the brain produces...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "virtues" or biological powers, moving from the purely nutritive functions to the "animal" and "vital" virtues. It explores how the temperament (complexio) generates the spirits (pneuma) that carry these powers from central organs like the heart and liver to the rest of the body.</meta>

<margin>
Here it is shown that man, just as an animal, possesses virtues (powers), in what ways, in what proportion, and in what location. From these, the difference between man and other animals is clear. Because of this, they move in different ways according to their appearance; and this is said not only of man but also of other things.
</margin>

The **temperament** <note>original: *complexio*; the balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note> consists of the four **spirits** <note>subtle substances or "vapors" that carry life force</note> which are members, or rather, from the members. They arise from the vapors of the **humors** <note>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> and their moisture, for every temperament generates its own spirit. According to the physicians, the **liver** exists as the primary principle of all parts; likewise, the **heart** is the principle of the primary fluctuation, which is the spirit. This comes from the temperament, which is held here in order to receive its own virtue or power. 

From these, other members are prepared to receive the **animal virtues** <note>original: *animales*; from *anima* (soul), referring to the powers of sensation and voluntary movement</note> and the remaining virtues. These animal powers reach the members through the spirits. Once the **vital virtue** <note>the power centered in the heart that maintains life</note> arrives, it prevents the animal powers in the members from being destroyed. Thus, a soul still exists even if it is not in a state of use; it is not destroyed by reason of the life-force, which is the least thing to be received. This arrives in one of two ways: either according to the ultimate judgment of sense and motion, or through the temperament itself which prevents the member from receiving them, or through a blockage <note>original: *opilatione*</note> that occurs.

In a member, **paralysis** occurs when the soul is, so to speak, conquered, and life remains without motion; the power is prevented from flowing to that member for sense and motion. The members themselves are pushed toward their own feeling through the vital power, and if they are blocked, they cannot receive it. We say that as long as a member is to be seen as living, the vital force must be present. If it is destroyed, it will not use motion. 

Perhaps a member is destroyed in some way, yet the whole remains living; perhaps through an operation, the member might be returned to motion. And this is the cause by which the soul's powers are said to suffice for performing motion. In **vegetative things** <note>plants or the basic growth functions of the body</note>, they act without receiving sense. It remains that these means follow the temperament, which is called the **vital virtue**. This is the first vital power which proceeds into the spirit from the substance of the humors. Then the spirit—which the **philosophers** and **Aristotle** say—receives that first vital power from which the other virtues flow. The operations of the soul do not happen without this; among physicians, it does not proceed except through the **animal spirit**, which is received not just for life, but for light.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "virtues" or powers of the soul, moving from the general concept of the spirit to the specific "animal" powers responsible for perception and thought. It specifically focuses on how animals and humans process information through both external and internal senses, relying heavily on the theories of Avicenna.</meta>

### Chapter 5: On the Apprehensive Animal Powers <note>original: *uirtutib(us) animalib(us) app(re)hensib(us)*; the powers of the soul related to perceiving and "grasping" information</note>

<margin>In another [version]: apprehension.</margin>
**T**hey say again that two powers are joined in the animal, since the animal itself is a genus. One is the comprehensive <note>perceptual</note> power and the other is the motive <note>movement-related</note> power. The comprehensive power is divided into two kinds: one is the **manifest** <note>external</note> comprehensive power, and the other is the **occult** <note>internal or "hidden" within the brain</note> comprehensive power. The manifest kind belongs to the senses and is known as the general sense, which is indeed divided into the **five senses**: it is split into the sense of sight and visible things, such as seeing; hearing and the act of hearing; smelling; tasting; and touch or the act of touching.
<margin>In another [version]: the virtue placed in...</margin>
And it is divided into five because they are distinguished by their own specific functions, which are determined by these powers. Each of these types of power acts by itself. Although in us it may seem like nothing, the path of touch and the tongue is distinct; and again, touch exists in the whole body, as both physicians and philosophers have categorized. And the power that is called the **occult comprehensive power** <note>the internal senses</note> is among the powers categorized by their types. One of these is the fourth sense of vision in the **phantasia** <note>the "common sense" that gathers data from the five senses</note>. Among physicians, there is one power; but according to **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian physician whose works were foundational to medieval medicine</note>, there are five internal powers according to the physicists, though some say two. The sense of sight is that which receives things perceived by the senses, and through their forms, they are joined in the phantasia. This power brings them back so that the forms of all things are present even in their absence. There are two aspects: one is for the present, and the other is for guarding or storing. Philosophers hold that these functions are located in the ventricles <note>chambers</note> of the brain.
One of these is called the **cogitative** <note>thinking</note> power when it acts in the middle. If it is used to create images, it is called the **imaginative** power; but it is called cogitative when it involves reason. Science investigates this as the **estimative** power in animals, which allows them to perceive "intentions" <note>non-sensory information, like "danger"</note> to perform their operations; this is called the imaginative power. And if it follows its natural spirit and returns to prepare itself, it is called the cogitative virtue. By this, it perceives and retains the dispositions of things perceived by the senses. This is the power that stores things in the imaginative faculty. It is a process of comprehension where the mind perceives forms even when they are divided from the objects—for example, an animal's ability to imagine flying. If the **phantasia** <note>imagination</note> acts to receive the senses, these forms are categorized by physicians and others.

<column-break/>

Thus, there is no doubt that in the animal there is a hidden and examining comprehension. This is defined by how an animal judges that one thing is an **enemy**
<margin>In another [version]: to perceive</margin>
and another is a beloved **friend** <note>original: *filius est dilectus*; literally "a son is loved," used here as an example of recognizing a friend or kin</note>. Since the soul naturally seeks every virtue, such as things that should be fled from. Secondly, this power extracts the "intention" <note>the inner meaning of a perception, like "this wolf is dangerous"</note> from the animal, which prepares itself in us. 
<margin>In another [version]: life</margin>
The animal comprehends these through the senses, but it is not the sense itself that judges them; that is the work of a higher power. And this occurs realistically in the temperament. 
<margin>In another [version]: aspect.</margin>
Doubtless, some apprehension exists in the natural state. Leaving aside the higher powers, these are united in a multitude of powers that lead to the animal state. And these are divided from the **fantastica** <note>the faculty of fantasy</note>; for the fantastic power follows its own logic. It holds its own distinctions within the sense.
It is separated from that which is called the **imaginative** and the **cogitative**. For those opinions do not follow hearing alone; they hold opinions only in the strength of that power. These operations are based on perceptions in the sense, making an opinion based on what is perceived. If the animal possesses a judge of the forms perceived by the senses, the **estimative** power is the judge of the "intentions" of those forms, reaching beyond the sense itself. That which resumes this power is called the **human imaginative power**, which acts as a kind of 
<margin>M' <note>likely an abbreviation for *Nota* or a specific medical authority</note></margin>
will in the deception of powers and the understanding of definitions. The physician must know how these powers are healed. # Chapter III. On the divisions of the dispositions of the human body and illnesses.

<margin>
<image-desc>A schematic diagram titled "Tongue" depicting a tiered architectural structure or base. Accompanying text: "In another version, concerning the purging of health at the end and of sickness at the very last", "or", "named from that which pertains to the column of the egg", and "concerning the joining together".</image-desc>
</margin>

There are three types of human **disposition** <note>the general state or condition of the body</note>. **Health** <note>original: *sanitas*</note> is the disposition through which the human body, in its **complexion** <note>the balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> and composition, exists in such a way that all its operations proceed according to its will. **Sickness** <note>original: *egritudo*</note> is a disposition contrary to this. Then there is a third disposition which is between health and sickness, in which there is neither perfect health nor terminal illness. This is found in the bodies of the elderly, or those recovering from illness, or in children. It may also occur because different things exist in one or two members at the same time: for example, a member may be healthy in its complexion but ill in its composition. Or one member may have two types of nearby causes, such that it is healthy in its quality and position, or healthy in two qualities but ill in its two faculties, or in the relationship between two things at two different times, such as

<column-break/>

that which is healthy and then becomes weak. Of illnesses, some are simple and others are compound. The simple ones are those which belong to one type of illness of complexion, or one type of illness of composition, which we shall name hereafter. Compound illnesses are those in which two types of illness occur together. We shall begin by speaking of simple illnesses. We say that simple illnesses are those that affect the members that are composed of similar parts <note>original: *partes siles*, referring to "simple members" like bone, flesh, or nerve, which are uniform throughout</note>; these are types of "bad complexion." And there are those that do not just affect the members with similar parts, but because the member is affected as a whole. It is possible to imagine these complexions appearing in any members whose parts are similar. Now, in compound illnesses, there is a class of illnesses of the **official members** <note>original: *membroz officialiū*, organs with a specific function like the heart, liver, or stomach</note> which are illnesses of composition; these happen to the members composed of various simple parts. The official members are the instruments of the soul's powers. And the second type of illness consists of those which happen to members with similar parts, but they occur in the "instrumental" parts insofar as they are instruments. Thus, they do not follow the instrumental accidents of simple parts. And it is also necessary to distinguish those which occur by the loss of **continuity** <note>original: *connuitatis*, referring to breaks, cuts, or fractures</note>, which happens to neighboring parts. This happens to simple members and those nearby that are composed. And it often happens in one, or all, or only in the vessels. Finally, we must ask what defines an illness. There are illnesses that follow a defect of complexion, illnesses that follow a defect of composition, and illnesses that follow the loss of continuity alone. Or an illness may follow one of these and exist from the comparison of the illness to the complexion; these are the ones we shall name.

## Chapter 4. On the illness of the solution of continuity <note>original: *solois ā tinuitatis*, "solution of continuity" is the medical term for any injury that breaks the skin, muscle, or bone, interrupting the body's continuous structure.</note> and its connection.

The illness of the breaking of continuity often happens because of a blow, a shaking, or a wounding. And it often happens to the flesh which is near it, and when it is fresh, it is called a **wound** <note>original: *plign*, likely *plaga*</note>. If, however, pus is made there, it is called an **ulcer**. Pus appears because the substances within it are evacuated, and the digestive heat cannot prevail. Now, in the first wound, the solution of continuity often brings pain to the wound which happens around the flesh. When it happens to the bone, it breaks it into two fragments, or into large parts, or into very small parts. Or it is split according to its length, making a crack.

### ->Chapter 10<-
### ->On the winds.<-

All winds have a season. The winds are varied...
<margin>Abundance</margin>
The North wind <note>original: "septētrional"</note> hardens the body and makes the flow of waters manifest. It aids the digestive power and is effective in strengthening the body. It is called a "durable wind" because it heals the foul, pestilential air. When the North wind follows the South wind, it prevents the fluxes <note>excessive flow of humors, like a runny nose or diarrhea</note> caused by the Southern air. It expels impurities to the exterior. Without it, many things would become liquid or putrid, and there would be a multiplication of fluxes from the head, such as coughs and eye pains. These Northern winds are the healers of those who have difficulty breathing or suffer from pains in the lungs.

### ->Chapter 11. On the southern winds.<-

<margin>Abundance</margin>
The Southern wind <note>original: "meridi uētis"</note> is often stormy and carries away the strength of the body. It moves the humors toward the exterior, which corrupts the exits of the body and makes the skin weak. It makes the body prone to epilepsy and affects the joints. It causes putrid fevers to arise.

<margin>from the sun</margin>

### On cold habitable places.

In cold habitable places, the inhabitants are stronger, taller, and digest less, as you have known. If the place should be humid, the inhabitants will be thick, fleshy, and have much humidity and fat, which comes profoundly from their way of life—

in the course of time, they will be heavy and pale.

### On humid habitable places.

In humid habitable places, the inhabitants are made beautiful because their limbs are soft by reason of the moisture, and they have a laxity toward the wind. Their summer is greatly heated and their winter is very much like it. And many deaths from fevers and fluxes of the belly come to them, and much blood from menstruation and hemorrhoids; indeed, hemorrhoids are multiplied in them, as are putrid ulcers, and putrefaction increases opulence <note>Original: "epulentia." In this medical context, it likely refers to a "fullness" or "swelling" of the body's tissues rather than wealth.</note> in them.

### On dry habitable places.

In dry habitable places, the inhabitant is dried out, and the fullness of the temples is furrowed, and the limbs are dried out. Their bodies are joined to dryness. Their summer is very hot and the winter is indeed very cold.

### On high habitable places.

In high habitable places, the inhabitants are stronger, very patient in labor, and they live for a long time.

### In deep habitable places.

In deep <note>Meaning low-lying areas, valleys, or depressions.</note> habitable places, the inhabitants, despite being productive, pass away after a short time due to debility and the watery humidity in the cold, especially if there is standing water, or milky water, or marshes. And as you have learned, their airs are bad.

# The Nature and Quality of Waters

The human substance <note>The physical makeup of the human body.</note> is not compared in this way. This is the substance that helps to liquefy mixtures and to sublimate <note>term: Sublimation; the process of turning a solid or liquid into vapor through heat to purify it.</note>; water helps and reaches the veins through openings in the earth, through layers like fissures, and is filled by the mixture. Yet this does not apply to all springs, but specifically to springs flowing over muddy ground; in the silt, however, a certain disposition is granted to each. It overcomes [impurities]. Or water that moves by itself, which, if it is not already "digested" <note>original: "digestiores"; meaning naturally processed or refined by movement.</note>, is purified lest it be spoiled by putrefaction.
