# Chapter 17. On the Enema.
<margin>In another [text] it is called a "sanzan."</margin>
The **Enema** is a noble medicine for expelling superfluities <note>Excessive or corrupt humors that caused disease.</note> that are in the intestines. It is used for pains in the kidneys and bladder, and for those who suffer from <term>colic</term><note>Severe abdominal pain caused by gas or obstruction.</note>. By its power, it eases the superfluities of the <term>liver</term><note>original: "epur"; the liver was seen as the site of blood production.</note>. When these things are trapped, they weaken the liver and lead to fever. From enemas, a clearing is made by expelling the remaining matters which they leave in the bowels. Regarding the form of the tube, as was said in the chapter on colic, the better it is made, the better it reaches the upper parts. Then let him turn himself to the side that hurts... it is better, however, to use warm rubs, which help to increase the flow and stop nausea. A bath is often used to make the humors "boil" and be purged. The purpose of these things is to release the air and humors that are held back. And for this reason, if you first use a bath, follow it with the enema. And if there are <term>pustules</term><note>Sores or ulcers.</note> in the intestine, or fever, or other ailments, do not let the enema remain too long in the anus, lest it cause harm by being used incautiously.

# Chapter 18. On Epithems.
**Epithems** <note>original: "Epythemata"; topical applications of liquid or poultices to the skin over a specific organ.</note> are named for the local places where the sickness reaches. And they perhaps have two powers: one that is soothing and another

<column-break/>

that is <term>astringent</term><note>original: "ingellanū"; having a tightening or drying effect.</note>. There is a greater necessity for soothing than for tightening. When the application is made during the time of soothing, it will prevent the disease from taking hold. These are used when the body is weak, such as using fractured barley to make an emplaster over the sores. Plasters are similar to epithems, but plasters are hard while epithems are more liquid. Epithems are applied with cloths. When they are placed over the principal members, such as the heart, they should contain things that fortify and bear a <term>substine</term><note>original: "s'ustinu"; perhaps a protective or supportive substance.</note> of great virtue. Epithems should have a pleasant odor, which the vital spirits love.

<margin>or adhering</margin>
<margin>in others they warm the principal [organs]</margin>
<margin>or they retain</margin>
# Chapter 19. On Embrocations.
<margin>An embrocation is an infusion used in two ways: either to dissolve something or to stop the flow of humors.</margin>
**Embrocations** are medicines specifically for the head or other members to resolve [humors]. It is beneficial to change them according to the need. In those members which must be "embrocated" with heat or cold, if there are superfluities that descend, let the embrocation be made of warm things. Let them be made from iron-water <note>original: "aq' f'rū"; water in which hot iron had been quenched, believed to have medicinal properties.</note> and washed. And if the matter is hard, let them use steam or cold water.

# Chapter 20. On Bloodletting.
<margin>generation (?) in another, generation</margin>
**Phlebotomy** <note>original: "Flebotomia"; the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood.</note> is an evacuation of the vital spirit which removes a great quantity [of blood]. It is used when there is an increase of humors, especially when they are too warm or too thin. Note that bloodletting should be done for one of two reasons: either for those who are currently ill, when the sickness or the person is strong, or for those who fear future illness. One is bled either because of a "multitude" of blood or because of the "malice" <note>toxicity or corruption</note> of the blood, or both. Among those illnesses it helps are: gout <note>original: "podagre"</note>, <term>sciatica</term><note>original: "arte tice"</note>, or when one spits blood from a rupture in the lung, or for those who have too much blood. It also helps with epilepsy, apoplexy, and melancholy when there is a multitude of blood. It is used for those whose hemorrhoid flow is restricted, and for women whose menstrual blood is restricted. The colors of the blood demonstrate whether one should be bled due to the darkness of the humors, or their clarity, or their purity. And for the one who has an incision, it helps all heat-related weakness, and for these it is better to bleed from the hand.

# Chapter 16: On Cupping

<margin>for</margin>
<margin>the part</margin> <gloss>that is, yourselves</gloss> **C**upping <term>Ventosae</term><note>The practice of applying heated glass or ceramic cups to the skin to create a vacuum, drawing blood or humors to the surface.</note> cleanses more effectively than <gloss>that is, bloodletting</gloss> phlebotomy. And it extracts more blood <gloss>if it were superficial</gloss> from the surface than from an abscess. And it is first known that they are useful in certain parts of the body for those who have [excess] blood and parts [affected], because from both it draws out blood. Unless it is drawn out in this way, indeed, it causes great difficulty in the limbs; <gloss>as in the highest law</gloss> <margin>Strength of ours</margin> <margin>the end</margin> the cupping is made available. And it is cautioned, <margin>Note</margin> especially that cups should not be applied at the beginning of the month, because the humors have not yet been moved or "boiled up" <note>Medieval physicians believed humors fluctuated with the moon, much like the tides.</note>; nor at the end, because the humors are then diminished. If in the middle of the month, the humors are ebullient <note>original: "ebullientes"; literally "boiling over," referring to the peak of humoral activity.</note> only with the increase of light [of the moon], and not for this reason following the increase. In the times of the increase of the sea and the water in the rivers, the rising [of humors] is not necessarily held. By the law of the moon or on the day, the second hour is better, for the reason that everyone should be careful with cupping lest he be bathed, unless the weakness was extreme; because he himself ought to bathe at another time. And afterward, the cups are applied mostly to the abdomen. Applying cups to the lower part of the head is not recommended for the elderly, because they always hinder the intellect. Cupping <margin>for the composition, i.e., of the veins of the breasts</margin> which is placed upon the <term>nucha</term><note>The back of the neck.</note> exists for heaviness; it is preferred over others because it alleviates the heaviness of the eyelids, and it cures the scabbiness of the eyes and the stench of the mouth. ### Chapter 17: On Leeches

It is said there that in a certain nature of leeches there exists a poisonous [quality], from which one must be cautious. Because they are of that kind with very large heads, and those whose colors are blackish-red <note>original: "antamoniales nigri"</note>, or the color of the day <note>Perhaps meaning pale or clear.</note>, or those having downy hair and similar to *mezemeris* <note>An unidentified creature or term, possibly a type of poisonous water-insect.</note>, and those upon which there exist lines of azure color. Because from that color it is permitted... <margin>David is colored in others / these</margin> In these there exists a poisonous quality, which sends from them fainting and syncope, and a flux of liquids, and fevers, and looseness, and bad ulcers. Do not take them from bad waters <margin>marshy</margin> in which there is mud and black... and the water of a dead bull stinks. If you choose those that are collected in waters with rabid eyes <note>original: "ocilibus rabiatum"</note> in which frogs dwell—do not pay attention to what is said, that those in waters where frogs dwell are bad. [Actually] they are whichever have the color of the "daughter of the thing" <note>A literal translation of a likely idiomatic or technical term for a specific hue.</note> upon which is said to be an index, and they have two lines of an arsenic color drawn over them. And the red, round ones which are the color of a "bee" <note>original: "epis"</note>; three which are like small locusts and which are similar to a mouse and live having their own heads; these are to be chosen. And choose none more than those having red bellies, and they are green, especially if they were from "golden" waters. And then, first, let some blood for the leeches be poured through and... <margin>they are opened through the middle of the belly / leeches</margin> which is done with... which is produced... which should be collected on a clear day, and then it must be done... <margin>of the anices [?]</margin> which is middle... it may be done for them because of the pure blood of the lamb. ### Chapter 29. From Avenzoar <note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162), a famous physician from Islamic Spain</note> on cauterizing medicine.

**A**venzoar says that cauterizing medicine is very useful for the living to prevent corruption from spreading, and to straighten a limb toward the depths in order to fulfill the desire to rectify it, and to resolve corrupt humors, and not to blunt them, and to restrain the flow of blood whenever it may be thin; gold is better than other metals. ### Chapter 30. On the sedation of pain!

**I**n the sedation of pain, it is divided into two ways: continuity and the virtue of the subjects, resolution and three-fold things. The second of the sedation which first comes to the cause of pain through the malice of the heat of the mouth, or cold, or moisture, or dryness, without any or in the middle it is demonstrated. Either to necessity, or the spirit. The pains which are sedated by the myrtle-like things of the subjects are dearer. And if the sedation seeks the uvula, it is never more precious. **C**oncerning the many occasions <gloss>turns</gloss> for wisdom in treatments, when we ought to be without them in needs. In which way a request of this kind exists, there is one caution: that one thing cannot be healed before another is itself healed. Just as with a purulent <term>purulent: containing or discharging pus</term> spirit <note>original: "aĩ" for anima, referring here to the vital spirit or pneuma</note>, it is joined. For in every medicine for an opening <note>original: "apertionis"</note>, the malice which comes with the spirit should be removed; otherwise, the spirit cannot be healed without the healing of the other, except in the medicine for ulcers. And the second caution is when one sickness is the end of another, just as happens with obstruction <term>oppilatio: a blockage in the body's vessels or passages</term> and fevers. The medicine is for the obstruction first, then for the fever. And if this were empty <note>original: "vaccuum," perhaps meaning the treatment was ineffective or the vessel is void</note>, and the obstruction is opened when heat falls into it, we will not help the fever. We will medicate that which is of the lung itself by drying it; we will care for the fever when it is impossible for the fever to be removed while its cause remains. And when its healing is a desiccation <note>original: "exsiccatio"</note> which causes harm to the fever, then there is one caution: that the one which is lesser should be released or held. Just as if it is joined with a cough and a pulse. The medicine is for the cough and also for the windiness <note>original: "flatudo"</note>. And concerning the pulse, we will not provide care. When, however, the sickness and the accident <note>original: "accidens": a secondary symptom or non-essential condition</note> are in the strength of the nourishment, the beginning and the end come upon them, and the cure for the accident is applied, and we do not wait for the sickness. Just as in colic, where stupefying medicines <term>stupefactiva: substances like opium or henbane used to numb the senses</term> are used so that the strength of the pain is moved. But the treatment of the colic itself is delayed. And it is among those things which we must do because of the weight of debility, or because of a coming flow which they suffer, or because of the presence of ease. And when we have delayed this work, we move the whole thing when we remove it, just as in the sickness of spasm. It is not the way that the humor is expelled; rather, something from it is left behind so that the motion of the spirit's movement is removed, lest that humor be resolved.

# Here begins the second book of the Canon on simple medicines. The words of the Prince, Abu Ali. <note>Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna.</note>

<image-desc>A large, ornate decorative initial 'L' in blue and red ink, featuring intricate scrollwork and filigree patterns, marking the beginning of the word 'Liber' (Book).</image-desc>

**THE BOOK** which completes the first part of the judgment on medical matters. And the second of these is the collected book on individual medicines <note>original: "medicianis singlaribv," referring to "simples" or single-ingredient drugs</note>. This book is divided into two treatises. The first of these concerns the universal rules which one must know regarding the matter of medicines. The second part concerns the power of medicines in medical practice. And the second of these [the second treatise] concerns the knowledge of the specific virtues of individual medicines.

The first treatise is divided into chapters.
Chapter One: On the temperaments <term>complexionibus: the balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</term> of individual medicines.
Chapter Two: On the knowledge of the temperaments of individual medicines through experiment.
<margin>one.</margin>
Chapter Three: On the knowledge of individual medicines through reasoning.
Chapter Four: On the knowledge of the opinions regarding the virtues of individual medicines.
Chapter Five: On the judgment of the actions of medicines applied externally.
Chapter Six: On the collection and preservation of medicines.

In the second treatise, however, we have placed the individual medicines in small cells <term>areolis: literally "little plots" or "cells," referring to a tabular or grid-like layout</term>. For each cell begins with the names of the medicines in alphabetical order, and the knowledge of their essence. And the second cell contains the element of their temperament. And the third cell contains the recollection of their qualities and virtues. And in the fourth cell, the properties of their parts and their universal dispositions—how they dissolve, how they digest, how they are prepared, and how they are perfected; and what things are similar to them among the operations which I shall state in the second treatise, and their qualities and other things signified by them; and the proof of them by their reception and color, so that their collection may be finalized. And in the fifth cell, their operations which proceed from beautifying or increasing, such as the removal of freckles, and rashes, and spots; or regarding the hair, such as its dyeing, its preservation, its lengthening, and its thinning; and those things that prevent unseemliness; and all of this I designate for you to find, so that it may be easy for you to find it in the tables, while it collects all the individual medicines which fall into use or are known. And in the sixth cell are the operations regarding [the muscles and nerves].

# First Treatise. Chapter One.
### The first treatise on the temperaments of medicines.

<margin><unclear>In the beginning of the position of the properties of the medicines in general...</unclear></margin>

Since we have already spoken in this book of individual medicines, we will find in our discourse the power—that is, this medicine is hot, or this is cold, or another is moist, or another is dry. And we wished to explain those things which are composed for the sake of the art, and that many things are composed generally from minerals, vegetables, and animals. The elements are the matter of each, and those things contained within them. For they act upon one another through a certain equality or through a derivation from that which they possess in themselves, and whatever subsists according to that. And the temperament and the quality of the elements of the compound are perceived by the recipient by the state of its power, which I believe I have shown universally according to the divisions of temperament. And whatever occurs to the person who is choleric, and whatever occurs to be equal in medicines. And I have shown that which is understood as the body's complexion through the action of its innate heat—not only whether it is lax or firm, or whether it is increased by nourishment, or whether it is harmed, or whether it is of these medicines, or whether it acts delicately, or whatever else is in its place.

...in each individual thing, there is a specific constitution. Then, you have a common principle that opposes it, so that it unites and joins them together; this commonality comes to them through a **secondary temperament** <term>complexio secunda: a complex mixture of qualities that creates a new, specific substance</term>.
And this secondary temperament is not what we spoke of before. For since it exists in itself, it is common in truth through equality, stability, and durability. And each thing is a true, simple entity in your view; or rather, it is a mixture. Nevertheless, there are two principles from which the secondary temperament arises through a **natural composition**, and not merely through a human art or craft. 
The secondary temperament occurs if there are two modes: either a composition of forms or a composition of substances. A composition of forms, for example, is when each part is joined to another so they become one. Just as our **innate heat** <term>calor innatus: the vital heat believed to drive life and digestion</term> is not only difficult to separate, but indeed inseparable from our nature, just as the heat of fire is difficult to separate from the fire itself. So it is with oil mixed with moisture and dryness; it acts in such a way that the integrity of the substance does not fail. In the second case, it is not so; rather, while the integrity remains, the parts dissolve so that they can be utilized. They hold together with their primary principles. For one does not act differently than the other in lifting the weight, just as one might argue the same for wood, but not for lead or water. 
Therefore, if the secondary temperament is firm, it possesses stability. It is not long before the temperament is separated by the years of innate heat, for it is made into a cloud. And while it is so, the temperament remains firm. If, therefore, there was a temperament, it will remain in the whole until it is resolved and its form is corrupted. And if it was declining or added to, it will remain in a certain way until its form is corrupted. And this remains as one thing, because it does not come from that one single opinion.

### Chapter Two: On the knowledge of the virtues of individual
### medicines, investigated through experimentation.

<image-desc>flourished blue and red decorative initial frame for the chapter title</image-desc>

**To know** the virtues of these individual things, one way is through known **experiments** <term>experimenta: clinical observations or trials</term>. The other is the path of rational distinction. **We**, however, in the experiment, will first state the definition. For through experimentation, one reaches the knowledge of medicinal truth with confidence, provided that the observations of the rules are kept.

<margin>Note VII: All the rules according to which things known through experiment are verified.</margin>
**One** of these is that the medicine should be free from accidental qualities acquired by it, such as accidental heat, or accidental coldness, or a quality that happens to it from something else rather than its own, or from the union <margin>likewise</margin> of another. **Water**, for instance, whose nature is cold, may be heated until it becomes primarily hot. And it is <margin>not</margin> according to its form that it should be naturally hot. So when it cools, it chills while it remains cold. And the almond, when it is cooked, is subtle. Then when it is transformed, it is primarily heated. **And** when it is weighed, it is cold. Then when it is salted, it heats potentially.

<margin>Second</margin>
**And** the second rule is that in each experiment, it should be a singular disease. For if the disease is composite, and in it there are two different signs indicating two cures, the experiment is not carried out in the matter of the medicines that are offered. For if there is a bitter thing in that medicine, where someone has a **phlegmatic fever** <term>febris flegmatica: a fever thought to be caused by an excess of the humor phlegm</term> and it is given in an unmixed state so that the fever is removed, it does not follow that the medicine acts because it is cold, since the patient was hot, which is the fever. Rather, and perhaps it does not help, except because it resolves the phlegmatic matter and evacuates it. And when the matter is deficient, it removes the phlegmatic fevers. **Which** truly is a help <margin>not</margin> in itself, but is changed into a help by accident; in itself because of its composition regarding the matter, and by accident regarding its composition to the fever. **And** the third <margin>m. / 3</margin> is that the medicine must already be tried in the opposites of its own qualities. So that with each of them at the same time, it may be transferred. And it is truly vindicated that it is the way of its own or another's. For perhaps it does not primarily help one of them in itself, but the other by accident. Like **scammony** <term>scammonaea: a potent herbal purgative</term>; if we try it in a cold migraine, it is not logical that it should help and heat it. **And** when its virtue is tried, in a hot migraine where there is a **tertian fever** <term>febris tertiana: a fever that recurs every third day, typically associated with yellow bile</term>, it may be concluded that it helps by evacuating the **choler** <term>colera: yellow bile, one of the four humors</term>. **Since**, therefore, it is so, confidence in the experiment of its heat or coldness is not acquired, except that we know that it effects one of the two things in itself, and the other by accident. **And** the fourth <margin>m. / 4</margin> is that the medicine should be of a quality opposite to the strength of the disease, so that the heat of the medicine is not overwhelmed by the coldness and strength of the disease. Wherefore, in the medicine it does not act...

The knowledge of the virtues of individual medicines through reason follows these rules... some is taken from the speed of their burning relative to the vigor of heating, and from the slowness of their burning. From these, one acquires manifest signs regarding unknown virtues. The first way is when a thing is of a similar nature and constitution. Knowledge of its nature or similarity is found in that whatever receives heat more quickly is hotter, and whatever receives coldness more quickly is colder. And for this reason, some things heat more quickly than others, as seen with **wine**. This increases the virtue that is in it and it becomes hotter. Just as our body differs from that which cools more quickly. And there are materials that open up viscous obstructions and dissolve them, such as those that resolve obstructions by thinning or thickening. And we define each of these ways by how the body is affected in removing them. For the dissolution of the material is intended to make the humors flow; perhaps it separates them into parts, and each is treated according to its likeness.

**A**ttracting medicines are those whose property is to move humors toward the place they encounter. This is due to their thinness and heat, as with **castoreum** <note>original: "castoreu'"; a yellowish secretion from beaver sacs, prized in historical medicine for its "hot" and "dry" properties</note>. **A**nd a **deep-acting** medicine is one whose property is to draw from the depths of the body; it is very strong in its action. It reaches the deep lobes of the organs, purging them, just as it might pull out thorns or arrows from the places where they are stuck. **A** **biting** medicine <note>original: "mordicatiua"; from the Latin 'mordere', to bite</note> is one that has a piercing and very subtle quality, causing a sensation of stinging or pain in the continuous tissues of the body. It "bites" even in small quantities, where each part is felt individually, but the whole is perceived as a single pain; such is the case with mustard mixed with vinegar, or vinegar itself. **A** **reddening** medicine <note>original: "rubificatiua"</note> is one whose property is to heat the limb it touches so strongly that a powerful attraction of blood draws the warmth to the exterior parts, making it red. This is seen with mustard, **monkshood** <note>original: "napellus"; a highly toxic plant also known as wolfsbane, used topically as a counter-irritant</note>, and **calamint**. **A**nd reddening medicines perform the work of cauterization, because they are sharp and heating, and they create a biting humor on the skin. **I**t creates a **stinging** sensation, leading to blistering, and eventually to...

**In its crude** state, its appearance is digestive. In its maturing state, its property is that it destroys the operation of natural heat through a gentle coldness, and it is also extinguished in a bad humor, so that it remains undigested in those who are ungrateful <note>original: "ingratis"; likely referring to patients whose bodies do not respond well to the treatment</note>.

**From** a stupefying medicine <note>original: "Ex stupefactiva"; a substance that numbs or induces sleep</note>, it is a cold medicine that, by chilling a limb, causes a loss of feeling, just as it determines the spirit of death to the power of motion and sense. **From** these are those that are totally putrefied in the stomach, which are found in a state of resolution of their acidity in the stomach; rather, it penetrates to the veins, then its properties remain in the limb.

**Cleansing** <note>original: "Mundicativa"</note> is the name for a medicine in which there is superfluous, external humidity in a limb, or where inflation is mixed in. Such are **mustard** <note>original: "a'zi'tu'"; likely sinapis</note> and **rocket seed** <note>original: "sem' eruce"</note>.

**Laxative** is the name for any medicine whose property is to wipe away, not by acting on the limb itself, but by the power of movement, signifying a purging of humidity. Through movement, it signifies an increase. It is a subtle cure because it goes over the openings of the veins; it eases the superfluous humors with its own humidity and removes them with its help. **Blocking** <note>original: "Sub ficitua"; likely *suffocativa*, medicines that close pores</note> is that whose property is to be spread over the surface of the body to block the passages of the channels and retain them in the limb so that it removes the spirit from it. **Constrictive** <note>original: "Constictiva"</note> is a medicine that makes the nature of a limb pull back from superfluous motion, and brings it back to gathering so that they are thickened in that place. It blocks the passages; it is a medicine from which comes the property that the parts are suddenly gathered together, making the subtle humors arrive, which leads to the repetition of the limb's form.

**Obstructive** <note>original: "Opilativa"</note> is a dry medicine that retains its own spirits through dryness, or through its gluey nature in its entry, which causes obstructions to be born in the limb.

**Conglutinative** <note>original: "Conglu'ttina"</note> is a dry medicine in which there is a little sticky humidity that adheres to the openings of wounds and blocks them, and retains the breath. These act like a fire in the limb, being glue-like, obstructive, and retaining.

**Sealing** <note>original: "Ex sigillativa"</note> is a drying medicine that dries the site of the wound so that a crust or scab forms over it, protecting it from external harms or accidents of nature. All these are medicines that dry without further medication.

**Purifying** <note>original: "Mundicativa"</note> primarily refers to medicines that lead to the corruption of superfluities, such as **euphorbium** <note>original: "euforbiu'"; a caustic plant resin used as a powerful purgative and external irritant</note> and...

<margin>**Alledazahad** <note>original: "Alledazahad"; likely a Latinization of an Arabic term for an antidote or bezoar stone</note> is said in its proper common use to resist poison: or just as theriac resists poison.</margin>
...for poison. Poison is a medicine that corrupts, not through dryness alone, but always by its own specific property. Such is **monkshood** <note>original: "napellus"; a highly toxic plant also known as aconite or wolf’s bane</note>. **Alledazahad** or theriac, however, are all medicines whose property is to benefit and strengthen the vital spirit against impulse, so that the harm of the poison is expelled by them. It is found that the name **theriac** is worthy of artificial preparations <note>original: "artificialibus"; medicines compounded by a pharmacist</note>. And the name **albedazahur** <note>original: "albedazahur"; likely referring to the Bezoar stone</note> is used for singular items that lack such worthy art. It seems that vegetables and minerals take the name theriac when they are among the worthy artificial compounds, while minerals alone take the name **albedazahur**. And it appears there is a great difficulty between them. The solution of the cause itself and the ways of leading them out are noted.

All medicines in which a dissolution <note>original: "solutio"</note> begins affect the protective spirit, such as in the herb **meadow saffron** <note>original: "miodactilus"; used historically for gout</note>, and as shown in pains of the joints; for when the dissolving power begins, it draws out the matter because it reaches the matter itself, nor does another follow it. In all resolving medicines where there is a logic, it equally brings about the softening of the joints and their inflammation, with rapid phlegms, and both heating and resolution. One of these benefits by destroying [the harmful humor], and when heating and resolution are gathered together, the fluidity becomes stronger.

### Chapter 5. On the judgments of certain external medicines.

Medicines are considered medicinal according to the dispositions by which they evacuate a part: those which are here concerning **decoction** <note>original: "coctio"; the process of boiling or 'ripening' a substance</note>, and operation, and administration with fire, and washing, and freezing in the cold, and profit in the property of other medicines. For there are medicines whose goodness is altered.

<column-break/>

For through these dispositions, their goodness is altered, partly because they are mixed with other medicines. Regarding those who speak of what is convenient in the composition of medicines: we say that some medicines are like thick or slow oils, which lose their virtues in boiling unless they are cooked with great labor [heat], such as **caper root**, **birthwort** <note>original: "aristologia"</note>, and **zedoary** <note>original: "zedoaria"; a root similar to ginger</note>, and those which are similar to them.

<margin>Note: the sweetness [or difficulty] decreed according to the medicinal spirit...</margin>
And among them are some equal mediums, for which a moderate boiling suffices; if they are resolved without violent labor, they are quickly drawn into the throat and recede, such as **senna**, and those which provoke urine like **teathos** and similar things.

And among them are medicines for which a very small boiling suffices; for if one boiling is added beyond the first heat, their virtues are dissolved into the steam, and they remain as a mere infusion, such as **dodder of thyme** <note>original: "epitimum"</note>. For if it is boiled much, its entire virtue is destroyed.

<margin>To the seventh. Note: he shows the medicinal sweetness.</margin>
And of the medicines, there are some whose virtue is destroyed by the heat of fire, such as **scammony** <note>original: "scamonea"; a harsh purgative resin</note>. For if it is ground beyond a certain heat, lest the heat cause damage, it breaks its virtue. Especially the grain-based ones are of this kind, in which the resolution is quieted in the heat. In every medicine, if it is boiled twice, the operations are destroyed. It is possible that the virtue is lessened according to its quantity and the proportion of its reduction. Indeed, it is possible that the reduction continues until it no longer has any effect. For it is necessary that just as the whole of something causes a movement, a half of it might move something. Just as a hundred men move a weight, one individual man cannot move a thousandth part of it. It is necessary that it be moved at least a little bit. If a medicine is divided until it becomes a singular part, it may no longer be able to cause a transformation. It is possible that the subject does not suffer a transformation from a half-dose as it would from the totality. Because the half is not as effective as the whole in the disposition of its singularity.

<margin>
This letter is difficult to understand. If it is made singular in the time of division, the other half may not move the matter afterward. It is possible that the half does not act with the same singularity as the whole. For as was said, they are not seen to be separated from the power. And this is seen in the maternal matter to which the medicine is moved; it becomes similar in the proportion of the whole matter upon which the total power acts.

For initially, it was a stone in which there was no sharpness, but when it is burned, it is turned into something sharp.

<margin>Note when burning occurs in medicines.</margin>

**Burning** <note>original: "adustio"</note> is performed for five reasons: either so it may be broken or ground more easily; or so that it may be sharpened; or so that its sparks may be removed; or so it may be made ready to be taken; or so that the "malice" <note>harmful or unwanted side effects</note> within it may be destroyed. An example of the first is **vitriol** <note>original: "colcotar"; refers to calcined green vitriol or iron sulfate</note>. An example of the second is **squill** <note>original: "scilas"; a sea onion used as a powerful diuretic and expectorant</note>. An example of the third is **burnt hartshorn** <note>original: "maris cornu cervi"; the antlers of a stag, burned to produce calcium and used as an absorbent</note>. And an example of the fourth is **senna** <note>original: "senat"; a powerful laxative leaf</note>. For if it is administered into the body, it is strengthened; and if it is administered into the nose, the quantity is different...

<margin>Note on washing.</margin>

**Washing** <note>original: "ablutio"</note> removes the fiery nature from every medicine that it acquired from burning. The reasons for **coagulation** <note>freezing or solidifying</note> are that those things which are frozen, like <unclear>tbal'</unclear>, are destroyed and coldness is added; thus it happens in the sun. Regarding **innovations** <note>referring to acquired properties</note>, it is because some medicines acquire qualities from external virtues so that their operations are resolved. For many medicines are cold or hot by their own specific properties, but they acquire [new qualities] from vicinity. Thus **zedoary** <note>original: "sevice"; an aromatic root similar to ginger</note>, and **cubebs** <note>original: "cusozby"; a type of pepper</note>, and **castoreum** <note>original: "castorei"; a secretion from beavers</note>, and **musk** <note>original: "musci"</note>, which have hot qualities, are made hot in the highest degree because of the place itself. Specifically, they possess a cold quality because they are obtained from the vicinity of **radical heat** <note>the vital, innate heat of a living organism</note>. # Anise
What is Anise? It is the seed of Roman fennel. It is sharp and sweet. **Selection.** The Roman variety is preferred. **Nature.** In which Galen <note>a famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> says it is hot in the second degree and dry in the second degree. And Dioscorides <note>the author of the primary Greek herbal 'De Materia Medica'</note> said it is both in the third degree. **Operation.** It is beneficial and opens blockages. By its nature it settles and aids the belly and resolves flatulence. It is very sharp. **Vulneraries.** It benefits inflation in the face and abscesses of the extremities. **Conditions of the Head.** Let a vapor be made to settle a headache <term>soda <gloss>a medieval term for a heavy, splitting headache</gloss></term> and dizziness. Or let it be mixed with rose oil and distilled into the ear. It heals what occurs in the inner part, whether from a headache, abscess, or its pain. **Conditions of the Eye.** It benefits [unclear] of the eye. **Members of Breath.** It provokes milk in nursing mothers. **Nutritive Members.** It takes away thirst caused by "borax-like" humors <note>original: "baurachis"; referring to salty or alkaline fluids in the body</note>. It benefits blockages of the liver and spleen caused by humors. **Members of Expulsion.** It provokes urine and menstruation. It cleanses the womb from the flow of white humors. It moves one to intercourse. It constricts the belly and aids the provocation of [unclear]. It opens blockages of the kidneys, the bladder, and the womb. **Fevers.** It benefits [unclear]. **Poisons.** It expels the harm of poisons and poisonous things.

# Wormwood
What is Wormwood? It is an herb with leaves similar to oregano. In itself, it has bitterness, heat, and sharpness. According to Hunayn <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a famous translator and physician in Baghdad</note>, there are many types of wormwood. Among them is *tozakenu*, and there is the Oriental kind, and others called *lucheir*, *lufu*, and *carfense*. It was called the "mother of herbs" by the ancients. There are five types: *tarfense*, *lufu*, *nabatu*, *torafani*, and Roman. The Nabataean kind has a good odor. And finally, in this herb there is...

**Sani <note>possibly *Sami* or a variety of *Symphytum*</note>** what it is: a herb having many female parts and a root that is entirely knotted. **Southernwood <note>original: "Abrot", for *Abrotanum*</note>** what it is: It has a fruit similar to the juniper <note>original: "uniuspen"</note>, but more vigorous and with a sharp human-like odor. According to the author, there are two species. One species has leaves like the leaves of parsley <note>original: "apstii"</note>, having many seeds that do not grow long. It is put into warming oils and burning oils, most often in oil made from bitter almonds. **In common wounds.** It helps with flowing matter in the limbs, for *esthomenus* <note>a "consuming" or gangrenous ulcer</note>, and for putrid wounds when mixed with honey. It prevents the spreading of "creeping" sores and blackened ulcers. Some use it for sores that do not heal because of its biting quality and intense heat, which dries them out. **Ailments of the head.** It is boiled in radish oil until it turns black, then it is distilled into the ear; this greatly helps with deafness.

**Antimony** what it is: It is a smooth stone of a leaden nature <note>original: "morau"; likely *marcasitae*</note>. # Ammoniacum
**What Ammoniacum is.** It is the gum of a tree. It grows where gold adheres, because through its grain and membrane <unclear>ulum</unclear> it is prepared. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the highest degree, just as it is in itself. **Applications and Petacos <note>original: "petacos"; likely referring to skin spots or lesions</note>.** It works by dissolving and drying on the outside, but it has no stinging quality on the outside. From it, a preparation is made for the ears when they are weak due to the narrowing of the veins; it is used in the treatment of blockages <note>original: "verrificatione solutioz"</note>, because in itself it has a smoothing and thinning quality.

<margin>Dissolve Dill and etc... (?) in place of (?) ...</margin>
# Anise
**Anise or *lothoi* <note>a synonym, possibly a corruption of a Greek or Arabic name</note>.** It is thin and dry. From it comes a cleansing quality. It is beneficial for the joints <note>original: "iūnētā'"</note> and for those who are thirsty. It is also a great remedy for the head <note>original: "sine capite"; literally 'without head', perhaps meaning it cures headless/aimless pains or migraines</note>. **Wounds and ulcers.** It benefits bad wounds, for it eats away bad flesh and creates a mass of good flesh. **The organs of movement <note>original: "Instrumēta uicturarū"; referring to joints and limbs</note>.** It helps with sciatic pain and pains of the flanks <note>original: "ylioz"</note>, when drunk with honey or barley water. If a plaster is made from it with honey and oil, it resolves the hardness of the limbs. When mixed with vinegar, wine, rose oil, and alkanet oil <note>original: "oleo de alchana"</note>, it helps with exhaustion. **The organs of the eye.** It soothes the roughness of the eyelids and itchy scabs. It wipes away white spots <note>original: "albugine"</note> and helps with watery eyes. **The organs of breath and the chest.** It helps with hardness and difficulty of breathing. For dilation <note>of the chest</note>, it is swallowed with honey or barley water. It cleanses ulcers of the lungs. It helps with suffocation caused by phlegm and black bile. **The organs of nutrition.** When it is drunk, it helps with hardness of the spleen and aids the liver; it is similar when taken with vinegar. It also helps with dropsy <note>original: "yopisi"</note>. **The organs of expulsion.** It provokes urine to such an extent that it may cause bloody urination. It provokes the menses and expels the *asaridē* <note>likely "ascarids" or intestinal worms</note>. It alone clears the womb and causes the expulsion of the fetus, whether living or dead. It provokes the menstrual flow. When placed over hardness of the testicles with vinegar, it softens them. **Substitution.** In its place, one may use the dross of a beehive <note>original: "sordinis alueari’ apū"; propolis or bee glue</note>.

<margin>Birthwort—both round and long. This one is noted for its difference in the stomach...</margin>
# Birthwort
**What Birthwort <note>original: "Aristologia"</note> is.** There is a variety that is black, which is stronger; this black type is found in ships <note>possibly meaning it was imported</note>. Its root is the primary type of Birthwort. Its nature is airy. It is difficult to digest and slow to take effect because its power and digestion are very slow. There is another type from gum. I shall make a separate chapter for it. It is better to use its decoction or its vinegar for the menses. **Nature.** Hot and dry as mentioned. **Applications and Petacos.** It is subtle, and its root causes flatulence. If one rubs with it, or with its juice, it draws poisons to the outside <note>original: "ext’iora u'iuose"</note>.

<column-break/>

**Beauty.** It removes the hairiness <note>original: "sitatē"</note> of the body. If a plaster is made from it with oil, it heals the bruising of blood in the eye. **Apothecary and Cleansing.** It helps with the removal of the menses when its root is mixed with plasters. It is also beneficial for scrofula <note>original: "scrofulis"; swelling of the lymph nodes, often tubercular</note>. **The organs of movement.** When mixed with orris oil or alkanet oil, it helps with almost all pains of the limbs. **The organs of nutrition.** Its root causes the bowels to be evacuated when used with orris oil. It helps with pains of the limbs. Its root causes the belly to be emptied. It is slow to digest, but it warms the stomach and comforts it, and it opens blockages. **The organs of expulsion.** When cooked with water, gum, and vinegar, it heals hemorrhoids of the anus. It provokes and causes a foul odor of the belly to be excited and expelled through the anus; it is harmful to the bladder. **Poisons.** It is a *bezoar* <note>original: "bedizahar"; an antidote or counter-poison</note> against poisons.

<margin>For large abscesses <note>original: "apostematibus"</note>.</margin>
# Long Birthwort
<margin>According to another interpretation.</margin>
**What Birthwort is.** The root is like a vine. It is similar to the annual variety in its nature, but it is inferior to it. **Nature.** Hot and dry, and dry in the final degree. **The organs of nutrition.** It purges and warms the stomach. It opens blockages. However, if it causes a biting sensation, its stay in the stomach is delayed and it becomes acidic. **Fevers.** It is a living protection against quartan fevers <note>fevers occurring every fourth day, often associated with malaria</note>.

<margin>The Birthwort mentioned previously... </margin>
# Round Birthwort
<margin>Birthwort is turning <note>original: "uertent"</note></margin>
**What Round Birthwort is.** It is *azararch* <note>from Arabic "zarawand", meaning Birthwort</note>. Some of it is weak and of no value. There is also a black, long, sandy, or mountain variety that is strong. **Nature.** Cold and dry in the final degree <note>this reflects a specific tradition, as birthwort is usually classified as hot</note>. **Opinions and Petacos.** It is for conquering and cleansing. **Sciatica and lothoi.** From its power, it gives help, for it helps with hot abscesses when applied as a plaster. **The organs of nutrition.** It comforts the stomach and liver, and it greatly increases thirst. **The organs of expulsion.** It constricts and helps with excoriation and the flow of blood from the lower parts.

# Aluuch <note>Likely "Alhuch", an Arabic-derived term for lead or lead carbonate (white lead)</note>
**Aluuch or *allallubar* <note>from Arabic "al-usruh", meaning lead</note>.** It is a black mineral in which there is much watery humor. It spreads like a fungus and in its substance it has acidity or a great multitude of parts. The sign of its quality is as Galen says: the speed of its liquefaction. Its sharpness comes from its extreme thinness. When it is dried, it leaves behind its moisture and swells. It is extremely cooling in its effect. **Nature.** It is cold and moist in the second degree. **Applications and lothoz.** A pill or a tablet is made from it. One should be rubbed with it, or it should be mixed with some oils. When it is dissolved in this way, it helps with hot abscesses and those that are itchy. It is also used as a pillar <note>original: "columna"; perhaps a suppository or a solid application</note> over scrofula, glands, and pains of the limbs. Glands are destroyed by it. **Wounds and ulcers.** As above.

It is bitter; this bitterness is more apparent in the other types. The remaining two species are more bitter than the first and of a stronger heat. And the root is of a stronger heat than the leaves. **Blemishes.** Used with flax and vinegar for "morphea" <note>a skin condition involving discolored patches</note>, which it draws out from the skin. The leaves are weaker than the root itself. In Lotus-like swellings. Similarly, the Bugloss medicament made from them with barley flour treats erysipelas <note>a red skin infection</note>. And similarly, the Amaleus root dissolves scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes</note> when placed upon them with fat. **On wounds and ulcers.** It is placed with wax upon all ulcers, and specifically for burns from fire. **Nutritive organs.** The root of Bugloss suits the stomach, and its decoction with alkaline water <note>original: "aqua alkami"</note> is valid for jaundice <note>original: "icterice"</note> and pain of the spleen. **Excretory organs.** A decoction of it with alkaline water or safflower water <note>original: "aqua cartami"</note> helps with kidney pain and stones in the kidneys. Also, if a woman applies the root to herself, it may cause an abortion. Its leaves, crushed with wine, bind the belly. This Bugloss resolves choleric humors, and the root... [mixing] leaves from it with hyssop and mustard <note>original: "kinapi" for *sinapi*</note>... it reduces humors... [something about] **fevers.**

<column-break/>

A decoction of Bugloss root with *alkarati* water helps with chronic fevers. **Poisons.** When the leaves of the red-colored kind are chewed and spit out <margin>Note</margin> upon venomous creatures, it kills them. The other two species are beneficial for the bite of a viper when drunk or applied as a liniment.

**What Almesu is.** <note>The identity of Almesu is unclear; it may refer to a toxic mineral or a plant like 'Almisu' (musk), though the description of toxicity suggests otherwise</note> It is said that Rhazes <note>a Persian physician</note> was truthful when speaking of this in the chapter on "Nuim"; however, we have brought the account of it into this chapter so it might be better known and more famous. **For:** They said that it is cold and dry, and others said it is hot and dry in its virtue. **Opinions and properties.** It is intensely cleansing; according to Dioscorides, it is inductive <note>drawing out humors</note> and putrefactive <note>breaking down tissue</note>. **Blemishes.** It cleanses the teeth by its whiteness. **Parts of the head.** They said that when held in the mouth, it strengthens the teeth. But this is among the things that are far from me <note>the author expresses skepticism here</note>. **Poisons.** It is a deadly poison.

**What Anise is.** It is an herb of pleasant odor, similar to amomum <note>original: "anamo"; a spice plant</note> in taste. **Blemishes.** It makes the breath smell good. **On swellings.** It helps with swellings... when applied as a plaster <note>original: "eplm" for *emplastrum*</note>. **On wounds and ulcers.** It prevents the spreading of ulcers and makes them firm by the drying power which is in it, and prevents the putrefaction of limbs. **Parts of the head.** It strengthens the brain and binds the gums, and prevents diseases of the mouth. **Organs of the eye.** It is mixed for ophthalmia <note>eye inflammation</note>. **Organs of breath and chest.** It strengthens the heart and all the internal organs. **Excretory organs.** It binds the nature <note>causes constipation</note>.

## Anacardus
**Anacardus** <note>The Cashew Nut or Marking Nut</note>, what it is. A fruit similar to a date stone, and its marrow is like the marrow of almonds, in which there is no harm. Its rind is very fragile, and its moisture is like a viscous honey with a good smell. There are people who chew it, and it does not harm them, especially the mind. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the fourth degree. **Operations and properties.** Its honey is ulcerating, opening, and burning to the blood and humors. **Aesthetics.** It eradicates warts and removes white leprosy <note>original: "albaras," from the Arabic term for vitiligo</note> and eradicates <unclear>lātiuūo</unclear> <margin>such as black pustules</margin> and heals phlegmatic hair loss <note>original: "alopitiā flegmaticā"</note>. **In appetite for washing.** <note>original: "Ju apinbs a lotūi," possibly referring to medicinal baths</note> It stirs up a hot appetite in those with corrupt humors. **Instruments of healing.** It is beneficial for coldness of the nerves; it softens the <unclear>ioiū</unclear>, the pulse, and twisting <note>original: "itorture," likely meaning cramps or spasms</note>. **Head organs.** It is beneficial for the corruption of memory. ## Anas
**Anas** <note>The Duck</note>, what it is. **Nature.** It is hotter than all domestic birds. It is said that its grease is cooling and its flesh heating, able to cause a fever. **Operations and properties.** Its fat is mixed in the second degree of heat, and by adding a biting quality in the profound <unclear>col</unclear>, it is better than the fat of other birds because it breaks wind <note>flatulence</note>. To the stomach, it is highly nourishing. **Aesthetics.** Its fat clears the complexion, and its use makes one fat. **Respiratory and chest organs.** It clears the voice. **Nutritive organs.** It is digested in the stomach <unclear>fuis</unclear>; likewise goose fat, but it is lighter than that, and the wings are best.

## Avellana
**Avellana** <note>The Hazelnut</note>, what it is. It is well known. It has a greater dryness than walnuts; it is more nourishing than a walnut because it is more solid, less windy, and of slower digestion. **Nature.** It inclines toward a certain heat and a little dryness. **Operations and properties.** It generates bile; in it there is a greater excess than in the walnut, and it creates inflation and generates windiness in the lower belly. **Aesthetics.** Because it is burnt, it dyes the hair. **Head organs.** It heals a splitting headache <note>original: "soda"</note> and is roasted as a remedy with pine and pepper; it ripens a cold <note>original: "couza," a catarrh</note>. ## Agnus castus
**Agnus castus** <note>The Chasteberry or Monk's Pepper</note>, what it is. It is a plant, and perhaps because of its size, it is a tree. It grows in places near water. ## Vitriol
Regarding **vitriol** <note>original: "Atramentum," which in medieval medicine refers to vitriols or metallic sulfates rather than just writing ink</note>. There is a difference between vitriol, alum, and tutty <note>term: <term>tutia</term>—zinc oxide, often collected from the chimneys of smelting furnaces</note>, which are pure and are used in stamping or forging. There is *calcathum* <note>green vitriol</note>, *calcadis* <note>white vitriol</note>, and *alsune* <note>a red or yellowish vitriol</note>. These are vitriols that receive a first dissolution from stones that do not otherwise accept dissolution. And this state itself... they receive a solution which, once liquefied, freezes or solidifies. Some are called *samnum*, and *alacadis* is white, and *calcathum* is green, or *rastitum* is red. All of these dissolve in water or reappear through alum; this is because of the nature of their body and solidification. And where this type of solidification comes from is vinegar <note>likely referring to the acidic nature of the sulfates</note>, or a sharpness that covers the layers. And because *rastitum* in its nature is similar to the unique ones <note>original: "unicoz," perhaps referring to rare gems or minerals</note>, its color is compared to them... it is understood that vitriol and tutty are produced from *colcotar* <note>term: <term>colcotar</term>—the red iron oxide remains left after the distillation of vitriol, used for polishing and medicine</note>. It is once covered with red powdered vitriol. This is the consideration. **Selection.** Egyptian green is stronger than *alkabrusi*. In great quantities, *alkobusi* is stronger. And if it is burnt, it is strong, or the burnt type is best. Some varieties are *alkaidis*... and the most refined of them is *assine* <note>likely another variation of "assune," a red vitriol</note>, and these do not resolve in water. There are some vitriols that shine like gold, which are called *alcodothur*. The best *alcodothur* is that which quickly turns into its own kind and is found pure, like the ancient kind. And from the... which they find in the ink-pot, which is noted as *sutu*. The best is hard, having a golden color with brilliance, or like *alcodothar*. The best *assune* <note>red vitriol</note> is that which is brought from Egypt, which breaks away from blackness, or has many veins, having an acidic and styptic <note>term: <term>styptic</term>—a substance that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</note> taste. All of its nature is similar. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the second degree. **Operations and properties.** All types are caustic and styptic, biting to the taste. ## What Birthwort Is
<note>original: "Aristologia," referring to Aristolochia or Birthwort, a plant used historically in childbirth and for treating snakebites</note>
Dioscorides says: there is the long kind and the round kind, and a kind that is like the shoots of a vine. The round kind is called the female, as if the long and round kinds were not both female. They have leaves similar to the leaves of the plane tree, which are similar. It is a twining variety that has a good odor, bringing the earth toward roundness <note>likely referring to the bulbous shape of the root</note>, having many long branches from a single root. And within its flower is something shining... having the form of a cap. The long variety is the male; its leaves are longer, and each shoot has the length of a palm. It has a purple flower throughout, upon which appears something like the flowers of a pine. Its root is one palm in length and has the thickness of a finger. And the vine-like kind has long shoots like vine branches; they are reddish, and the leaves are like those of the evergreen <note>original: "semper viva"</note>, with a flower like the flower of rue. The root itself is excessively large, having the thickness of a rope, which merchants use in the middle of creating oils. **Nature.** All species are hot to the point of stinging, and dry in the third degree. **Operations and properties.** It is cleansing <note>term: <term>abstersive</term>—a medicine used to clean wounds or skin</note>, opening, resolving, and thinning. Its sharpness draws out thorns and splinters. The long kind is more worthy for growths in ulcers because it is more cleansing and hotter, but in other operations the round kind is stronger, for infusions, tampons, and restorations. Truly the long kind is similar to the round in its heating quality, indeed stronger in its superfluity... the round kind is better for the stomach and settles pains in the joints more effectively. The third kind is weaker than them. **Regarding coloration.** It benefits morphew <note>term: <term>morphea</term>—a skin condition causing discolored patches</note> and cleanses spots. It carries away their filth, especially the round kind, and clarifies the complexion. **Wounds and ulcers.** It is a cleanser of filthy and malignant ulcers and hollowed-out wounds. It helps the long kind to drain, and is used for the putrefaction of small fractures and private parts. When it is used with honey, it fills the wound with flesh. **Internal organs.** It benefits the joints, for it is used as a compress for gout <note>original: "podagra"</note>. Especially the round kind; and when those suffering from gout drink it, it helps them. **Parts of the head.** It cleanses the filth of the ear and helps hearing when placed in it with honey; and it helps the gums if they rot, especially when administered

<column-break/>

with pepper. It cleanses the superfluities of the brain and helps epileptics, and mitigates frenzy <note>original: "phrenesim"</note>. **Parts of the breath and chest.** It benefits asthma, especially the fresh kind, and cleanses the chest and lungs; it also benefits side pain <note>likely pleurisy</note> when drunk with water. The round kind is stronger in all these matters. **Nutritive organs.** It is good for the tongue and spleen when taken with oxymel <note>term: <term>oxymel</term>—a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note>. And when smeared over the spleen with vinegar, it helps greatly; the round kind is stronger in all other respects. **Expulsive organs.** It preserves against retention, and when drunk, it effectively dissolves gas and colic, and benefits the same. When the long kind is drunk with myrtle and pepper, it purges the superfluities of the womb in those giving birth, provokes menstruation, and expels the fetus. **Fevers.** It helps with the chills of fevers. **Poisons.** It benefits the stings of scorpions, especially the long kind. As they have said: two drams of the long kind are drunk, or a plaster is made from it; it benefits the stings of venomous creatures and poisons. **Poisons.** In place of the round kind, one may use an equal weight of zedoary <note>original: "zurumbet," a root similar to ginger</note>, or half of this...

<margin>Alchana [Henna], but it is said by me to be a plant that turns its head to the sun</margin>
## What Henna Is
<note>original: "Alchana," referring to Lawsonia inermis</note>
The name of a fruit. Henna is cold in the first degree, dry in the second. **Operations and properties.** It has the power of dissolving, numbing, and constricting without harm, and it is resolving and cleansing against the bite of poison. With oil, it is very helpful, heating and relieving. **Abscesses and pustules.** Its extract benefits hot and phlegmatic abscesses through its drying action, and it opens blood. **Wounds and ulcers.** Its decoction benefits burns from fire and scalds. It is said that it acts in wounds like a cloth soaked in dragon's blood <note>original: "sanguinis draconis," a bright red resin from several different plant genera</note>, and for bone fractures with vinegar. **Organs of the joints.** Placed on the hand, it benefits pains of the nerves when it is included in poultices for paralysis and tremors. Its oil resolves weariness, relaxes the nerves, and benefits bone fractures. **Parts of the head.** It is used with vinegar on the head or forehead for headache <note>original: "soda," a medieval term for headache derived from Arabic</note>. Similarly, it benefits ulcers of the mouth. **Parts of the breath and chest.** It is suitable for pleurisy and is included in plasters. **Expulsive organs.** It is suitable for pains of the womb.

<margin>A. Gum called Asafoetida</margin>
## What Asa Is
<note>original: "Asa," likely referring here to the resin *Asafoetida*</note>
It is a species of gum; one is stinking and the other is fragrant, having a strong odor. The stinking one is hotter. It is a plant of the veterinarians <note>original: "herba ueterinis"</note> known in its entirety. And the best of this species is the "anerese" <note>unclear term</note> and it is the gum of the "almaror" <note>unclear term</note>.

### Nature
It is hot in the fourth degree and dry in the second. 

### Operations and Properties
It breaks up "windiness" <note>original: "uē̄tositates," meaning gas or flatulence</note> or drives it away through its resolution; it is very effective at dissolving thick blood and clotted blood found in the body. 

### Decoction
It helps with hair loss <note>original: "alopit̄ē"</note> when washed with

<column-break/>

vinegar and pepper. Sometimes it is administered to improve the color of the skin, and it removes warts that are like nails. 

### Preparations
When properly prepared, it counters the "biting" fraudulence of the limbs <note>referring to sharp, stinging pains</note>, and if a wing is held over it, it prevails <note>perhaps a reference to its strong scent driving away pests</note>. It is humanely used to stimulate the appetite. 

### Wounds and Ulcers
It helps with impetigo <note>a skin infection</note>. 

### Joints and Limbs
When drunk with water, it generates a great amount of milk and helps with pains of the nerves, namely tetanus and paralysis. If a ring is made from it, it may soothe the headache called "acra" <note>original: "atcr̄m," likely a variant of *acra* or *soda*</note> when swallowed, or it is hissed into the soul <note>original: "sibilat̄ aīm̄o," perhaps meaning inhaled</note> with pepper and rue. 

### Parts of the Head
It fills the soft movements <note>likely referring to the brain's pulses</note>. It is rubbed with oil and placed upon the belly. It is effective in the treatment of epilepsy. And when used as a gargle, it eradicates leeches attached to the throat. 

### Parts of the Eye
It is used as an ointment or "alcohol" <note>original: "alcohol," in the sense of a fine medicinal powder or eye salve</note> made from it with honey. 

### Parts of the Chest and Breath
When dissolved in water and used as a gargle, it clarifies the voice immediately and helps with chronic roughness of the throat. If swallowed with eggs, it helps with chronic cough and cold pleurisy. It is also used by the elderly for rot in the uvula. 

### Parts of Nutrition
If administered with dry figs, it treats jaundice <note>original: "hyctiac̄"</note>. It is said to be harmful to the stomach and liver if not used properly. 

### Expulsive Parts
It helps with hemorrhoids, increases the strength of sexual intercourse, and provokes menstruation and urine. It helps with piercing pains of the belly and ulcers of the intestines. Galen said that he considered this to be a substance that dissolves slightly through its astringency; it is healthy for the mouth and improves the color of old blood. 

### Fevers
It is used for quartan fevers <note>a fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria</note>. 

### Poisons
It is placed upon the bite of a rabid dog and the bites of venomous creatures, especially scorpions and shrews <note>original: "ructelle"</note>. It helps against all of these when drunk. Rubbed with oil, it expels the harm of a poisoned arrow. 

### Composition
In place of the "scice" <note>unclear term</note>, use an equal weight of the fragrant kind, an equal weight and a half of serapinum <note>a resin from a Persian plant</note>, a bit of horehound <note>original: "mar̄ob̄"</note>, and half its weight of the gum of rue.

The oil of almonds is lighter than the nut itself. **Beautification.** The bitter almond helps when placed upon pimples, freckles, skin roughness, and various ailments; it smooths the appearance of the face. When the root of the bitter almond is cooked and smeared on the face, it is a powerful medicine. Eating sweet almonds fattens the body. **Opening the bowels.** The bitter almond with wine [helps] a flux... **Wounds and ulcers.** It is smeared with honey upon spreading ulcers and "formica" <note>likely shingles or a creeping skin rash; literally "the ant"</note>, and with vinegar and wine upon impetigo <note>a bacterial skin infection</note>. The bitter variety is the most effective for all of these.
<margin>Sar <unclear>sabaphar</unclear></margin>
**Parts of the head.** They are very good for ear pain and ringing in the ears. This is especially true of the bitter oil. If the head is washed with them and alum, it cleanses moisture and dandruff <note>original: "fursures"</note> and makes the hair grow.

<margin>To prevent drunkenness.</margin>
<margin>Taking five is enough.</margin>
<margin>As they are eaten during the meal.</margin>
When bitter almonds are taken before wine, they prevent drunkenness; for this purpose, five is the usual number. And [it is said] that bitter almonds, when held [in the mouth] or mixed with vinegar and rose oil and applied as a plaster to the forehead, help with a "soda" <note>a medieval term for a splitting headache</note>. Oil of bitter almonds also helps with this. **Parts of the eye.** It helps the vision. **Parts of the breath and chest.** Bitter almonds with [linseed] are good for spitting of blood, and they help those with chronic coughs, asthma, and pleurisy. This is also true of sweet almond oil. Almonds are praised for helping with coughs and the spitting of blood. **Nutritional parts.** They open obstructions of the liver and spleen. The bitter ones especially open acute obstructions in the extremities of the veins. When fresh almonds are cooked with their hulls, they cleanse the moisture of the stomach; though they are difficult to digest, they provide good nourishment. When eaten with sugar, they pass through the system quickly. Their sweetness moves the bile. **Parts of expulsion: the bitter variety.** They open obstructions of the kidneys. The oil of bitter almonds cleanses the kidneys and bladder, and it breaks [kidney] stones. It is also drunk with iris. When made into a plaster with rose oil and wax, it helps with pains of the womb and its hot obstructions, as well as "suffocation of the womb" <note>a historical diagnosis for various female health issues</note>, difficulty of urine, and kidney pain. As a suppository, it provokes menstruation. The sweet ones help with colic because of their [soothing] properties. The bitter ones are more medicinal; their oil is commonly used. **Poisons.** It helps with the bite of a rabid dog.

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of Parsley and mineral substances into a comprehensive treatise on the medicinal properties of different types of Water (Aqua), including sea water, sulfurous water, and mineral-rich springs. It continues the format of categorizing effects by "Nature," "Operation," and specific "Ailments" (Debra) of the body parts.</meta>

<margin>From the source.</margin>

# Water. Selection.
We have already spoken of good and praiseworthy waters in the first book. These are healthful. However, those waters that are standing, or found in lagoons and pools, are harmful. Also bad are those over which a strange and foreign odor lingers for a long time, and those that are yellowish or thick. One should be wary of waters that quickly turn to stone <note>referring to heavy mineral sediment or calcification</note> or those upon which bad moss floats. Foreign, harmful things do not freeze upon the surface of [good] waters. And know that the purity of waters is noted when they are mixed with milk, wine, or starch <note>original: "amulo"</note>. They are better when they do not have a fierce odor, or a smell of unripe fruit, or a scent that is laxative or provocative. Corrupted or stagnant waters are rectified by adding substances such as garlic <note>original: "aleū," likely allium</note>, onion, and leeks. These inhibit the bile in the water, remove its malice, and purify it. When water is harsh, it is either because it is sharp or cutting. Just as water of that spirit cleanses that which you wash with it, bitter water rectifies sweet water. Water [preparations] are also made with dried wood <note>original: "xilocurate," possibly a corruption of xylo-</note> and various virtues; the great master Rhazes <note>original: "zaroz," referring to the Persian physician Al-Razi</note> speaks of this, as well as of hot mud and fennel. Vinegar also cleanses and rectifies bad waters.

## Nature.
Sea water is sharp and hot, and it is a "hateful" water <note>original: "aq' i'visa," meaning unpleasant to the senses</note>. It is easily made into a drying agent. There are also copper-bearing and iron-bearing waters. Cold water harms those suffering from obstructions <note>term: <term>oppilations</term> (blockages of the internal organs, common in medieval pathology)</note>, yet it benefits those with thinness of the body and promotes the flow [of humors]. Those who have these qualities find their strength more quickly and are comforted in their conditions. If it is digested internally, it is restorative to the complexion.

## Operation.
Sea water helps against chills when mixed with vinegar, and it treats ulcers and kills lice <note>original: "pediculos"</note>. It dissolves clotted and frozen blood. Sulfurous waters are good for diseases and for [cleaning] wool.

## Roughness and Joints.
Sulfurous waters benefit the opening of the joints and help those with suffering nerves.

## Wounds and Ulcers.
Sweet water is bad for drinking when one has ulcers because it moistens them too much. The use of sea water is very helpful for scabies and impetigo <note>original: "ipragini"</note>. Sulfurous waters are also good for scabies and impetigo, provided one bathes in them.

## Joints.
Sea water similarly benefits the flesh around the joints, especially when a bath is taken for paralysis, numbness, and similar conditions. Sulfurous waters act similarly. And

<column-break/>

they are present for all pains of the joints and cold flows [of humors].

## Ailments of the Head.
Epidemics <note>or perhaps skin eruptions</note> are helped by lukewarm water and calmed by hot water. The vapor of sea water helps with epilepsy. Copper-bearing water benefits the ears.

## Ailments of the Nostrils.
Bituminous water <note>original: "asfalti"</note> is bad for the eyes.

## Ailments of the Breath and Chest.
Very cold water is extremely bad for the chest. Indeed, water is harmful to the flesh of the lungs because of the moisture it introduces, whereas the lungs require drying. Lukewarm water is good for ailments of the throat, the uvula, and the chest. Sea water is effective against ailments of the breasts. Water [preparations] are sometimes given for the lungs. Aluminous water <note>water containing alum</note> is for the spitting of blood. Iron-bearing water benefits a hardened spleen, and copper water is the primary remedy for it.

## Ailments of the Stomach.
Nitrous water benefits a "moist" stomach because of its nitrous quality. Aluminous water benefits vomiting and inhibits it. Similarly, styptic aluminous waters and sulfurous waters benefit ailments and pains of the spleen, and likewise the liver. Very cold water harms the stomach by causing obstructions. Sea water is also very bad for the stomach. The vapor of sea water benefits dropsy <note>original: "ydropisi," an old term for edema/swelling</note>.

## Ailments of Expulsion.
Sea water is used in an enema <note>original: "clistere"</note> for piercing pains, and when drunk it dissolves [blockages]. It is also drunk to calm the "biting" of the gut. Aluminous water prevents miscarriage <note>original: "abortu"</note> and the excessive flow of menstrual blood. Sulfurous waters benefit pains of the womb. Very cold water is bad for sexual intercourse <note>original: "coitui"</note> as it restricts the veins and calms the movement of sperm. Saline water dissolves [humors] as it dries them out. All mineral waters cause difficulty of urine and affect the bladder wall. Drinking much of them causes a drying dissolution. Some aluminous waters cause colic to occur. Thick/impure waters cause stones to form in the kidneys and bladder. Water in which iron has been extinguished <note>a common medicinal preparation</note> benefits the spitting of blood.

## Fevers.
Sulfurous waters, if not used carefully, cause acute fevers; they can even cause quartan fevers <note>malaria-like fevers that recur every four days</note>.

## Concerning the Vein.
For a dead [worm or growth in the vein], one sits in sea water, which helps it. This is done similarly for other such things.

## Maduum. <note>possibly a resin or mineral substance</note>
<margin>Its moisture. Bad heat.</margin>

### Nature.
It is harmful. It is cold and dry in the first degree.

### Operation.
It performs many functions. In it, there is a power of cleansing and softening. It must be cooked with its own example <note>likely meaning cooked in its own juice or a specific decoction</note>.

## Debility.

...[Socotrine] <note>original: "gibilis," likely a corruption of "Socotrinus," the highest quality aloe from Socotra</note>, Egyptian, and Arabic. Yemeni alum, that is, *feileh*. Round alum, that is, *manicum*. It has a sharp, acidic stypticity <note>astringency</note>. And it is as if it were the "flower" of the alum. There is a species found in *Sela* in which there is no stypticity to the taste. And this itself is not of the genus of alum. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the third degree. **Operations and Properties.** In it there is a power of prohibiting and drying. Barley <note>original: "Hordeu"</note>. **Nature.** Its heating property is between the second and third degree, and its drying property is between the first and second. And when it is burnt, its drying property is in the second degree. **Operations and Properties.** It is a maturative <note>helps abscesses ripen</note> for cold humors, a sedative for pains, it gives substance to the belly, and it is drying; its oil is similar. In it there is the highest softening power, both in itself and in combination, and it is primary among things that ripen and open wounds. Its drying power is even greater than its resolving power. It is a maturative and it opens ulcerated wounds. It also helps with trembling ulcers. **Healing the Parts.** Its oil helps with pains of the joints and similar things. **Parts of the Head.** A compound may be made from its oil or its dry powder; it helps with melancholic pains of the ear and dries the moisture of the ear. **Parts of the Eye.** Constant eating of it weakens the sight. **Parts of the Breath and Chest.** An infusion of it or its "milk" <note>barley water</note> is made for the elderly; it is helpful for those with light humors because it increases milk <note>in nursing mothers</note>. **Natural Parts.** It helps with hiccups and fullness of the stomach caused by things swimming in the stomach. In that way, it is easily born in the stomach. Yet its seed is harmful to the stomach. **Parts of Expulsion.** It helps with piercing pain in the belly. One may mix the seed to make a clyster <note>enema</note> or sit in a bath of it. And its seed makes hemorrhoids flare up. And its essence is mixed with *loriano*, black, and *teshail*.

Here he speaks of the power of fats.

<margin>
