It is effective for cracks in the face and lips.

## Hard Swellings and Cleansings <note>original: "Asura et lotrix." "Asura" likely refers to "al-asrah," a term for hard swellings or abscesses; "lotrix" refers to a cleansing wash.</note>

Pure fat is effective for abscesses <note>original: "apata," a corruption of "apostemata"</note> and for "leonis" <note>likely referring to "elephantiasis leonina," a skin condition</note>. It resolves long-standing abscesses.

## Wounds and Ulcers

Top-quality fat is effective for burns caused by fire.

## Parts of the Head

Goose fat soothes ear pain. Fox fat is also extremely helpful for this. Hen fat is beneficial for roughness of the tongue.

## Parts of the Eye

Fish fat is beneficial for watery eyes and sharpens the vision when mixed with honey. Fresh viper fat, if applied first <note><insert>hr</insert> likely "habetur," meaning "is held" or "applied"</insert></note>, ensures that eyelashes that have been pulled out do not grow back.

## Internal Maturations <note>original: "Intrunita maturarũ," likely a corruption of "Iuncturae" or "Intrinseca," referring to internal ripenings or abscesses</note>

Bird fat is beneficial for those suffering from wasting diseases <note>original: "fusino," possibly a corruption of "phthisis"</note>.

## Excretory Organs

Goat fat is beneficial for the stinging of the intestines <note>colic or irritation</note> when it is administered, and it helps their ulcers. Goat fat is stronger in the treatment of intestinal ulcers, as is pig fat. This effectiveness is due to the speed with which it congeals. If the fat is applied, it gently soothes the stinging. Camel fat from the hump, when used as a fumigant, is beneficial for hemorrhoids. All light fats, such as hen fat and others, are beneficial for pains of the womb <note>original: "matris," literally "of the mother"</note>, though in some cases they are ill-suited; goose fat specifically serves the womb.

## Poisons

Fat is beneficial for the stings of venomous creatures. Elephant fat, when used as an ointment, drives away venomous things. Goat fat is beneficial for those who have been bitten. And deer marrow is beneficial for wasting diseases.

# Garlic and its kin

## Nature

<margin>Raw garlic, that is, shallots; wild garlic, that is, *skorom* <note>original: "skorom," likely scordion or water-germander</note>. These two chapters are one.</margin>

It is cold <note>The text notes cold, though most medieval sources classify garlic as hot; this may reflect a specific variety or a transcription error in the original source</note> in the first degree.

## Application

It is smeared over skin abrasions when mixed with vinegar.

## Wounds and Ulcers

It heals fresh wounds. It is smeared over abrasions with vinegar and heals them. One may also wrap the skin of the garlic itself over a wound, and it will be healed.

## What Garlic Is

Garlic is a well-known substance. There is another type called "pittirium" <note>possibly "ophio-scorodon" or "viper's garlic"</note>, which is wild. In the wild variety, there is bitterness and astringency. There is also a variety called "serpent garlic." Leek-garlic <note>original: "porrinū," likely a hybrid like elephant garlic</note> is a composite of garlic and leeks.

## Nature

They are warming and drying. The wild variety is more so than the garden variety.

## Operations and Virtues

It resolves inflammations strongly, particularly those that are ulcerated. It is also beneficial for those affected by a change in water <note>traveler's sickness</note>.

## Beautification

A decoction of mountain garlic is drunk to kill nits and lice, and it is also rubbed over them. When applied with honey over bruises or "exultations" of the eye, it is beneficial for hair loss <note>alopecia</note> caused by putrid humors.

## Hard Swellings and Cleansings

It should be applied to feces <note>possibly as a suppository or for cleansing</note>, and its use serves as a cleanser.

## Wounds and Ulcers

It treats ulcerated

<column-break/>

spots. Applying it with honey over "impetigo" <note>a skin infection</note> heals the ulceration. Wild garlic also causes "fraudulent" <note>stubborn or non-healing</note> wounds to close when it is placed upon them in its own way.

## Joint Problems

When a clyster <note>enema</note> is made from it, it is beneficial for sciatica, as it alone clears the pain from the choleric joints.

## Parts of the Head

Garlic causes foul breath, and for that reason, it is avoided. However, it soothes toothache, and a gargle made from its decoction helps with dental pain, especially when mixed with frankincense.

## Parts of the Eye

It weakens the vision and causes a discharge in the eye.

## Parts of the Hearing and Chest

A gargle of the decoction clears the voice. It is beneficial for a chronic cough and for chest pains caused by cold. It also expels leeches from the throat.

## Nourishing Parts

It helps with tremors. It is used in a preparation made from garlic, olives, and nuts.

## Excretory Organs

Sitting in a decoction of garlic leaves provokes urine and menstruation, and it expels the afterbirth. The same is true when it is applied topically or drunk. If one suffers from the "famos" <note>unclear; perhaps a skin condition or specific infection</note>, the aforementioned preparation is very beneficial. A certain quantity of it taken with honey-water extracts phlegm and expels worms. It also acts as a natural laxative. However, it should be used carefully because its rapid drying and resolving power can be harmful. If it is cooked in water, its heat is reduced so it does not dry out the body as much, though this may generate flatulence in the system. One should not be concerned if it cannot expel the gas immediately. Because it is highly penetrative, it should not be avoided when used to stir the desire for intercourse.

## Poisons

It is helpful for the stings of venomous creatures and the bites of serpents when drunk with wine. We have already experienced its success this way; also, when mixed with cumin and rubbed over the bite, it is beneficial.

# What Marshmallow is

## Nature

The name is Greek, derived from a name for various living things <note>referring to "althaea," meaning "to heal" or "that which heals"</note>.

## Nature

It is hot and moist.

## Operations and Virtues

In it are the powers of softening, maturing, soothing, and resolving. Both the leaves and the roots are beneficial. The root is stronger than the leaves, being more drying and firming.

## Beautification

It is smeared over bites with vinegar while sitting in the sun. It softens powerfully.

## Abscesses and Cleansings

It softens abscesses and prevents them from hardening; it resolves bloody and mature

**Asphodel** <term>Afodillus</term>
What it is: its leaves are like those of the leek and the rush <note>original: "scenu," from the Greek *schoenos*</note>. It has a smooth stem, upon the head of which is a flower. It has long, round roots like nails or clubs.

**Its Nature**

It is hot and dry. Although some have said it is cold and moist, they are far from the truth.

**Operations and Properties**

It is cleansing and resolving. When its root is ground, it becomes warming and drying, even more so in its root and its sap <note>original: "lac," literally 'milk'</note>, which has the power of dragonwort <note>original: "dracōtre criste"</note>.

**Cosmetic Uses**

It benefits hair loss <term>alopiatiē</term> and skin rashes <term>lerpigini</term> when the roots are scraped and smeared on white patches <term>morphee albe</term> <note>a skin condition like vitiligo</note> while sitting in the sun.

**Abscesses and Swellings** <note>original: "Asūcta al'vetoz," a corruption of *Apostemata et elevatio*</note>

Its root with wine dregs is placed on all glandular abscesses and on carbuncles. When a plaster is made from it with barley flour, it helps at the onset of hot abscesses.

**Wounds and Ulcers**

When its root is applied with wine dregs to deceitful and filthy ulcers, it benefits them.

**The Joints**

It benefits the muscles and twisting.

<column-break/>

**Parts of the Head**

When its juice is distilled alone, or with frankincense and honey, it benefits the throat. When dropped into the ear, it provides relief for toothache and molar pain.

**Parts of the Eye**

In the juice of its root, there is help for the eye.

**Parts of the Breath and Chest**

When given as a drink—half a gold coin’s weight <note>original: "aurei"</note> with wine—it benefits pain in either side and coughs. Its root with wine dregs is good for abscesses of the breast.

**Nutritive Parts**

It benefits jaundice <note>original: "bicice," likely a corruption of *icteritiae*</note>.

**Organs of Expulsion**

It provokes urine and menstruation. Its fruit and flower, when given in a wine drink, are purgative. A plaster made from its root and wine dregs is used for abscesses of the testicles.

**Poison**

Three gold weights of it are given for the bite of venomous creatures. When the fruit and flower are given to drink with wine, it wonderfully benefits scorpion bites; it purges the body.

**Hellebore** <term>Heleñ</term>
**Nature**

It is composed of heat and dryness, although some say its coldness is more dominant. In some varieties, there is a sharp heat; in others, an abundant coldness.

**Operations and Properties**

It is strongly drying, which prevents the flow of humors to the internal parts; it thins and cleanses. When drunk or poured over a flow of blood, it stops it. It prevents vomiting and stops abscesses and the putrefaction that can occur. It aids digestion and helps with phlegm and bile <term>coleras</term> and harmful black bile <term>melancolias</term>.

**Observations**

It is smeared with honey on the traces of blood.

**Abscesses and Swellings**

It prevents the gathering of abscesses and the spreading of gangrenes. It heals "eaten-away" erysipelas <note>original: "erisipila comestū"</note> and redness of the uvula, as it prevents the spreading of all abscesses. It benefits itching, shingles <note>original: "formice," literally 'ants,' a term for herpes or shingles</note>, and erysipelas when smeared on them. It is also used on the sites of abscesses, wounds, and ulcers.

When wool soaked in vinegar is placed over wounds, it prevents them from abscessing. It benefits wandering ulcers, scabies <term>scabia</term>, and impetigo <term>īpētigini</term>. It also helps with burns from fire or bruises.

**The Joints**

It is beneficial for the shoulders <note>original: "hūis," likely *humeris*</note>, and when bathed with sulfur upon gout <term>podagrā</term>, it helps.

**Parts of the Head**

When mixed with vinegar-oil or rose oil, or when milk is poured over it and it is placed on the head, it benefits a hot headache <term>soda</term>. And similarly from it and...

**Agaric.** <term>Agaricum</term> <note>A medicinal fungus, typically the Larch Agaric, used as a purgative</note>. It is also called the wild fungus of the larch tree. ### Substitution
Or in its place for fevers, sumac <note>original: "sum' sir"; likely *sumach* or a specific syrup</note> is used.

## Balsam <note>The balm of Gilead or *Commiphora gileadensis*, highly prized in antiquity</note>. What it is.
It is an Egyptian tree growing in a place called "of the Sun." Its leaves resemble those of wild rue, but they tend toward whiteness. Its height is the stature of the *cusia* tree <note>likely the *cassia* tree</note>. Its oil is better than the plant itself. And according to the strength of its wood in all ways, its oil was such that it is extracted with iron after an incision is made, and that which exudes from the wood is gathered with ivory [tools]. It does not produce in a year more than forty to sixty pounds.

### Selection
From the experience of this oil: it causes the curdling of milk immediately when it drops upon it. When mixed with water, it thickens and preserves its solidity in the water. From its beginning with vinegar, its scent is subtle. It is adulterated with plum oil, oil of mastic, or resin dissolved in alkanet oil. The best kind is reddish; the worst is that which is dark or greenish.

### Nature
Its vigor is hot and dry in the second degree <note>Medieval medicine classified substances on a scale of 1 to 4 based on their "qualities"</note>. Its seed is hot in the same way. Its oil is hot even to the beginning of the third degree. And there is no doubt about its heating property, as some think.

### Operations and Benefits
It opens obstructions and is beneficial for colic.

### Wounds and Ulcers
<gloss>it bites</gloss> It cleanses ulcers with *yrcos* <note>likely a medicinal resin or iris</note> and extracts bone fractures. <gloss>this</gloss> It helps ailments of the belly. It is useful for sciatica when drunk. It is drunk with vinegar for the breath.

### Parts of the Head
It is useful for ulcers of the head and cleanses the head itself. It is beneficial for epilepsy and vertigo.

### Parts of the Eye
Its oil wipes away film [pannus] from the eye.

### Parts of the Breath and Chest
Its wood and its seed are useful for pain in both sides and help with asthma or shortness of breath and lung pain. Its seed is beneficial for cold phlegm and coughs. Likewise, its oil is a supreme help for the internal organs located above the *mirach* <note>an Arabic anatomical term referring to the abdominal wall or epigastrium</note>.

### Nutritional Parts
It helps with weakness of digestion, cleanses the stomach, and strengthens the liver.

### Parts of Expulsion
It provokes menstruation and helps with pains of the womb. It extracts heavy vapors when drunk and helps with coldness. It is used in fumigation for all pains of the womb. Its decoction opens the womb. A wax-salve <note term="cerotum">a cerate or wax-based ointment</note> made from it with rose oil...

<column-break/>

...helps with coldness of the womb and difficulty of urine.

### Chills
Its oil removes rigors [shivering].

### Venoms
It resists poisons and is beneficial for the bite of a viper. With oil and henbane flour, when drunk with milk, it is a remedy for poisons and scorpions.

## Belem <note>likely *Behen*, the root of *Silene* or *Centaurea*</note>. What it is.
Rough pieces which are dried roots, similar to cabbage. There are two kinds: one is white and the other is red.

### Nature
It is hot and dry in the second degree.

### Beauty
It is fattening [to the body].

### Parts of the Breath and Chest
It greatly strengthens the heart and helps with heart palpitations.

### Parts of Expulsion
It clearly increases semen.

### Substitution
In its place, use an equal amount of "the Jew" <note>likely *lapis judaicus* or Jew's stone, used for urinary issues</note> and half its weight of "bird's tongue" <note>the seed of the ash tree, *Fraxinus*</note>.

## Berengella <note>a variant name for Southernwood or a similar aromatic herb</note>, which is Southernwood. What it is.
It is a plant similar to southernwood. One species has shorter stems and larger leaves. The leaves are small, white, and rounded, appearing in summer. Galen says there are two types of flavor...

### Nature
It is hot and moist in the first degree.

### Operations and Benefits
It is restorative and very beneficial... 

### Parts of the Head
It is useful for cold [ailments] of the head when applied as a plaster... when cooked in water it becomes more effective. It helps with nasal obstruction and catarrh.

### Parts of Expulsion
It breaks stones in the bladder and provokes menstruation, best when used as a decoction. It helps ulcers... and opens the appetite for food when drunk, or when applied as a plaster... taken up to five drams.

## Burach <note>Borax or Nitre (Natron)</note>. What it is.
It is a strong kind of "lime" which is of an oily nature, and its astringency is not minimal. When it is put in a vessel over glowing coals, it is easily removed.

### Selection
The best is the *sarmenū* <note>possibly *saracenicum* or a specific grade</note>, light, flaky, brittle, porous, white, or purple, or rose-colored, and pungent. When compared to other *baurach*, it is as salt is to other things. But *baurach* is not eaten unless mixed with water. The "foam of baurach" is a refined form and has its virtues. The best of these is the marble-like foam, easily broken.

### Nature
It is hot and dry at the end of the [second] degree...

## What Buchu is.
It is a substance brought from Yemen. It is said to arise from a medium-sized <note>original: "midia"</note> [plant or resin]... <note>OCR is unclear; possibly referring to a gum or aromatic</note>. **Selection.** The best is clear, light, and of good odor. The white variety is poor.

**Nature.** It is hot and dry in the first degree. According to some, it is cold in the first degree.

**Operations and Properties.** It strengthens the limbs.

**In Beauty.** It cleanses and dries out the humors that are under the skin, makes the body's odor good, and removes the smell of the armpits <note>original: "p̃hiloz"; likely *paxillos*</note>.

**The Nutritive Organs.** It is good for the stomach.

## What Blete is.
It is the same as [Blitum]. <note>likely *Blitum capitatum* or a similar leafy plant like beets or spinach</note> **Nature.** It is cold in the first degree, [moist] in the second, and moist at the end of the second. When its seed is dried, it is then moistening; rather, it dries in the first degree. Its root is drying.

**Operations and Properties.** That which is mature is beneficial. When immature, it causes phlegm <note>original: "sputa"</note>. Furthermore, it matures things in their nature... <note>Text here is difficult to decipher; likely discussing digestive properties</note>. The "melon" variety <note>likely a specific cultivar or shape of the plant</note> is better than the rest. When it is dry, it is digestive and cleansing, except for its seed. <column-break/>

**The Eyes.** It is used so that it adheres... preventing a flux from reaching the eye.

It is said that it should be taken with savory. It causes nausea and vomiting; but if one drinks oxymel <note>A mixture of honey and vinegar</note> while warm, it moistens the [stomach]. **In Poisons.** When it corrupts in the stomach, it takes on the nature of poisons, so that it should be expelled quickly.

## What Berberry is.

**Instrument of Healing.** It benefits those suffering from [excessive] humors, cold illnesses such as paralysis <note>original: "pilisi"</note>, and "torture" <note>original: "tozture"; likely refers to twisted limbs or cramps</note>.

**The Nutritive Organs.** It kindles the fire of the stomach and is preferred for nutrition. It enters into [various medicinal mixtures].

**The Excretory Organs.** It constricts the bowels and dries out flatulence <note>original: "uētositate"; windiness</note>.

## What Belleric Myrobalans are.
They are close to the Emblic myrobalans <note>original: "ebli con"; Indian gooseberry</note>. Their pith is sweet, similar to [almonds].

**Nature.** Cold in the first degree, dry in the second.

**Operations and Properties.** In them is a strengthening power and a constricting power.

**The Excretory Organs.** It purges the bowels... and according to some, it lightens the bowels. This is manifest in those who prefer it...

### Lemon Balm
<note>original: "Beiderezeguu"; likely a corruption of the Arabic "Badranjbuyah," or Melissa officinalis</note>
**Nature.** It is hot and dry in the second degree <note>Medieval medicine graded the intensity of a substance's qualities from the first to the fourth degree</note>. **Opinions and properties.** It benefits all ailments caused by phlegm and melancholy <note>two of the four bodily humors; an excess of melancholy was thought to cause sadness and skin issues</note>. **Beautification.** It removes sores and all spotted wounds. ### Maidenhair Fern

Loth, the son of Mesogue <note>Mesuë the Younger, a famous 11th-century physician</note>, says it works in this manner. **Poisons.** Drunk with wine, it helps against the bites of serpents, rabid dogs, and other venomous creatures. **Substitution.** In its place, one may use an equal weight of its flower or oil with half its weight in licorice juice.

### Baurac
<note>Nitrum or Borax; in medieval texts, this often referred to naturally occurring sodium carbonates or borates</note>
Which is... It is river nitre. Some say it is glass... It is well known, and its oil is powerful. It possesses certain virtues. **Nature.** It is hot in the first degree, inclining toward dryness in the first degree. It contains a superfluous moisture. **Operations and Properties.** It is naturally styptic <note>contracts tissues to stop bleeding</note>, but it can also dissolve humors. It resolves certain inflammations but has a tendency toward putrefaction, and it generates the bad humor of melancholy. **Applications.** When mixed with rose vinegar, it is applied to the head for heat. **The Head.** Its juice is distilled to stop nosebleeds, especially when mixed with vinegar. It also removes numbness of the teeth. It can soothe or stir the temperament <note>complexio</note> depending on the condition. **The Eyes.** It helps with throbbing in the eyes and treats dimness of vision by moving and drawing out moisture. Its juice strengthens the sight when made into an eye salve <note>original: "collirio"</note>. **The Respiratory and Chest Organs.** It greatly strengthens the heart and dries the lungs and chest. A rinse made from its water helps with the spitting of blood and increases the flow of milk. **The Nutritive Organs.** It is difficult 

<column-break/>

to digest and prone to rapid putrefaction; it is bad for the stomach, especially its leaves. **The Excretory Organs.** It binds, yet it can also dissolve and provoke humors. It helps with difficulty in urination in the elderly. **Poisons.** It is placed upon the stings of wasps, scorpions, and the sea dragon <note>a venomous fish</note>.

### Bercurum
<note>Likely Dog's Mercury (Mercurialis)</note>
Which is... They say it is *azar*, a leaf that resembles the leaf of sorrel. **Operations and Properties.** Its leaves are styptic. It heals wounds and ulcers. **The Head.** Its juice is best for old ulcers of the ears. It is made into a syrup <note>original: "rob"; a thickened fruit juice or syrup</note> to treat these ailments.

### Ballomon
<note>Likely a species of Spurge (Euphorbia)</note>
Which is... It is wild *arfarsac* and is a type of spurge <note>original: "titimmallus"</note>. Its seed is "fiery," as are all spurges. **The Excretory Organs.** It purges the bowels.

### Bebiluli
<note>Possibly the Frothy Poppy or a similar plant</note>
Which is... It is what is called the pitted and frothy poppy. It is thought to have the same purging power as spurge. **Nature.** It is very hot. **The Excretory Organs.** It purges like spurge.

### Bener Guuide
<note>Likely Barberry (Berberis)</note>
Which is... It benefits the complexion and treats "wind" <note>gas or bloating</note>. When mixed with oil, wax, and egg yolk, it heals ruptures. With wine, it provokes urine and menstruation and causes abortion. With cardamom, it is effective for hemorrhoids and fevers. It also benefits shivering. **Poisons.** It is effective against the toxins of minor venomous creatures. **Substitution.** In its place, use *tossilore* <note>possibly coltsfoot</note>.

### Bacasica
Which is... It is *lebelkebs* <note>an Arabic name for Lablab or a similar climbing bean</note>; with its black seeds, it is used in gardens.

### Bilu
Which is... It is the stalk of the *fistula* <note>Cassia fistula, the Pipe-tree, used as a laxative</note>. We shall narrate the secrets of the *fistula* stalk in the chapter on *Hubium*.

### Beus Defendu
Which is... It is an eye salve brought from Armenia. **Applications.** It is applied to hot inflammations and is used for hot gout <note>original: "podagram"</note>.

### Ballaustia
<note>The flower of the wild pomegranate</note>
Which is... The flower of the wild pomegranate of Persia or Egypt. It can be red, white, or rose-colored. Paulus <note>Paulus Aegineta</note> says it is cold at the end of the first degree and dry in the second. **Operations and Properties.** It is binding <note>original: "glutinatina"</note>; it stops flows and generates melancholy. **The Mouth.** It is good for the gums and for healing wounds and ulcers. It consolidates injuries.

# Blatum. Nature.
<note>Possibly *Blitum* (Strawberry Blite) or *Blatta Byzantia* (an aromatic sea-shell operculum), though the description of being "moist" and "nourishing" strongly suggests the plant Blite</note>
It is hot and moist in the first degree. Its degree of moisture is particularly high. **Operations and Properties.** It is ripening, resolving, and softening. Its ability to resolve <note>break down morbid humors</note> in moderate bodies is not difficult, and in delicate bodies <note>original: "corpib' veneris"; likely referring to women or those of a soft constitution</note>, it acts with ease. Its juice is drying. It easily constricts, acting as a sedative for the pain of matters flowing to the limbs. **Decoctions.** Anointing the body and the belly with a decoction of it nourishes and fattens the person. **Wounds and ulcers.** It benefits wounds of the nerves, fills up ulcers, and purges them. **Head organs.** When drunk as a medicine made from it, it helps bruises of the facial membranes and ailments <note>original: "asuita"; likely *accidit* or *assueta*, meaning habitual conditions</note> radiating to the ears, nose, and mouth; it also helps conditions of the throat and jaws. When the flesh <note>pulp</note> is used as an ointment on the throats of infants, it is beneficial for the mouth and belly. **Breathing organs.** It benefits those with coldness, especially when prepared with almonds and sugar; it is also useful for pleurisy and pneumonia <note>original: "piplemoia"</note>. It makes spitting easy and ripens the phlegm. If taken with almond oil, its ripening power is greatest. Used alone with water, its cleansing effect is less than its ripening effect. It is used for phthisis with the spitting of blood, and it benefits the vomiting of blood and pus when one and a half ounces are strained with honey. **Excretory organs.** It is a softening agent, and frequent use of it loosens the bowels. If used as a clyster <note>enema</note>, it helps hot inflammations and hardness in the intestines, as well as first-stage wounds of the bladder's opening. **Poisons.** It resists poisons, especially when the bite of a viper is anointed with it.

# Barba Hirana. Nature.
<note>Likely *Barba hirci* or Goat's Beard (Tragopogon)</note>
In this substance, there is a mixture of heat and coldness, such that its heat is at the end of the first degree, and its dryness is intense, reaching the second degree. **Operations and Properties.** It is styptic <note>contracts tissues to stop bleeding</note> to the core, and its root possesses the strongest binding quality. It is useful for hemorrhages and for organs that need to be constricted. Its juice has the stypticity of rose seeds. **Wounds and ulcers.** Its leaves, when applied, benefit

<column-break/>

### Column 2

chronic ulcers; in these matters, its flower is the most potent. **Head organs.** Its root is among those medicines that wipe away filth from the ear and dry its ulcers while preserving the sense of smell. **Breathing and chest organs.** Its flower, leaves, and root, however prepared, benefit ulcers of the lungs and the spitting of blood when drunk with barley water. **Nutritive organs.** It comforts the stomach and prevents the pouring of excess fluids into it; its juice acts in this way. **Excretory organs.** It is the strongest medicine for ulcers of the intestines when drunk, whether as its flower or its juice with wine. It is also used for the flow of blood from the womb, applied either as a suppository or drunk.

# Jewish Bdellium and Meccan Bdellium.
<note>Resinous gums from the *Commiphora* tree, prized in antiquity for medicine and incense</note>
**What it is.** There is Jewish bdellium, another called "Sicilian" <note>original: "ficulu"; likely an imitation or a specific regional variety</note>, and another called Arabic, which is said to come from wild palms. **Selection.** The better of the two gums is that which is variegated, clear, and bitter in taste; it should be clean, easily dissolved, and have a sweet or pitch-like odor. Some say Jewish bdellium comes from Alexandria for drying purposes. **Nature.** Meccan bdellium is cold and dry. Others say it is hot at the end of the first degree. The Sicilian variety has a softening quality, while the Arabic kind is more drying. **Operations and Properties.** It resolves coagulated blood and is softening, ripening, and breaks up windiness <note>gas</note>. When used with strong softening agents, it is very effective. The Arabic kind is particularly strengthening. **Opening and Dissolving.** It resolves hard swellings <note>original: "afiata"; likely *apostemata*</note>, which can be dissolved with the saliva of a fasting person. Likewise, it resolves other "cold" ailments. Meccan bdellium, which is not from wild palms, is the same as Jewish bdellium; it removes freckles or spots. Its decoction is drunk for internal and hard swellings. **Wounds and ulcers.** Anoint with vinegar upon the affected area. **Hardness of the joints.** It benefits bruises, lacerations, spasms, hardness of the nerves, and anything congealed. **Breathing and chest organs.** It benefits conditions of the windpipe <note>original: "canne pulmonis"</note> and its roughness; it also benefits an old cough and pains in the side. The Arabic variety benefits swellings of the epiglottis and the throat. **Excretory organs.** It benefits hemorrhoids when drunk, used as a suppository, or as a fumigant. It cleanses the blood, benefits stones in the kidneys, and because it is a resolving agent, it prevents the scraping <note>abrasion</note> of the intestines and provokes urine and menstruation. Bdellium <note>a fragrant resin similar to myrrh</note> is an Arabian substance used for purification, as a quantity of two *aurei* <note>original: "aureor(um)"; a weight based on the gold coin, roughly 7–9 grams</note> of it is taken and drunk with honey-water to diminish phlegm. Both types of bdellium resolve "ranulas" <note>swellings under the tongue</note> and abscesses <note>original: "apostemos"</note>; it opens closed passages and cleanses the womb. It also resolves abscesses of the rectum and anus. **Poisons.** It helps against the bites of venomous creatures.

# What Old Butter is.
<note>original: "Butiru(m) n(on) recens"; aged or salted butter was distinguished from fresh butter in medieval medicine for its stronger heating properties</note>

It performs the same actions as butter but is stronger in its ability to change, soften, and soothe; it is heating. I have already mentioned the pure substance of it in the chapter on raw butter, but I will add more here. **Nature.** It is hot in the highest degree and moist in its own degree. **Operations and benefits.** It is ripening and resolving <note>meaning it breaks down "bad humors" or swellings</note>. It is used in ointments for the body. **Abscesses and swellings.** It ripens abscesses, especially those behind the ears and specifically in women's fistulas. It is unsurpassed for such conditions in the body. **Head organs.** It ripens abscesses occurring near the ears. **Breathing and chest organs.** It soothes the chest and ripens the fluids within it when mixed with honey, sugar, and bitter almonds. **Excretory organs.** It helps when taken with almonds because it binds by its own property and also dissolves matter. **Poisons.** It acts as a theriac <note>an antidote or universal cure</note> for poisons that have been swallowed.

<margin>Also called asphalt</margin>

# What Jewish Bitumen is.
<note>original: "Bitumen iudaicu(m)"; also known as "Jew's Pitch" or asphalt, often harvested from the Dead Sea</note>

It is said that bitumen is a substance that flows from certain mountains, while another kind floats upon certain waters. The black variety is considered of poor quality. It is great and light; the kind that animals chew with difficulty has a [distinct] flavor, but it is brittle. **Selection.** The best kind is purple, clear with brilliance, strong, and heavy. The black, dirty kind is bad. **Nature.** It is hot in the second degree and dry in its own degree. **Operations and benefits.** Its virtue is nourishing. It comforts the stomach and liquefies congealed blood in the belly when it is drunk. **Cosmetic use.** It helps with vitiligo <note>original: "alleri"; likely *albor*, white skin patches</note> of the nails when applied as a liniment. **Abscesses and swellings.** It helps with scrofula <note>swollen lymph nodes, often tubercular</note>. **Wounds and ulcers.** It is smeared over ruptures and over the abscesses of wounds, and it does not permit them to open. **Joint organs.** It is used as a poultice for gout; it is drunk and smeared on for sciatica. **Breathing and chest organs.** It helps with coughs and ulcers of the lungs, and aids in spit-

<column-break/>

-ting <note>expectorating</note> and expelling pus from the chest. It also helps with tonsillitis <note>original: "alumnis amigdaluru(m)"; literally "almonds of the throat"</note> and quinsy <note>severe throat inflammation</note>. **Excretory organs.** It helps with hardness of the womb. When used as a suppository, it benefits it; it also prevents the prolapse of the womb during painful labor. When an enema is made from it with water, it is beneficial for the bowels.

# What Rennet is.
<note>original: "Coagulum"; the substance from a young animal's stomach used to curdle milk, used here to stop bleeding or dry out fluids</note>

There are many types of rennet, and we shall discuss each specific rennet in the chapter concerning animals. **Selection.** Among them, the best is from the fawn and the hare. **Nature.** All types are hot and dry. **Operations and benefits.** It resolves congealed blood and has a [drying] power; it coagulates every fluid. It is highly desiccative <note>drying</note>, prohibiting all flows, including the flow of blood in women. There is no doubt that it is a drying agent. According to Galen <note>an influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note>, in some cases rennet can cause obstructions. **Head organs.** It helps with epilepsy when drunk, especially camel rennet. **Breathing and chest organs.** It resolves congealed blood in the lungs. **Digestive organs.** It resolves curdled milk in the stomach when drunk with wine, and it resolves congealed blood in the stomach, though it is generally bad for the stomach. **Excretory organs.** When used as a suppository, it purges the menses and helps with conception. It also helps with "suffocation of the womb" <note>an old term for hysteria or uterine displacement</note>. Camel rennet helps with ulcers of the intestines, as does the rennet of a horse foal. **Poisons.** All types are theriacal <note>antidotal</note> and help against the "black poison." The rennet of the kid, calf, and lamb are the most helpful. It heals against venomous bites... when drunk with [specific] herbs.

# What Juniper is.

It is well-known. An oil is made from it by burning, and the oil from its bark is particularly strong. There is also a preparation made from its flowers. **Nature.** It is hot and dry at the end of the second degree. Its pulp is hot in the first degree and moist in itself. Some say it is cold and moist in the first degree, but its coldness is greater. Its milk is cold and [dry] in the second degree, and its seed is hot in the second degree. **Operations and benefits.** The pulp causes flatulence. Its leaves also cause flatulence, while its flower is more subtle.

# What Ceruse is.
<note>original: "Cerusa"; white lead, a lead-based pigment used both in cosmetics and as a topical medicine despite its toxicity</note>

It is the "rust" of lead, or made from lead. And it is said that it is made from lead when it is burned... it acquires a surplus of substance. All ceruse is made with vinegar. And some is made with salts, and some in other ways used in this art. **Nature.** It is cold and dry in the second degree. **Operations and properties.** That which is made with vinegar is faster in its effect and penetrates more deeply. In other forms, it is agglutinative <note>meaning it helps wounds close and stick together</note> and cooling <note>original: "alesfreg"; a medieval Latin term for a soothing, cooling agent</note>. **Benefit and harm.** It softens strict and hard swellings, wounds, and ulcers. It is put in plasters and fills ulcers, generating new flesh in them; however, it can be corrosive because it is a strong astringent and cooling agent. It is very powerful in the generation of flesh. **Eye organs.** It helps for distortions of the eye. **Excretory organs.** It is among the remedies used for conditions of the anus. **Poisons.** It is itself among the poisons. And the detailed reminder of its [toxic] nature is in the chapter on poisons.

# What Chamomile is.
<note>original: "Camomilla"</note>

There is one kind whose flower is white, another that is purple, and another yellow. It is well known, and its leaves resemble its flowers. Its root is dried. Galen <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note> says it is close to the healing power of the rose in its substance, but it is hot. **Nature.** Hot and dry in the first degree. **Operations and properties.** It is opening, thinning, and softening; it is "resolving" without causing irritation. It has a high status among medicinal ingredients. **Benefit and harm.** It calms hot swellings by softening and resolving them. It softens hardness that is not yet very tight. And it is drunk for thick swellings and ulcers. **The instrument of neighboring parts.** It softens tension and strengthens the sinewy parts of the body. It is among the remedies that most benefit weariness, because its heat is similar to the natural heat of an animal. **Head organs.** It strengthens the brain and the senses. It is used to evacuate "superfluities" <note>excess humors</note> from the head because it resolves them without irritation. It is also beneficial for sores of the mouth. **Eye organs.** It heals the eyes. **Breathing and chest organs.** It eases the coughing up of phlegm. **Digestive organs.** It removes jaundice. **Excretory organs.** It purges the womb and breaks stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, especially the variety with the purple flower. And with chamomile...

It also provokes menstruation and is used as a decoction. ## The Onion <note>original: "Cepa"</note>
It is well known. Its quality is very sharp, bitter, and astringent <note>original: "sliptiatas"</note>. The best kind is the long and sharp variety. White onions are more acute, the dried ones are more moist, and the roasted ones are more daring <note>original: "audũ"; perhaps meaning potent</note>. **Nature.** It is hot in the third degree and contains superfluous moisture. **Operations and properties.** It is cleansing for the senses. Because of this, tears happen when it is handled, as the vapors from its flowers <note>referring to the onion's pungent scent</note> seize the eyes. It causes bloating <note>original: "inflatio"</note> and draws blood to the surface, as it is a "rubefacient" <note>a substance that reddens the skin by increasing blood flow</note>. A decoction of it is used as a nutrient to help whatever needs healing. The juice <note>original: "llexa"</note> of the onion is not as bloating as the onion itself. It is nourishing when cooked together with other things. Onions also protect against the harm of "bad waters" <note>a common medieval belief that onions could purify water or protect the drinker from waterborne illness</note>. In some provinces like Persia, the scaly kind <note>original: "scosa"</note> is very common. **Beauty.** It reddens the face and removes skin spots. When mixed with figs, it is very effective for hair loss <note>original: "alopitue"; alopecia</note>. Mixed with honey, it eradicates warts. **Wounds and ulcers.** It is useful for dirty ulcers and helps against the spread of gangrene when used with calaminth. **Head organs.** The head is purged with its juice; it cleanses the head. Dropping it into the ear helps with earaches, ringing <note>tinnitus</note>, and discharge in the ears. It is one of those things that causes thirst. Frequent use causes lethargy <note>original: "suber"; a heavy, stupor-like sleep</note> and is harmful to the intellect because it generates bad humors. It also increases saliva. **Eye organs.** Its juice helps with cataracts <note>original: "aq̃ dẽscendẽs"; literally 'descending water'</note> and clears the vision. From its seeds, a fine powder <note>original: "alcbvlol"; from the Arabic word 'kohl'</note> is made with honey for white spots on the eye. **Breathing and chest organs.** Onions with honey benefit those who are choking. **Nutritive organs.** Generally, it is difficult to digest, and some types provoke vomiting. Because of its sharpness, it strengthens

<column-break/>

the stomach and creates an appetite. When twice-cooked, it is not very nourishing but becomes quite suitable. It is beneficial for jaundice <note>original: "byctiae"</note>. **Expulsive organs.** It opens the passages of hemorrhoids. All types of onion excite sexual intercourse, and onion juice provokes menstruation. **Venoms.** It helps with the bite of a rabid dog when the juice is smeared over the wound or when it is applied as a plaster with salt and rue. The onion also expels the harm of poisonous "winds" <note>toxic gases or vapors</note>. It is said that there is a certain moisture generated in it that draws out the power of poisons.

## Coral <note>original: "Corallus"</note>
It grows in the seas that are in Africa. It is said that when it is ground, it fills the cavities of weak teeth and roots them firmly, and strengthens the gums. It is supreme for the health of the gums. Galen <note>a famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> believed that burned and washed coral, used in the weight of one drachm <note>approx. 3.5 grams</note> with gum arabic and egg white, given with cold water, helps with the spitting of blood and its rising <note>hemorrhage</note>, and stops the flow of bile. This is red coral. It benefits all diseases of the stomach, especially if placed directly over it. Galen said: "I have experience with this; I hung it on the neck of one who suffered stomach pain, so that the coral was over the opening of the stomach, and the pain was removed." When I took it away,
<margin>Note.</margin>
the pain returned. I have had similar experience with a certain wood for epilepsy. Those who hang red coral on their necks during their healthy days will be free from stomach pain. For this reason, it is hung on the necks of children. **What it is.** It is a stone-like substance. Some coral is red, some black, and some white. **Nature.** It is cold in the first degree and dry in the second. **Operations and properties.** It is used to stop the flow of blood. Its drying power is greater than its cooling power. **Wounds and ulcers.** It cuts away "proud flesh" <note>excessive growth of grainy tissue in a wound</note>. **Eye organs.** It strengthens the eye by drying the unhealthy fluids within it, provided it is burned and washed. It clears away cloudiness and stops excessive tears. **Breathing and chest organs.** It stops the spitting of blood and helps with coughing. Black coral is especially good for this when burned and washed. It is one of the medicines that strengthens the heart and helps with heart tremors <note>palpitations</note>. **Nutritive organs.** Drunk with honey, it helps with diseases of the spleen and softens it. **Expulsive organs.** It helps with swellings <note>original: "aposteitaly"</note> of the intestines.

<summary>This page details the medicinal properties of onions, including their use as a skin treatment and digestive aid, and coral, which was used for dental health, stomach pain, and as a protective amulet for children.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical pharmaceutical list of "simples" (individual medicinal ingredients), following the entry for the Onion. It moves from botanical roots to animal products (Castoreum) and dairy (Cheese), detailing their humoral qualities and specific applications for various ailments.</meta>

# Zedoary <note>original: "Cepazir"; likely a corruption of "Zedoaria," a root related to ginger used to treat digestive and "cold" ailments</note>
Zedoary. What it is: It is a root that grows with a shared stem <note>The OCR "stilis opē munis" likely refers to "stilo communis," a common stem</note> in its rocky environment. Branches grow in its place, and it is more stable than them. **For expulsion.** It soothes cold pains of the womb <note>original: "matris"; in medieval medicine, the womb was often called the "mother"</note>. **Poisons.** It is effective against the poisons of bees or scorpions. It is taken as a drink or applied as a poultice with a bandage <note>original: "fiaulo"; likely "fasciola," a small bandage</note>. **Substitution.** Use as much of this as you would of zedoary, or two parts of cloves <note>original: "gariofilis"</note>.

# Castoreum <note>original: "Astoreu"; a pungent secretion from the scent glands of beavers, famously used in medieval medicine for nervous disorders</note>
Castoreum: what it is. It is the testicle of an animal in the water <note>original: "ī manni"; likely "in mari" or "in amne," referring to the beaver's aquatic habitat. Naturalists at the time wrongly identified the scent glands as testicles</note> which are black. They are found hanging together from a single root, like two hollow, dried skins. It has a thin skin that is oily and breaks when touched. **Selection.** The best is that which consists of two testicles clinging together; this is not adulterated. Adulteration is often done with opopanax <note>a medicinal plant resin</note>, gum, and other things mixed with oil and a little real castoreum, then dried in a bladder. Those who work to obtain this from the animal's limbs do so because when it is poured out, it is like honey; it is then dried together. **Nature.** It is substantial and strong in its ability to heat and dry. It is hot to the end of the third degree <note>Medieval medicine graded the intensity of a substance's "humoral" effects from 1 to 4</note> and dry in the second degree. **Operations and properties.** It resolves inflations <note>bloating or gas</note>. When applied as an ointment, it warms the body. The gummy substance in its center is stinging and provides intense heat. **For acute conditions and lethargy <note>original: "Asuta ⁊ lvtlvi"; likely "Acuta et litargia"</note>.** It helps with hot illnesses. **Wounds and ulcers.** It helps with pernicious <note>dangerous</note> wounds. **For the urinary organs.** It helps with coldness and provides heat; it also helps with tremors and "moist" spasms, as well as with numbness, stupor, and paralysis. **For the head.** It helps with forgetfulness and lethargy <note>a state of sleepy indifference</note> when mixed with vinegar and rose oil. If a fever is present, it is drunk with honey and pepper; it helps and does no harm. The dose should be a spoonful. It resolves "cold" headaches caused by windiness <note>gas or vapors in the body</note> and helps with "cold" deafness. Nothing is more helpful for windiness in the ear than castoreum the size of a lentil, dissolved in oil of nard and dropped into the ear. **For the chest and lungs.** Inhaling the smoke through the nostrils helps with lung ailments. **For nutrition.** It is drunk with vinegar for hiccups and to cause thirst. **For expulsion.** It removes piercing stomach pain when drunk with vinegar and resolves 

<column-break/>

windiness. It provokes menstruation. Two drachms <note>a unit of weight, about 3.5 grams</note> drunk with oxymel <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note> helps with the flow of the saphenous vein <note>a major leg vein</note> and brings out the fetus. It removes coldness and windiness from the womb. **Poisons.** It helps with the bites of poisonous creatures. It acts as an antidote <note>original: "t̄ypnaca"; likely "theriaca"</note>. If it is dark or blackish, it is poisonous if taken in one day. If someone suffers from this, use vinegar and ass's milk as an antidote. **Substitution.** If castoreum is unavailable, use the same amount of marjoram <note>original: "oziano"; likely "origano"</note> and half as much pepper.

# Cheese <note>original: "Caseus"</note>
Cheese: what it is. Cheese is made from milk or from whey <note>original: "seru"</note>, such as that which is called ricotta <note>original: "receta"</note>. **Nature.** Fresh cheese is cold and moist in the second degree. Old, salty cheese is hot and dry in the third degree. In the "water of cheese" <note>whey</note>, there is a cleansing property. **Selection.** The best is the medium kind, not that which is hard and brittle; others are poor. Good cheese is recognized by its color and a flavor leaning toward sweetness. Goat cheese made from mountain-grazing goats is better than that from goats that graze on nothing <note>likely meaning low-quality pasture</note>. **Operations and properties.** It helps against thirst. Fresh cheese is nutritious and fattening; it should be eaten with honey. Old cheese is hot, astringent, and cleansing; it draws out choleric humors. Whey is very fattening for dogs and nourishes them. Ricotta is very resolving <note>breaks down humors</note>. **For chronic ailments <note>original: "Ju de ozanaē"; likely "In de ozena" or a similar term for chronic sores</note>.** Whey is a medicine that cleanses melancholy <note>black bile</note>. Fresh cheese cooked in wine helps with facial spasms. Old salty cheese thins the humors. **For acute conditions and lethargy.** Fresh, unsalted cheese prevents sores from burning. **Wounds and ulcers.** It is good for bad ulcers and recent wounds. Fresh cheese soothes heat in the limbs and prevents the swelling of the hips, especially when used with herb leaves and vinegar. Whey is drunk to treat the "scabies" <note>a general term for itchy skin rashes</note>. **For the urinary organs.** It treats the bladder when mixed with oil or water.

<summary>This page describes the medicinal properties of Zedoary, Castoreum (beaver secretion), and Cheese, focusing on their "hot" or "cold" natures and their effectiveness in treating conditions ranging from lethargy and paralysis to skin rashes and digestive issues.</summary>
<keywords>Zedoary, Castoreum, cheese, ricotta, whey, medieval pharmacology, humors, cold diseases, toxins, reproductive health, skin treatments</keywords>

... it is made into a plaster <note>original: "eplin"; abbreviation for "emplastrum"</note> for a divine void <note>original: "diuine uacuatuū"; likely a reference to a specific type of swelling or hollow ulcer</note>. And it is used externally like gypsum without impediment, and it is a very great help. **Parts of the eye.** From this, with saliva, a plaster is made for the extremities of the eyelids. **Parts of the breath and chest.** When cooked with cheese <note>original: "caseu"</note> in water and given as a drink to nursing women, it increases the milk of the breasts. **Nutritive parts.** Cheese <note>original: "Ballē"; a variant or corruption of "caseus"</note> is bad for the stomach, especially for those who do not salt it. Unsalted cheese is somewhat difficult to expel. And it is said that fresh cheese <note>original: "ꝛrecn̄s"</note> is heavy on the stomach, or it is due to its ambiguity <note>its uncertain humoral nature</note>. Salted cheese is not older than the other, and it is faster in digestion; it descends more quickly. Ricotta <note>original: "Reaxeta"; likely "recotta," a fresh whey cheese</note> is less harmful to the stomach than the common cheese. **Parts of expulsion.** It generates stones in the kidneys and bladder, and it is harmful. [Fresh cheese] does not salt the humors, but water [whey] by dissolving it leads out the bile and helps it. It is useful when prepared with honey, becoming a more helpful medicine—especially that which is made from the milk of goats and sheep. Also, its whey <note>original: "ſcus"; likely "serum," whey</note> is useful for ulcers in the intestines and for roasted meats; it prevents flux [diarrhea]. When roasted cheese is taken, or a clyster <note>an enema</note> is made from it with rose oil and [common] oil, it helps those who go to the stool with blood <note>original: "ſurgētī ad ſellā cū ſanguine"; refers to dysentery</note>. **Poisons.** And when mixed with mountain calamint <note>an aromatic herb</note>, it is applied over poisons.

# Cinnamon: what it is.
<note>original: "Cynamomū"</note>
It is [a root/bark], and one good species is somewhat reddish in color, growing in the mountains, thick and short. Another variety is white, loose, inflated, and fragile, having a skin that tends toward softness. There is also a black species, flat and slightly knotty, which is like "cassia lignea" <note>"wood cassia," a cheaper relative of true cinnamon</note> tending toward greenness, or a bark like red bark. Among these, the variety that lasts for a long time is the true one. And there is a type made from that which is prepared with wine. Furthermore, there is a species called "false cinnamon" <note>original: "cinamomū mendosu"</note>; it has a certain odor and is harsh, and its power is weak; oil is made from it. **Selection.** The best is that which has a good, sharp odor and a biting taste <note>original: "mordicānā"</note>. Its color is pure and unmixed. Some say the best is blackish, declining toward green or red, smooth, with branches close together, in which there is sweetness, saltiness, and a little bite. It is not very fragile. Because of its longevity, its scent should overcome all other odors, so that no other smell is

<column-break/>

perceived with it. The bad variety is that which has the odor of must <note>mold or dampness</note> or frankincense, or a saltiness, or any bad odor, or is white and fragile, or smells of rancidity. The flat kind that radiates in pieces is also bad. It is preserved for use in a vessel, but if not [stored well], it weakens after a period of fifteen years and its strength stands still. It is best when taken from a plant that grows from a single root. If it is falsified, it is not suitable. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the third degree <note>in Galenic medicine, the third degree indicates a very potent substance</note>. **Operations and properties.** It is the ultimate in "subtlety" <note>the ability to thin thick humors</note>; it is digestive, opening, and rectifies against putrefaction. It has a power that destroys the sliminess of corrupt humors. It is very hot and resolving <note>able to dissipate fluids or swellings</note>. **Skin.** It is placed over freckles or spots on the cheeks with vinegar, and treats eruptions. **Wounds and ulcers.** It is suitable for treating deep ulcers. **Instruments of the joints.** Oil of cinnamon is wonderful for tremors <note>shaking of the limbs</note>. **Parts of the head.** It helps the brain. Its oil strengthens the head and cleanses it, drawing out moisture from it. It also settles the pain of the ears. **Parts of the eye.** It helps with "pin and web" <note>original: "pūno"; likely "pannus," a growth over the eye</note> and darkness of the sight; its power brings light to the eyes and consumes the moisture of the eyelids. **Parts of the breath and chest.** It eases the cough of the trachea and cleanses the chest. **Nutritive parts.** It opens obstructions of the liver and strengthens it. It strengthens the stomach and dries its excess moisture. **Parts of expulsion.** It helps with the pains of the "mother" <note>the womb</note> and the kidneys. It is a resolution for the stomach when used with a little oil, wax, and egg yolk, so that it does not overflow but is cleansed. It provokes urine and menstruation, and can cause an abortion. With seasoning, it helps against cold humors. The oil is beneficial for pains of the womb when broken down with rose oil and wax. **In fevers.** It helps against rigors <note>shivering fits</note> and its oil is helpful. **Poisons.** It resists the bites of venomous animals. A plaster is made from it with myrrh for the stings of scorpions.
<margin>On white hellebore</margin>
**Substitution.** In its place, one may use the bark of cassia lignea, or double the amount of "calcite" <note>likely a mineral or a plant corruption</note>, or double the amount of "bealtel" <note>possibly balsam</note>.

# Brain: what it is.
<note>original: "Erebuū"; a corruption of "Cerebrum"</note>
**Selection.** The best brains are those of birds, especially those found in the mountains. Of all [others], the most durable is the brain of a goose, then of other living creatures. **Nature.** It is cold and moist.

<meta>This page continues the pharmaceutical inventory, transitioning from the properties of animal brains (concluding a previous section) into detailed entries for Saffron (Crocus) and Colocynth (Coloquida). ## Opinions and Uses
It generates phlegm <note>original: "flegma"</note> and corrosive humors. **Parts of the head.** Chicken brain is preferred for a flux of blood from the nose <note>original: "fluxui sanguis narū"; a nosebleed</note> stemming from the membrane. And camel brain, when it is dried and drunk with vinegar, helps; it is preferred for epilepsy. **Nutritive parts.** It causes nausea during its digestion and destroys the appetite. And it is necessary that it be seasoned with seeds. He who wishes to avoid vomiting from its food should take it upon an empty stomach. It is slow to digest and coats the surface of the stomach. **Parts of expulsion.** It lightens the belly. And duck brain is a medicine for ailments of the anus. **Poisons.** Brains are healthy against the ingestion of poisons and the bites of animals when they are eaten.

## Saffron
**Selection.** The best is fresh, of a good color, and of a good odor, having a little whiteness upon its hairs, and being of a deep hue. <note>The text describes high-quality saffron threads, which should be vibrant but may have pale tips.</note> It should not be easily broken into pieces. **Nature.** It is hot in the second degree and dry in the first. <note>Medieval medicine categorized substances by "degrees" of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness to balance the body's humors.</note> **Opinions and uses.** It is astringent, resolutive <note>capable of breaking up congestion</note>, and maturative <note>promoting the ripening of sores</note>; because of its astringency, it is binding. Its heat is tempered and it affects phlegm. Galen said its heat is stronger than its astringency. Its oil is warming, and it is said it never alters its moisture, but rather helps with its quality, rectifies putrefaction, and strengthens the viscera. **Decoration.** By its color, it makes the skin look like wine <note>referring to a healthy, glowing complexion</note>. **Its Disturbance.** It resolves swellings and helps in cases of erysipelas <note>original: "ensipila"; a skin infection</note>. **Parts of the head.** It causes a heavy headache <term>soda<gloss>A medieval term for a splitting headache or migraine, derived from the Arabic 'suda'.</gloss></term> and is harmful to the head. It is drunk with syrup to the point of intoxication, and it induces a sleep that creeps upon the senses. When drunk in wine, it intoxicates so much that it produces rheum. It is preferred for hot swellings in the ear. **Parts of the eye.** It clears the vision because it stops the flux of humors to them. It helps with a <term>pannus<gloss>A medical condition where a veil-like tissue or film grows over the cornea.</gloss></term> and is used to make an eye-salve <note>original: "alcosol"; likely a reference to kohl or a specific medicinal collyrium</note> for spots acquired in the eyes. **Parts of the breath and chest.** It strengthens the heart and is soothing; it is given to those with pleurisy and those suffering from chest pain so that they may sleep. Its oil makes breathing easy and strengthens the instruments of the breath <note>the lungs and airway</note>. **Nutritive parts.** It causes nausea and destroys the appetite because it is the opposite of the acidity found in the stomach, yet it can also help the appetite. It strengthens the stomach because of its heat, balance, and astringency. It is also said to be beneficial for the spleen. **Parts of expulsion.** It excites sexual intercourse and provokes urine, and it helps with the condition of the womb.

<column-break/>

...more deceitfully <note>referring to adulterated saffron</note> in itself, when it is mixed with honeycomb or with marrow with double the amount of oil. Someone said that when the aforementioned is brought to the light, they are purified and their part is made. **Poisons.** It is said that three gold coins' weight of it restores joy <note>literally "establishes rejoicing," suggesting it acts as an antidepressant or antidote to "melancholy" poisons</note>. **Substitution.** An equal weight of costus <note>an aromatic root</note> can substitute for it, or spikenard, or an equal weight of the bark of woody cassia.

## Colocynth
**What it is.** There is one kind of Colocynth <note>original: "Colloquida"; also known as Bitter Apple</note> which is male, and another which is female. The male is hairy, and the female is smooth and whiter than the others. **Selection.** The one to be chosen is white and of a smooth whiteness; if it is black, it is bad, and if it is hard, it is bad. It is necessary that the pulp not be agitated when it is collected from the belly of the fruit; rather, let it be left to dry inside it. It is weakened otherwise. And it should not be gathered until it is at its greatest maturity. The roundness should be kept whole. And the air of it is known to be bad. It is said that it is necessary to remove both the rind and its seed. When there is only one colocynth upon the vine, it is bad and prone to rot. The male is hairy and firm, and the female is loose. It is necessary that it reaches the height of yellowness, and there should be nothing in it that is not finely ground; for even the smallest part, if not sensed, when it finds moisture, it inflates and leads to paralysis, as well as twists in the intestines and worms <note>original: "ascar'"; ascaris or intestinal pinworms</note>. It is necessary that it be sat upon <note>perhaps referring to a steam bath or suppository</note> with honey, then dried and used. Its rectification—that is, the expulsion of its malice <note>its toxic or harsh effects</note>—is best done with tragacanth <margin> rather than gum </margin> because gum helps the strength of the medicine more. **Nature.** It is hot in the third degree and dry in the fourth. Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchind'"; a famous 9th-century Arab physician</note> however estimated it to be cold and moist, but he is far from the truth of medical experience. **Opinions and uses.** It is resolutive, "cutting" <note>meaning it breaks up thick, sticky humors</note>, and eloquent. <margin> annaua </margin> Its green leaves stop the flux of blood. **Skin conditions.** It is rubbed upon leprosy and elephantiasis. **Swellings and winds.** The green leaves resolve swellings and mature them. **Instruments of the joints.** It benefits pains of the joints, the hips <note>sciatica</note>, and cold gout. **Parts of the head.** It purges the brain. It is necessary to gargle it with vinegar for toothache, or it is preferred that it be held in the mouth; vinegar helps with the hot pain. When cooked in oil, the oil is beneficial for dripping and ringing in the ear, and it makes the extraction of teeth easy. And there is an extract of that which is in the colocynth...

It is applied to the mouth and helps with tooth pain. **Parts for breathing and the chest.** It helps when prepared as a treatment for chronic shortness of breath. **Nutritive parts.** Its root helps with dropsy <note>original: "ydropisi"; an accumulation of fluid in the body</note> and jaundice <note>original: "me malatto"; likely a corruption of "malattia," referring here to the "evil sickness" of jaundice</note>. **Parts of expulsion.** It dissolves and draws out thick and viscous phlegm and aids through purging; by itself, it helps greatly with windy colic. ### Chickpeas
There is a white variety and a red one; there is also a black one and a green one. Likewise, some are cultivated and others are wild. The wild variety is honey-like <note>original: "melle"; likely referring to the sweetness or consistency of the sap</note>, digestible, and of a more intense heating nature. The cultivated variety is effective in its [nutritive] presence. Indeed, the nourishment of the cultivated type is as oily honey compared to the wild. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the first degree. The black variety is the strongest. **Operations and properties.** Both cause flatulence <note>original: "inflatiua"; gas-producing</note> yet are softening; they aid in chewing and are more nutritious than beans, being more solid. Some varieties are especially helpful for the lungs. The "clean" chickpea generates fewer superfluities. **Beauty.** It wipes away freckles and creates a good complexion when used and eaten. **Swellings and wounds.** It helps with hot and hard swellings, and other tumors, such as those in the glands. **Wounds and ulcers.** Its oil is thick, and its flour is used for treacherous cancerous ulcers and itching.

<column-break/>

**Joint instruments** <note>original: "Instrumenta iuncturarum"; the joints and connective tissues</note>. It helps with back pain. **Parts of the head.** It helps cleanse the head and helps with the onset of pains. It helps with heat in the gums and swellings around the jaw. **Parts for breathing and the chest.** It clarifies the voice and nourishes the lungs better than almost anything else, especially when taken as a broth made from chickpea flour. **Nutritive parts.** If the decoction <note>a concentrated liquor made by boiling the substance</note> is strong, it helps with dropsy and jaundice <note>original: "hyctitie"</note>, and opens blockages of the liver and spleen caused by humors or black bile. One should eat it in the middle of a meal. **Parts of expulsion.** Its decoction breaks stones in the bladder and kidneys when taken with almond oil, radish, and parsley. All parts of it produce [strong] breath, and it is bad for ulcers of the bladder. It greatly increases sexual desire <note>original: "uehementẽ addit in coitu"</note>, and it even aids male animals and camels; an infusion of it makes them... when drunk with wine. It helps the nature of the body and opens blockages of the kidneys. The black variety is as described. They say that when soaked in vinegar and eaten, it is helpful... for half a day... he says that in vinegar there are two qualities separated by boiling: one is salty and softens the nature, and the other is sweet and provokes urine. The sweetness in it causes gas and excites sexual intercourse.

### Chickens
Among chickens, those that cannot fly have excessive heat and moisture. But those that fly are lighter. Their eggs are of a hotter nature. **Operations and properties.** In chicks, there is an excess of moisture. **Parts of the head.** Their blood helps with the flow of blood from the nose <note>nosebleeds</note> coming from the brain's membrane. **Parts for breathing and the chest.** Flying birds are easier to digest and provide better humors than chicks. It is necessary to eat them warmed with verjuice <note>original: "agresta"; the tart juice of unripened grapes</note>, coriander, and [marrow]. Their eggs are of a bad flavor.

### Camphor
The species of camphor are *alcaulutim* and *artagite*, then *alezand* and *aleitice uara*; it is that which is mixed from its wood, because it is sublimated from its wood. Some have said it is a large tree, providing shade for men... unless one reaches it at a [certain] time of year; it is like a marine sponge...

<meta>This page continues the medical properties of Camphor (Canfora) before moving into entries for Woad (Vndis), Clete, Sausur, and Zinniu (Orpiment). It maintains the standard medieval structure of organizing effects by "degrees" and by the specific "parts" of the body affected.</meta>

...but; what he has extracted. That wood we have seen many times already. It is a white, brittle, and light wood. In its essence <note>original: "in au'"; possibly *in auro* or *in aura*, referring to its composition</note>, it more rarely pertains to the shavings of a wood-cutter. **Nutritive [Properties].** It is cold and dry in its mode <note>meaning its medicinal "degree" or temperament</note>. **Beautification.** Its use causes gray hair to appear more quickly. **Pustules and Swellings.** <note>original: "Aputa & bothor"; from the Arabic terms for ulcers and skin eruptions</note> It benefits hot pustules. **Parts of the head.** With vinegar, it benefits the flow of blood from the nostrils. Or when one has a headache <note>original: "sodā calidē"; *soda* was a common medieval term for a burning headache</note> caused by immature heat, or with the water of *muru* <note>possibly a corruption of *myrrhae*, myrrh-water</note> or water of *alledaroz* <note>an obscure medicinal water</note>. In **fevers**, it causes wakefulness and strengthens the senses that have been overheated, and it strongly cures *alliolā* <note>an unidentified inflammation or swelling</note>. **Parts of the eye.** It is useful for moderate cases of hot ophthalmia <note>inflammation of the eye</note>. **Parts of expulsion [the excretory system].** It suppresses sexual desire and generates stones in the kidneys and bladder. It also restrains the choleric flux of the belly.

**What Woad is.** <note>original: "Vndis"; likely *Isatis tinctoria*, a plant used for blue dye and medicine</note> It is the plum-colored <note>original: "plumū"; possibly referring to a leaden color</note> dye from a root. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in its mode, reaching the fourth degree. **Actions and properties.** It is cleansing, purifying, ulcer-forming, sharp, and biting in its qualities; it cuts through phlegm and black bile. **Beautification.** It removes white spots <note>likely vitiligo</note>, dead skin, and black marks. **Pustules and Swellings.** It benefits scabies <note>original: "scabiei"; a contagious, itchy skin condition</note>. **Parts of the head.** It causes ringing <note>original: "tiiuitatiē"; likely *tinnitus*</note>. It is a purifying smoke for the ears and clears out the cavities that are within them. It also resolves the accumulation of wind from the nostrils, which *alcaseu* <note>another obscure Arabic-derived term</note> brings about, by opening the blockages in the nasal passages. **Nutritive parts.** It causes strong vomiting and dissolves the hardness of the spleen. **Parts of expulsion.** It is a resolvent, provoking urine and flow <note>original: "fluppiē"; likely menstrual flow</note>. It provokes the menses, extracts the fetus, and breaks stones. **Substitution.** In its place, one may use an equal weight of its burned charcoal <note>original: "pūe urēuoicu"</note> together with an equal weight of pepper.

**What Clete is.** <note>original: "Clete"; possibly *Chelidonia* (Celandine) or a similar plant</note> It is a herb similar to madder <note>original: "rubee"</note>; it comes from Italy. **Nature.** Some have said that in its essence, with its quality, it is cooling to the second degree. **Actions and properties.** It is appetizing and useful for those prone to sharpness [of humors], and it reaches the [liver], taking the place of cinnamon. **Wounds and ulcers.** It is good for putrid ulcers in the limbs and for *gruguiis* <note>an unidentified skin condition or ulcer</note>. **Parts of the head.** It is good for putrid sores in the mouth. **Parts of breathing and the chest.** When held in the mouth, it clears the voice. **Nutritive parts.** It is strong in opening obstruc-

<column-break/>

-tions in the liver. **Parts of expulsion.** It cleanses the urinary tracts, provokes the passing of sand <note>likely small kidney stones</note>, and extracts stones from the kidneys and bladder. Its juice, when chewed, is pleasant to those who use it.

**What Sausur is.** <note>original: "Sausur"; likely Willow (*Salix*) or a similar bitter, styptic plant like Saussurea</note> It is a substance wrapped around itself, having leaves. It has a small white flower in which there is bitterness and stypticity <note>an astringent, mouth-drying quality</note>; that which is most bitter is the most effective. **Nature.** It is purely hot in the first degree and dry at the end of the second, although it has its own unique virtues. **Actions and properties.** It is purifying and extracts thicker superfluities from the veins; it works in this way because of its stypticity, cleansing the veins and drawing out the excesses within them with its slippery quality. **Nutritive parts.** It strengthens the stomach because of its astringency. When drunk with vinegar, it settles hiccups and opens obstructions of the liver; indeed, it truly strengthens it. It has virtues against *hycūiat* <note>possibly a corruption of *icteritia*, jaundice</note>. Its juice, taken with strong wine, benefits a weak stomach. **Parts of expulsion.** It cleanses the impurities of the womb <note>original: "uetr'is fetus"</note> because it cleanses the veins, and it provokes urine and menses. It eases the pain of the veins and stops the flux of blood. Because it is astringent and purifying, it restrains the flux of menstruation. **Fevers.** Its seed is very useful for ancient fevers.

**What Zinniu is.** <note>original: "Zinniu"; a corruption of the Arabic *Zarnich*, referring to Orpiment or Arsenic sulfide</note> One type is *Kermenu* <note>Persian orpiment</note> and is from Persia; another is *Emu* which is Nabatean. *Kermenu* is black in color, and the Persian variety is dark-colored. The Persian is stronger than the other. The Nabatean is what is found in other places. Of all of them, some are wild and some are domestic. The wild ones are stronger in their power. Of the wild kind, there is a species or seed similar to the seed of a lily. **Selection.** The *Alkermenu* is stronger than the Persian, and the Persian is stronger than the others. **Nature.** It is hot in the third degree. **Actions and properties.** It expels wind and resolves [humors], though it has a harmful and drying effect because of its stypticity. **Beautification.** When the face is washed with its water, it clears the skin; likewise when taken internally with measure. However, if used too much, it turns the face dark. **Pustules and Swellings.** It is applied with a wax salve <note>original: "ceroto"</note> or oil and bean flour over internal pustules, or rather with oil and honey. **Wounds and ulcers.** It heals wounds...

...wild <note>likely Wild Cumin, *Cyminum silvestre*</note> whose seed is similar to the seed of a lily. It is beneficial to the sight. **Parts of the head.** When mixed with vinegar and an ointment is made from it, it stops the flow of blood from the nostrils. The wild variety is inserted into the nostrils for this purpose. **Parts of the eye.** When chewed and mixed with oil and dropped upon a pterygium <note>original: "ungula"; a wing-shaped growth on the white of the eye</note> and upon clotted blood in the eye, it brings relief. And when chewed with salt and the spit is dropped upon the itch <note>scabies</note> and eyelid growths, it removes the growth from the exhaustion <note>possibly meaning irritation</note> and is effective against "sand" <note>likely refers to granular conjunctivitis</note>. The juice of the wild variety clears the vision and draws out tears, and is helpful for the nose. It also aids those with accidental inversion of the eyelashes in the eye <note>trichiasis</note> when they grow inward. **Parts of the breath and chest.** When drunk with vinegar mixed with water, it aids difficulty of breathing, as Galen <note>a famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose work formed the basis of medieval medicine</note> says, as well as shortness of breath and heart tremors caused by cold. **Parts of expulsion.** It is administered with oil for external openings. When administered with a wax salve, or with oil and bean meal, it breaks stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>. The wild variety is also effective for the dripping of urine <note>strangury</note>, bloody mucus, stinging pain in the belly, and inflammation. The juice of the wild variety, when taken with honey-water, loosens the belly. Rufus <note>Rufus of Ephesus, another influential ancient medical author</note> says that Nabatean cumin loosens the belly, but the "black" variety <note>original: "lcernumū"; likely a corruption of a specific type</note> does not loosen it, but rather constricts it. The wild variety provokes bile in the urine. **Venoms.** It is given in a drink with wine for the bites of venomous animals. It is the wild variety whose seed is similar to the seed of a lily.

# Caper
<note>original: "Capparis"</note>
What it is: It is a fruit and has a root. Others say that the caper is sharp and hot... it is sharp and hot... and it prevents boiling in the stomach just like mustard. Its root is bitter and sharp. Its essence is such that it makes the mouth of the reader <note>possibly "eater"</note> water until it opens the gums. **Selection.** The most useful part is the bark of the root. **Nature.** Born in hot earth and is quite hot. The heat of the whole thing when dried is in the second degree <note>medieval medicine ranked the intensity of a plant's qualities from the 1st to 4th degree</note>. **Operations and properties.** It is resolving, opening, and cleansing. With honey, it is healing and purifying. In its bark, there is bitterness, sharpness, and astringency. The nutritional value of its fruit is small, especially with salt. When it is moist <note>fresh</note>, it is more nutritious than when it is dried.
