Because of its heat, it dissolves those things. **Venoms.** It is an antidote <note>original: "tynica"; likely a corruption of *tyriaca* or Theriac</note>.

# Cabbage
<note>original: "Caulis"</note>
What it is. Nature: In its substance it is moist... and highly hot and effective. It is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. One type of cabbage is domestic, another is wild, another is marine, and another is aquatic. The wild variety is smaller, sharper, and more distant from... <margin>the Greeks call this "alphos" <note>referring to white skin spots or leprosy</note></margin> ...cabbage with water... it nourishes the blood poorly when it is not dissolved, and it causes flatulence... it causes pain in the body. It is not as changeable as the winds. **Operations and properties.** It is ripening, softening, and drying, especially when it is boiled and the first water is thrown away. Its taste is strongly drying, and it has the property of calming pain. Its nutritional value is small, and the moist nourishment it provides is light. The blood it produces is bad. However, when it is cooked with fat meat and hens, it becomes somewhat good. **Swellings of the places.** The wild, marine, and domestic varieties ripen...

Mixed with honey and oil, it treats the marks of wounds. With bean flour, lentils, or maple flour, it treats scrofula <term>scrosul: a swelling of the lymph glands, often in the neck</term>. Galen says it dissolves scrofula because it is cold. It is possible that it acts through its deep, penetrating substance. If it is drunk, the heat resolves it quickly while the cold remains. It heals erysipelas <term>erysipela: a painful, spreading skin infection</term> because it is cooling or because it is mixed with melancholic or phlegmatic humors. **Parts of the head.** It aids vertigo caused by choleric or phlegmatic vapors, and epilepsy caused by these. The moist variety causes sleep and prevents nosebleeds <note>original: "ductū sanguinis narū"</note>. Two or three measures of it with "tongue-water" <note>possibly *aqua linguae avis* (ash-seed water) or bugloss</note> restrains the spitting of blood. **Nutritive parts.** It is slow to digest. It comforts a warmed stomach. When prepared, it prevents vomiting. It also soothes belching that occurs after food. **Parts of expulsion.** Its seed, when prepared, constricts the sperm. It is said that its seed with "rob" <term>rob: a thickened, sweet fruit syrup</term> alone expels worms. With honey and oil, it aids hot swellings of the testicles. The moist and dry varieties diminish the power of intercourse by drying out the sperm. **Poisons.** When four ounces of its juice are drunk, it becomes a danger, for it can cause death even from syncope <term>sincopi: a sudden loss of consciousness or fainting</term>. One should not take too much of it.

**The Dog.** **Decoration.** Dog urine is applied to warts. It is said of dog's milk that it scrapes away hairs and prevents their growth.

...of hairs of any sort, and I think it is in vain <note>original: "uanu," meaning ineffective</note>, as Galen estimated in certain places. Indeed, Galen wrote canons in which he said that dog's blood prevents the growth of hair in any place. **Aspects of Expulsion.** In the words of Galen: his claim was refuted where he estimated that its blood acts as **poisons**. Red dog blood is useful against the bite of the dog itself and against the poison of the Armenian arrow.

**What Flesh Is.** Good meats are sheep’s flesh, because in its heat it is subtle <term>subtle: in medieval medicine, this refers to substances that are fine, easily broken down, and capable of penetrating the body's channels</term>, and the meat of bulls and goats. The meat of these animals, when it is pure, is more susceptible to digestion and provides a more subtle nourishment. Kid meat has fewer superfluities <term>superfluities: waste products or excess humors produced during the digestive process</term> than lamb. The meat of a suckling animal is good if the milk it consumed was praiseworthy; but if the milk was not praiseworthy, the meat is bad. The meat of a decrepit sheep is bad. Similarly, the meat of an emaciated animal is poor. The meat of young animals is lighter and more pleasant. Likewise, the meat of males is preferred. Red meat from various animals that are very fatty is heavier, while others are lighter. Varied meat provides less nourishment and is more difficult in the stomach <note>original: "natiꝰ in stō," likely referring to a heavy or "floating" sensation in the stomach</note>.

**Selection.** The better and more digestible meat is that which is one year old. The right side, being lighter, is better than the left. The meat in the middle of the flanks <note>original: "lactoꝝ"</note> is cleaner than the meat of the nerves. Soft meat where a nerve is present is perhaps pleasant, following the character <note>original: "p̄gnantiā"</note> of milk, such as the meat of the breast, or the character of saltiness, such as the root of the tongue. When it is nourished and digested... <unclear>elonū</unclear>. In some men, it produces phlegm; the quantity of its nourishment is not like the natural nourishment of other meats. The meat of the milk-glands and the testicles is not good at all, for it exists more as a support, such as the tissue between the veins of the liver, the heart, and similar roots. Breasts provide long-lasting nourishment; if there is milk in them, the meat is like the milk. Testicle meat is better than some others. Among birds, the better meat is that of partridges, and chickens are more subtle than those. If they are eaten with the nourishment of the meat of geese and other similar birds... Furthermore, all animals of a dry complexion <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's or food's nature</term> do not have the best meat, except for kid meat, which is good. The meat of she-goats is not very good, and its character is perhaps very bad. Hyena meat is absolutely bad. Wolf meat is bad. And all large water birds with long necks and beaks, such as kites and marsh birds, are tough and fully winged...

...their generation produces melancholy <term>melancholy: the humor associated with black bile, considered cold and dry</term>; such are thrushes and sparrows, and they are bad. Sturgeon meat and wild boar meat <note>original: "poria siluris," likely porcina silvestris</note>: for while wild meat is lighter than domestic meat, it provides strong and full nourishment and is fast to digest. All these things should be considered regarding the dispositions of animals in their age, their proper age, and the rest as was mentioned in the section on milk.

**Nature.** Bird meat is generally more flatulent <note>original: "flaior," meaning it causes wind or gas</note> than the meat of quadrupeds. Beef is more flatulent than goat meat. Goat meat is dry and more difficult to digest than sheep's meat. Sheep meat and the meat of old animals is "combustive" <note>original: "adūstiua," referring to its tendency to overheat the humors</note> to such an extent that it heats our humors. Hare meat is hot and dry. The meat of large birds and geese, such as kites, and water birds... is fast... and preferred before all other meats. Certain parts, which by their nature are moistening, like fatty meat and that of ducks, are hot but not moist.

**Properties and Ages.** Meat is a food that strengthens the body. It is the food most closely related in its conversion to blood. The nourishment from meat cooked in a pan is more flatulent than that which is roasted. The nourishment of boiled meat is moist. That which is roasted with... <unclear>serū uibꝰ</unclear>... is rare. Fat and rinds are of poor and little nourishment, and lack subtlety. Meat that is salted <note>original: "saltita"</note> has its moisture removed, and thus it becomes delicate or thinning, having a drying quality. Its nourishment is small. Fatty meat loosens the belly with its poor nourishment, and because of the speed of its conversion into fumes and bile <term>bile: also called choler, the hot and dry humor</term>, it is quickly digested. The meat of the flanks <note>original: "ylioꝝ"</note> is naturally tenderer than fatty meat, but it is bad for digestion and nourishment.

Beef is very nourishing; cow's meat is melancholy, generating melancholic illnesses. That which is better is the meat of calves. Meats, with the exception of beef, are said to dissolve the rinds of melons. Meat is better at the hour in which the animal is killed in spring and the beginning of summer. However, water is said to cleanse them; it does not have the same viscosity as their own fluids.

## Beautification

Cow meat <note>original: "vacana" for "vaccina"</note> generates morphew <term>morphew: a skin disease characterized by scaly or discolored patches</term>. The fat of a wild donkey <note>original: "asini siluris"</note> is a light for skin eruptions. Likewise, duck fat makes one fat. And the burnt meat of a goose <note>original: "anerim" for "anserum"</note>, when smeared over morphew, is useful. Burnt meat of a turtle <note>original: "rurani"</note> is useful for alopecia <term>alopecia: hair loss or baldness</term>.

## Rough and Smooth

Beef meat aggravates cancer. And similarly, coarse meats resolve the rough and hard things in them.

## Wounds and Ulcers

Cow meat generates scabies and bad impetigo <term>impetigo: a contagious skin infection</term>. And similarly, burnt duck meat, when smeared over St. Anthony's fire <note>original: "ignem sagrum" for "ignem sacrum," likely referring to erysipelas</note>, provides relief.

## Health of the Joints

Cow meat generates leprosy, elephantiasis <term>elephantiasis: a disease characterized by thickening of skin and tissues</term>, and smallpox <note>original: "varias" for "variolas"</note>. And similarly, the meat of geese and fatty meats. A plaster <term>plaster: a medicinal paste spread on cloth and applied to the skin</term> placed over the back of the neck alleviates death <note>original: "morte," likely referring to a death-like lethargy or coma</note>. The decoction of hare's meat <note>original: "lepris"</note> soothes the specific pains of the joints. Its operation is specific, like that of fox wine. The meat of a doe <note>original: "damule"</note> provides nourishment when placed like a plaster over joint pains. The meat of gazelles <note>original: "dorcalium"</note>, softened with costus oil <term>costus oil: an aromatic oil from the root of Saussurea lappa, used in ancient medicine</term> and used like a plaster, is specifically applied over joint pains. The fat of a wild donkey softened with costus oil, used like a plaster, is specific for pains of the lower back and neck. And the meat of a viper and the heart of a hare—but that is discussed in its own chapter. And the meat of a hedgehog <note>original: "enici" for "ericii"</note> is a remedy for leprosy.

## Members of the Head

Cow meat and other coarse meats are bad; they cause alienation <note>original: "alienationem," likely delirium or mental distress</note> through drying. And doe meat mixed with wine is drunk for headache <note>original: "sodam," a medieval term for a splitting headache</note>.

## Members of the Eye

The fat <note>original: "cinum" for "sevum"</note> of a dog or goose is preferred for spots in the eye <note>original: "albugine"</note>. The meat of wolves... is good for the eye and fixes its vision.

## Members of the Breath and Chest

River crab <note>original: "cancer fluvialis"</note> is preferred for those who are very emaciated. And the meat of chickens is beneficial and not harsh.

## Nutritive Members

The meat of the aforementioned birds benefits the spleen. But beef seasoned with dry coriander and vinegar prevents humors from rising to the stomach. And the meat of the camel <note>original: "alcatu," likely derived from the Arabic "al-qatu"</note>

<column-break/>

is mentioned in the summaries as being good for corruption of the complexion, dropsy <term>dropsy: an old term for edema, or fluid swelling</term>, and blockages of the spleen and liver. And it is better if it is taken when wide-spread <note>unclear reading: "pili oge lata"</note>, so that it does not stir up thirst. As for what suits the ox, he praises the meat of wolves for coldness and moisture due to its noble quality and speed of digestion, and it resolves the thickness of the belly by its subtlety. Meat prepared from domestic silurus <note>original: "filuris," likely the sheatfish or catfish</note>, according to what is said, is quick to digest and relaxing. And it is highly nutritious and viscous. And the meat of tree-dwelling animals, because of its thickness, is quick to digest. Meat eaten with oxymel <term>oxymel: a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term> is preferred for dropsy. And camel meat is for the blockage of the liver and its weakness, and for the corruption of humors in dropsy. And the meat of wolves—specifically the snout and claws—the stomach abhors.

## Members of Expulsion

Beef meat prevents black bile from reaching the stomach. Roasted hare meat is useful for intestinal ulcers. When dried with oxymel, it is then good for kidney pain. The broth of a cock and for colics and melancholy fires. The fat of a wild donkey with costus oil also takes away kidney pain and lower back pain. And the meat of wolves, their snouts and claws, is a wash for hemorrhoids. The juice of beef with vinegar and a little salt for colic is an effective bread <note>original: "panx," likely "panis"</note>. And similarly, its meat jelly with crushed coriander and its sharpness is similar, with dry coriander and a little saffron. And similarly, bird meats, roasted or not, loosen the belly; but stronger than them is camel and its fat <note>original: "alaucbrum"</note>, which purges and draws water from them. Camel meat provokes urine. And fatty meats thin the nature more vehemently than others.

## Fevers

Beef meat, and that of wild pigs and great birds, causes quartan fevers <term>quartan fever: a fever that recurs every third day, usually associated with malaria</term> to occur.

## Poisons

Dried doe meat taken in wine as a drink protects against poisons. Burnt goose meat protects against the bites of snakes and scorpions and drives them away when taken with wine. And frog meat is a remedy for punctures of the nerves from poison.

**Cassia, what it is.** It is said to be the bark of a root in the mountain of Ascenu. And there are several species, one of which is red, with a good flavor and odor. ## Costus
<note>An aromatic root from the ginger family, highly prized in medieval medicine.</note>
Costus is what it is. And there are three species. One is expensive, known as "Arabian," which is white, light, and aromatic. The second is "Indian," which is black and light, or like the first. The third species has a heavy odor and is called "Galnotic," or a lesser version of these species. It is the one whose scent is like pine, tending toward blackness. And what [is found] among these species is the root. It is similar to *ascinur* <note>possibly asarabacca or a similar root</note>, but it has the scent of laurel. Good costus, however, is often falsified <note>adulterated or faked</note> with the roots of elecampane <note>original: "enule clunis," likely *enula campana*</note>. And because of this, one should check if it bites the tongue or if it has a powerful odor. **Selection.** The best is that which is white, fresh, full, not hollow, and not smelling of decay, biting the tongue when tasted. Next is the Indian, which is black, light, and less sharp. And the best is of the [quality of] manna and possesses a leathery bark. **Nature.** It is hot in the third degree and dry in the second. **Opinions and Properties.** In its substance is a bitter quality, very sharp, and a heat that is sharp to the point of being stinging. It is beneficial for all things that require heating, and by which humor is drawn out from the depths [of the body]. **Anatomy.** It pulls at the skin, cleansing it when applied with water and honey. **Wounds and Ulcers.** In its substance is an [ability to treat] ulceration. And that which is bitter dries out ulcers and moist sores. **The Joints.** It helps in the softening of stiffness and the making of ligaments. It [heals] the pain of sciatica when applied as a plaster. **The Head.** It helps with lethargy. **The Chest.** It helps with pains of the chest. **Expulsion.** It provokes menstruation when drunk, used as a fumigant, or as a suppository; it kills the fetus <note>used as an abortifacient</note>, provokes urine, and expels intestinal worms <note>original: "aschandes ūumes," ascarids</note>, and gives strength for sexual intercourse. It is also applied for pain of the womb, and benefits the cold color of the womb when drunk or by sitting in a decoction of it. It moves the bowels <note>original: "mouet naturā," literally "moves nature"</note> when drunk on an empty stomach. And when it gives strength for intercourse, it is not because of excessive moisture, but because of the "windiness" <note>gas/spirit</note> that is in its substance. **Fevers.** It helps with shivering when applied with oil. **Poisons.** It helps against all bites, such as the bite of a viper and others, with wine or wormwood. **Substitution.** In its place, use half its weight in pepper.

## Zedoary
<note>Cedoaria: A root similar to ginger or turmeric.</note>
Zedoary is what it is. It is said that it is a wild fennel...

<column-break/>

...wild. **Selection.** The best is that which has a good odor, is heavy, black, and is not woody. And when it is dissolved, it tints water with the color of saffron. And when chewed, it stains the teeth with a strong, lasting dye. **Operations and Properties.** It is heating and ripening. **The Eyes.** It is an "abstersive" <note>cleansing agent</note> for the eye. And its oil helps with dimness of vision. **Expulsion.** It provokes urine.

## Dill
<note>Anebū: Likely *Anethum*, or Dill.</note>
Dill is what it is. A fleshy seed; with it, one works against redness, which is a lesser redness than the stone found in the gall of a lion <note>a reference to a legendary medicinal stone or a specific mineral</note>. **Nature.** It is hot in the second degree. **Operations and Properties.** The son of Mesue <note>an influential Persian physician</note> says that in its substance is a styptic <note>tissue-contracting</note> quality for animals. **Expulsion.** It binds and expels worms and intestinal parasites.

## Cadmia of Gold
<note>Climia auri: Zinc oxide or metallic dross from smelting gold.</note>
Cadmia of gold is what it is. The best is that which is golden, shining like glass, coming in the form of scales or flakes, and reddish. **Nature.** It is balanced, leaning toward dryness in the second degree. **Operations and Properties.** The parts washed from it are more styptic than Cadmia of silver. In its substance, it is drying and cleansing. **Wounds and Ulcers.** It fills wounds, cleanses their filth, removes proud flesh <note>excessive granulation tissue</note>, and heals fraudulent <note>persistent or deceptive</note> wounds. **The Eyes.** It helps with white spots in the eye when mixed with water and strengthens the eye.

## Cadmia of Silver
<note>Climia argenti: Metallic dross from silver smelting.</note>
Cadmia of silver is what it is. All Cadmias are produced from gold or silver, and sometimes from copper or marcasite. It is the dross that rises above the place where the metal is melted or poured, and it is scaly. **Nature.** It is the opposite of Cadmia of gold, for it is colder. **Operations and Properties.** In its substance, it is drying and cleansing with balance, without stinging; the same is true of that which is washed from it. It is more suitable in plasters, and its drying and cleansing power is [better] for the warm bodies of men than for those with hard flesh. **Wounds and Ulcers.** It helps with difficult and moist wounds and ulcers when powdered and used in plasters.

## Vitriol
<note>Calcanum: Also known as Chalcanthum or Copperas; a metallic sulfate.</note>
<margin>Vitriol and its species.</margin>
Vitriol. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the fourth degree. **Operations and Properties.** It is drying, hardening, and thickens the body; in its substance, it is styptic and caustic. **Wounds and Ulcers.** It helps with fistulas <note>abnormal passages</note> of the nose. **The Head.** It stops bleeding from the nostrils. And what distills from it, a single drop dissolved in water...

## Chalcitis
<note>original: "Alcazar," a transliteration of an Arabic term for Chalcitis, a metallic ore or copper sulfate used as a caustic and astringent.</note>
Chalcitis is what it is. As Galen says, it is called Chalcitis because it is made from a copper-like stone. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the [second] degree. **Operations and Properties.** In itself, there is a powerful burning and an astringency to the flow of blood, as well as a drying effect; the burning is of the highest drying power and of the least stinging quality. And in it, there is a great deal of saltiness and a great deal of heat. **Abscesses.** It is beneficial for shingles <note>original: "foxmice," referring to *formica*, a creeping skin ulcer</note> and erysipelas <note>a skin infection</note> when smeared on with water. It is powdered over fraudulent and spreading ulcers; it consumes excess flesh and causes a scab to form. **Head Organs.** It helps with the flow of blood from the nostrils and helps with gum swellings. **Chest and Lung Organs.** It is beneficial for swellings of the tonsils <note>original: "gallonis"</note>. **Eye Organs.** It is put into kohl <note>original: "alcofol"</note> to wipe away whiteness <note>cataracts or corneal scarring</note> and the hardness of the eyelids. **Organs of Expulsion.** It stops the flow of the womb.

## Chicory
<note>original: "Ancheri," likely *Cichorium intybus*. Known for its bitter, liver-cleansing properties.</note>
Chicory is what it is. **Nature.** Hot in the first degree. **Operations and Properties.** It is a subtle cleanser. Paul [of Aegina] says it generates melancholy, but this is corrected if it is cooked with milk. **Beauty.** It cleanses the skin and morphea <note>skin discolorations or leprosy-like patches</note>. And in truth, it is a substance most helpful for eating away filth and scabs <note>original: "eptox," likely impetigo</note>; it removes small blemishes from women. It is also natural. **Wounds and Ulcers.** From it alone, a plaster is made for scabs, and it helps with fraudulent ulcers on the breast. **Head Organs.** A purge for the head is made from its root, and it helps with thick humors in the brain. **Chest and Lung Organs.** It opens obstructions of the lung and cleanses it. **Nutritional Organs.** It opens obstructions of the spleen and liver. **Organs of Expulsion.** Its water loosens the bowels. It is a plaster for hemorrhoids and removes piercing pain in the belly; it resolves uterine pain and extracts bad, thick humors; it opens obstructions of the liver and spleen. **Poisons.** It is a plaster for all poisonous bites.

...Ladanum, which is a substance upon which you should place a cloth... with flowers of Ladanum.

## Cistus
<note>original: "Elfus," referring to the *Cistus* shrub, from which the resin Ladanum is harvested.</note>
Cistus is what it is. There are three types: black, white, and red. They are all sharp [column-break] and astringent. One species of it is that which produces Ladanum. Some say it is in the root, and some say otherwise; they are of similar types. **Nature.** Its leaves tend toward heat. Perhaps in some of its parts, it is cold. But Ladanum itself is hot at the end of the [first] degree. **Operations and Properties.** It is a cleanser, a healer, and astringent. It is also found in solutions. In its flowers, there is an astringent quality. That which is called Ladanum is warming, opens the mouths of veins, and is soothing. **Beauty.** Its Ladanum is a cleanser for lice. Ladanum with wine or honey wipes away the marks of ulcers and the scales of the head <note>dandruff</note>. When mixed with wine, myrrh, and myrtle oil, it prevents the falling out of hair. It is not used for this unless it is applied with a plaster, because its dissolving power is small. **Wounds and Ulcers.** A decoction of it in wine is very beneficial for ulcers. A plaster is made from it, and it helps against fraudulent swellings. With wine, it is used for fire burns. **Joint Inflammation.** It is noted for this. **Head Organs.** When its juice is mixed with oil, wine, honey, and nitre, it dissolves old earwax. When its black juice is taken and warmed in the bark of a pomegranate and distilled into the ear, it helps with painful swellings. A head purge made from its water is excellent for cleansing the head. It washes old filth from the ear and dries its ulcers. **Nutritional Organs.** When a plaster is made from its decoction with vinegar, it helps the spleen. **Organs of Expulsion.** When three parts of the white flower are drunk with wine, it helps dysentery, to be drunk twice a day. When a plaster is made from its red heads, it provokes the menses. When a fumigation is made from it to purge the menses, it prevents pregnancy. And the small part of its head used as a suppository provokes the menses and ejects the fetus. A fumigation of Ladanum is made for the afterbirth and to cause abortion. Its flower binds the nature. **Poisons.** Its water drunk with vinegar and wine helps against the bite of a spider <note>original: "ructielle," likely referring to a venomous spider or insect</note>.

## Anabasis
<note>A genus of desert shrubs used in antiquity for their drying and diuretic properties.</note>
Anabasis. **Operations and Properties.** Its seed drives away winds <note>flatulence</note> and dries out the humors.

### Glandia what it is.
It is a plant in which there is a resemblance to alyssum <note>original: "alusen," a herb historically used to treat madness or rabies</note>. **Nature**. Hot and dry in the first degree. **Actions and benefits**. It helps and heats to cause fattening, and it is useful in those thirsts and against slight bloating. **Respiratory and chest organs**. It is made into a gargle with milk and its salt. And its decoction helps quickly with meat that is prepared with oil and its heat. **Digestive organs**. It alone draws out the watery fluid which is late-arriving <note>original: "seru," likely *serum*</note>, and its juice. And women use it, though weakly. **Excretory organs**. It provokes urine and generates foam, and it expels bile and wateriness from the living body. The dose of it is from one-third of a pound to two-thirds.

### Grasa.
**Nature**. Hot <gloss>by the pound.</gloss> in the first degree, dry in the second. **Actions and benefits**. It prevents the flow of blood from a burn of the same. **Burned clusters**. From the decoction of the burned substance, it prevents catarrh <note>original: "cathaphar"</note>. **Head organs**. From the decoction of the burned substance, it prevents the flow of blood from the nostrils.

<margin>Aristolochia [Birthwort] of the fields</margin>
### Aristolochia what it is. 
It is among the species of birthwort <note>original: "aristolochie," a plant used historically in childbirth and for treating snakebites</note>. **Nature**. It is hot in the second degree, moist in the first. **Actions and benefits**. In its seed there are laxative <note>original: "lenitiua"</note> powers; they help with bile.

### Gaubita.
**Nature**. Cold and moist in the second degree. **Actions and benefits**. That which is cooked <note>original: "clisata," perhaps related to elixation or boiling</note> helps in some matter and is swift to cook; if it is not corrupted in digestion, for if some thing is generated from it, it is a bad humor or a very fatty humor which mixes with the bad humor. And it can certainly be stored like other fruits. And the humor generated from it is tasteless; it is not distinguished by anything that is certain. For if water arrives to it, its humor is harmed, and it is commendable for colics. And it is known if the water stays: and for what it is generated. Truly because it brings

<column-break/>

the colon. It doubles the effect, and from the moisture <note>original: "fetate," likely moisture or fluidity</note> which is there, a homogeneous nourishment is generated for that which is fostered by it. For when dried and eaten with mustard, a bad, acidic humor is generated from it; or with salt, a salty humor is generated; or with frankincense <note>original: "thyitias," likely a resinous or incense-like preparation</note>, and a frankincense-like humor is generated from it. And it is entirely harmful to those dominated by melancholy and phlegm, and good for colics. And that which is raw does not enter into medicines, except that it impresses cooling and heating if the soul is drawn to it for pleasure. **Head organs**. Its juice settles hot ear pain, especially with rose oil. It is also beneficial for inflammation <note>original: "fursem," possibly *phrenitis*</note> in the parts of the brain, and it is a confection for throat pain. **Respiratory and chest organs**. The juice of the gourd <note>original: "cucurbite"</note> with honey is beneficial for chest pain caused by heat. **Digestive organs**. And their decoction is for hot superfluities in the stomach, and it removes them. And a drink is made in water <gloss>it is like a melon</gloss> very much, and it quenches thirst. And it is also a food that generates fire in the stomach very much, so that it is suitable for children and adolescents. And it is not a medicine that harms the stomach, whence it is used. And the harm it brings to the colon is very great. **Excretory organs**. Furthermore, its water, mixed with honey and drunk at the proper time, lightens the belly. And similarly when it is buried [in ashes] and cooked thus, and it is drunk <gloss>with melon</gloss> with its juice. And it harms the intestines very quickly, especially the colon. **Fevers**. It is beneficial for bilious fevers.

### Gaumar what it is.
The seed is like that of a melon and is dry in effect. And that which is better is the larger one, which is ripe. **Nature**. Cold and moist in the second degree. **Actions and benefits**. It settles heat and bile. If the food is bad, it leads to putrefaction and minor fevers. The "Badeca" <note>original: "Badecã," an Arabic term for watermelon or a specific variety of melon</note>, however, is of faster corruption than what is seen. And in that which is not yet ripe, there is a withholding [astringency]. And the seed is like the melon seed in effect. The food, however, is of longer digestion and stays in the veins, and it generates chronic bilious fevers. That which does not help expels [menses or fluids] or causes the speed of bloating in the stomach. **Burned clusters**. Its leaves are placed with honey upon phlegmatic sores, and it is beneficial for them. **Head organs**. [The scent] of it comforts the spirit if its odor is smelled. **Digestive organs**. Before meals, it settles thirst and comforts the stomach, though it is not well digested. ### Camphor <note>original: "Camfora"</note>
Camphor is a <term>resolvent</term> <note>a substance that thins or dissolves thickened humors or swellings</note> and it resolves. 
It comes from a tree from which the juice of the herb is collected... it takes its fruit at the end of summer through which it is useful... and it is suspended in a pine tree so that its water may flow out. It is dried in a dish over water and when it is on a table it is kept in the shade. 

**Alecco** <note>possibly a specific grade or type of refined camphor</note>. The good kind is that which is white, straight, and sharp-pointed. It is helpful. Its sound is [distinct], and that which is white, flat, and light, which falls in threads, is preferred.

**Nature.** It is hot and dry in the third degree. 

**Opinions and Ages.** It is of a subtle <term>resolution</term>. <note>meaning it breaks down substances easily</note> Erta <note>likely a corruption of a cited authority like Galen or Rhazes</note> said that its leaves and fruit are astringent, they resolve, and they dry the bark even more. And the juice of the root and its leaves is the same. 

**Beautification.** Its juice, or the juice of the root and leaves, is brought for <term>pityriasis</term> <note>original: "hyatiae," a skin condition involving flaky patches</note>. When it is dried and powdered by itself, it deletes the marks in black scars and cleanses the filth of the face. 

**Ipita Botlor** <note>possibly a corruption of *Epithymum* (dodder of thyme) or a specific plant preparation</note>. When it is made from the root and leaves with barley meal, it resolves and opens [blockages], heals <term>icterus</term> <note>original: "anneru," referring to jaundice</note>, and it ruptures abscesses when mixed with white gum or its juice. 

**Wounds and Ulcers.** When the dried part of it is powdered over <term>scabies</term> <note>a contagious skin infestation</note> and <term>impetigo</term> <note>original: "pringine," a skin infection</note>, it brings them relief. 

**Urinary Instruments.** It relieves the pains of urination. Its decoction used as a clyster <note>enema</note> brings a sense of fullness. A plaster made from it with vinegar is applied for <term>podagra</term> <note>gout, specifically in the foot</note>. 

**The Head.** Its juice resolves phlegm and bile. A purge of the head is made from it with honey and milk. It heals <term>epistaxis</term> <note>original: "nares auctiae," nosebleeds</note>. It consumes the primary superfluities and helps in <term>gallegate</term> <note>unclear, possibly a corruption of a specific head ailment or "alligate," meaning bound/chronic conditions</note> of the past, as the ancients hated. The juice of its leaves is weaker. When the juice is distilled into the ear, it soothes the pain therein.

**Respiratory and Chest Organs.** A solution made from its juice or essence is helpful for those who have badness of breath. The palate is smeared with its juice, honey, and oil to provoke [the clearing of] phlegm. 

**Digestive Organs.** It helps <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "ydopisi," modern edema or swelling</note> by drawing out water in a marvelous way without harm, when one and a half <term>rings</term> <note>original: "annulus," a medieval unit of weight</note> of its root is given in a drink. Also when half a pound of it is boiled with two <term>kustis</term> <note>an ancient measure of volume</note> of wine and given in a drink, three to five "rings" per day. And when one and a half rings of the root is taken, or of its <term>aconite</term>...

...which [is taken] without a doctor, it causes the vomiting of phlegm and red bile. It is drunk with honey-water and it acts vehemently and clearly, provoking the bowels without injury to the person, and it is not harmful. For those who need to be loosened [laxatives], it is made so that its juice is mixed with double the amount of salt. Then it is made into pills like herbs and drunk with water. **Excretory Organs.** It draws out phlegm and bile, and its juice provokes urine and menstruation, and it expels the fetus if applied [as a pessary].

### Horn <note>original: "Cornu"</note>

**Respiratory and Chest Organs.** Burned and washed horn helps with the spitting of blood. 

**Digestive Organs.** It causes swellings to subside and does not harm the stomach because of its [cleansing] nature.

# Cassia fistula <note>The Golden Shower tree, used as a laxative</note>

Regarding this, Galen said: the marrow of this fruit is not exported to other regions. **Organs of excretion.** It is very evocative...

# Mallows
And it is said that the wild type <note>original: "siluris," likely a corruption of "silvestris"</note> is the mallow, and the <term>molokhia</term> <note>an edible green popular in Middle Eastern cuisine</note> is the domestic kind. And <term>caleze</term> is a certain species called "white molokhia," and it is the same as Marsh-mallow <note>original: "itia est altea"</note>. It is also called Jew’s herb. And let it not be long-winded as to what its species are; the best of them is known by its appearance. **Selection.** The wild type is shorter and more delicate, and the strength of the domestic water-mallow is less than that of the wild. 
**Nature.** It is cold and moist in the first degree <note>In medieval medicine, drugs were graded 1 to 4 based on the intensity of their effect on the four humors</note>. And it is said that the domestic type is hot and dry, according to what is said there by Paul <note>Likely referring to the physician Paul of Aegina</note>. And it seems his intention was directed toward the Jew’s herb, since he himself names it <term>al-muludria</term>. **Operations and Ages.** In its use, there is a softening quality which is better than that which is harsh or rough: it is similar to the wild type, and more cleansing and drying. And that which is called domestic warms slightly and resolves [humors] quickly because of its moisture and its viscosity; it is used with <term>almurī</term> <note>a savory condiment or brine</note> and oil. It is easy to digest. And its moisture, according to what is said, is better than the moisture of lettuce. Paul says it binds, expels wind, and resolves without biting <note>original: "mordicatioe," a sharp or stinging sensation</note>; it seems he intended that to refer to the Jew’s herb. **Preparation.** It is effective against "ants" <note>likely referring to "formica," a creeping skin rash or shingles</note> and hair-loss, and its leaves are used as a pottage; it also treats burns from fire. Similarly, a decoction of it and its broth is the domestic type, which is used for the onset of a hot headache and its reduction. **Wounds and Ulcers.** If someone chews it raw with salt and places it upon fistulas, it works for them as a medicinal dressing for the eye. **Head Organs.** A plaster made from it for ulcers of the head with quicklime <note>original: "uiua," likely "calce viva"</note> is very effective for them. And it is chewed for the neck. **Eye Organs.** When its leaves are chewed and applied with a little salt, it cleanses fistulas in the eye and stops the growth of [unwanted] flesh. **Breathing and Chest Organs.** Its leaves and flower soften the chest and cause milk to abound; they also soothe a cough arising from heat and dryness. And its seed, and that which is taken of it with honey, removes the roughness of the chest. **Nutritive Organs.** The domestic type is bad for the stomach, and its use leads to blockages of the liver. **Organs of Excre-**

<column-break/>

**-tion.** Its flower, when drunk or applied with oil, is effective for ulcers of the kidneys and bladder. And the seed of the molokhia is effective for abrasions and ulcers of the intestines. The branches of the domestic mallow are useful for the intestines and bladder by softening the nature [of the bowels]. It also helps with pains in the hips. And this is when the "water of the hips" <note>possibly referring to joint fluid or a specific wash for sciatica</note> is drunk, which is made from it... And it is said a decoction of it treats the hardness of the womb by sitting in it [a sitz bath] and by making an enema with it. And it is used as a fresh remedy. As for the wild mallow, it is used because it alone is effective, and it dissolves thick and windy humors. And when it is applied externally, it is accustomed to draw out blood. 
**Venoms.** Its leaves soothe the stings of wasps and the bites of <term>epu</term> <note>possibly a type of venomous insect or spider</note> when applied with oil. Similarly, its seed is drunk, and it often induces vomiting, and it helps the movement of the bowels.

# Swallow-wort
<note>original: "Chaueū," likely a phonetic variation of "Chelidonia"</note>
What it is. Someone said it is a "vein," and it is what is called <term>mēūue</term>. And another said it is small. And when the swallow chicks are blinded, the mother bird brings this plant and sight is restored to them; it adds strength to the eyes. ## Audreceq
<margin>A plant that heals... breaks... from... <unclear>alm.</unclear></margin>
A plant growing in dry places annually, having hollow stems tending toward redness, thick and hard, and knotted with mature nodes. And at the nodes, there are many small, thick, scale-like leaves. ## Anemone
**Nature.** Some have said it is excessively hot, and others say it is hot and dry in the third degree. But the first is true. **Operations and Properties.** It is sharp, and sharply putrefactive and burning. **Aesthetics.** It eradicates warts when smeared on or made into a wax salve. It is smeared on for the whitening of the nails and benefits them. It eradicates nail fungus when made into a plaster. It removes <term>morphea</term> and <term>albaras</term> <note>terms for various skin patches, including leprosy and vitiligo</note> when smeared on with vinegar. And when it is used with mustard as a liniment, it makes hair grow.

And if it is boiled with oil, it thickens. **Swellings and Abscesses.** It is smeared upon cancerous abscesses and resolves them. **Wounds and Ulcers.** It is smeared upon scabies and impetigo <note>contagious skin sores</note>. **The Eyes.** Mesue the Younger <note>original: "fili’ mesague," a famous medieval medical authority</note> says it cleanses the "nail" <note>likely referring to a pterygium or film over the eye</note> greatly. **The Digestive System.** A drink of it provokes urine greatly, so much so that it also helps with dropsy. **The Excretory System.** A drink of it provokes urine greatly. And a drink of it also helps the "middle" <note>the vessels</note> to provoke the discharge of harmful things. It provokes menstruation and causes abortion. Some say that one drink of it causes a discharge from the bladder, but my experience does not support this; yet if three <term>talenta</term> <note>a unit of weight</note> are given in a drink, it ulcerates the bladder. Galen said: "Everything in this category ulcerates the bladder." This is especially because it makes sharp humors incline toward it, which the body cannot evacuate except through the bladder.

## Glue
**Nature.** Glue <note>original: "Colla," referring to animal-based gelatin or glue</note> is hot and dry in the first degree. Fish glue <note>isinglass</note> is less hot, but is dry. **Operations and Properties.** All glues are binding and drying. **Aesthetics.** Glue from skins is used in cleansing washes and in whitening medicines. And when glues from hides and common glues are combined, they are washed and used in place of <term>tutenag</term> <note>zinc ore/white ointment</note> for the nourishment of the tendons. **Swellings and Abscesses.** Glue from hides is smeared on for various things and helps with the blisters from burns. And also glue from skins. And glue from cowhides, when smeared with vinegar upon impetigo, is beneficial. It reaches deep down and helps. When smeared with honey and vinegar upon a wound, it helps. ## Dauigum. What it is:
It is the flower of the Hermodactyl <note>original: "hernodactuli," likely *Colchicum*, historically called "fingers of Hermes"</note>. And its virtue [healing power] is the same as that of the Hermodactyl.

## Brugum. What it is:
A woody, rooted herb about the size of a thumb-joint to the tip of the nail. It is white on its face [inside] and golden on the outside, inclining toward a divine suitability. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the second degree. **Operations and Properties.** It thins out gassiness <note>original: "uentositates," referring to bodily "wind" or bloating</note>. **Organs of Breath and Chest.** It strengthens the heart and greatly aids heart tremors. **Organs of Excretion.** It dissolves gassiness that occurs in the womb. **Poisons.** It helps against poisons from the stings of venomous creatures and scorpions, drunk in various ways. **Substitution.** In its place is put an equal weight of it, or two-thirds the weight of cloves <note>original: "de gariofilis"</note>.

## Emesit. What it is:
The Laurel tree <note>original: "Arbor lauri"</note>. Its gum <note>original: "guma," likely the resin or oil</note> and leaves are used. However, the gum is stronger in action than the leaves. Regarding the roots and their various uses, they are sometimes mentioned here, but the full account of them will be found in the chapter under the letter "G," where Laurel is discussed in detail. **Nature.** It is hot in the third degree and dry in the second. <note>Medieval medicine graded the intensity of a plant's "heat" or "dryness" on a scale of 1 to 4 to balance the body's humors.</note> **Operations and Properties.** It is used for softening the nerves <note>original: "lani," likely a corruption of "nervi"</note> and for the hair. **Organs of the Head.** It is used as a wash for tremors. **Nutritional Organs.** It helps in opening obstructions of the liver and spleen. **Organs of Excretion.** It is beneficial for colic.

<margin>Dardi: an herb which is Ivy</margin>
## Eusier. What it is:
Ivy <note>original: "Hedra"</note>. Its leaves are like lily leaves but smoother. Its fruit has two or three coverings which are almost like hairs on the outside. They are dry juices that make for a better wash. **Nature.** It is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. **Operations and Properties.** Its powers are drying and "resolving" <note>meaning it breaks down or dissolves morbid humors</note>. **Preparation and Washing.** It has a thinning property that hardens in the sting and prevents issues in the hypochondria <note>the upper abdomen, below the ribs</note>. **Beauty.** From its shoots, a preparation is made to remove alopecia <note>patchy hair loss</note>. **Organs of the Eye.** It helps with eye sores.

## Ordar. What it is:
It is the Pomegranate tree <note>original: "Arbor amiai," likely a transliteration of an Arabic term for pomegranate</note>, from which "inflated" heads emerge, which is how the fruit is formed. Its leaves are eaten green, similar to olives. **Operations and Properties.** It possesses styptic <note>constricting or blood-stanching</note> qualities. The bark is styptic, while the root is "aperitive" <note>opening the body's channels</note>. **Beauty.** It cleans the scalp of scurf. The bark, when used with vinegar while it is still fresh, removes "albaras" <note>white skin spots or depigmentation</note>. **Wounds and Sores.** The bark is used as a bandage over strikes and wounds to solidify [heal] them. Similarly, the leaves, bark, and flowers are beneficial for wounds. The same applies to the shavings that fall from the bark, which fall away like flour.

<column-break/>

It prevents fraudulent applications. Regarding what is said about the decoction of this plant being given to horses, it is used as a drench. **Nervous System and Joints.** From the decoction of the roots and leaves, it heals broken bones. **Organs of Excretion.** When a decoction of it is drunk with wine, it helps; otherwise, taken with cold water, it expels phlegm <note>one of the four bodily humors, associated with coldness and moisture</note>.

## Ouidar. What it is:
It is the gum of the *Alebel*, which comes from India. Its wood is similar to *zurut* wood. It has a hollow center which contains a "milk" [sap] that is hot and sharp, causing thirst. **Nature.** It is dry in the third degree, and its heat is even greater. **Operations and Properties.** The sap has a burning sharpness, while the wood itself has a mild styptic quality. **Nervous System and Joints.** It is good for softening the nerves and for the hair. It is helpful for treating various ailments when applied. **Organs of the Head.** It is beneficial for "cold" obstructions in the brain, and for apoplexy and epilepsy. **Nutritional Organs.** Its sap causes thirst. **Organs of Excretion.** It breaks stones in the kidneys and bladder, and it helps the veins. It is used to soften the bowels by sitting in a decoction of it.

## Daucus. What it is:
The seed of the Wild Carrot <note>original: "dauce silvestris"</note>. The distinction of its use is found in the chapter on wild plants. **Nature.** It is hot in the second degree and dry in the first. **Operations and Properties.** It is a powerful "aperitive" [opener of blockages] and stimulates the appetite. **Organs of Excretion.** It provokes urine and menstruation.

<margin>Oende, that is, Cataputia</margin>
## Onde. What it is:
The seed of this plant is also called *fistia*, and the seed is similar to rue seed, but with black spots. It is smaller than some seeds and larger than others. Its core <note>original: "medulla"</note> is oily. **Nature.** The potency of the core diminishes over time until it is consumed. **Selection.** The best and strongest is from India. The white variety is poor; it works slowly, causes disturbances, and creates stinging pains. Everyone should be careful because the thin bark can burn the lips; it destroys their color and causes white spots. When peeling it, a small "tongue" [germ] emerges from the bark; one should leave that part and only take the core. **Nature.** It is extremely hot. **Beauty.** It is used for treatments of the teeth and to prevent the graying of hair. **Organs of Excretion.** It purges superfluities. A potion of it is made with grape juice. In purging, it draws out moisture, melancholy <note>the "black bile" humor</note>, and phlegm.

## Odochisa
What it is: An Indian bark <note>original: "cortex indus"</note>, which is very styptic <note>a substance that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</note>. **Operations and Properties.** It is styptic. **Organs of the Breath and Chest.** It is good for spitting blood from the chest and for pleurisy <note>inflammation of the chest lining</note>, and it clarifies the voice. **Organs of Expulsion.** It is beneficial for ulcers of the intestines.

## Orusatanus

## Tragacanth
What it is: It is the gum of the *alauda* <note>possibly the "lark-spur" or a similar plant associated with the gum-producing astragalus</note>. **Nature.** It is cold, declining toward dryness. **Operations and Properties.** It is similar to other gums, though there is a slight drying effect in it, just as there is in gum [arabic]. **Organs of the Eye.** It is placed in eye-salves <note>original: "alcol," from the Arabic *al-kuhl*</note> in place of other gums.

# Liver. Actions and Properties.

It is useful if the flesh is irritated by the fat of newborns <note>original: "natis pinguis"</note> or the fat of chickens. <term>Parts of the Head.</term> Goat liver applied by itself is said to cleanse epilepsy. And whoever suffers from epilepsy and eats it, it helps the condition. The liver of a spotted lizard <note>original: "stelliois"</note> placed upon a molar <margin>Stellio: that is, a green lizard, or perhaps a lizard <note>original: "ligur"</note>.</margin> tooth settles the pain of them. <term>Parts of the Eye.</term> This same goat liver is eaten or applied as a plaster <note>original: "malafos," likely malagma</note> over the eyes, or even just its vapor is used. <term>Nutritive Parts.</term> Burnt liver is a remedy for pains of the liver. Galen says: "I also, through my experience with medicines, have tried it. I found nothing to increase the help more than that which comes from the lobe of the liver <note>original: "lo foli," likely lobo follis</note>." Furthermore, the liver is pounded... <term>Poisons.</term> The liver of a rabid dog is dried and applied over the bite. And they say that even those who fear water <note>A reference to hydrophobia, a symptom of rabies</note>, if they live by the hair that was used... they are cured and healed by divine help.

# Galbanum. What it is.
A hot gum <note>A resin obtained from certain Persian plants</note>, the power of which lasts for three or four years. That which is many years old tends toward paleness and thinness; it does not dissolve in oil except with difficulty. And it is fresh in those hulls... <term>Selection.</term> The best of it is fresh and clear, tending toward paleness, with a sharp odor and a bitter taste. It is often adulterated with sarcocolla <note>a tree resin</note> or other gums. <term>Actions and Properties.</term> It is cleansing. It has a burning <note>original: "**Bale**," likely an error for "habet"</note> and caustic power. When fresh, it provides a foreign heat to the soul, though it is not as hot as other gums in its warming power. <term>Joint Ailments.</term> It is mixed with those applications made for the joints, such as pepper, cinnamon, and seseli <note>an aromatic herb</note>, and is applied healthfully. It heals the joints <note>original: "artaxes"</note> of the bones in one day. It is used to reduce the flesh in the cavity of the bones when made into an ointment with vinegar. It is rubbed on paralysis <note>original: "parisis"</note> with pressure, and it is very effective. <term>Parts of the Eye.</term> When an eye-salve <note>original: "colliriũ"</note> is made from it, it is cleansing, though its stinging lasts the whole day; for this reason,

<column-break/>

it is mixed with honey and other eye-salves. <term>Excretory Parts.</term> It helps in thin water with cold [symptoms] for those who have colic. It is also used as a potion with the seeds of the "lotus." Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Tralles, a 6th-century medical writer</note> says that it constricts the mouth of the womb <note>original: "matris uterinę"</note>, so much so that it prevents mid-wives from causing abortions. <term>Excretory Parts.</term> By dissolving, it washes away viscous phlegm. It is effective against many types of intestinal problems, according to what has been said. <term>Poisons.</term> It happens sometimes that if something poisonous has stung someone... it appears in the flesh... and if it persists for three days, it may ulcerate the intestines.

# Hinnus <note>Possibly referring to a mule or animal-based remedy</note>. Actions and Properties.
Its action is immediate. <term>Washing Water.</term> The ash of a chicken, if burned, can be used with water on a place to restore it. <term>Parts of the Head.</term> They say that those burns that are on the "knees of horses" are healed by these ashes with vinegar. <term>Excretory Parts.</term> The rennet <note>original: "coagulu"</note> of it is for the flux of the bowels and ulcers.

# Iron Rust. Actions and Properties.
Its nature is cooling and astringent. <term>Excretory Parts.</term> It helps with the flux of those in childbirth.

# Elecampane <note>original: "Nula," likely Inula helenium</note>. What it is.
It is a garden plant. Its leaves are from one span to one cubit in size, spread over the earth. The part that is most helpful is its root. <term>Selection.</term> It is found in marshy places. The best way to prepare it for nourishment is to let it stand with vinegar to temper its heat. <term>Nature.</term> It is hot and dry in the second degree, and in it is a superfluous moisture; because of this, it does not heat the body excessively when it is encountered. <term>Actions and Properties.</term> It helps all injuries and cold pains, and the movement of wind and inflation <note>flatulence</note>. It has a reddening power. <term>Joint Ailments.</term> It helps sciatica and joint pain. A plaster made from its root and leaves helps cold pains and coughing.

### Operations and
### Properties

The white variety is of a violent bitterness and its power is of intense heat. No animal eats it. It is prepared purposefully for the belly; even mice eat it in honey [as a poison]. Then there is the bark in pieces, which is broken up and made into barley water so that nothing remains in the throat or stomach. There is also the powdered form with honey-water, but this is the one that causes the most harm because it remains in the vessels. Therefore, one must have remedies ready for those who take the stronger dose, such as chicken broth, or a drink of *chrysocome* <note>Goldylocks plant</note> with *nitrastrum* <note>a salt or soda compound</note> to lighten it, or fragrant oils like those made from lily or narcissus. The physician should have sharp vinegar, fragrant apples, quinces, warm bread, and fragrant wine ready. If the patient suffers from [over-purging] or fainting, or if they lose their hearing or sight, or if they have tremors, use cupping glasses. When they are distressed by the bitterness, offer cold water and let them smell fragrant things. If they suffer from weakness, then crushed pine nuts in wine or honey-water should be given. When it is necessary for them to vomit, bread soaked in [water or wine] is useful.

## Lees <note>The dregs or sediment of wine or vinegar, known as "Faex"</note>.
### Selection.
The best dregs are those of wine. Those that are similar to vinegar are also good. Intense use is required so that it may burn, but it should be dried first. Thus, let it be burned like sea foam in the first glass vessel, washed from mud or a pot. The end of its burning is when it becomes white and can be powdered. It should be used while fresh. Whatever harm might come from it is removed by burning; then it should be administered. That which is old is weak in its power. Everything that is used should be prepared in a vessel and not exposed to the air. If it is washed, it is washed like earth.

### Operations and properties.
Vinegar dregs are stronger than other dregs. Their power is cleansing and styptic. When burned, they have an additional caustic and putrefactive virtue.

### Blemishes (Indecorations).
When burned and administered in a whitening ointment with pine gum, it corrects the skin.

### Swellings (Apostemes) and Blotches.
Unburned dregs, when boiled, dry out blotches and ulcers.

### Members of the breath and chest.
Unburned dregs extinguish inflammation of the body and that which pertains to the chest and fainting.

### Nutritive members.
Unburned dregs prevent the flow of humors <note>original: "ausu(m) maticez(um)"</note> to the stomach.

### Expulsive members.
When the material is applied as a plaster made from unburned dregs, it benefits the flow of menstrual blood.

## Gall or Bile
<note>original: "Fel"</note>

The strongest galls are those from beasts of prey. First is cow gall, then the adult bear, then the sheep. Among birds, the largest gall is from the rooster, the *duragi*, and the *aibuagi* <note>likely specific game birds</note>. The galls of birds are generally stronger than the galls of four-footed animals. The gall that is particularly strong for the sides <note>ribs/flank</note> is that of the *zapatu* <note>uncertain: possibly a bird or a large fish</note>. Weak galls include those from the pig and those from roasted meat. The gall of a tortoise is stronger than that of four-footed animals, according to Dioscorides <note>a famous Greek physician and botanist</note>. The exterior of the gall should be washed and boiled in a quantity of water until it reaches three boils; then it is stored in a vessel and kept in the shade.

Gall is hot and cleansing. It is distinguished between male and female, and according to the state of thirst, hunger, satiety, and the species and quantity.

**Poisons**

**Mushrooms.** **Selection.**
The better species is the well-known kind that grows on trees <note>original: "alaitabie," a Latinization of the Arabic *al-ghada*</note>; none of them should be eaten raw, as colic <note>original: "colica passio"</note> results from them. Those that are properly prepared are not entirely bad.

**Nature**
They are cold at the end of the third degree and moist in the first.

**Actions and Benefits**
They generate a bad, sharp humor. Their correction, however, is that they should be boiled and served with dry and moist herbs, mountain oregano <note>original: "origanum montanum"</note>, and pure wine should be poured over them.

**Organs of the Head**
They cause stupor and apoplexy <note>stroke</note>.

**Organs of Breathing and the Chest**
They cause difficulty in breathing when a suffocation occurs, which happens from a lack of evacuation.

**Organs of Nutrition**
It is said that they cause a "choleric passion" and sudden suffocation when eaten in large quantities. They are difficult to digest and provide poor nourishment. They cause a biting sensation in the stomach, fainting <note>original: "lincopis," likely leipothymia</note>, and a cold sweat.

**Organs of Expulsion**
They cause difficulty in urinating.

**Poisons**
Among them are those that are deadly. These are the ones that grow near poisonous seeds, or in rotten and damp places, or where poisonous reptiles dwell, or near certain trees that are decaying, such as olive trees. Among the signs of poisonous mushrooms: they have a slimy, putrefactive moisture on them. They change color, and eating them leads to hiccups <note>original: "vips," likely corruption of singultus</note>, shortness of breath, and fainting. Their cure is a preparation of masterwort <note>original: "masuis"</note> and calamint with honey and bishop's weed <note>original: "ameo"</note>, taken immediately.

It opens obstructions of the liver because of its bitterness and aromatic quality. It is used in medicinal drinks. Its nourishment is very slight.

# Fennel <note>original: "Feniculum"</note>
Which is called *baralme* in Persian. Which is... This truly is the seed of the wild variety, similar to the seed of hemlock <note>original: "conia-du"</note>. It has an appearance like *silunio*. If it is weak, it is because it lacks strength; if it is strong, it is *silunio magno*. **Nature.** Fennel is of a heating and drying quality, and it is ranked in the third degree. The grains <note>seeds</note> do not have as much heat; their dryness is in the second degree. **Actions and Properties.** It opens obstructions <note>term: "opilationes" – blockages in the vessels or organs, often the liver</note>. **Organs of the Eyes.** The plant and its gum provide clarity of vision. And it is said that it is effective in wine for this purpose. Democritus claimed that because of its potency, if they feed on fresh fennel seed, their bodies become strong. It is also said that serpents rub their eyes upon it when they emerge from their dens after winter to illuminate their sight <note>A common medieval belief that snakes restored their vision by rubbing against fennel</note>. **Organs of Breath and Chest.** It increases the flow of milk <note>original: "lac exumat lacit"</note> and helps with chronic coughs. **Nutritional Organs.** If drunk beforehand with cold water, it helps with nausea and inflammation of the stomach. However, it is slow to digest and leaves behind a bad residue. **Organs of Expulsion.** It provokes urine and menstruation. The wild variety breaks stones in the bladder or kidneys and aids the flow of urine to the kidneys and bladder. Wild fennel is also given with milk for the dripping of urine <note>strangury</note> and to cleanse the kidneys. When water is distilled from its root and its stalks, it is very effective. **Fevers.** It is beneficial for chronic fevers. When taken as a drink with cold water, it relieves nausea during fevers and inflammation of the internal organs. **Poisons.** Prepared as an electuary <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note> cooked with wine, it treats the bites of poisonous creatures. The root, when placed upon the bite of a rabid dog, is also beneficial.

---

# Fumitory <note>original: "Fumus terre" – literally "smoke of the earth"</note>
**Selection.** The best is that which is green, fresh, sharp, and bitter. **Nature.** It is cold in the first degree and dry in the second. **Opinions and Properties.** It purifies the blood. Because of the property of its bitter flavor, it clarifies the complexion. If it is cold, it is even stronger in this effect. **Wounds and Ulcers.** It is drunk to treat itching and scabies <note>term: "scabiem" – a general term for itchy skin eruptions or mange</note>. **Organs of the Head.** It benefits the blood of the gums. **Nutritional Organs.** It strengthens the stomach and removes obstructions of the liver. **Organs of Expulsion.** It softens the belly <note>acts as a mild laxative</note> and provokes urine. A portion of it is taken as follows:

**Column 2**

from the weight of 10 drams <note>original: "x. 3"</note> up to half a pound; and up to two pounds when mixed with sugar or syrup. When used in a decoction, half a pound is used, down to 10 drams. In cases of severe stomach distress, it is ground up to seven times. **Preparation.** For scabies, use the old roots, taking a middle weight of them along with senna...

# Figs <note>original: "Ficus"</note>
**Which is figs in itself.** This is *chalnauna* here. Leaves are taken from its branches and boiled with syrup or water. From this, it is used for lingering fevers. It is said that in its actions, it is similar to honey. **Selection.** The white fig is best, then the red, then the black. That which is well-measured is better <gloss>and the roots</gloss>... And the fig is praiseworthy in its actions. However, some say it does not generate good blood and can produce lice <note>A common medieval medical theory that excessive sweet fruit led to the generation of parasites</note> unless taken with almonds, which removes all such faults. **Nature.** The fig that is moist and hot is best. When moist, it is most balanced. The immature fig is styptic <note>term: "ab stiua" – contracting or binding</note> and leans somewhat toward coldness in its milky sap. The fig is hot in the first degree, and by the end, it is subtle. **Opinions and Virtues.** The dry fig is sharp and strong in its binding and resolving powers. The fleshy part is very laxative. It is used for clearing the throat, for coughs, and for obstructions. It is sharper and stronger in its effects than other fruits. Because it is laxative, it draws humors to the exterior. It causes flatulence. When its juice is taken with the root of *almezeni* (not the black kind), or when its leaves are dried and boiled, it treats skin eruptions and the scales of scabies. The juice of the leaves is heating and softening. It is a supreme softener. It expels superfluities to the skin and induces sweating. When taken, it sedates heat. The wild variety, I believe, dries and expels humors to the exterior and causes sweating. Its milk coagulates milk just as blood does. Its sap is somewhat congealed, and while moist, it is very nutritious.

### Poisons <note>original: "veneni"</note>

Its milk benefits the puncture of a scorpion's sting. And similarly it helps against the bite of a mad dog <note>original: "rutele," likely referring to a rabid animal</note> when mature leaves are applied over the bite. And a plaster made from it with mustard <note>original: "berlo," likely watercress or a similar pungent herb</note> over the bite of a weasel is beneficial. The water of its load <note>possibly decoction</note> also helps the memory when given in a drink with rue. And the wild fig benefits poisonous punctures when drunk or smeared on the skin.

**Dried Lees** <note>original: "Fax siccatio," referring to the dregs or sediment of oil or wine</note>. The best are the lees of oil made from crocus grains. 

### Nature

The lees from the pressing of oil are in the highest degree of heat.

### Actions and Benefits

It is also said that the lees of chickpea oil bind the tongue and

<column-break/>

the teeth in such a way that it produces a stain like a dyer's tint. 

### Wounds and Ulcers

The lees from the pressing of oil are among those things that resolve ulcers and treat them in dry bodies. 
<margin>A. Leaven or that which is fermented.</margin>

**Leaven** <note>original: "Fermentum," yeast or sourdough starter</note>. 

### Nature

In its nature, it is in the highest degree of heat and dryness. It cleanses because of the quantity of its saltiness and its vigor. 

### Actions and Benefits

It is digestive and fermentative. In its first stage, it is somewhat cold but restrains humors from moving to the exterior and resolves them. 

### Instruments of the Organs <note>original: "Iustru men caium," likely "Instrumenta membrorum"</note>

A plaster is made from it for pain in the lower part of the foot.

**The Acorn** <note>original: "Glans"</note>. Note that it is constricting. If the chestnut is constricting, there is even greater constriction in the acorn; it is more effective when ground. 

### Nature

The acorn is cold and dry. Its coldness is in the first degree. However, it contains some heat in its sweetness. And the leaves of the acorn are of great astringency <note>term: "stipticitatis" — the quality of shrinking or constricting tissues</note>. 

### Actions and Benefits

In the chestnut there is constriction; it is used for all flows in the belly and prohibits the flux of blood. The chestnut is slow to digest but provides good nourishment, especially if mixed with honey. Galen <note>note: Galen of Pergamon, a famous Greek physician whose theories dominated medieval medicine</note> says it is more nourishing than all other wild fruits, though it produces little blood. The chestnut is more nourishing because of its sweetness, and its nourishment is praised. It is prepared with salted pig fat and benefits hard swellings. The fruit of the acorn also benefits those with hot temperaments. 

### Wounds and Ulcers

For creeping ulcers <note>likely referring to gangrene or spreading infections</note> and wounds, the leaves of the acorn are applied and powdered on top to heal the wounds. 

### Organs of the Head <note>original: "Membra capitis"</note>

It treats headaches <note>original: "soda"</note> by its natural astringent quality. 

### Organs of Breath and Chest <note>original: "Membra anhelitus"</note>

It benefits the spitting of blood. 

### Digestive Organs <note>original: "Membra nutmitia"</note>

It benefits excess humidity in the stomach. 

### Organs of Elimination <note>original: "Membra expulsionis"</note>

It constricts and benefits dysentery and intestinal pains...

# The Pine Nut <note>original: "Glans," usually meaning acorn, but here explicitly described as the pine nut</note>. What it is.

It is the fruit of the larger pine tree. It provides better nourishment than the common nut, though it is slower to digest. It is composed of the elements of water and earth; there is little heat <note>original: "frictā," likely meaning friction or innate heat</note> in it. As a completion of our discourse, let this be governed by the chapter on the pine tree. 
**Nature.** It is considered similar to the almond, being slightly warm. 
**Actions and Applications.** It is a very strong nutrient and is not harmful. It corrects corrupt moisture in the intestines, though it digests slowly. If the digestion is to be corrected in those with cold temperaments, it should be taken with honey. In those with warm temperaments, it acts as an extractor. It significantly increases nourishment when infused in water; this process removes sharpness and helps with gnawing sores <note>term: "carcinomata" — here referring to "mordicatio" or stinging, corrosive ulcers rather than modern cancer</note>. It is so highly nutritious that even a small amount provides a great deal of sustenance. Small pine nuts from smaller pine trees are found in every region. 
**Benefits for the Body.** It heals pains of the joints and back and is useful for softening the tissues. 
**Organs of Breath and Chest.** It greatly cleanses the lungs and restores health where there is pus or humors from the bones. 
**Organs of Elimination.** It excites sexual desire and provides nourishment to the brain. It removes stones from the bladder. 
**Poison.** When joined with figs and dates, it offers protection against the sting of a scorpion.

# Gentian. What it is.

These are leaves found near the root of the plant; they are similar to walnut leaves and the leaves of plantain <note>original: "aruoglose," a corruption of arnoglossa, the herb plantain</note>. Its color is red. The center of the plant is earthy and absorbent. It has a smooth taste and grows to a length of two cubits. Its leaves are spaced far apart from one another. Its fruit is found at the tips, and its root is long, similar to the root of birthwort <note>term: "aristologie" — birthwort, a plant traditionally used in childbirth and for snakebites</note>. It grows in mountains, in cloudy areas, and in damp places. It is said that wherever gentian grows, it cannot be ignored by those who know it; it was discovered by King Gentius <note>original: "germina rex," referring to the Illyrian king Gentius, the namesake of the plant</note>. It grows on high mountains. A juice is prepared from it by soaking it in water for several days, 

<column-break/>

then cooking it, allowing the dregs to settle, then straining it and thickening it with honey. 
**Selection.** The Roman variety is better, especially if it is reddish and sweet, and if the woody stem has the thickness of a finger and a dark color leaning toward black. The juice made from it should have a similar appearance. 
**Nature.** Hot in the second degree, dry in the second. 
**Actions and Applications.** It is an opener <note>term: "apitiua" — an aperient or substance that opens obstructions in the body</note> for those with blockages. Its root soaked in water is useful for many things. 
**Benefits.** Its root breaks the power of bites and stings. 
**Wounds and Sores.** It heals wounds and corrosive ulcers, especially when the aforementioned juice is used. 
**General Benefits.** Two drams <note>original: ".z̄. due," a measurement of weight</note> are drunk with wine for bone pain; it also helps those who have fallen from a high place. 
**Organs of the Eye.** A liniment is made from it for ophthalmia <note>term: "ob talmie" — an old term for severe eye inflammation or conjunctivitis</note>. 
**Organs of Breath and Chest.** Two drams of its juice are good for pleurisy. 
**Nutritional Organs.** It is an opener of obstructions in the liver and spleen, and it aids the coldness of the stomach. It is effective if the syrup is taken when the body is not firm due to cold. 
**Organs of Elimination.** It purges the urine and provokes the menses. A suppository made of its root cleanses the womb and can cause abortion. 
**Poison.** It is the ultimate medicine for the sting of a scorpion; for this, two drams are taken with wine. It also protects against all poisons and the bite of a mad dog or a wolf. 
**Substitution.** Half a portion of this can be substituted for the root of the caper plant.

# Larch Fungus <note>original: "Gibber," likely referring to Agaricum, the wood-rotting fungus found on larch trees</note>. What it is.

It is a grainy substance found in high places, leaning toward white, which is gathered from the larch tree. Like coral, it becomes one when mixed with water and honey. 
**Nature.** According to Paul <note>note: Likely referring to the 7th-century medical writer Paul of Aegina</note>, it has a cooling and drying effect. 
**Actions and Applications.** It stops the flow of blood. 
**Beautification.** It makes the body fat. 
**Wounds and Sores.** It heals ringworm...

# Galbanum. What it is.

It is a primary resin... which some say is the seed of black fennel. The bark of its root is white and broad. It comes from India and is similar to papyrus. 
**Benefits for the Body.** It is given in a drink for those suffering from paralysis.

## Gypsum. What it is.
It is a laminated gypsum stone, white and small, the utility of which increases when added to an ointment. **Nature.** Cold and dry. **Operations and Effects.** It is a "glutinating" <note>term: "Glutinativus" — a substance that "glues" or binds the edges of wounds together</note> agent. It is placed upon wounds flowing with blood, and it stops them. It is discussed in its own chapter, regarding how it acts as a binder. It causes adherence and has a thickening quality with stickiness. When a part is moist, it adds a certain delicacy to it. **Organs of the Head.** From it, a plaster is made for the forehead or a covering like a cap, and it restrains the flow of blood from the nostrils. It is especially effective when the gypsum is prepared with Armenian bole <note>original: "lolo armenico," likely a scribe's error for *bolo armenico*, a medicinal red clay</note> and meal. It is distilled with rose water, and instead of wine, with vinegar. **Organs of the Eye.** It is mixed with egg white so that it becomes like a stone, and it is placed over bloody ophthalmia <note>term: "ob talmia" — an old term for eye inflammation</note>. **Poisons.** It is a remedy against poisons through its drawing properties.

## Gips. What it is.
It is the same as gypsum.

## Ginisectum <note>Possibly referring to *Genista* (Broom) or a related leguminous plant</note>. What it is.
It is a plant with threads and fibers like the lupine. **Operations and Effects.** It is cleansing, opening, and soothing to inflammation, and it is detoxifying in itself. **Nutritive Organs.** It resolves the humidities of the viscera in the stomach and is beneficial for the "sours" <note>original: "srois," likely *syrosis* or sour stomach</note> of infants. **Organs of Expulsion.** It helps with flatulence of the womb.

## Gezar <note>The Arabic term for Carrot (Daucus carota)</note>. What it is.
Note that its seed is strong like the seed of seseli <note>original: "siluris," likely *seselis*</note>. According to Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, there is one species of it whose leaves are smaller than the leaves of fennel, which it resembles in form. Its stalk grows to the height of a palm, and the part above is dark. The flower is white, sharp, and has a long scent and many branches. It grows in sunny, solitary, and stony places. The garden variety is similar to Roman parsley, being sharp, burning, and of a good scent. Its leaves are like the leaves of coriander or celery.

<column-break/>

It is white, and the medicinal parts are the tops and the fruit. It has living heads full of seeds which are shaped like cumin. **Nature.** It is warm in the second degree and moist in the first. **Wounds and Ulcers.** Its seed and leaves, when bruised and placed upon corrosive ulcers, are beneficial; they also help with pleurisy. **Operations and Effects.** It is difficult to digest. When cooked, it is easier to digest and benefits those with dropsy <note>term: "ydropisi" — edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</note>. **Organs of Expulsion.** It settles stinging pain in the belly and breaks up gas. It provokes wind and is itself a wild plant; its seed and leaves also promote coitus. The seed of the domestic variety causes great inflation [gas]. The seed of the wild variety is counted among the best; it excites coitus more than the garden variety. It provokes menstruation and urine. The wild variety is better and more potent. Its seed and root together do not fail to help with the difficulty of conception.
