### Dragon's Blood <note>original: "Sanguis draconis"; this is actually a red resin obtained from plants such as the Dracaena tree, not real blood</note>
It is a well-known red juice. **Nature.** It is not very hot. Some even say that it is cold and that its power is found in the second degree. **General Operations.** It is constrictive <note>acts as an astringent to tighten tissues</note>; it is effective against the flux of tongues <note>possibly referring to oral bleeding or excessive salivation</note>. **Wounds and Ulcers.** It consolidates <note>heals or closes</note> ulcers and large wounds. **Nutritive Organs.** It strengthens the stomach. **Organs of Expulsion.** It restrains and benefits dysentery and anal fissures.

### Blood <note>original: "Sanguis"</note>
It is said that human blood and pig blood are similar in nature, so much so that some have been deceived into eating human flesh as if it were the flesh of a pig. This remained hidden until it was discovered in the market by the law of the land. It is also said that there is much power in blood; however, the blood of small animals is of weaker virtue than the blood of larger ones, though they are similar. We should note that what we are discussing now concerns the various types of blood and the many uses found for them. **Selection.** It is necessary that the blood administered in medicines be taken from healthy animals, neither melancholic <note>suffering from an excess of black bile</note> nor putrid. **General Operations.** Horse blood is caustic and corrosive; it is of a bilious nature, especially that which is drawn out. **Beautification.** Warm rabbit blood is used for spots and skin discolorations. Bat blood <note>original: "vespertilionis"</note> is used, according to many, to stop the growth of hair, especially on the breasts. The blood of green frogs and the blood of white snails are even better for preventing hair growth. It is also said that bat blood preserves the breasts from drooping if it is applied correctly. **Hard Swellings.** Rabbit blood matures hot abscesses; goat blood acts similarly and is administered for congealed blood. Also, the blood of a goat <note>original: "m dītuus", likely "hedinus" or kid-goat</note> is applied over erysipelas <note>a skin infection</note>. Warm frog blood is used for hard abscesses, as is warm rabbit blood

<column-break/>

for soft abscesses. **Instruments of the Joints.** All kinds of blood are used for instruments <note>the parts of the body</note>; warm blood is applied to hot gout <note>term: <term>podagīā</term> — a painful form of arthritis, often in the big toe</note> and benefits it. Vulture blood, when it is distilled and warm, is applied to skin excoriations of the joints which are painful; it is best when mixed with warm rose oil. Galen <note>a famous Roman physician whose theories dominated medieval medicine</note> says this should be used at the time the pain is felt. If this is not available, one should administer warm rose oil in its place, as it has a similar effect. The same is said of chicken blood. Donkey blood is used for bile and issues in the anus such as protrusions. Wild turtle blood cures epilepsy when taken with wine. Similarly, lamb blood and camel blood are said to benefit epilepsy, though this is not as well known. Galen says that this is not done without some doubt, but I say that perhaps it may be verified by experiment, as it approaches the virtue of the medicine <unclear>mo ae</unclear> which is living. **Organs of the Eye.** The blood of the eagle and the lizard strengthens the sight. The blood of the bat <note>original: "allvule"</note> prevents hair from regrowing on the eyelids. The same is said of the blood of a Mediterranean lizard, though experiment has not verified this. Pigeon blood and the blood of the *alguarcscen* <note>possibly a transliteration of an Arabic bird name</note> are used; the blood of a bat is distilled over a cataract. The same effect is had from its gall. Similarly, if the shafts of feathers are dipped in this blood and applied, Galen says it is for the sake of the vision. **Organs of Breath and Chest.** Owl blood greatly benefits asthma. Similarly, the blood of a dog is useful. It is said that bat blood preserves the breasts so that they remain standing and do not sag at the root. From the blood of a goat, taken directly before it congeals, mixed with vinegar and used for three days while warm, it cleanses and benefits the chest. **Organs of Expulsion.** Kid-goat blood is used for fluxes, as previously stated according to experience. Hyena blood and camel blood are used to restrain fluxes. Goat blood, when drunk with honey, benefits dysuria <note>painful urination</note>. Dried goat blood is also used for those suffering from kidney stones. **Poisons.** The blood of goats, camels, and rabbits is used against poisons; it is effective against the bites of venomous creatures when drunk with wine. ## Asparagus. What it is.
According to Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years</note>, it is said that it is neither heating nor cooling in nature; however, this appears in the [medical] process. But I say it is not far from sharpness. And therefore, they induce more [digestion]. It strengthens by its heat. And it appears upon the skin of animals as something very biting <note>original: "mordicium"; referring to a stinging or acrid sensation</note>. **Operations and powers.** Its root is truly cleansing; it effectively opens obstructions <note>original: "opillationes"; blockages in the vessels or organs</note> of all the viscera, especially of the liver and the kidneys. It also aids in the resolution [of fluids], especially in the process. **Nutritive instruments.** It is drunk as a decoction for pain of the ribs <note>likely pleurisy</note> and for sciatica. **Parts of the head.** A decoction of its roots when cooked with vinegar is useful. Likewise, the seeds of the roots are used for the pain of the teeth. **Nutritive organs.** It opens obstructions of the liver and is preferred for jaundice. It is also known to cure nausea. **Organs of expulsion.** Rufus <note>Rufus of Ephesus, a Greek physician</note> stated that it helps against hiccups. And it is strengthened for the provocation of the bowels, provided it is boiled. Many have said that it is effective against phlegmatic or windy colic. A decoction of the roots provokes urine and is preferred for difficulty in urinating; it also increases sperm and libido. It is preferred for difficulties in pregnancy. Likewise, its seed, when taken, provokes the menses and opens obstructions of the spleen. **Poisons.** With water, it helps against [poisonous] breath, and it is preferred for the stings of shrews <note>original: "rutete"; likely referring to the *araneus* or shrew-mouse, thought to be venomous in antiquity</note>. And its decoction is used so that the bite does not become infected.

## Grime <note>original: "Sordities"; refers to various types of oily residues, earwax, or skin scrapings used in ancient medicine</note>
**Nature.** Grime in the ear is heating at the end of the second degree, and the best of it is from the nest <note>likely referring to residues found in beehives or bird nests</note>. And the grime of wool <note>lanolin or sheep grease</note> which is impregnated in it is heating in its quality. And the grime of the gymnasium <note>original: "lutianu"; referring to the *sordes* or *gryphes*—the mixture of sweat, oil, and dust scraped from athletes</note> which is also called bath grime. Grime from the gymnasium has two species: one is that which is collected from the bodies of those who anoint themselves with oil mixed with dust. The second is that which is collected from the walls from their vapors and sweats, and that which is collected above the dirt of the game. **Opinions and powers.** Both are resolving and maturing <note>bringing an abscess to a head</note> with equality; they burn strongly, and therefore they extract boils and thorns. **Decoction.** Grime in the ears is preferred for inflammation <note>original: "pinnitiũ"; likely a typo for *pinnulas* or related to ear inflammation</note> and helps with cracks in the lip. **According to Al-Zahrawi** <note>original: "aluoroz"; referring to the famous Arab surgeon Albucasis</note>. It resolves [problems of] the skin. The grime of the gymnasium is of this sort...

<column-break/>

...of woolly garments. **Wounds and ulcers.** Grime from the walls of the gymnasium is useful for wounds of a certain nature. Grime from the ears is very cleansing in pregnancy. **Nutritive instruments.** Grime from the bodies [of athletes] in the gymnasium is useful for sciatica when it is placed upon it with a spatula like a plaster; it also is preferred for hardness of the breasts.

## Sea Foam. What it is. <note>original: "Spuma maris"; usually refers to cuttlebone, halcyonium, or dried marine remains</note>
There are five species: the spongy kind, which is formless in its shape; the second is like the bone of an octopus, which is thick and muddy in the hands. The third is spongy, white, long, light, and has a rolling scent. The fourth has the form of a mushroom, flat and rough in material. The fifth is called "the way." **Nature.** It is hot in the third degree. **Operations and powers.** It is a modifier of grime, detergent, and caustic <note>original: "adustiua"; capable of burning or scouring</note>. The third type is... **Decoration.** The kind that is [found] in the sea is used for alopecia <note>patchy hair loss</note> and boils; it is administered for the scouring of hair and is preferred for morphea <note>a skin condition causing discolored patches</note>. The spongy kind is included in washes and in medicinal lotions for the side and the face, and for old infants <note>likely referring to older children</note>. The rest is used for scouring hair. **Parts of the head.** The flat kind is very useful for the scouring of the teeth and is generally powerful for the scouring of the gums. **According to the authors.** The flat kind is suitable for those things which are like nails upon the skin <note>warts or calluses</note>, and for troches <note>medicinal lozenges</note>. **Wounds and ulcers.** It benefits ulcerative scabies and impetigo, especially the spongy kind. **Nutritive instruments.** It is useful for digestion when mixed with oil of roses. **Nutritive organs.** It is preferred for the spleen and for dropsy <note>original: "yd’ropisi"; swelling caused by excess fluid</note>. **Organs of expulsion.** It is used for difficulty in urinating and for purging the sand found in the pain of the kidneys.

Dung is not administered when it is fresh because of the excess of its heat. The dung of goats, [and other animals], is administered when dried. **Nature.** None of the dungs are cooling; rather, they are moisturizing. The dung of pigeons is the hottest of the species which are administered; those that are raised in houses are less [hot] than the ones previously mentioned. **Operations and powers.** The dung of goats which have been moved <note>perhaps referring to wild vs. domestic</note> is administered in all fluxes of the womb. Dung is caustic when burned, and...

## Spodium. What it is.
It is the burnt roots of reeds <note>original: "radices canarum aduste"; spodium was often a substitute for burnt ivory or zinc oxide, here using burnt plant matter</note>. It is said that some collect it by fanning the extreme ends. **Nature.** It is cold in the second degree, dry in the third. **Operations and properties.** In it there is a binding <note>original: "stupnatas"; referring to astringency</note> and a "derivation" <note>diverting of humors</note>, and a little resolution. Its stimulation is very great, though its ability to resolve and prepare humors is small. Through its binding nature, it causes strong drying, and it is suitable for many things. **Parts of the head.** It benefits *alcola* <note>aphthous ulcers or thrush in the mouth</note> and melancholy proceeding from anxiety. **Parts of the eye.** Spodium benefits hot inflammations of the eye. **Parts of the breath and chest.** It strengthens the heart and benefits hot tremors of the heart. For the flow caused by the effusion of bile to the stomach; drunk or applied, it benefits melancholy from anxiety, and previous tumors, and those about to break. **Nutritive parts.** It benefits coughs and inflammation, and weakness of the stomach, and it prevents the effusion of bile into it. **Parts of expulsion.** It prevents bilious loosening of the bowels. **Fevers.** It benefits acute fevers.

## Spleen. Selection.
The best of spleens [to use medicinally] is the pig’s spleen. The white type is bad as food. **Operations and properties.** In it there is a certain binding quality, and it generates melancholic blood. **Nutritive parts.** It is slow to digest because of its binding nature.

## Sambucus <note>Elderberry</note>. Nature.
The white is warmer... and the dark purple... a type of 

<column-break/>

warm salt for the face. **Operations and properties.** It is a blessed remedy under [certain] heights, and its oil benefits [wounds]. **Beautification.** It removes spots <note>original: "puni"; likely pimples or facial blemishes</note> and makes the face a reddish color; it has a multitude of fragrances. **Instruments of the joints.** And its oil benefits cold ailments in the nerves and joints. **Parts of the head.** And its odor relieves *soda* <note>a medieval term for a splitting headache or migraine</note>; truly, when its scent is released, it treats headaches caused by phlegm. And its pure oil, when warmed, makes blood flow from the nostrils when it is smelled.

## Sulphur. What it is. Known. Flame.
It is hot in the third degree, reaching toward the fourth. **Operations and properties.** It is heating and "attractive" <note>drawing out substances from the body</note>. **Beautification.** It is used for whiteness... when it is touched by fire. And when it is mixed with lime <note>original: "al luti"; likely a corruption of "calce"</note>, it eradicates the marks that are on the nails. With vinegar, it is placed upon bites. **Wounds and ulcers.** It is placed upon a burn that has ulcerated, and it binds it; mixed with vinegar, the body is washed with it to treat [skin conditions]. **Instruments of the joints.** Its use with [other substances] applied upon gout is beneficial. **Parts of the head.** It restricts catarrh <note>runny nose/mucus</note> by fumigation; and it is mixed with vinegar and honey to be placed upon the ears.

## Sage. What it is.
According to the species and according to the individual complexion [of the patient]. It is said to be altogether maturing and "resolutive" <note>able to disperse swelling</note>. **Beautification.** It cleanses spots, blackness, and the blood from bites. **Wounds and ulcers.** Rubbed into a wound with the saliva of a fasting person <note>original: "salivat... ieiuni"; medieval medicine often attributed special healing powers to the saliva of someone who had not yet eaten</note>, it strengthens it. **Parts of the head.** Sage, when distilled into the ear, benefits the hearing and clarifies the senses, restoring them immediately. **Poisons.** Sage resists poisons; and when a fasting person spits upon a scorpion, it dies many times over.

## Stavesacre <note>Larkspur</note>.
It is the "mountain raisin" and the "caper grain," found much in Mount Lebanon. **What it is.** It is mountain raisin and it is a black grain, like black maple. **Nature.** It is hot in the third degree. **Operations and properties.** It is burning, corrosive, sharp, and acrid. **Beautification.** It kills lice, and it is used with arsenic and resin to treat [skin]...

# Savory.
<note>original: "Satureia"; Winter Savory (*Satureja montana*), a herb known for its sharp, peppery taste</note>
**Nature.** Its nature is sharp and acrid. **Operations and properties.** By its corrosive nature, it is cleansing; it has a resolving and drying effect if applied to **wounds of the throat.** Savory of the woody kind <note>original: "Satarua ligni"</note> solidifies wounds; when taken with wine, it treats [unclear] and fungal growths upon cavernous ulcers <note>original: "ulcei fornicalia"</note>.

# Sal ammoniac.

## The Serpent: what it is.

The meat from the snake is cooked with water, salt, and dill; it is administered this way. It yields an oil, which is administered with the water in which its flesh was cooked, and it is applied to the ears. We will speak further about the different species in the fourth book. **Selection.** The best meat is that of the female, and it is better than that of the male. **Nature.** The drying effect of its flesh is powerful, provided that the heating is not excessive. **Operations and properties.** The property of its flesh is such that it causes superfluities to penetrate to the skin, and it purifies a person when they are cleansed <note>original: "mūdificat"; a term for purging or cleansing the body's humors</note>. There is a certain effect regarding a large swelling in the neck <note>original: "exturā ī collo maḡ"; likely referring to scrofula or a goiter</note>, as it opens it and draws out all that is within it. And the flesh, when taken, aids in the healing of wounds and strengthens life. **Cooking.** Cooking it with figs <note>original: "fic̄"</note> destroys skin blemishes, because it expels superfluities to the skin; it is very beneficial for leprosy and is administered for hair loss <note>original: "alopica"</note>, where it brings great help and promotes growth. Its flesh, specifically from its extremities, prevents the growth of scrofula <note>original: "s̄crofularū"; swelling of the lymph nodes</note>, and it is held in high regard. **Nutritive instruments.** It is used by removing a measure of one finger's length from the head and the tail, and it is boiled. And if it is eaten with a certain ratio, it takes away the pain of these areas. **Parts of the head.** When its ear <note>original: "auris"; possibly a specific anatomical part or a misspelling of 'flesh'</note> is cooked in wine and distilled, or when the bone is distilled from vinegar in which its flesh was boiled, it aids toothache. The best part for this is the ear of the male. Galen thought that because a thread <note>original: "filū"</note> dipped in the blood of a living snake and wrapped around the neck or throat appeared to provide a maximum and wonderful benefit for the sight. **Parts of the eye.** Its broth and the aforementioned flesh strengthen the sight, and it is said that its fat prevents the flow of water <note>original: "s̄ttu aque"; referring to cataracts or "suffusion" of the eye</note> into the eye.

<column-break/>

**Venoms.** It is poured and placed upon the bite of the viper itself, and it settles the pain.

## Spodium <note>original: "Spodiū"; often refers to metallic ash, burnt ivory, or the residue from furnaces used as a cooling agent</note>: what it is.

It is spoken of in the chapter on the serpent.
**Nature.** It is cold in the second degree and dry in the third. **Operations and properties.** It retains blood <note>original: "Retinet sanguiē"; a hemostatic agent</note>. **Occasion.** It prevents the falling out of hair. **Substitute.** In its place, one may put an equal weight of *seluzalutaz* <note>original: "seluzalutaz"; likely a variant of 'sellyria' or a specific earth</note> and a third of its weight in reed root.

## Camel Grass <note>original: "Sceleos"; likely Schoenanthos or Camel Grass</note>: what it is.

It is a certain coin-like plant <note>original: "alamanū ē nūmū"; possibly a reference to the shape of the leaves or a regional name</note>. It is found in the logic of the principles <note>unclear: "logico ī p̄arīp̄"</note>, which have a white interior. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the second degree. **Operations and properties.** It is resolutive, soothing, cleansing, and carminative <note>original: "carminatiuū"; helping to relieve gas</note>. Its root and its seed are used for internal pains, and they work against congealed phlegm. And it is given in a drink for the internal organs, and it increases purification. It is drunk in wine and prevents coldness; it is also taken with pepper. **Nutritive instrument.** It benefits the complexion. **Parts of the head.** It helps with "soda" <note>term: soda - a medieval term for a splitting headache</note>. **Parts of the breath and chest.** It helps with asthma, difficulty breathing, and shortness of breath, as well as an old cough; the root and seed work similarly. And when the root is prepared with honey and swallowed, it cleanses the chest of humors. **Nutritive parts.** It resolves inflammation, settles the pains of the stomach <note>original: "m̄sērū"; likely a contraction for viscera or stomach</note>, and its root digests food; it is good for the stomach. **Parts of expulsion.** It resolves the inflation and pain of the belly and acts as a pure diuretic. It removes the difficulty of urinating and resolves pains of the womb. It is beneficial for the pains of the bowels. The juice of this and its seed are used for retention, and three measures are drunk for ten days; it heals the pain of the kidneys, being a total remedy for them.

## Strengi <note>original: "Strengi"; likely an astringent juice or a specific type of harsh wine</note>: what it is.

<margin>It is a juice which, through its power of scent, is suitable for stopping stench.</margin>
It is a juice from *Strengi*, which is stronger than wine. **Nature.** Cold and dry. **Operations and properties.** It is styptic <note>original: "stypt̄'"; an agent that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</note> and is used for fragile areas. Being used primarily in baths, it prevents fluxes and heals wounds.

### Scammony: what it is. 
<note>original: "Scamonea"; the resinous juice of the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*</note>. It is the juice of a climbing plant, which can last for up to thirty years. **Selection.** The better quality is that which tends toward whiteness. It should be fragile like a sea shell, easily powdered, soluble, and "living"—meaning it dissolves in water, turning it white like milk. The best kind is that which must be prepared; it is baked inside a fruit <note>original: "pomo"; specifically a quince, used to buffer the harshness of the resin</note> and mixed with anise water, by which its "malice" <note>the harsh, toxic side effects common to strong purgatives</note> is removed. Another way it is made bad is when the scammony is not rectified by being baked in an unripe quince or processed with anise or fennel, or dissolved with almond oil. **Nature.** It is hot and dry in the third degree. Its heat is greater than its dryness. **Operations and properties.** Within it are cleansing and resolving powers, which purify the stomach and the liver. **Decoration.** It cleanses morphea <note>localized skin discolorations</note>, white spots, and scales. **Wounds and ulcers.** When it is cooked with honey and applied as a plaster upon wounds, it resolves them. **Skin and washes.** It is applied with vinegar upon ulcerated scabies. **Instruments of the joints.** With vinegar and leek <note>original: "lauch"</note>, it is placed upon the pain of the joints and hips as a plaster. **Members of the head.** The root is used for chronic headaches <note>original: "soda antiqua"; 'soda' was a common medieval term for a persistent headache</note> when applied with vinegar and rose oil. And when scammony is mixed with other things and placed upon the head of one who has a chronic headache, it heals it. **Members of the breath and chest.** It is among those things that harm the heart. **Nutritive members.** It harms the stomach and liver greatly. Its "malice" is broken when it is baked in a quince. It is oppressive, causes nausea, and destroys the appetite for food, causing weakness. **Members of expulsion.** It purges yellow bile <note>original: "colerā"</note> strongly. Indeed, its effects vary by region, so much so that I have seen in some healthy coastal areas it acts as a very strong purgative. It harms the intestines and can lead to abortion. When the root is drunk in a dose of one gold coin's weight <note>original: "pōd' aurei"; a reference to a specific weight, likely a denarius or solidus</note>, it purges sharp bile and phlegm. Some say that if scammony is drunk in an excessive quantity—and half a drachm <note>original: "ʒ"</note> is the limit—it causes nausea and provokes a cold sweat; finally, it brings about

<column-break/>

death with its excess and is insufficient <note>likely meaning it causes more harm than the intended medicinal effect</note>. Some have said that when small amounts are taken, it provokes movement and purges. Its power is lesser when mixed with aloe. Similarly, it is mixed with salt lupins and fragrant seeds. When placed in a wool suppository, it cleanses the female parts. We rectify its malice when we mix it with quince water or rose water. When it is provided to a stomach that can tolerate it, it can be beneficial; it acts on the internal organs and excites the members, and is given in the necessary quantity. **Poisons.** It benefits the stings of scorpions, both when drunk and when applied as an ointment.

### Sagapenum: what it is. 
<note>original: "Serapinū"; a gum-resin derived from species of *Ferula*</note>. It dissolves quickly in water. It is sometimes adulterated with galbanum <note>another medicinal resin</note>, as it is similar to white galbanum. The best kind is from Isfahan <note>original: "spahan"; a city in Persia famous for its drug trade</note>. **Nature.** It is hot in the third degree and dry in the second. **Operations and properties.** It is resolving, opening of fistulas, carminative <note>relieving gas</note>, heating, and cleansing. Regarding the **instruments of the joints**, it benefits palsy, ruptures of the muscles, and their tremors. It dissolves materials that are stuck in the hips and is taken as a drink. Similarly, it is good for bad complexions of the joints. **Members of the head.** It resolves cold and windy headaches and benefits epilepsy. **Members of the eye.** It benefits obscurity of the eye, "sun-spots" <note>original: "mako sol"; possibly macula</note>, and redness of the eyelids which irritates the eye. It is among the best medicines for "water ascending in the eye" <note>a medieval description of cataracts or glaucoma</note>. It is diluted with water and placed over the eye to clear it. **Members of the breath and chest.** It benefits chest pain, asthma <note>original: "statis"</note>, and old coughs. It is drunk with the pressed water of rue, in a dose of one drachm, for ailments of the breath; it cleanses the chest powerfully and transforms bitter humors. **Nutritive members.** It benefits dropsy <note>original: "ydrophisi"; edema</note> and clears out the watery fluid. **Members of expulsion.** It benefits windy colic when drunk, and stinging pain in the belly. ## Spikenard: what it is.
<note>original: "Spica"; Spikenard (*Nardostachys jatamansi*)</note>
There are two kinds of Nard: one is Syrian and the other is Indian. And it is the Nard spike, weaker in strength than the Indian, and used for its specific diseases. It is provocative <note>likely meaning it provokes urine or menses</note>. Its nature is that of the Syrian plant. And that which is otherwise is pulled up with its root and comes forth. It is sometimes adulterated with plants that are similar to it. Among these is the "Saurian" <note>original: "s̄arı̄̄"</note>, which is preferred because of its wonderful odor. And it comes from the mountains; its leaves are like the leaves of the Gratian oat. Its stalks are not flat in the manner of the <unclear>invisis</unclear>. It has roots, but no anise, no fruit, and no flower.

### Selection.
Choose that which is of a light color. The smell of the hairs <note>the fibrous roots</note> should be pleasant and incline toward redness. The third test is the smell of cyperus <note>a fragrant sedge</note>. And the small spike is not as cheap or long, but more of a wrapped spike, of a wonderful odor... roots from the dust in great quantity. And it is sometimes adulterated by soaking it with warm water and mixing it with small antimony. Therefore, it is said that they test it with antimony and the color of antimony. After that, they sell it in the weakness of Damascus...

### **Lycium**
<note>original: "lycor̄"; an extract made from the juice of the Boxthorn or Buckthorn bush</note> itself. It is said [to come from] Rhodes. The black is common, but the red is better. It is said that the best is that which is rosy in color, has a light odor, many roots, is woody, and is easily broken. That which is chosen should be inclined toward whiteness <note>on the inside</note> and have a certain scent. 

**Nature.** It is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. 

**Properties and Actions.** It is aperient <note>opening</note> and resolutive. From its bark <note>original: "l̄ntīai," likely *lentia*</note> it is very astringent <note>original: "stipnatııs"</note>; its heat is minor. Thus it is praised for its ability to tighten and scrape [the humors] without excessive heat or sharpness. From the aromatic spice a powder is made to be used in temples <note>likely a reference to incense or topical application</note>. Therefore, the spice is used for cleansing, as it is good for creating a pleasant odor. 

**Tough Swellings.** It resolves tough swellings and resolutions. 

**Parts of the Head.** It stops rheum <note>original: "r̄eumātısmos"; runny discharges</note> and strengthens the brain. 

**Parts of the Eye.** It makes hair grow on the eyelids when there are spots <note>original: "malcosol," likely *macula*</note>, and it is used as a powder on the eyelids to aid vision. 

**Parts of Breathing and the Chest.** It helps with tremors of the heart, cleanses the chest and lungs, and prohibits the flow of humors to them. 

**Nutritive Organs.** It is good for the liver and stomach and strengthens them. It is beneficial for jaundice <note>original: "hıcterıc̄e"</note>, prevents the flow of humors to the stomach, and relieves its biting pains. When it is drunk with wine, it benefits the spleen. 

**Organs of Evacuation.** It provokes all [flows, such as urine and menstruation]. It is stronger when it is hotter and less astringent. It eases all roughness by soothing them. It helps the colon and kidneys and prevents the movement of humors to the intestines. It has the power to restrain an excessive flow of matter.

<note>original: "SAmch"</note> What it is. This is spoken of in the chapter on *Rhus* <note>original: "tıa r̄oīdē"</note>.

### **Sebesten**
<note>original: "STantıū"; the Assyrian plum (*Cordia myxa*)</note> What it is. It is a seed that reduces flatulence <note>original: "uētuosıtatıs"</note> and other seeds. It is easily handled. Some say its oil only benefits melancholy, but it actually fattens and moistens the body. It is a liquid obtained from a certain kind of fruit. 
**Selection.** Its body is stronger than the oil itself. 
**Nature.** It is hot in the middle of the first degree and moist at the end of it. 
**Properties.** It is glutinous and softening,

providing equal heating. Its oil has the same properties and is softening. Its nature is somewhat astringent. The whole fruit, when prepared, is of little harm.

It lengthens the hair. When the leaves are applied, they relieve those who suffer from fissures. Its oil, when decocted, preserves the hair and makes it strong and hard. 

**Tough Swellings.** It resolves hot swellings. 

**Wounds and Ulcers.** It can be placed upon burns. Its oil, when drunk, removes many phlegmatic and sanguine humors, especially when mixed with an infusion of aloes and water or wine. 

**Ointments.** A plaster is made from it for those with redness. 

**Parts of the Head.** Its oil helps with headaches caused by heat <note>original: "sodaadııstıuē"</note>, and the leaves heal fissures of the skin. 

**Tough Swellings.** It helps when applied to swellings and opens them. 

**Organs of Breathing and the Chest.** It is good for constriction of the breath and asthma. 

**Nutritive Organs.** It is bad for the stomach, causing nausea and slowing digestion. It is better when eaten with honey; this removes the harm and aids digestion. It softens ulcers. When prepared, it is less harmful. It is very nutritious. It is best taken with its skin <note>original: "coııace suo"</note>; when the skin is removed, digestion is slowed. 

**Organs of Evacuation.** It benefits the intestines. An infusion of it is a powerful provoker of menstruation, so much so that it may cause the fetus to be expelled. When eaten cold with cucumber seeds, it does not allow humors to irritate the spine. 

**Venom.** It benefits the bite of a rabid dog <note>original: "carııs rabıosı"</note> and protects against deadly poisons.

**Members of nourishment.** It benefits moistures of the stomach and benefits the breath of infants when it is placed upon their heads, according to what is said in the gloss.

**Members of expulsion.** It benefits winds <note>flatulence or gas</note> of the womb.

## Sebia
<note>original: "Sebia"; identified by the description as Scammony (*Scammonia*), a powerful and dangerous purgative resin</note>
What it is. Having two names... and it has hairs and leaves like tarragon leaves, as they stand out, and it also has a milk <note>latex</note>.

**Nature.** That which is best is light, tending toward redness, and smooth, like a wrapped skin. And that which is with two stalks, closed and thick, tending toward redness and hard. And that which is like a thread is bad, and nothing of it should be administered. <margin>The thread-like [kind] is bad.</margin>

**Nature.** Avicenna says it is hot in the first or second degree, and thus in the end of those. Its milk is at the highest point of [heat]... that is, in the third degree.

**Operation and utility.** In [the body] it is stripping and sharp, and causes the disruption of the openings of the veins. There is no other medicine by which it is repelled. And when it is rectified <note>processed to be less toxic</note>, there is no... in its place because of what we have said. It is entirely harmful, especially for those with hot [temperaments].

**Members of the head.** Its milk helps in curing the teeth.

**Members of nourishment.** It harms the stomach and liver, and leads to bile and the transformation into dropsy <note>edema/swelling</note>. And everything that is first infused in the viscera... and is dissolved by these... it dries out. For this reason, one will need a little salt and myrobalan or aloes [to balance it], and it provides help to the sounds.

**Members of expulsion.** It purges only phlegm, melancholy, and water. And if its administration is usual for laxatives, it was afterwards diminished because it harms sexual intercourse and sperm, and because it disrupts the veins of the anus. And for this reason, its rectification is made... it is infused in a hollowed-out quince or a... for a time, and it is renewed many times. This weakens it and destroys its operation in all bad ways. If it is found to be used, mix it with anise, fennel, and cumin. And of it we take in drink up to 4 [scruples]. Regarding its herb: in its milk there is no... and it is not seen to be given in drink, and it flows only upon the... which should be hidden by sitting in cold water. And when it is given in drink for colic, it is drunk with salt ammoniac, bdellium, and... and a little salt, as narrated in the chapter on colic.

**Fevers.** It repels those fevers that are generated.

**Poison.** A weight of two [ounces/drachms] of it acts as a poison.

# Wolfsbane <note>original: "Strangulatori adib"; from the Arabic *ad-di'b* (wolf). This refers to *Aconitum lycoctonum* or Wolfsbane</note>, which is: "I cut through."
It is the flesh of the wolf among the ancient and old ones, and it is pure. 
It is [artificial/harmful] and is not administered internally, nor externally <note>A warning about the extreme toxicity of Aconite</note>.

# Willow <note>original: "Salix"</note>, which is: It rises toward the sun when they [the branches] split; it has a strong gum. **Operations and properties.** Its fruit and leaves are <term>styptic</term> <note>styptic: an agent that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</note> without a stinging sensation. 
And for them, drying is sufficient. And its juice is of a vehement drying nature. 
And when made into <term>plasters</term> <note>plaster: a soft, heated mass applied to the body as medicine</note> against heat, it retains the flow of blood. And when its leaves are split, there is gathered from it a gum of vehement [astringency] which is [soothing]. **The Belly.** Its juice eradicates warts and helps when used with vinegar. **Wounds and ulcers.** Plasters are made from it for major wounds, both from its fruit and its leaves. 
And its ash removes calluses when it is smeared on with vinegar. **Organs of the head.** Its decoction in its own water is sedative for various pains. And there is nothing more effective than the juice of its leaves in the cavity of the ear when it [the ear] aches. **Organs of the eye.** The fruit is placed in its water over the [film] of the pupil. And its gum greatly benefits weak vision. **Organs of nutrition.** Its decoction benefits obstructions of the liver and jaundice. **Organs of expulsion.** Its fruit, strongly decocted, stops the flow of blood.

# Sardinian Plant <note>original: "Sardicus"; possibly *Ranunculus sceleratus*</note>. **Organs of the head.** Its oil is valid for ear pain when it is poured into the ear. And similarly its "body" [the plant material] when it is thoroughly pounded.

# Dross <note>original: "Scoria"; the slag or byproduct of smelting metals</note>. **Selection.** The dross of the strongest drying power is iron dross. **Nature.** Iron dross is dry in the [second] degree. **Organs of nutrition.** Iron dross strengthens the stomach and dries its superfluities; it moves [the bowels] to soften them when it is prepared in wine or water, or drunk with wine. 
**Organs of expulsion.** Iron dross prohibits the flow of bleeding hemorrhoids. When the patient sits in wine or water in which it has been soaked, it prohibits [conception] and prevents a [uterine] flux of blood, and it is the ultimate remedy for this.

### Tarragon <note>original: "Tarascon"; likely *Tarchon* or *Artemisia dracunculus* (Tarragon)</note>.
Tarragon, which is: It is well known what species this is in the teachings. **Nature.** It is cold in the second <term>degree</term> <note>Medical theory classified substances by 'degrees' of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness from 1 to 4</note> and its moisture is similar; elsewhere it is said to be in the first degree of moisture. **Operations and virtues.** It is cooling, similar to celery. **Organs of the eye.** It helps to wipe away white spots in the eye <note>original: "albugines"; cataracts or corneal scars</note>. **Organs of nutrition.** And its juice is very helpful for dropsy and it opens obstructions of the liver. **Poisons.** It resists poisons. <unclear>...</unclear> it is made into a <term>plaster</term> for stings. <unclear>...</unclear> for the sting of a scorpion.

### Marking Nut <note>original: "Anacardis"; the *Anacardium occidentale* or more likely the *Semecarpus anacardium*, known for its caustic juice used to mark fabric and treat skin</note>.
Marking Nut. **Operations and virtues.** Within it, there is a binding property and a restraint in cleansing. It wipes away "figs" <note>original: "ficus"; a common medieval term for external fleshy growths or hemorrhoids</note> and warts. And also its water is cleansing and drying; the water derived from it is more drying than the nut itself. And just as its drying property is for binding, so its fruit and medicine are used for stings. And it is so great that it is like balsam, and among other things, it is powerful for unifying wounds in place of green <term>gallnuts</term> <note>gallnuts: growths on oak trees used for their high tannin content to stop bleeding</note>. **Decoration.** And a <term>decoction</term> <note>decoction: a concentrated liquor made by boiling herbal material</note> of it brightens ivory, for those who fight <note>original: "preliatios"; possibly referring to ivory chess pieces or warriors' gear</note> and for their justice. **Preparation and washing.** If it is dissolved and placed on the head, it stops a discharge. **Wounds and ulcers.** And just as it dries moist ulcers when they are loose. And just as vinegar in it dries difficult ulcers, it eats away all excess flesh. **Organs of the head.** A decoction of its leaves in wine helps the pain of the teeth; a mouthwash made from it helps with "figs" of the mouth, if one has them. **Organs of the eye.** And the fruit stands in the place of gallnut for diseases of the eye. **Organs of breath and chest.** It helps with chronic spitting of phlegm, made from its fruit. **Organs of nutrition.** If indeed they are dissolved in vinegar, a plaster made from them helps the spleen. And for the spleen, one drinks wine in which its leaves have been boiled. And vessels for those with spleen issues are made from its wood. **Organs of excretion.** It helps with pain of the anus. And one sits in a decoction of it to aid the flow of the womb <note>original: "matas"; shorthand for *matrice* (womb/menses)</note>. ### Medicinal Earths <note>original: "Tera"; referring to medicinal clays like Terra Sigillata</note>
What they are: They are found in the chapters of our primary sources. In them, there is acidity and a certain bitterness, and they have a pungent taste. **Selection.** The better of them are the white sandy earths, in which there is no bad odor. Those that are dry and earthy are [by nature] moist. Those that are extracted through dregs and filtration with hazelnut water and salt water, and then cooked with oil—which some call *almun resep* <note>a corrupted technical term for a processed oil</note> or *alif*—are the best. And also in their genus are the mushrooms <note>original: "fungi"</note>, which grow under trees and in poor soil. **Operations and virtues.** They are very caustic <note>original: "causa"; likely meaning "constricting" or "heavy"</note>, and they nourish those who suffer from melancholy; one should not approach them [without caution]. Their antidotes <note>original: "tyriaci"</note> are pure wine and warming spices. And if they are boiled and then cooked with these, they produce nourishment that resists bad humors, though they have no taste of their own. **Organs of the joints.** Paralysis is feared from [the misuse of] them. **Organs of the head.** Apoplexy results from them. **Organs of the eye.** A flow of water is caused by them in the eye, particularly in those who are washed; this is restored by the best doctors and others. **Organs of nutrition.** They are slow to digest and heavy; they generate a thick and burnt <term>chyme</term> <note>the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</note>. Galen, however, says in a certain place that they are not of bad humor. **Organs of excretion.** They cause colic and difficulty in passing urine.

### Tortoise <note>original: "Estudo/Testudo"</note>
**Organs of the head.** Its blood, which is like that of the sturgeon, is said to be beneficial for epilepsy in youths. And the gall of the tortoise is effective for eye-salves <note>original: "cola"; likely collyria</note> and is dripped into the nostrils of those suffering from epilepsy. **Organs of breath and respiration.** Its egg is good for a persistent cough, and its gall is applied to scrofulous ulcers <note>original: "scrofulas"; swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck</note>. **Poisons.** That which is prepared with manna and [garlic] is a remedy for poisonous wine and for those who have drunk henbane <note>original: "latiamum"; likely hyoscyamus</note>.

<margin>Tench in nature <note>The tench (Tinca) is a fish often associated with medicinal properties</note></margin>
### Yew <note>original: "Taxa/Taxus"; the text describes it as hot/dry, though the margin notes "Tench"</note>
**Selection.** The best is that which is lighter in weight and more intensely black by nature. It is entirely hot and drying, both in its raw state and in its powdered form; it never contains any internal coldness. **Operations and virtues.** It is entirely drying. It opens that which is blocked. ### Almonds <note>original: "Amandi/Amygdalae"; the text compares them to prunes</note>
**Selection.** The better ones are the fresh ones, not those that have reached old age, for those are dried out and their acidity is too strong. **Nature.** They are cold and dry in the second <term>degree</term>. **Operations and virtues.** They are laxative; they are more "subtle" <note>refined/easily absorbed</note> than common plums and have less moisture. **Organs of nutrition.** It benefits those with a multitude of bilious humors and fevers, and it soothes a cold stomach that has been made raw by excessive vomiting. **Organs of excretion.** It loosens the bowels effectively, and wine made from their decoction should be taken in the amount of half a pound. **Fevers.** It helps in burning fevers accompanied by fainting and flux, because its nature is light and cooling.

### Germander <note>original: "Teden/Teucrium"</note>
Which is called *Iugo* by Dioscorides <note>the 1st-century Greek physician</note>; it is an herb having leaves similar to the leaves of horehound <note>original: "prassium"</note> and a square root. And when mixed with wax and myrtle oil, it benefits ulcers...

## Manna <note>original: "Teraniabin"; from the Persian *taranjubin*, a medicinal manna</note>. What it is:
It is a dew that falls mostly on the "marosca" <note>likely a type of thorny shrub, *Alhagi maurorum*</note> in places near rivers. And it falls mostly in our region upon stones. **Selection.** The white, grainy kind is better. **Nature.** It is a substance naturally balanced toward heat. **Operations and virtues.** It is a soothing substance suitable for clearing the throat. **Organs of the breath and chest.** It helps the cough and soothes the chest. **Organs of nutrition.** It quenches thirst. **Organs of expulsion.** It loosens and draws out bile easily, especially when taken with the skin that is found upon it. And its dosage is from 10 aurei <note>a unit of weight or currency used here as a measurement</note> to 20 aurei.

## Tutty <note>original: "Tucia"; a medicinal zinc oxide collected from smelting furnaces</note>. What it is:
It is the soot of the smoke that rises when metals are purified, and the stones that assist in this, and the slag that is made from them. And when it is refined, it is made into a powder. That which is refined is white tutty, and that which remains at the bottom is *climia* <note>cadmia or zinc dross</note> which is not as effective. Common tutty is white, another is yellow, and another inclines toward redness. And it is said that what is gathered during the washing process is like the dregs in the water used for washing, which is more pleasant. The difference between the "pleasant" kind and tutty is that tutty is refined [sublimated] and the other is not refined, but remains at the bottom in the channels through which the copper flows. And this is like the *climia* of the copper. And that which is refined is refined from the "coruna" <note>the furnace or crucible</note>. **Selection.** The best is the white, "flying" kind, which is easy to crumble, and has the color of pistachio or henna. And that which is not old is better than all others. **Nature.**

<column-break/>

Cold in the third degree, dry in the second. **Operations and virtues.** It is of a drying nature without causing stinging. And that which is washed helps ulcers so that they are healed into scars. **Organs of the eye.** It helps with eye pain and prevents harmful fluids from being constricted in the veins of the eye or entering the tunics; especially that which is washed. **Organs of expulsion.** It helps with ulcers in the intestines and their parts. It is helpful. One type is mineral and another is artificial, which is called "gold-binding" <note>original: "capistrum auri"; likely chrysocolla or a similar flux used in metalworking</note>. **Organs of the head.** It helps with toothache and the erosion of the teeth by its potency.

### Asmarach. Its nature.
It is hot and dry. **Operations and virtues.** It is a strong cleanser.

### Iusa. Its nature.
It is dry and removes white spots from the eye. And a plaster made from its fat is placed over its own bite, and it cuts the pain immediately.

### Myrobalan <note>original: "Embul"; likely the Emblic Myrobalan or Indian gooseberry</note>. Varieties.
It is cold in the third degree, dry in the second. **Operations and virtues.** It is astringent and drying. **Organs of the head.** It strengthens the flesh found at the roots of the teeth. And if it is chewed for a long time, it always helps with that. **Organs of nutrition.** It strengthens the stomach, and it should be chewed for a long time.

### Euphorbium <note>original: "Efise"; a caustic resin derived from spurge plants</note>. What it is.
It is a gum... [referring to a previous mention]. **Selection.** Do not overlook the green and fresh kind. And when it is placed on a part of the body, it weakens the ancient [condition], as it is a cleanser that helps and dissolves humors, which are superfluous impurities. **Nature.** It is very hot and caustic, having a quality of heating and drying. And in it there is a superfluous moisture that is dried out, yet it does not sting immediately. **Operations and virtues.** It is cleansing, dissolving, thinning, and breaking down; it does not gather its superfluous moisture except over a long time. And it is among those things that draw out or extract from the depths of the body, though it takes time due to its superfluous moisture, and it does not act instantly because of its heat. **Decoration.** It makes hair grow and helps greatly with alopecia. And it is never used except with oil. And we have already mentioned its uses in the third chapter. And it helps with the hidden flow of blood, provided it is not left on the part for too long, lest it burn and leave marks, especially on white skin. **Instruments of the joints.** It is joined with compounds such as those that soften the nerves and for sciatica, and it is mixed with cold things. And it is used as a liniment for joint pain <note>original: "arteticam"; refers to gout or general arthritis</note>.

# **Grapes** <note>original: "Uııe," likely referring to Uva or wild grapes</note>
**What it is:** It is as Pliny describes it. Under the "dog grape" <note>nightshade or wild bryony</note> is the white kind. It is said to be more hot in its nature.

### **Operations and virtues.**
It is cleansing, purifying, and opening to the pores.

### **Eliminative organs.**
The medical weight of it resolves difficulty of urine. A weight of 5 drams <note>the symbol '3' indicates a dram</note> expels both living and dead fetuses. A dose of half a dram up to 3 drams provokes the menses. A dose of 3 drams is a laxative that draws out water in cases of dropsy <note>original: "hydro pı," or edema</note> in this way.

### **Poisons.**
A weight of 5 drams is effective against the poison of pests. And from a fumigation <note>burning and inhaling the smoke</note> with wine, it is seen to put to flight poisonous creatures.

# **Nettle** <note>original: "Urtıca"</note>
**What it is:** The color of its seed is similar to the seed of a leek. It is found in stable places <note>common on disturbed ground near human habitation</note>; it is long in its growth. It bites <note>stings</note> whatever it touches, and even affects the intestines.

### **Nature.**
Nettles are hot in the third degree and dry in the second. The seed is of less dryness than the plant itself.

### **Operations and virtues.**
It is astringent, burning, and resolving with a caustic power. And there are some who say its heating is not foundational. It is used for opening [sores], and its leaf is used for the cleansing of biting ulcers. And when it is cooked with meat, the meat dissolves <note>a historical observation of the enzymes in nettles</note> through its operations.

### **Treatment of Abscesses.**
A plaster of it with raisins dissipates hardness and helps with swellings. And its seed helps with cancer when used for a long time, as well as with "cyanus" <note>likely bluish skin discolorations</note>.

### **Wounds and ulcers.**
With salt, it helps ulcers that happen from dog bites, as well as malignant ulcers and cancers.

### **Instruments of the joints.**
A plaster made from it with salt helps with the twisting of the nerves <note>original: "toz sıoı̃ ūuoı̃," likely gout or muscle spasms</note>.

### **Organs of the head.**
The burnt leaves cut off the flow of blood from the nostrils. Its seed helps with the blockage of the nostrils and opens severe obstructions. And from its seed

<column-break/>

a plaster is made; it is recommended for the eradication of teeth <note>to loosen a tooth for removal</note>. A plaster of it also helps with abscesses behind the ears and is a cleansing agent.

### **Organs of the breath and chest.**
When drunk with barley water, it cleanses the chest. And when its leaves are cooked in barley water, they draw out the thick humors <note>original: "ııuõ re8 crostıos," thick phlegm</note> that are in the chest. Its seed is very strong; it removes asthma and the dilation or constriction of the chest.

### **Eliminative organs.**
It excites sexual intercourse <note>original: "excıtat coııtū"</note> especially the seed taken in wine, and it opens the mouth of the womb so that it receives the sperm. When applied as a suppository with myrrh, it provokes the menses and draws the womb [into place]. A decoction of it with myrrh is beneficial, and its fresh leaves, when placed as a plaster, return a displaced womb to its location. As a laxative, it draws out phlegm and raw humors by its cleansing power and its natural dissolving virtue. Its oil dissolves phlegm more than the oil of safflower. A decoction of the leaves with shells <note>original: "o stııııı8," likely crushed sea shells</note> softens the belly. And if you wish it to dissolve [the humors] in this way, take the marrow of its seed, mix it with lye <note>original: "lıuııch"</note>, put it in a tube, and drink it. One should drink something of oil afterward so that it does not burn the throat. When it is rolled with honey and applied as a suppository, it resolves [internal issues].

# **Urine** <note>original: "Urina"</note>
**What it is:** It is well known. Most authors agree that among the urines of living creatures, the urine of the Arabian camel is the most potent, which is called *negib* <note>original: "negib," from the Arabic 'najib,' meaning noble or excellent</note>. Human urine is weaker than most other urines, yet the urine of domestic castrated pigs is even weaker. Generally, the urine of any castrated animal is weaker than its uncastrated counterpart. Among all, human urine is the most frequently used.

**Nature:** It is hot and dry.

### **Operations and virtues.**
It is entirely cleansing <note>original: "absterget," meaning it wipes away impurities</note>. Human urine, especially when applied with its sediment <note>original: "ande," likely referring to the dregs or 'amurca' of the liquid</note>, helps at the site of a blood flow to stop it. Camel urine is beneficial for fissures <note>cracks in the skin</note> when washed with it. Bull urine acts similarly.

### **Beauty.**
It wipes away morphea <note>original: "morfeũ," a skin condition involving painless, discolored patches</note>.

### **Wounds and ulcers.**
Ass’s urine is beneficial for spreading and moist ulcers. Human urine is used for the same, especially that from a healthy person who has not been drinking much. It is used for "white spots" <note>likely leucoma or skin depigmentation</note> when mixed with glass <note>powdered glass was a common abrasive in medieval medicine</note>, or with water and vinegar. It is also applied to erysipelas <note>original: "crisipilã," a bacterial skin infection causing a red rash</note>, and when smeared on, it helps with running sores and ulcers of the feet. For dark ulcers, it is mixed with ash.

### **Organs of urination and joints.** <note>original: "Instrum̃tu micturini," though the context discusses joint pain (iuncturarum)</note>
It is beneficial for pain in the joints, particularly the urine of domestic goats. Likewise, urine is used for spasms and tensions <note>original: "extũsioĩ"</note>. Similarly, it is used as a head purge for tension.

### **Members of the head.**
Bull’s urine, when dissolved with myrrh <note>original: "mura"</note>, is dropped into the ear to soothe pain effectively. Goat’s urine alone does the same. Old human urine stops the flow of putrid matter from the ear. Camel urine, when cooked, helps with the stench of the nostrils and opens obstructions of the ethmoid bone <note>original: "collatorij"</note> when used with a strong scent.

### **Members of the eye.**
It helps with "coagulations" <note>cataracts or thick humors</note> in the eye; it also treats albugo <note>white spots on the cornea</note> and scabies of the eye. This is especially true of the urine of young boys. It is similarly effective when mixed with the dregs mentioned before.

### **Members of breath and chest.**
The urine of nursing infants is beneficial for the dilation of the breath <note>asthma or shortness of breath</note>.

### **Nutritive members.**
Human urine is extraordinarily helpful for those with spleen issues; it was observed that a patient would drink his own urine every day while dreaming that he should do so. He began this practice and found it to be a miraculous cure. Both human and camel urine are beneficial for dropsy <note>original: "ydropisi," or swelling caused by fluid retention</note>. It is especially effective for a hard spleen or the beginning of dropsy. Dog urine is particularly moving <note>purgative</note>, especially when it has a sharp smell. Likewise, old pig urine mixed with strong wine is used for these conditions.

### **Expulsive members.**

<column-break/>

Human urine breaks stones in the kidneys and bladder and provokes them to be expelled from the body. Ass's urine is beneficial for kidney pain. Human urine, when collected and used in a sitz bath <note>original: "sedet in ea"</note> by women once every five days, helps with uterine ailments.

### **Poisons.**
Human urine, when drunk, is beneficial against the bite of a viper and should also be poured over the wound. This is particularly true if the person has eaten stony plants <note>possibly Lithospermum or similar</note>. Mixed with nitre <note>natural soda</note>, it is effective against the bite of a rabid dog and for all bites and punctures. Old urine is an antidote for all poisons, including sea-hare <note>a toxic marine mollusk</note>.

# **Usnea** <note>original: "Usnea," refers to tree moss or lichen</note>
**What it is:** It is a moss. It is a certain growth similar to a black moss found on the surface of round trees, growing in clusters. It is found on trees like the cedar, the fir, and the apple tree, or in places where there is much water and moisture.

**Selection:** The best is that which is fragrant, flat, and light in color; the others are less effective.

**Nature:** It is cold and dry in the second degree, though some say it is slightly warm. It is composed of a watery substance and a superfluity of digested moisture. It is generally considered cold and dry in the first degree.

### **Operations and virtues.**
It is a resolvent <note>it breaks down humors</note>. It resolves various humors whether applied externally or taken internally. It has a strengthening and soothing effect. It is said that when used as an ointment, it settles the nerves.

### **Beauty.**
It eradicates bad nails <note>fungal infections</note> when applied with arsenic.

### **Abscesses and swellings.**
It resolves cold abscesses and comforts the heat within them.

### **Wounds and ulcers.**
It soothes old ulcers and those that are malignant.

### **Urinary organs.**
It eases urination when applied with wax, especially when mixed with pine resin.

### **Members of the head.**
It is beneficial for cold abscesses of the ear when mixed with oil of pomegranate.

### **Nutritive members.**
It eliminates issues of the spleen when placed upon it with other strengthening things, such as figs.

<margin>acorns</margin>

# **Vermiculus** <note>original: "Vermiculus," literally 'little worm,' referring to the Kermes insect</note>
**What it is:** It is a type of insect. It is one of those mentioned previously; some say it is like the "hundred-legged" worm <note>centipede</note>, but it is more powerful and penetrates deeper. Others say this little worm is collected from various parts, specifically from trees that bear acorns <note>original: "gladios," but the margin clarifies "glandes" or acorns; Kermes insects live on the Kermes oak</note>.

**Nature:** This genus of worm is purple in color and is drying in its nature. Galen says that there is a moderate numbing <note>original: "stup'iacas"</note> quality in it.

**Wounds and ulcers.**
This little worm is beneficial for wounds of the nerves when applied with wine or vinegar.

## Frankincense. Nature.
**Frankincense. Nature.** <note>original: "Olibanus"</note> It is hot and dry in the fourth degree <note>Medieval medicine ranked the intensity of a plant's "complexion" from 1 to 4</note>, and it has a cleansing property. **Operations and properties.** It is resolutive and opening. And note that it is not fatty but brings about extreme dryness; it is igneous <note>fiery</note> in nature, but its drying power destroys its watery parts, and it never fails to cleanse. **Decoration.** <note>Beauty treatments</note> It makes the hair grow and prevents lice. **Wounds and ulcers.** The leaves are beneficial for large wounds, especially when cooked in wine. A plaster made from them is applied to "Persian fire" <term>ignis Persicus: a term for shingles or similar burning skin rashes</term>, which is called acute. **The Head.** When distilled, it quickly takes away pain in the ear, especially when mixed with rose oil or leek juice. It also helps with old, chronic wounds of the head. **The Respiratory organs and chest.** It is useful for the chest and lungs and cleanses the breath. **Nutritive organs.** It removes obstructions of the liver. And its leaves with vinegar are good for the spleen. **The Excretory organs.** In a certain solution, it draws out "burnt choler" <term>choler: yellow bile, one of the four humors</term>. Sometimes it is used in a thick solution to stop the flow of blood.

## Shepherd’s Rod.
**Shepherd’s Rod.** <note>original: "Virga pastoris," referring to the Teasel plant</note> There are male and female varieties; the male is stronger. **Operations and properties.** It is helpful when applied. Because of its great repulsive power, it thins the flow of matter because it is drying. **Wounds and ulcers.** A plaster is made from it for skin ulcers and sores 

<column-break/>

of the face. It is used to open and cleanse the womb. It consolidates and heals recent wounds. **The Head.** Its juice dries out ulcers of the scalp. **The Respiratory organs and chest.** It is useful for those who cough up blood. **Nutritive organs.** A plaster is made from it for inflammations to cool them down. **The Excretory organs.** It checks the flow of blood from the bowels or ulcers of the intestines. It is used for those with a prolapsed anus; it provokes urine and aids digestion, and it helps to regulate the menses.

## Raisins. Nature.
**Raisins. Nature.** <note>original: "Uva sicca"</note> They are hot and moist in nature. **Operations and properties.** They are helpful for various conditions. **The Head.** They benefit the gums and the color of the teeth. **The Eyes.** The juice is used for thinness of the sight and clears away film or "white" <term>albugo: a white opacity of the cornea</term> from the pupil. **Nutritive organs.** They help with obstructions of the liver, especially when taken with starch and white gum.

## Grapes.
**Grapes. Nature.** <note>original: "Uva"</note> White grapes are more praiseworthy than black ones, as they contain more nourishment. Regarding their collection: those gathered two or three days after ripening are better than those gathered at the same hour they ripened. **Nature.** The skin is cold and dry. **Operations and properties.** Grapes gathered immediately are flatulent <note>cause gas</note>. Their nourishment is similar to the nourishment of figs. They are very nourishing, though they can be harmful if not fully mature. When a grape is old, its nourishment is "dry." **Nutritive organs.** Raisins are a friend to the liver and stomach. **The Excretory organs.** Grapes are used for pain of the intestines. And raisins benefit the kidneys and bladder. Grapes collected at the same hour they ripen move the belly and cause bloating. And all grapes, if eaten in excess, may harm the bladder.

## Vutros.
**Vutros.** <note>Possibly a corruption of "Vitis" (the Vine) or a specific grape variety</note> **Operations and properties.** Old grapes are very nutritive, but they do not digest quickly in the stomach. **Nutritive organs.** They provide the highest nourishment.

## Iris, what it is:

It is the root of the heavenly lily <note>original: "lily celesti," referring to the Blue Iris or Iris florentina</note>. And its essence is produced from this; its flowers are of diverse colors, from white and yellow to celestial blue and purple. And they are called "Iris" after the rainbow <note>original: "arc' cuis," the bow of the sky</note>. And then the roots are knotty, and its leaves are small. And when they are old, they are better for use. 

### **Selection.** 

Which is of moderate heat. It is diverse, tending toward a pale or compact brown, declining somewhat toward redness. It should have a light odor, not smelling too much of sleep-inducing things. And it is biting to the tongue, moving the saliva with its strength. 

### **Nature.** 

It is hot and dry at the end of its degree. 

### **Operation and Benefits.**

It is digestive, spiritual, and cleansing. And its juice is dissolved with honey-water, and it purges thick phlegm and leads it out. 

### **Beauty.** 

With equal parts of liquid hellebore, it cleanses the skin of spots and freckles, and makes the face clear. 

### **Obstruction of the Liver.** 

That which is from it softens hardness and thick obstructions of the liver, and scrofula <term>scrofula: a swelling of the lymph nodes, usually in the neck</term>, and it eases the bowels. 

### **Wounds and Ulcers of the Eyes.** 

It helps foul ulcers, for it makes flesh grow in fistulas <term>fistula: an abnormal passage or hole in the body tissue</term>, if it is powdered, and it consumes proud flesh. 

### **Instruments of Youth.**

Its oil resolves weariness, and when drunk with vinegar or wine, it helps with spasms. It is used in milk, and from its extract, it is used against gout. 

### **Headache.** 

It induces sleep and removes old headaches. And when it is mixed with rose oil and vinegar, it is effective for many types of headache. And a mouthwash made from its decoction soothes the pain of teeth. Its decoction is beneficial and serves to promote love.

# Ypericon <note>St. John’s Wort</note>
In Arabic it is called *alhanb*. In Syriac it is named *una demois*, which means "Blood of the Demon" <note>likely a reference to the red juice of the crushed flowers</note>. It has a stem and a dusty flower. Its sign is that it tends toward a dark red color. Its figure is like that of sumac, but it is less red. **Selection.** It is healthy in a drink made from its seeds, or from its flowers alone. **Nature.** It is hot and dry at the end of the degree. **Operations and Properties.** It is a thinning, opening, liquefying, and resolving agent. **Abscesses and Tumors.** It is useful for cold, hard, and large swellings. **Wounds and Ulcers.** A plaster made of its leaves is beneficial for fire burns and solidifies great wounds and evil ulcers. When it is held and powdered over a wound, it helps rotting and putrid limbs. **For Scrofula and Sciatica.** It is beneficial for the color of the face and the skin. A decoction made with wine, when drunk for forty consecutive days, heals sciatica <note>original: "scaticā"</note>. **Expulsive Organs.** It provokes urine and the menses; such is its property. In a solution, it draws out choler. **Note.** Its location is placed in the house of the frequent [remedies], and that which is taken from the root is used.

# Moist Oesypum <note>original: "Sopus huida," referring to Oesypum, or crude wool grease/lanolin</note>

# Edania <note>likely Doronicum or Leopard’s Bane</note>

In my opinion, it is a species that resists Monkshood. **Poison.** It is a theriac <term>theriac: a universal antidote or "wonder drug" against poison</term> against poisons.

## Juzaber <note>from the Arabic *Juz al-barr*, likely the Wild Nut or Nux Vomica</note>. What it is.

## Zuzar <note>likely *Ziniar* or *Zujar*, meaning Verdigris or copper rust</note>. What it is.
The species for making *zuzar* [verdigris] are when one scrapes copper... and moistens it with oil and vinegar, and buries it in a moist place. Or one may take scrapings of copper and place them over a vessel... so that *zuzar* is made from it. And it is also made with sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used as a flux in metallurgy and in medicine</term> and burial in a moist place as is known. And if you wish to make *zuzar* very well, take vinegar of cinnabar, and mix it in a bronze mortar with a bronze pestle, and let it sit in the hot sun... until it thickens. It is composed with alum and salt in measure. When it is made, it dries. It is placed upon... then it is healthy. It is kept in a moist place... and when it dries, it is gathered. Frequently *zuzar* is found growing on stones in great numbers. And it is found in common use.

### Selection.
That which is better is... of a green color. And it has a sharp taste because it is made with sal ammoniac.

# Sugar
**What it is.** The sugar cane... it is used for its soothing and smoothing qualities. **Nature. Cold** <note>The text notes a debate on its temperament</note> **and it is subtle. It functions differently than other types of sugar, for its sweetness is light on the stomach and the liver. **Excretory members.** It benefits the kidneys and the bladder.

## Gingania
**Gingania. What it is:** I say that Gingania <note>This likely refers to *Agrostemma githago*, commonly known as Corn Cockle or Gith, a common weed in grain fields</note> is named after darnel <note>original: "ioliis," referring to *Lolium temulentum*, a grass often infected with a toxic fungus</note> for two reasons. One of them is the "silius" <note>perhaps a reference to a specific variety of grain-weed</note> from which various small breads are made. It is said that Gingania is very common; some avoid it because it is a "bad honey" <note>original: "melia iocē malā"</note> which generates heavy pain. **Selection.** The better kind is that which is lighter than those previously mentioned, not fragile. If it is viscous when chewed and inclining toward a reddish color, it is not of a small nature.

## Metel Nut
**Metel nut. What it is:** It is a poison. That is, it is a stupefying substance <term>stupefactive: a drug that induces a state of stupor, numbness, or insensibility</term> similar to the "wolf nut" <note>likely a reference to *Aconitum* (Monkshood) or another toxic "nux"</note> which has short, sharp spines. It is a thing similar to the Nux Vomica <note>The "Strychnine tree," though here it likely refers to *Datura metel*, the Thorn-apple</note>, and its seed is similar to the seed of the latter. **Special Opinions.** It is stupefying. It harms the head and causes foolishness <note>original: "stultit," referring to delirium or madness</note> through its evil bitterness. It is a poison. It is harmful to the heart. It is called a poison for this reason.

## Lupins
**Lupins. What they are:** It is a complex-shaped, bitter grain like a lentil, pressed flat in the middle, and it is the "Egyptian bean." **Selection.** The wild kind is stronger in its virtues than the cultivated one. **Nature.** It is hot in the second degree. **Special Opinions.** It is styptic <term>styptic: capable of contracting tissues or stopping bleeding</term> in its power. And the bitterness of the lupin is of a resolving nature <term>resolving: a quality that breaks down or disperses "morbid" matter in the body</term> without being stinging. Regarding this, Galen says: When the bitterness is removed from the lupin by water, it is edible, but it remains long in the stomach as a gluey substance. Because of this, it is difficult to digest and generates "gross" <note>thick or sluggish</note> humors in those who do not digest it well. Those who hate the smell or sweetness <gloss>the flavor after processing</gloss> find it to be a great medicine. When the decoction is well-prepared, it is good for bad humors. **Beautification.** It thins the hair and cleanses the skin of pustules and facial spots <note>original: "morfee," likely skin discolorations</note>. It should be boiled with water until it dissolves. **Aid and scent.** It provides a wash for the face to cleanse it. The decoction, when infused, is beneficial for cancerous sores and their condition. **Red wounds.**

# Or the part concerning fevers, and there are four types.
## The first treatise on ephemeral fever.

<margin>
Question
regarding
fever
---
sharpness
</margin>

<image-desc>A large ornamental initial 'F' in red and blue ink, decorated with white cross motifs and delicate floral and vine filigree patterns characteristic of high-quality medieval manuscript illumination.</image-desc>

**Fever** is an extraneous <note>original: "extraneus," meaning heat originating from outside the natural balance of the body</note> heat kindled in the heart; and a part of it is spread from the heart by means of the spirit <term>spiritus: in medieval medicine, this refers to the "vital breath" or subtle substance that carries life through the arteries</term> and the blood through the veins and arteries into the whole body. It is inflamed by an inflammation that harms the natural functions. This heat is not like the warmth of movement or the labors of the soul, which also inflame, but it hinders natural operations so that they cannot remain steady. And according to this state, fever is divided into two primary divisions: namely, into accidental fever and disease-based fever. Accidental fevers are sometimes called "sharpness," because accidental fevers are named for the way they converge in this discourse. A disease-based fever is that which is caused by an actual illness, and the fever is not the medium here but the result of the rotation. Corruption is its cause without a middle step; now corruption itself is the disease, or rather the cause of the disease. A fever of "sharpness" is a certain cause that follows the sharpness. Thus, the disease is in the spirit itself. And it should be known, as was said above, that the sharpness of the fever follows its heat. It cannot be the color itself; it is similar to an accidental fever, so that it is mostly ephemeral <note>original: "effimere," from the Greek for "lasting a day"</note> or accidental. It is often followed by a "pricking" sensation <note>original: "pūtcōe," likely punctio</note>, because in the beginning, the beginning is not the cause of the sharpness, but rather as if it were pricked. And the actual cause is corruption. Sharpness is the cause of it and the pricking. And it is known that this lightens the accidental fever. Rather, it is understood through it that sharpness follows, and the sharpness announces its arrival. Similarly, the disposition of putrid fevers is through operation and putrefaction. Or rather, in these kinds of descriptions, there are things that do not have anything intermediate, but make a medium part between themselves and the inflammation which perhaps hindered it from before. We have made this easier for those who follow. We shall say, therefore, that those fevers of sharpness and obstruction are "sharp" fevers, and other fevers are actual diseases. It is time to say how both are like a plague following its own path. For there is a movement of heat and moisture in the spirits, which is a calculation of "prickings," baths, moisture, and odors; and the cause is the conjunction of water and the vital spirit coming through the channels, even when they are poured out. There is a calculation of the bile <note>original: "ācr bilia," likely referring to black or yellow bile</note> which persists so that it heats and remains one of these types. If they cause fever in the radical members <note>the fundamental organs or "roots" of the body</note> by a burning heat everywhere in the moist point or by the sun

as the sun burns. Or by an approaching poll <note>possibly a reference to a head-fever</note> in the generation of fevers, it becomes a hectic fever <note>original: "febrica ethica," a fever that dries out the body's solid parts</note>. And if the feverish heat occurs in the humors, then it happens in three ways. This causes it to flow into the heat within the vessels and enter the surrounding parts. Or the hot force takes it into the branches of the vessels. Then the generation of the fever does not change the humor. And if the fever occurs in its movement in the spirits and in the waters, it kindles heat in the members and the moisture, just as it is pricked towards the bile. Because of this, it heats the air within it and pricks the water and the stinging parts.
