And it does not last more than a day or its night; it does not belong to another genus of fevers. The division of fevers is by the way they approach in nutrition or potential events. And fevers are divided in another way: namely, some fevers are acute, and some are in remission, and some are numerous. Some are natural, and some are diurnal <note>occurring daily</note>. And some are healthy... they are inseparable, for they are inseparable from those to whom they belong. And there are those in whom there are intensifications, then those in whom there are fortifications; then they are similar. And some are fleeing... as in an obstruction. These are of three kinds; then they are sharp.

### On the signs of fever

Just as when the body is pricked toward fever, the signs are heat and moisture. In the soul, moisture is the form of heat, not because there are cold sweats in the onset of the illness. And they cause heat and dryness in the onset of hot fevers. Then the pricking appears. They follow the movement toward the point and toward the burning. This causes action in hectic fever, which is balanced in moisture and dryness and double heat. These signs were from the genus of the body in which the fever begins and is heated. The vital air approaches the moist fever; those in whom heat is balanced, then moisture is multiplied. This is regarding putrid fevers and those that begin in cold and moist branches. And the logic of the cause is that it moves from the ephemeral.

### On the locations of fevers

And the cause is thus a sign of the disease. First, the weakness, then the heart and the creatures. And there are those which are pricked, such as through a paroxysm <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or increase in the intensity of a disease or fever</term>, through love <note>original: "āmore," medieval medicine recognized "love-sickness" as a physical ailment</note>, or through pain. It precedes the motion out of the fever, and the cause is told. And first, it is from the anger which the internal heat kindles in the branches. When the mind is not open in the case, they are not divine, nor is the flight finished. And first, that which is in the mind of the whole disease. <meta>The text continues the analysis of how various fevers manifest in the body. While the previous page focused on the internal movement of heat and the initial stages of putrefaction, this page provides diagnostic criteria for distinguishing between "ephemeral" fevers (short-lived) and "putrid" fevers (caused by corrupted humors), specifically looking at the pulse, breathing, and the timing of the fever cycles.</meta>

Likewise, the cause of the heat is a moderate amount of "smoky" vapor; this is the cause of an **ephemeral fever** <note>A "one-day" fever caused by temporary factors like overexposure to sun or exhaustion, rather than deep infection</note>. It is also the precursor to fevers caused by putrefaction, which happen when the humors are collected and stirred.

And short-windedness, which is a state of being dissipated; when the heat in the internal organs does not reach the point of becoming a true fever, it instead manifests as a weariness or fatigue in the extremities. Such a condition is governed by the motion of sleep and the swelling of the humors. At times, this inner heat hinders breathing. It is not necessarily a "venereal" sensation <note>referring to physical desire or excess</note>, but rather a weight or pressure in the head, and a throbbing within the skull. If this condition is prolonged, it causes the patient to fall into **putrid fevers** <note>Fevers resulting from the literal "rotting" or corruption of the bodily fluids</note> or causes an acute illness combined with weakness. This often benefits from a change in the color of the skin. When the nourishment is revolved within the spirit, it falls into a fever that frequently overflows into the stomach, causing nausea, vomiting, or the discharge of much putrid matter, as well as dizziness and exhaustion if the quality of the humors remains disturbed.

The pulse in acute cases is stretched out, either from a loss of strength or from some other cause. <insert>So that a narrowing or constriction occurs in the vessels, and then the power already begins to wane</insert> which is seen in the "shivering" of the pulse <note>original: "s̄brīio pulsūs"; likely sub-vibration or a faltering pulse</note>. These pulses differ in how they happen; they may be large and strong, or faster and stronger, but they are distinguished during the increase of the sickness by signs of putrefaction. Even if this does not appear clearly in the patient's nature, it often appears through the lightness of the "matter" <note>the corrupted humor</note> being purged.

<margin>

</margin>

There are also signs that indicate whether a fever is putrid, such as sweating during the first period of the cycle. This is a sign of an ephemeral fever’s increase, for in that first stage, there is no heavy cause, but rather a lightness that leads it forth. In ephemeral cases, they do not usually proceed to full putrefaction. However, when the fever has been acquired and is already established, it is not so easily dismissed. A great increase in the pulse's magnitude and heat signifies a further increase in the sickness. Moreover, it may be "medullary" <note>deep-seated, as if in the marrow</note> in its beginning, starting with a chill or a blockage and hardness, often accompanied by sweating and a thirst that returns. Or it may be "vesperal" <note>occurring in the evening</note>.

<margin>
Other times
</margin>

In times of ephemeral illness, the urine often returns to a state of being cleansed and modified. And when several symptoms occur at once, such as a headache, a blackened tongue, and multiplied restlessness, it signifies an increase in the struggle of the "matter" <note>the humor causing the disease</note> which is about to break. This is why the patient raises their hand, as if trying to flee the heat. The pulse then tends toward greatness and strength, or toward smallness and weakness. When the pulse is hard, it is almost always a sign of a fever associated with an abscess or a hard swelling in a limb. This hardness may also be caused by the application of cold water or something else that hardens the pulse. The <insert>diversity in these</insert> pulses and their increase comes from the presence of putrid fevers and their powerful signs. Even if it appears to the natural sense to be very light to the hand, if the pulse is strong, it should not be fast.

<column-break/>

With the aforementioned speed, an ephemeral fever does not advance to full corruption. This is because the matter at the beginning is not yet "digested" <note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" or "concoction" refers to the body's process of ripening and neutralizing harmful humors</note>. It may perhaps be an acute fever. <term>And it should be known</term> <note>original: "Et sciā"; a standard scholarly formula used to introduce an important rule</note> that in acute fevers, the evacuation of the bowels is a form of relief. This does not happen in the internal organs themselves, but rather the fever is alleviated when the "filthy" matter is moved toward the place where the pain first appeared.

### Insensible signs of fever.

This section treats the declarations of the pulse which make a fever very apparent. For the most part, these things cannot be described in words, but the fever is raised and remains within the vessels of the humors. Nature is strengthened by what we call the "radical" dispositions <note>referring to the "radical moisture," the fundamental life-fluid believed to sustain the body's heat</note>, as seen in the blackness or darkness of the signs. These signs signify the cause is a persistent and sharp conflict at the beginning of the sickness’s expansion. It changes when...

### On the things in which certain fevers differ. He says it is seen.

In a fever that comes from the putrefaction of **choler** <note>Yellow bile, associated with hot and dry qualities</note>, there is a movement of nature toward the beginning of the vessels. Or there is a burning sensation, for these fevers are scorched. This movement is toward the vessels of the site, as seen in the "shivering" of the pulse. **Tertian fever** <note>A fever that spikes every third day</note>, which is caused by putrefaction, does not have a natural prevalence; rather, the heat is great and moderates itself according to the nature of the choler. This heat is such that it may be light to the touch, but it is deep within the nature as it digests.

### Tertian Fever

Natural tertian fever is always associated with the spirit. It can be "pure" or "not pure." A pure tertian fever is one that follows a regular cycle of three days, rather than an erratic one. Its opposite is a fever that lasts a whole week. That which comes from the putrefaction of blood involves the spirit and the "black" humors. Its heat is often relieved and moderated by the choler. When putrefaction occurs in these treatments, it is said that **Phlegmatic** <note>Related to the humor phlegm, which is cold and moist</note> fevers happen every day. This is from a very cold humor that lasts a long time because of its lack of speed. It is characterized by a great multitude of humors. When the corruption of the spirit is involved in the cycle, it is because it is absorbed by the corrupted heat. This leads to bad symptoms arising from the flow of fluids. This type is more similar to "hectic" fever <note>a chronic, wasting fever</note>, but is generally more diffuse even if it becomes hard. It is not a "pure" fever because of the motion of the putrid humors.

### Quartan Fever

As for the cycles: **Quartan fever** <note>A fever that spikes every fourth day</note> is not soul-driven but is a long phlegmatic <note>Note: usually Quartan is associated with Melancholy/Black Bile, but the text here links it to a long phlegmatic duration</note> condition that perhaps extends for a year. The cycles are shorter than the spirit's cycles, but they create a swelling over a long period because they follow a sequence of fast-moving accidents.

### Quotidian Fever

**Quotidian fever** <note>A fever that occurs every day</note> is a persistent illness that is not "expelled" but arises from "smoky" vapors, often originating in the stomach or the belly. Or...

The cure for these <term>Epialos and Liparia: types of continuous fevers; Epialos involves simultaneous shivering and internal heat, while Liparia involves internal heat with cold extremities</term> is to be handled before the onset of the paroxysm... if they have a sonorous way. The regimen for Liparia fever requires more subtlety than any other regimen.

# Treatment of Pestilential Fevers

The summary of their treatment is based on our knowledge. For when that air is revealed, the way is through the cooling of the belly; all urine should be sent toward evacuation. If the patients are young and have a sanguine <term>sanguinea: a "complexion" dominated by blood, thought to be hot and moist</term> nature, let a phlebotomy <note>original: "flebotom̄a"; the practice of bloodletting to balance the humors</note> be performed. If there are other humors <term>humores: the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</term>, let them be evacuated. And it is necessary that the physicians be well fortified, as well as the wealthy, and that the heart be strengthened with fragrances and cooling vapors. They should be surrounded by cooling fruits and their extremities should be cooled. Let them use juices expressed from fragrant cooling fruits, and use camphor and rose water, which is highly praised. One should not go a single day without rose water, or things similar to it. If there is a flowing spray of rose water in the house, it is better.

One should receive an acid diet in a clean place; they should have things like citron. Do not give cold water, but rather the water of sour milk, such as buttermilk. Also, let them be rolled in that clay or fat with vinegar... for this is a correct remedy. Likewise, cold rain water is very helpful. Let them be given oil of spikes <note>likely lavender or nard</note>, which strengthens and balances the heat. Avoid long vigils <note>lack of sleep</note> so that they may retain their strength when the cold is extreme. Long vigils and frequent anointing... when you see the chest... then it harms... the external heat... when the appetite falls... it returns to the heart... many of them who have water as mentioned above are troubled by the mass and are not relieved. It harms them and they should be restored... And it is necessary that they be given things that are acetous <note>vinegar-based</note> and drying... for their food should be such that it does not add to the corruption.

# The second part of the treatment of the pestilence concerns the locations

The second part is to correct the air of the sick rooms. No one who is healthy should stay in a place where the air is not purified and blown through with good odors. If there is any putrefaction, let the air be rectified with wood of aloes, or with amber, or musk, or rose water, or with the flower of mace, or frankincense and laudanum, or honey of roses, and blessed Egyptian unguent, or with hyssop, or laurel, or cypress, or sweet rush, or acorus <note>a fragrant medicinal root</note>, or bitter almonds...

### Smallpox: On the Care of the Limbs and Their Defense Against the Harm of Smallpox

<margin>
Because of this, it is said to be "smallpox-pitted."
</margin>
The body parts that must all be protected from measles and smallpox are the throat, the eyes, the upper parts of the nose, the lungs, and the intestines. These are the parts where smallpox strikes; the eye is perhaps destroyed, or perhaps a white film <term>albugo</term> <note>original: "albugo," a white opacity of the cornea that can cause blindness</note> develops in it. In the throat, suffocation may occur, or perhaps an ulcer forms which prevents the swallowing of food; and perhaps it reaches the [stomach] so that itching or irritation occurs there. In the upper parts of the nose, ulcers may occur which block the passages of smell. In the lungs, it may happen from the pustules <note>original: "botty," from the Arabic *bothor* for eruptions or pustules</note> of smallpox and measles that the breath becomes violently constricted; and perhaps it leads to a [coughing of blood?] when it is ulcerated. In the intestines, excoriation <note>a painful scraping or wearing away of the internal lining</note> may occur, which is difficult to treat.

### The preservation of the eyes is best achieved by making an eye-salve <term>alcohol</term> <note>original: "alcohol," referring to a fine medicinal powder or kohl for the eyes, not liquid spirits</note> for the eye with alum, and with rose water, and with rose water in which sumac and camphor have been placed at the time of the eruption, or with alum alone.

### On the Hemitritreos.

<margin>
[This is the definition of the hemitritreos]
</margin>
The Hemitritreos <term>hemitritreos</term> <note>original: "Mitteus," a scribal corruption of the Greek-derived term for a semi-tertian fever</note> is a fever composed of two fevers. One of these is a continuous phlegmatic fever <term>flegmatica</term> occurring in one day. These are either daily or follow a tertian cycle <note>original: "tenuta," likely referring to the three-day cycle of a tertian fever</note>, or they follow the nature of the combination or its truth. Because they are two continuous fevers, they arise from two sources of putrefaction.

And it is strong to be given when the fever is prolonged. It was used so that the thirst would not be strong from the heat. Here it is noted that it is possible for pepper to be cooled in its effect, so that its warming power is mediated. Nature shortens the sickness by destroying its superfluity. Galen speaks of those who are ignorant of how pepper inflames a fever, and he mocks those who forget to use proper judgment.

The intention of the <term>crisis</term> <note>The "turning point" of a disease, where the patient either begins to recover or declines toward death</note> is a separation of judgment in the expressions. In itself, it is a sudden expulsion of one thing [disease matter] or the other, which happens suddenly, either toward the safety of health or toward the side of sickness. In this time, the significance which arrives is a medium... just as a declamation is a sickness of the body, almost like an enemy outside a city. Indeed, the light things which are in the soul, and so a battle occurs between both, which happens then from the signs of the violence of the battle... he roars, there is pain, there is a cry. The dared restoration is languishing. This happens at the seventh time <note>The "seventh day" was traditionally considered the most critical day for a medical crisis</note> in the sensation of the action. Either the Lord conquered the external [enemy], or they saw the King was immune to the external. And the victory which shall be either complete—in which there is a complete overcoming and dismissal of one of the two parts—or it is incomplete, in which the philosopher returns to a reversal, so that the battle happens another time, or badly. Which occurs on the seventh [day] at the end of the [symptoms]. And so when the Lord overcomes, he expels the master of the tower. He either expels him by total expulsion, so that the city rests from him... or he expels him by universal expulsion, driving him from the city. Then he can drive him from other places entering the city. Similarly, it may happen to the soul. Either it expels the harmful matter from the foundation, which is the heart, or from these principles, or from its members which are the extremities. Or it expels it from the foundation... but rather brings it to a change of state. This most often happens in chronic sicknesses, in cold evils, which signs of love... and similarly all sickness which turns either into the path of the crisis or the path of drying out. The best is that the crisis is complete, in which there is manifest trust, appearing with safe accidents... which some say indicates the crisis will fall on the day of the crisis, laudably. And every crisis is either laudable or bad; and each is either complete or diminished. A complete one is when nature expels the matter by total expulsion. And on the day of the crisis, that which is diminished is that which follows the time... either in resolution, or in bad drying out. In diminished crises, the days indicate the day of the crisis falling in the sickness... by a strong external virtue. Signs above in the throat in illnesses... and it is not bad if it follows a flux of the belly. And it happens in inflammation of the stomach. And the pulse of the heart in stomach conditions with the heat of fever is bad. A bad sign above from the anterior limbs. Another bad one follows a flux of the belly, and similar things.

In wakefulness, it is bad... better in the weeping of infants <note>original: "insect," likely a transcription error for 'infantum'</note>. And that which appears in a paralysis of the chest... and those signs which preceded the deaths of the ancients were observed, and those following were their conclusions. Bad signs from the part of the tongue <note>original: "leinuder," possibly 'lingue'</note> and in hearing. It is a bad sign. And if the voice flees, and in odors and colors... it is a bad sign. It signifies the weakness of the vital spirit <note>original: "spiritus," the life-force believed to animate the body</note>.

### Signs seen in the eyes
Sunkenness of the eyes on the third day with flux of the belly and wakefulness. A continuous gaze is a [troubling] sign. And darkness of the white of the eye, or its redness tending toward the color of a peacock or a sky-blue <note>original: "celestem"</note>, is a bad sign. Sharpness in both eyes in acute and burning illnesses is very bad. And if the sick man sees anything [hallucinates], it is a deadly sign. The distortion or twisting of the eye <note>original: "retorsio"</note> is a very bad sign. And if this distortion was from the animal spirits of the eye without a sound brain, then that sign is bad, for there is no mixing of strength, and similar things. Signs above from that which is seen with a brightness—which brightness does not signify health—and it floats like water to the upper parts. And it signifies a union with other signs. The falling of a tear without will, especially from only one eye, is a bad sign... and other signs of the flow of blood from the nostrils signify it. And if it is said that tears flow in multitude... with heat or cold, with or without will. Fleeing from the light is a significant sign. Just as a love of darkness is mortal, unless there be speed and pain. If the gaze is fixed without blinking and movement, it is bad, for it indicates the loss of the vital spirit. And a multitude or accumulation of humors <note>original: "luptudis," likely 'voluptuosity' or 'multitudo'</note> is a very bad sign. And the heaviness which that volume generates in the eye... in the morning... in hard matter.

...as it is said to occur because of a softening <note>original: "malaundia," likely a corruption of "malacia," a medical term for softening of tissues</note> which is judged to be a powerful sign regarding the eyes, as if an external pressure were present. For in the beginning of a digestive disturbance, the eye in this condition appears like a fig <note>original: "ficus," possibly referring to a swollen or granular appearance</note>, which is a clear sign. It is also similar to the dryness associated with inflammation <note>original: "lippitudinis," referring to bleary or inflamed eyes</note> of the eyes.

### Signs related to the eyes.

If something floats over the pupil like a spider’s web <note>original: "tela aranee"; medieval doctors often used this to describe cataracts or visual disturbances called "muscae volitantes"</note>, and then these things recede toward the pupil, this is a sign of inflammation. When it does not cease in this state, it is a sign of approaching death. Likewise, a film over the eyes <note>original: "tectis oculi," covered eyes</note> and their persistence during acute fevers is bad; this is signaled near the brain <note>original: "cebucalum," likely "cerebellum" or "cerebrum"</note> and also in the mouth, as well as a change in color to a pale hue, which happens quickly. The constant opening of the eye and a change in its brightness are significant bad omens; perhaps this is due to excessive "hot matter" <note>this refers to the medieval theory of humors, where heat caused bodily fluids to rise and affect the head</note> and an opening in the parts of the brain. A trembling of the eyelids during sleep, when not habitual, is not a good sign. Dryness of the eyelids is also a bad sign. If the eyes remain open during wakefulness and the sight seems to dim while the eye palpitates, this is a sign of death. A forceful opening of the eye accompanied by a wandering mind <note>original: "ai' alienati'," alienated soul or delirium</note> and weakness is fatal. If a pustule like a white lentil appears under the eyes, the patient may die on the tenth day; it appears when there is a loss of "sweetness" <note>likely referring to a lack of healthy moisture or vitality</note> in the body.

<margin>Note concerning an acute abscess through the nose.</margin>

### Signs taken from the nose.

Thinness <note>original: "tenuositas," referring to the nose appearing pinched or sharp</note> of the nose is bad and signifies the proximity of death, especially when the breath is foul and deadly. A flattening of the nose is likewise bad. When there is a sharpness in the nose during an acute fever, that is not a good sign. In women, if there is a profound scent of honey or a burning smell, or a discharge <note>original: "lua'," possibly "lues" or discharge</note>. The dripping of sharp fluid <note>original: "aque acris," acrid water</note> from the nose in acute fevers is perhaps a sign of approaching death. However, if the patient does not sneeze or if the passages are obstructed, it is a sign of death and the destruction of the senses; similarly, if it does not cause blood to flow, or if there is a slight redness.

<margin>Note on the bad sign of placing a finger to the nose or other parts.</margin>

If the sick person constantly puts his finger to his nose to clean it without cause, it is not a good sign; to do so when there is an itch is also bad.

### Signs taken from the ears.

A stretching of the lobes, their change in color, and a coldness of the extremities are bad signs. It is said that if the discharge of the ear becomes sweet, it is a bad sign according to Galen <note>Galen was a famous Greek physician whose writings dominated medieval medicine</note>; it is fatal among the young. A leaden color in the ear during an acute fever is a sign of "amorosis" <note>likely "amaurosis," a type of vision loss, or a general darkening</note> and is fatal, unless something ruptures in the lower parts. In young people, it may originate from a movement that seems healthy but is instead a sign of internal corruption.

### Signs taken from the teeth.

Any grinding <note>original: "tnuu," likely "stridor"</note> of the teeth in acute fevers, or if the patient tries to eat something that is not food, is not a good sign. Note that when the teeth are covered in a film during a fever, as is common, it signifies that the fever is deep or returning. It also signifies intense heat and "viscous matter" <note>thick, sticky bodily fluids</note> that is slow to resolve. When a sick person tries to clean his teeth at every hour without it being his habit, it is not a good sign. A grinding of the teeth without

<column-break/>

habit perhaps indicates mania <note>delirium or frantic mental state</note>. And if mania occurs and the eyes then fail, it signifies a loss of strength <note>original: "allopnatitẽ," likely "lipothymia" or fainting/collapse</note> and that no strength will flow back to him because of the weakness of the heart. Grinding of the teeth occurs from any of these causes. Dampness of the gums is also a bad sign.

### Signs taken from the tongue and mouth.

Every trembling of the tongue and that which makes it heavy is a sign of declining toward illness. Dryness of the mouth and saliva, or a loss of speech, is bad. If the dryness causes the tongue to become parched and then turn black, it is fatal, often occurring on the fourteenth day. Know that a powerful foul odor of the mouth in acute illnesses is a sign of death, as it signifies the corruption of the internal humors. The lifting of one or both lips in acute "lyric" <note>likely "lyricis," referring to a specific type of fever</note> fevers is bad.

<margin>Note on the distortion of the lips.</margin>

A distortion of the lips in acute fevers signifies an excess of inflammation or a hidden corruption of the heart; coldness of the lips is also bad. If the mouth remains open in acute illnesses, it is a bad sign. An excess of dryness on the tongue is not a good sign, and when it appears on the tongue in an acute fever like a black bitterness, death is near. This is often accompanied by a loss of taste for hot things, or a dryness of the tongue, which is a sign of "phthisis" <note>a wasting disease, usually tuberculosis</note>. If there is a roughness of the tongue and a change in its color, it signifies an excess of illness. Know that if the tongue is freed from all dominating humors in any condition, it returns to its natural state or helps the neighboring members to recover.

### Signs taken from the extremity of the throat; if it happens suddenly on the day of crisis, it means death.

Suffocation with foam <note>original: "spuma," froth at the mouth</note> is a very bad sign. Foam occurs when the lungs are overheated, which destroys the lungs and the diaphragm, which are made to balance the breath of the soul. This appears as a rattling in the throat due to great weakness. Frequently, this occurs at the beginning of an illness alongside a cough. At the end, when it happens in a strong fever, the patients are suffocated and death arrives, because the heart requires a great deal of breath to counter the intense heat. If the airway is blocked, the heat inflames the heart and creates an excess of "malice of complexion" <note>an imbalance of the body's basic qualities: hot, cold, moist, dry</note> which seeks a way out. Likewise, difficulty in swallowing is a bad sign. This happens either because of a displacement of the vertebrae <note>original: "spodil," spondyls</note> or because of extreme dryness. Do not give any vinegar or sharp things during such a fever. If swallowing cannot be performed without great effort, it is a very bad sign; the same is true if water is swallowed and then returns through the nose. Likewise, if the patient sighs at every hour, it is not a good sign.

### Bad signs taken from the "Faces of Hippocrates" <note>original: "fortũ ypxas," referring to the *Facies Hippocratica*, the classic medical description of a dying face</note> which appear in the veins.

Redness appearing in the veins and the eyelids is bad.

### Bad signs taken from the softening of the body, and weakness, and lying on the back, etc.

Softening of the body and weakness indicate extreme debility.

### Bad signs

Lying on the back above **because of the manner of lying.** The position in which one sits or lies is formed by one's way of life; rather, it settles through the mixture of the belly and the presence [of humors], and it is a bad sign, especially when at the end one's breathing gradually pants toward its end. This is seen in one who previously lay down and felt relief on his back, but now shows a uncovering of the extremities <note>referring to the patient restlessly kicking off covers</note>; and besides these things, it is a sign alongside other signs of a very manifest heat. And if there is great distress <note>original: "agustia," meaning "angustia" or respiratory distress</note> and the body is as if it were a single justice <note>likely an error for "unity" or "stiffness"</note>, while the strength is sluggish. If you see the body quickly softening, yet diligent in its scattered state so that the mouth stays quiet at the hour he sits in this form, or if pain is prevented by lying on the back. For that occurs from something where the love of the usual space is magnified by lying on the back, and by fainting, and by other things. Because if there was an indistinct state of health in acute illnesses, it is bad and enough to be a sign of the "love of lying on the back" <note>this likely refers to a patient's involuntary preference for the supine position due to extreme exhaustion</note>. This is either through much fluid of this humor in the organs, or through dryness of the vessels of this nature, which weakens the sides <note>original: "lactos"</note>, or through weakness of the vital breath <note>original: "aie," likely "animae" or "spiritus"</note> of the side from another part. And if the desire to lie on the back arises, or another deprivation, or rather a failure to sit up, it is a bad and fleeting sign. And the primary thing is that because of the breath, there is a difficulty in the air, a non-vital precipitance in the increased moisture, in which there is enough to distinguish from what preceded it. And if he tries to flee from you, as if toward protection, it is a sign that is not good. And turning over in sleep onto the belly without being accustomed to it is bad; it must be either due to a change in the voice or a lack of appetite <note>original: "alexia," likely referring to "orexia" or lack of desire for food</note> that is found. And this sort of thing is highly praiseworthy, unless it occurs with a fistula that was receiving the place...

### Signs regarding the air.

When the breath fails, or is so weakened that when you draw it out, it does not return to its place, that is a bad sign. Breathing out warm vapors from the air with a fleeting breath is a ruinous sign. And it happens because the heat of the heart is finished.

### Signs regarding the belly and palpitation.

A swelling of the belly in acute illnesses, with little folding of it <note>referring to a distended, rigid abdomen that does not crease</note>; if this is present and only in the belly, it is a sign of death. Especially when there appears in it a pustule of a dark color, and a protrusion. And the swelling of one side of the belly is more increased than the other. And similarly, the swelling of the whole side is an increase that similarly limits 

<column-break/>

the end. It is then received and similarly the movement is led by a certain gentleness, which inflates the abdominal wall <term>mirach: the medieval term for the abdominal muscles and skin</term> in an increase of phlegm and dryness. But if it is an abscess <note>original: "apa," likely "apostema"</note>, it will have neither color nor darkness. A hiding of the genitals <note>original: "prodioz," likely "pudendorum"</note> without pain and a sinking toward the lower parts is a sign of mania, as is a turning toward the upper parts without pain.

### Signs from the eye.

Eyes in acute fevers that move by themselves are a bad sign.

### Signs from wakefulness.

A restraint of the eyelids <note>insomnia or inability to close the eyes</note> is a bad sign. And similarly, a searching or scratching in acute illnesses, or a wrinkling of the eyelids, signifies death in a short time, or the pain of dizziness or a pollution <note>nocturnal emission or discharge</note> in the peak of the illness; it signifies a long life if it happens at the end of the illness.

### Signs from the matrix.

An exit of the woman's nature <note>likely referring to a prolapse or discharge from the womb/matrix</note>, not in childbirth but in an acute fever, is a bad sign.

### Bad signs from the tongue.

These are according to quantity: **to be mute.** Also, if it is cold and thinned with the heat of an acute fever, or if it is fixed and cannot move, it is a sign of ruin. A bad sound <note>original: "cacuonia," likely "cacophonia"</note> with a horrible smell in acute fevers is due to a greatness in the moisture of the belly, or in the loss of innate heat, or the bringing on of fainting and dissolution. And the strongest sign is the coldness of the extremities in acute fevers toward death, which is a sign in the beginning of the illness. And similarly, if the breath is cold and does not grow warm, it signifies the flight of the blood of the heart to the interior parts. This is preceded by a darkening of the fingers and hands and the nails. It is a mortal sign in one who is thinned out, and if it happens suddenly, it is more ruinous. Because of the darkening, as with anyone who is born <note>possibly "dying"</note>, if it occurs in the fourth [day], it signifies a weakness of the animal virtue, and darkening signifies a weakness of the innate heat, and redness signifies a corruption of the return of these humors. And blackness is better than darkening or redness. And with this, it is far better if the patient is saved. And the thinning of the body when it is altered, and a burning and trembling of the stomach <note>original: "tremit ventrit"</note>, and hands with coldness of the belly, is a sign of eternal death. And from these, on the part of their difficulty, if a frothy spitting occurs because of the humors of the belly, it is mortal. And from the animal nature and the violence of the fever, it is a sign of death.
<margin>Note on the pollution of sleep and what it signifies.</margin>

### Signs from the sleep of the throat.

If sleep becomes heavy and harmful, it is a sign of ruin; and if one sleeps more than others, it is worse. This is a corruption of the senses, which leads to a deep sleep, because it is a sign of a change in the fevers and others. In the beginning, or if it happens many times, it does not hurt. And to be weighed down by sleep with a weakness of the pulse is bad; it is because of a weakness of the actions, or because of the moisture of the brain, or because the soul permits the senses to be quieted by the putrefaction of cold humors, especially if it increases harmfully.

A confusion of reason follows. The exercise of cold reasoning <note>original: "ratiocinatio frigidorum," referring to a chilling or detached delirium</note> is an evil thing. Thus, if a lightness of speech follows the patient's judgment, it is a bad sign.

### **Bad signs concerning Smell**

A person may turn pale in the reaching of the hands <note>original: "appetitione manuum"; this refers to "carphologia," the involuntary picking at bedclothes or air, a grave clinical sign</note>. This happens to all men when things are gathered and scattered as if by a sting <note>original: "ex punctura"</note>. It is a bad sign. It occurs when a vision is produced by vapors that rise to the brain, which cause the patient to imagine things that are not actually present to the eye, appearing in the white humor of the eye <note>original: "humiditatem albugineam," referring to the aqueous humor or the white of the eye</note>.

**Signs taken from various pains** of the mind and acute [sufferings]. It is a bad sign. It signifies a vehement onset, or a great delirium of the mind, or a loss of control over all the limbs; and if it is followed by a sudden, complete quiet without cause, that is an evil sign.

<margin>ordered speech</margin>

**Signs taken from the voice and speech**

A very [weak] voice is of this nature. **In delirium,** this is bad; and a variability [of speech], more and more, signifies a strong pressure in restlessness, or the softening of the muscles of the tongue and the epiglottis, or their thickening, or the destruction of the imagination which is the beginning of speech. When the sick speak with variability... finally, the rarity of speech signifies a loss of general understanding. And a great deal of talking in a state of variability signifies a great alienation of reason. **Signs taken from the movements of the soul and nature according to reason.**

Breath [comes] little by little in the head... it is safe; but if it indicates apoplexy <note>original: "apoplexia," a sudden loss of consciousness or stroke</note>, it is mortal. **Signs and warnings taken from movements, manner of moving, and restlessness. It is a bad sign.**

The eyes [turning] toward the temples... or a vision of woods and flowers? <note>original: "visionem silvarum et effloresci"</note>. This is a bad sign, and it is because of respiratory distress <note>original: "angustiam"</note>, or because of a prediction of a loss of reason, or a gasping for breath and suffocation. And if pneumonia is worsening, it is because of this suffocation, or because it stands in the way of recovery, or occurs for other causes. And when the limbs are heavy and cannot be moved, it is a bad sign. And when the nails grow dark, death is present. And trembling is a bad sign, especially when there is a burning of the uvula <note>original: "ar_sis inter uva"</note>. **Signs taken from the three-day fever <note>original: "trinatione," likely a tertian fever</note>** and first the loss of movement... then of the tremors.

**Judgments taken from heat and other things.** Others occur in those parts that do not move, such as the milky arms <note>original: "brachia lactola," possibly meaning pale or flaccid</note>, so that matter may be expelled from them; matter is scant and obedient to digestion in that one whose nature is in its power. And if the heat should change to cold against nature, it is a bad sign; and it signifies many times that they are not born to be resolved <note>i.e., the disease will not reach a "crisis" or resolution</note>, either because of the multitude of the matter or because of the weakness of the virtues <note>original: "debilitatem virtutum," the patient's vital strength</note>.

**Signs taken from dreams.**
Often one sees in a dream a sign of that which has been... as if one enters a bath. **Signs taken from the appetite.**

The destruction of the appetite in illness... is bad; and a great [hunger] in acute [diseases] is likewise. And at the highest, it signifies corrupt men, or a natural death. And when the thirst is destroyed in such conditions, it is a bad sign. **Judgment of signs.**

And if a hiccough occurs after the seventh day, it is usually a sign of health, provided other good signs are joined to it. And many times it happens because of a complete crisis, and it signifies praise <note>a positive outcome</note>. But it signifies malice if it is joined with a lightness [of the head]. **In acute fevers, signs taken from the breath.** Acute [fevers] come from the openness of the passages and from the extremity; it is worse when it happens through those open ways because of fevers from putrefaction. ...to the great [signs]. It happens that he desires a golden hue <note>original: "cellum auri"; likely referring to a yellowing of the vision or skin associated with jaundice</note>. He dies on the twentieth [day]. ### **Further Signs**
**D**erivation <note>original: "ypreas," likely a corruption of "diaphoresis" or a specific vascular condition</note> may occur from the part of the veins. Small veins appear in the forehead, and those in the eyelids and the calves are a bad sign. The redness <note>original: "alcitas," likely *alacritas* or *rubicunditas*</note> of the visible veins [is noted], appearing at a distance and of a purple color. The appearance of those [veins] which did not appear before is not a bad sign in itself.

### **Further Signs from Blackness**

**A** sign of a full reduction <note>original: "pline reducionis"</note> in a small fever with a debility of the vital force is mortal. And regarding the end of the vital force: when the fever does not remove the soul <note>original: "febrio anieo," likely referring to the vital spirit</note>, then it is a long [illness]. And the rule of all [signs] is that if the [bodily] heat <note>original: "caualatio," likely *caliditas*</note> does not help, then the fever settles with him. And if he seems to be helped by it, it signifies that he moves toward a [crisis]. But that which cannot be expelled is an evil thing. Indeed, it is bad if it occurs only once; perhaps it signifies a turning point <note>original: "asorsiu iudicis," the crisis or judgment of the disease</note> either through the debility of the surplus strength or something else.

### **Judgment of Evacuation**

**E**vacuation that helps through the flux of vomiting and the bowels and other [means] is that which is predicted. When humors are evacuated like water in such a way, it leads to a feeling of lightness. These are the signs of the evacuation of humors which the physician evacuates, or [signs] if the physician [should intervene]. It is so that the evacuation of the humor begins [properly]. And the concern is that its end should change toward an exit of [the disease’s] sharpness, such as toward black blood, or a stinking humor, or a pure humor, and thus a change [of state]. And when the evacuation is altered before it achieves what it should achieve, it is not helpful. And when the evacuation is superfluous before digestion begins, then it is not [good], nor is it a clean movement. A weak or meager evacuation signifies that nature did not move [the matter] when it [tried to] evacuate. If it becomes bad, it signifies death; if it becomes very bad, it signifies a long-delayed judgment <note>the 'judgment' or 'crisis' is the moment the disease is either defeated or kills the patient</note>.

### **Judgment of Sweat**

**S**weat of this kind in acute illnesses comes from the phlegmatic [humors]. It opens the way for the spirits [of the body] and the swelling of the viscera.

### **The Cause of Multitude**
**S**weat multiplies, or there is a mass of sweat, when it occurs through no [particular] day of its own, or through its own goodness, or when the strength is either expelled or [the body] is softened. Or the cause is [the pores] dilating; this dilation decreases the sweat through that [opening]. Sweat is gathered in abundance when it moves away [from the center].

### **Diversity of the Limbs**

**T**he members which sweat the most while sweating, and those which [sweat] with...

<column-break/>

...are those in which the matter is refined by heat, as in the [vital organs]. And those which are [cold] are the members where the matter is not refined. And those which do not [sweat] have a strength of the soul <note>original: "ūte q̄ ē," *virtus que est*</note> that prevents it, or a constriction of the spirit which guards against it. For the liquids find natural ways toward [the member], and it is helped by it. Sweat which multiplies in the prior strengths, or in the back more than in the [limbs], signifies a [crisis]. It multiplies in the upper parts more than what happens in the lower parts, where a diversity [of symptoms] is perceived. 
<margin>Note.</margin>

**S**leep disposes one to sweat more than anything else. One sweats more in sleep than in wakefulness, because the heat in the members acts more upon the humors. Those who [sweat] in the [middle of the night] move the matter toward the judgment <note>the crisis</note>. Great sweat in sleep from a frequent cause signifies that the body is more affected than it can tolerate. If, however, that sweat comes from a high [fever], it signifies that he needs evacuation. Great sweat with health does not [usually] occur unless it is through a multitude of matter that nature wishes to expel. And that multitude, if it is from a [repletion], will be cured [by the sweat]. This repletion is expelled if it has been refined. Sweat which is expelled by nature, as happens in a long [illness], does not happen only from superfluities. It is an exercise of nature to cleanse [the body] through them. Through sweat, a strength is brought forth; it is thin and [cleansing], and it releases the seized [limbs]. Nature loves to expel the [excessive] humor through this, unless [the illness] debilitates her. And know that as much as the heat of life is stronger, the resolution [of the disease] is more hidden. When sweat is accompanied by other [signs], you may speak of the soul <note>the prognosis of life or death</note>, for it is either due to a multitude [of humors] or a dilation [of the pores], or a failure of the strength to hold it in.
<margin>
Note. 
Note how much the color of the sweat, namely if it is red, is more [significant].
</margin>

### **Days in which it multiplies**

**S**weat in illnesses moves [the matter]. It occurs most greatly in the [third] and fourth [days]. It does not [always] appear in the fourth, but it appears together with sharpness [of symptoms] in the fourth or [third]. And when it is from the blood, sweat always changes [the state]. The sick man sweats on the twenty-seventh, the thirty-seventh, and the twenty-fourth [days].

### **Signs of the Modes of Sweat**
**T**he signs of the modes of sweat [are as follows]:
By the touch of it, whether it is hot or cold. It is signified by its color, whether it is clear, or thin, or [bright]. It is signified by the taste, whether it is bitter, or sweet, or [salty]. It is signified by its odor, whether it is stinking, or sweet, or otherwise. It is signified by the flux, whether it is watery or viscous. It is signified by its location, whether it is over the whole body or from the [limbs]. And that [member] in which it [starts] is where the illness is. It is signified by its hour, whether...

### The Significance of Sweat Regarding the One Sweating.

Cold sweat, as [noted] above regarding the one sweating, in the heat of a fever is a very bad sign. It signifies that a fainting spell <note>original: "uoillo"; likely a corruption of "volo" or a similar term for a sudden fall</note> is taking hold, and it signifies syncope <note>a temporary loss of consciousness or fainting</note>, even if it is not cold. Because cold [sweat] is worse in the process of sweating, as it signifies [the heat] which was [previously] present. When a fever removes a great deal of the internal heat, it is characteristic of these cold sweats, for the innate heat is not driven out. Rather, it is often [stolen] from them when [the body] separates the humors <note>the bodily fluids like blood, phlegm, and bile</note>, so that the external heat prevails. Internal sweat is bad, and a great amount of sweat signifies a long duration <note>original: "loquacite"; literally 'loquacity' or 'talkativeness,' here meaning the disease persists</note> of the illness due to the multitude of matter. And if it is found with a foul odor <note>original: "fletor"</note>, it demonstrates the person's debility. Moreover, if it is found at the start of the illness, it is not a sign that it has reached its peak; then it is a bad sign. Also, sweat with a foul odor in the beginning of an illness is bad and signifies a multitude of [corrupt] matter. It is not like the humidity of the air or much rain, for then, despite its malice, the illness is of a lesser malice. And many times when an illness begins with sweat, the fever follows and is prolonged. And when goosebumps <note>shivering or "orripilatio"</note> occur from sweat, it is not good; rather it is bad, because goosebumps signify the expulsion of humors and a very bad sign. That which signifies sweat is similarly stated; indeed, those things are bad because they are caused by the nature of the humidities which are not resolved by the flux. It signifies that the matter is not resolved toward a healthy outcome, for it debilitates the patient. If the pulse and the flow [of sweat] occur together, it is a bad sign. If the pulse falls during sweat, then death is near. However, long-lasting sweat is beneficial if it occurs after the pulse is stabilized, and that which happens on a critical day <note>a day when a disease is expected to change for better or worse</note>, then you may consider it joined [to a recovery], and the patient is always relieved by it. It follows that if lightness follows, it leads to the removal of the heat and cold, with the odor and taste, and the quantity in its multitude. Whether [the illness] is in its beginning, its peak, or its decline, or how it sounds from the fever in its intensity, or its debility, so that it may be eased in the future. And know that in convalescence <note>the period of recovery</note>, sweat is increased by the remaining matter, which is not a bad sign as it makes [the illness] diminish.

<margin>Note that a great multitude of sweat does not bring relief unless it is of a good quality.</margin>

### The Significance of Sweat Concerning the Pulse.

A hammer-like pulse <note>original: "pulsus martellinus"; a pulse that feels like a rhythmic striking</note> regarding the pulse... or a wavy one <note>original: "undosus"</note> is bad. A "gazelle-like" pulse <note>original: "gazelui"; a jerky, uneven pulse compared to the leap of a gazelle</note> accompanied by debility is bad. And there is a diversity in those who are vehemently infected; the weak [pulse] of those who are dying... is indeed a very bad omen of death. It is different when the pulse is frequent, and a rapid pulse on the right side is nothing when accompanied by debility; then the significance is bad. Many of these pulses have been diverse and bad without [an obvious] illness...

### Judgments on the Flow of Blood from the Nostrils.

<margin>Note</margin>
The outflow of blood from the nostrils <note>epistaxis</note> occurs when there is pleurisy <note>inflammation of the chest and lung lining</note> or an affliction of the liver. In the region of the hypochondria <note>the upper abdomen, under the ribs</note>, the flow of blood from the nostrils completes the crisis <note>original: "cri"; shorthand for crisis or turning point</note>. First, [consider] from which nostril it comes, or if it is from both. These occur in moderate fevers. If it is from the lungs <note>original: "p’plemona"; likely peripneumonia</note>, it does not happen... and pleurisy is a middle condition. It is well known that a flow of blood from the nostrils happens in a certain way... and that it be pure... It happens on the fourth, fifth, or ninth day. And when a flow of blood from the nostrils is expected, it should not be from debility. One should see if it occurs with a hot sensation <note>original: "calide"</note> over the head or with a sensation as if a superfluity <note>an excess of humors</note> were being moved... and it happens with a windiness <note>gas or pressure</note> above the hypochondria. And the best flow of blood from the nostrils is that which follows the lower part [of the body]. A nosebleed is more convenient for this than [other evacuations]. These are the things that were [mentioned] above. But in the beginning of a phlegmon <note>an inflammation of the soft tissue</note>... it is prolonged and a certain recovery is expected through the flow of blood from the nostrils. It should not be expected in a cold beginning, or in peripneumonia <note>lung inflammation</note>.

Here, it is clear regarding the flow of liquid [from the nose]: unless it is truly pure, it is bad. Also, a flow of blood from the nostrils is bad if the blood is black. If the blood that flows is pure and bright red <note>original: "ruteo splendido"</note>, it is [better]. And a flow of liquid from the nostrils which occurs on the fifth day signifies difficulty for the patient <note>original: "aialo"; likely animalis, the living being</note>.

The changes in the nostrils occur at the peak [of the illness]. First, we speak of the signs of the humors...

## On the signs that an abscess becomes a discharging sore.

When there is pulsation in the bladder, for the most part, or a prolonged hardness with heat, it is extended by a stronger force so that it becomes a discharging sore.

## On the signs of mildness and all maturations, and the sign of it, and bad maturation. Judgments of pus.

All praiseworthy evacuations are those which are white, smooth, and do not have a horrible odor, and in which the union [of the skin] is not broken; in which there is no tearing or sharp pain coming forth. Nor is lightness brought about unless it is prepared by the digestive power <term>digestive power: in medieval medicine, this refers to the body's ability to "cook" or process raw humors into a refined state, like pus</term>. This is not signified for long by the operation of the said mass and its obedience [to nature]. And all that occurs with a violent, horrible odor is far removed from healthy maturation and is closer to putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the decay or "rotting" of humors within the body</term>. They also said that sometimes another color in the members is indicative of white [pus], which does not resemble it, and the previous signs do not prevail over it.

## And bad pus is a certain sign of putrefaction, which is contrary to healthy maturation.

And it signifies the mastery of external heat. And when the pus comes out with different parts having various colors and shades, it is a sign of the degradation of the humors. Not all pus comes about in order to heal, whether through putrefaction, or maturation, or diminution, or by being altered with something else.

## The significance of how much heat is found in a single mass.

From the dregs, chills <note>original: "conpilationes," referring to the shivering or rigors associated with fever</note> and fevers occur. And in these there is an order: the pain becomes more violent, which is due to the shivering in the members over a longer space of time. Then the white spaces are hidden, and the weight of the abscess increases. You should know that when a discharging sore occurs, it arrives at its own collection [of matter], and at that time the pains in these members are more violent. And the more it approaches its state, the more it is known; but when the eruption occurs in the members, there is a "loss of continuity" <note>original: "solutio continuitatis," a standard medical phrase for a physical break in the skin or tissue</note>, and the pain that comes from it is gathered together. And when the matter becomes pus, a strong heat is felt, and in the inflammation, a fever occurs through its connection with the heart. And you should know that the hardness of the pulse is a great testimony. And when the sign of the discharging sore appears, and there is hardness in the lower parts, and the pulse is not weakened, it indicates beforehand that an internal discharging sore is forming. In such a case, it is perhaps in the viscera, or rather in the infection

<column-break/>

of the viscera themselves. And then there is the feeling in the side in which there is a cavity [pointing] toward the throat which extends from it, and it is dangerous.

## Signs of maturation.

When the signs of maturation <term>maturation: the process of an abscess "ripening" or coming to a head, indicating it is ready to be drained</term> occur in a member, it generally happens that the fever and the shivering and the pain are completed. And a heaviness remains, which shows that the matter is already being changed and maturation is present.

## Signs of the characteristics of eruption and [rupture].

When the pains recede, but there was intense piercing and stinging, and the heaviness becomes more violent, and fevers are brought on, then the eruption is approaching. When a sudden rigor <note>shivering or chill</note> occurs and there is an abundance of pain, then the eruption has already been made. And when the flesh appears evacuated, the stinging which was there no longer exists. And it is empty, so that there is a drying of the part and a weakness of the dried areas. And when a sudden eruption occurs in the viscera, many things return [to the body]. Then perhaps a palpitation of the heart occurs, and a bad syncope <note>fainting or loss of consciousness</note>, and perhaps death occurs because of the dissolution of the vital strength. And perhaps there occurs what is called a "loosening of the belly" <note>diarrhea</note>, and perhaps a great spitting of pus occurs suddenly when it has exited into the chest. And perhaps suffocation occurs when a great amount of matter erupts into the interior suddenly.

## When the pus has exited, which was not appearing before.

If maturation follows its own path, nature moves and brings forth the "wickedness" <note>referring to the diseased matter</note> to a single mobile member. This is not hidden from the foolish. It was a hollow thing which the cause points out. And from pure heat when there were discharging sores. That which concerns the regimen <note>medical treatment plan</note> is the removal of that which weighs upon the members. And that is according to two modes of regimen: when the regimen is given according to the reasoning of the physicians, while the illness departs from that which is customary. And it is as if the magnitude of the matter is doubled so that it becomes pus, which is interrupted before that. So that you may observe the patient, you should serve him so that the cause of pain does not advance and cause a sudden rupture. Many men die this way by the shivering and the drying up of their strength. Rather, the physician should observe the strength and preserve the patient with that which is healthy. Note that one should have a thinning <note>original: "subtilief," likely "subtiliens" or "subtiliatif," referring to medicines that thin the humors</note> treatment... for an internal sore in the viscera when all maturation should be thinned.

And the second is a regimen departing from the usual because of the known disposition [of the patient]. And since when the illness is great and the discharging sores are present in their great size, that which is customary is used. And there is a haste in the moderation of the maturation within it. Because of the maturation of the plaster <note>original: "illitōr̄," likely "illitoris," meaning an ointment or plaster applied to the skin</note>, this brings maturation to its mark. Then it is natural to perforate it with caution, lest that which follows the discharging sore accidentally touches the noble members <term>noble members: the vital organs, such as the heart, liver, or brain</term>. **Sometimes hardness of the joints occurs.**
In neighboring parts, hardness moves the joints with difficulty and without sense of touch; sometimes it is joined with a certain numbness, and sometimes with fleshiness, and its cause is that which is harmful. 

**Owl's Eye** <note>original: "Oculus noctue"; a type of callus or corn</note>
Wolf's nail <note>original: "Lupus clavi"</note>, or <term>al-musmar</term> <note>Arabic term for a corn or callus</note>, and so forth. It is a round, white nodule, like the head of a nail. It happens first from pressure and rubbing, and because it is made of dead flesh, it multiplies. It happens first in the feet, the toes, and lower parts, and it harms the "canals" <note>veins or tendons</note> that run through there. It is necessary that an incision be made upon it, and from that time, let it be moved by hand always and pulled out from the depths, for sometimes it is such that it is not possible for it to come out entirely. And the first thing that happens if it is not cared for is cancer.

**About cancer and carcinoma.**
Cancer is an abscess of black bile <note>original: "melancholia"</note> arising from burnt black bile or burnt choler, or from colicky matter which is called "combusted" but is not a clean swelling. It differs in its sensation from others by its color, its hardness, and a certain throbbing, because of the speed with which the matter changes and inflames. It differs from a phlegmon <note>a hot, red inflammation</note> because it has "feet" <note>veins</note> that it shows in its growth toward the limb; that is, when the "feet" of the cancer are not red as in a phlegmon, but are dark because of the thickness of the matter. And it is distinguished from other things because it first appears in the opening and comes forward from the flesh. It differs from other tumors because there is sensation, whereas in others there is no sensation at all. It happens most often in "branching" limbs <note>original: "membro ramoso"; likely referring to the breast due to its milk ducts and veins</note>, and this is more frequent in women. At the beginning, its disposition is hidden. When a cancer appears, it is unmistakable; its signs appear clearly. In the beginning, it is like a small bean, hard, round, and dark in color, with a certain greenness. Some cancers cause extreme pain, and others are somewhat quiet. Some lead to ulceration <note>original: "ulaiaitōē'"</note>, which happens from black bile and the burning of the blood and choler. Others are dry and do not ulcerate. When it changes from non-ulcerated to ulcerated, the lips of the wound appear thicker and harder. And one sees that this happens for one of two reasons: either because of its tenacity in the limb or because of its round shape and its color, and the "registry of veins" which are like its feet, as was mentioned before. 

**Cure.** That which must be avoided regarding cancer is that in its beginning, it is perhaps possible to prevent it from increasing beyond what it is, and to keep it so that it does not...

### What leprosy is, namely the cause...

**L**eprosy is an evil illness arising from the combustion of choler <term>colere</term> <note>Yellow bile, one of the four bodily humors, believed to cause heat and dryness</note> entering throughout the whole, which corrupts the complexion of the members—that is, their form and their shape—and perhaps it corrupts in the end their very substance, so that it is recognized in the mind as the heat which comes from ulceration. <margin>Note on the causes of leprosy.</margin>
### Concerning the causes and efficient factors
The evil of the ancients arises from the corruption of the body and is very prone to heat and dryness, whereby they turn blood into melancholy, either in the complexion of the whole body or otherwise, so that it makes the blood acquire bit by bit a heavy state. And its material cause is from melancholy and this follows. When the body has within it unhealthy qualities, or heat operates within them, which resolves the subtle parts and first breathes out the melancholic spirit and refills it. And the eating of superfluities leads to this cause in youth. And the causes for the winemaker are the blockage of the pores, which provokes innate heat, and the blood is chilled and thickened. Or it happens when the spleen is joined weakly, and it does not burn to purify the blood from the melancholic humor. Or it is because the expulsive powers <note>original: "mēuicāily"; likely a corruption of "medicinales" or "mechanicales" referring to the body's natural functions</note> are weak, and from the expulsion of that, you find the matter is placed there. And because the corruption of the air aids that whole thing, or through the proximity of lepers, because the breath is contagious. And because it occurs hereditarily, or because of the complexion of the mother from whom he is created, because of the cause which is either clear or an acquired matter, according to the disposition which is in her, just as it happens during the indistinct inception of menstruation.

And concerning this sickness which is weak, it is difficult to treat. And from another name, it is strong, where there are scabs. And "alopecia" <note>original: "mapies"; likely referring to hair loss</note> which is more susceptible. And it is confirmed more by the softening. And it is made from the melancholy of choler, and is more foul, and with more harmful things and more difficult occurrences. Or it is seen as an ulceration, thus more susceptible to hearing. And that made from the dregs of the blood is safer and quieter. And if they ulcerate, those made from burnt melancholy in a choleric way with its accidents, it will be more slowly understood by its greed. And because the sickness does not cease to corrupt the complexion of the members through which all the quantities of the coming life—that is, heat and moisture—pass, it arrives at the principal members and remains there. And it begins first from the extremities and the light members, and there it is moved by their nature, and changes the color, and perhaps it comes to ulceration; from there it goes bit by bit through the whole. For although at first when the infirmity is there, it is through a small trace with those being among the extremities because they are weaker, yet when its path is measured and the malice pricked, there appear ulcers in the principal members. And it is more for him to pertain to it by the malice of its complexion.

### On the Suturing of the Abdomen

Column 1

<margin>
Perhaps the points <note>original: "pūcta"; meaning the stitches or sutures</note> are made above.

Since it is necessary that this matter be prepared, it is so that one may grasp that which is called the **mirach** <term>original: "mirach"; the abdominal wall, including the muscles and fat</term> and the **siphac** <term>original: "siphac"; the peritoneum, the thin membrane lining the abdominal cavity</term>. For it is not just anywhere that you should begin, but you must change the manner of the skin from the outside to the interior part. When the point of the needle has penetrated into the skin, then direct it back according to the straightness and the length of the whole belly. While you are between the margins of the *siphac*, do not introduce these letters <note>A figurative reference to the stitches or the sequence of the suture</note> during the preparation. And make the needle penetrate into this margin from the inside to the outside; then make it penetrate from the inside to the outside in the other margin of the *mirach*. And when you have made it penetrate there, then make it penetrate beneath this same margin of the *mirach*, or from the outside to the inside. And while between the margins of the *siphac* which is on the similar side, make the needle penetrate the other side from the inside to the outside. And make it penetrate with an active penetration into the *siphac*, in the margin of the *mirach* which is on its side, until you have made it penetrate the whole. Then in that same place, go from that same side, which is the margin of the *siphac* on the other side. And extract the needle from that part which it penetrated; then bring the needle back into that margin of the *siphac* which is on the other side near the margin of the *mirach*. And extract it from that part which is on its side. And do this once in a similar way, until you have treated the whole wound according to this example.

In the middle of the stitches, however, beware of excess in width or tightness, because the width should hold just as much as is required. And the tightness brings [the edges] together. And if there is a defect in your cord <note>likely referring to the suture thread or ligament</note>, let it be guided toward the distribution. And if it is soft, let it be cut away. And let it be tied with a light closure. And the thread, if it is able, should be of silk <note>original: "daucī"; perhaps a corruption or specific term for silk or flax</note> for the suturing. For if the thread is too long for the stitch, the belly will remain squared within itself, and the boundary will not be united. And according to its equality, I say that the instruction regarding the influence <note>the flow or healing process</note> must be attended to in the *siphac* with the *mirach*; it will strongly unite and become flesh, since it is muscular. And some have performed it according to this mode: It is necessary that the needle be fixed in the outer margin of the *mirach*, and make it penetrate to the inner parts, and while between the margins of the *siphac* entirely, let the needle be brought back to the inside. And make it penetrate to the interiors; then let the needle penetrate from its own part which is joined. Then make it penetrate in the other margin of the margins of the *mirach* according to this. And in this manner of stitching, it is held to be better, as it comprehends four margins in one stitch. And this is so because with this construction, the belly which we have already discussed is now covered, and the *mirach* is renewed and joined with it in that preparation. Afterward, place upon it the incarnative medicines <note>medicines intended to promote the growth of new flesh</note>. And then the manner for binding it is with bandages and wines for the wound. And moisten a wide cloth of linen with warm oil, and wrap it over another short one, and by the grace of God, it will be healed safely, near to some softening of the [tissue]. ### Medicines that Heal Wounds

**The powers** of these medicines are determined by their placement. And it is indubitable that a poultice of them is of less power than that which is made from them with oil and wax. There are also those that are produced from oil and cerates <term>original: "cerota"; waxy ointments</term>, and the types of medicine that are made of hematite <note>original: "hemastenyi"; a blood-stanching mineral</note> and other minerals that extend deep and do not penetrate superficially. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of wounds, transitioning from the treatment of bleeding to the classification of chronic wounds known as fistulas and various types of ulcers, including their discharges and signs of healing.</meta>

...with internal depth. And an ulcer that has such depth and is not emptied until it has already been cleansed, and becomes curved, is what is primarily called a **fistula** <term>fistula: a pipe-like, narrow tunnel that forms under the skin, often draining fluid from an infection</term>. It is thus a hollow passage penetrating into a limb, or one that hardens into something like a hidden and hollow nostril.

When someone speaks of a "hidden extension," they mean that which has elongated from a [source of] discharge <note>original: 'bauie', likely referring to 'bavia' or 'pavia', a discharge of fluid</note>; it creeps away from it and becomes a hollow in which it bends through the flesh and dilates the passage. Some say that a deep fistula is a dilation of a vein—not a common vein, but a deep-seated one. In such cases, the hardness of the ulcer appears as a constricted opening.

And certain fistulas are "evil" <note>meaning malignant or difficult to treat</note>; those are the ones that age within. Their malice <note>severity</note> is judged according to the length of their extension and their upward path. Some are even. Among these, some are oblique, traveling toward the belly, causing pain or irritation; when they are touched at their lower end, they react. Perhaps the operation is difficult in those members where the fistula reaches the bone. When it reaches a ligament, it is that which runs along it; truly, the pain is monstrous and the ligaments <margin>or twisted</margin> may perhaps not be enlarged. Those that go to the bone are more difficult when they are on a slope or at a great depth. From the decay near the veins, waste <note>original: 'fex', referring to dregs or morbid matter</note> frequently exits. From those that reach the flesh, the fluid is oily, or thin, turbid, and raw.

Many times there are "acidic" fistulas that occur in the <unclear>lining</unclear>. There is a distinction between a fistula and an ordinary ulcer.

Often it pours out a fluid in such a way that the nature of this flow is livid. Then it is not truly "fistulous," but a discharge of another color emerges; for the discharge of a fistula is white, dark, and hot.

And ulcers are divided into ten types of divisions. Some are painful, and some are deprived of pain. Some are open, and some are deprived of color or pale. Some are "clean," and some are "unclean." Among the unclean ones, some produce an excessive amount of fluid and copious moisture, which is a bad sign in a fistula. Some of these are filthy, and some are "un-numbered" <note>likely meaning irregular or difficult to categorize</note>. Regarding these ulcers, they are discharging <note>original: 'purdy', likely 'purulenta'</note>. The most harmful among them are those with a sharp, stinging moisture and internal heat. Some are "corrosive," some are "ambulatory" <note>spreading or wandering</note>, and some are soft, either cold or hot. Soft ulcers are those that cause the hair to fall out from the area they occupy.

And there are sometimes ulcers that "flee" <note>refractory or receding</note>, from which a hot limb is produced; perhaps it is hot with a burning sensation that, if it comes together, mortifies the flesh—a bad thing. Some are difficult to solidify <note>to heal or close</note>. Putrefaction <note>decay</note> is a corrosive process. If it is "ambulatory," it spreads. Perhaps it is corroding and corrupting that which it touches.

Hot ulcers tend toward redness and are relieved by cold.

When these bad ulcers are infected by a malicious heat of the body, like a leaden or dark hue, that is a sign of extensive corruption of the body's composition, and a corruption of each of the pathways, because solidification <note>healing</note> becomes difficult.

Ulcers whose roots are deep, or which produce sharp excesses, are acute. Those whose roots are otherwise, and where the fluids in that place are copious, are cold.

Ulcers generated from a discharge of sickness are bad, for they expel the dregs of corruption from excessive illness.

Ulcers that cause the loss of hair from the surrounding area are bad.

The better signs—those indicating the health of ulcers and wounds—are when the discharges tend toward healthy **pus** <note>original: 'saniem'</note>.

And concerning the signs <margin>through their own property</margin> of the location: when it is breathed through, <margin>note</margin> it is a mild wax, and the reason is more quickly destroyed.

The causes of malignant ulcers are twofold: when they occur in a body filled with malignant excesses, or through a corrupt regimen <note>diet and lifestyle</note>, and when they follow bad pustules. The malignancy of the ulcer is signified by its putrefaction, its initial spreading, and the corruption of that which it occupies <margin>of it.</margin> or the difficulty of healing in the elderly, where a re-opening of the wound occurs during the healing process.

### The Fourth Medicine of Alexandria.

Take opoponax <note>A medicinal gum resin derived from the Hercules-allheal plant.</note> and roasted sarcocolla, colcothar, and flower of copper, and the juice of alum. One part of each; let it be surrounded by half a part. Let it be made into a powder. Or of any plasters, or silver with vinegar in which vitriol has been boiled. ### Concerning proud flesh added upon a wound.

For these are the names of wounds called "certainly drying." And the less they cause "biting" <note>Stinging or caustic irritation.</note>, the better they are. And it must not be expected that nature alone will assist to prevent flesh from growing; for the growth of flesh is the work of nature, and nature cannot act without the help of medicine, or without its assistance. This is the opinion on nature. Because of this, it is necessary that there be a great deal of support for the medicine. And know that what is prepared for this does not benefit those who wander from the ancient and correct path; and if there was anything living from it, it will be necessary in doing so to observe caution, lest it prevail in a place where it does not corrupt the action. And these things are to be praised for this: dry waxes, if they are needed, which I have found healthy, and to make them into troches <note>Medicated lozenges or discs.</note> and shapes like water-tablets. This is more effective. It is required that those which need it have hot water of arsenic, and that is for the resolution of hardness, and to revive that which was corrupted. And the medicine which is caustic and of a "fixing" power is more helpful in this chapter, not in part only, for perhaps it is subtle alone; this is because its thickness from the air and its moisture of combination is less, and its fixation with its own spirit is greater. And these medicines are such as burnt shells, and two parts of burnt things with their flesh. Truly, it remains in the skin more than is necessary. And perhaps beyond that which is marvelous is the flower of native stone, and the strong dross [scoria] of copper which is a glue, gold, and colcothar, and roasted sarcocolla; [roasting] dimin-

### Regime for wounds that break open despite previous consolidation.

For the power of the first [treatment] comes to help the consolidation. The "disruption" [breaking open] occurs when bad flesh is taken, and the bone that follows it, from the lack of care or desire for it, but which you seek.
