### Dislocation of the Jaw.

<margin>en-</margin>It is the nature of this part that it may be dislocated from its proper order so that it remains open. Although this may occur on one or both sides, it most frequently happens from a full fall, or when the dislocation occurs because of a softening <note>A loosening of the ligaments due to excess "moisture" or humors</note> that overcomes the strength of the joint. The application of one part to the other is then distant. This prevents the movement of the jaw <note>original: "lactis suis," referring to the muscles or "milky" ligaments of the jaw</note> which comes to it from the <term>apophyses</term><note>The bony outgrowths where muscles attach.</note>. When the dislocation occurs on one side, the visible form of it is a leaning of the jaw toward the healthy side with a swelling. At other times, it is universal <note>occurring on both sides</note>. Then the surgeon must hasten to reduce it. For if it is not brought back, it leads to hardships or injuries, or there is little hope of restoration. For if it is not restored, the surrounding ligaments and nerves <note>original: "ūcloziō"</note> are stretched and can cause <term>inseparable fevers</term><note>fevers that do not break or remit</note> and immediate headaches because of the violence of the displacement of the jaw muscles. This may perhaps be a small thing at first, until inflammation sets in. And when it happens that it is loosened by a flow of superfluous humors or purging, or if they vomit similar things, one must hasten to the cure. <gloss>And the method of managing this</gloss> is for the head to be held firmly. Then the <term>restorer</term><note>original: "restaūator," the surgeon or bone-setter</note> shall find a way to place his thumbs inside the mouth. He should move the lower jaw to soften it from every side; for there are the muscles which are the substance that bears the violence of the dislocation. Afterward, let him move the jaw to the right and left, then extend it suddenly, and then push it back. The jaw will then return to the place from which it was separated or moved backward. It is necessary to extend it so that it matches its own socket. The sign of its correction is the equality of the two sides and the closing of the mouth. Then it should be stabilized with small cushions, or a wax salve, or roses, or oil of roses. Then leave it be; when it is healed quickly, recovery is possible.

**If it is not stabilized**
then hardness will occur. It will be necessary to apply softening treatments. The easiest way to treat the hardness is with warm water or oil in a bath of feathers <note>a warm compress using feathers to retain heat</note>. Then let it be anointed. Afterward, the restorer should sit behind the patient and hold the jaw at the back, where the joint is said to be joined. Or, if that is not possible, lay

<column-break/>

him back upon a pillow or something full and soft, and keep his head firm so that it does not move until the healing is complete.

### Dislocation of what is called the Fork, or separation of the collarbone...

That which is called the <term>furcula</term><note>literally "little fork," the medieval term for the clavicle or collarbone</note> is the separation of the collarbone... It is widely known because it is joined with the chest <note>original: "p’core," for *pectore*</note> and not entirely separated from it. For this reason, it may move from either side. If the bones suffer deformity through great violence or cold, they are squeezed. This should be treated with applications that resist the cold. But when the extremity that follows the shoulder <note>original: "humenū"</note> is separated from it, it is a complete dislocation. Although there are two heads <note>the sternal and acromial ends</note> that prevent this, or many from the single head of the <term>spatula</term><note>the shoulder blade or scapula</note>. The collarbone does not move with a swift motion because it is always placed against the chest for support. In other animals, the collarbone is different. If a dislocation occurs from wrestling or a fall, when it is equalized, it is returned to its place by hand or with round compresses <note>original: "pillullis plīnis"</note> which are placed over it with a binding that is tight. This should be done at the ends where it is separated, reducing it to its place. And that which binds the collarbone and the shoulder is a cartilaginous bone, and it is wrapped in a <term>membrane</term><note>original: "mialen̄ō," likely *medulleno* or referring to a connective tissue</note>. When it is moved, it protrudes; but it is not our experience that the head of the shoulder itself is separated or gone from its place. Rather, the protrusion of the collarbone is seen clearly, and the place below it appears hollow. Truly, it must be distinguished by these signs. And the management of it is such that in no way should it be pulled toward the head, nor should the shoulder be moved similarly.

### Dislocation of the Shoulder

When the shoulder <note>the humerus</note> is dislocated, it is a displacement of the shoulder joint from the socket of the <term>spatula</term><note>scapula</note>. They are easily displaced. Truly, when the joint of the shoulder is dislocated by an accident, it is easy to see, for the socket is not deep and the ligaments are not strong; rather, they are smooth and short to allow for easy motion. Its dislocation is a thing that does not often happen in my experience in one specific way: it does not dislocate upwards, because the prominence of the shoulder <note>the acromion process</note> prevents it. Nor does it go backwards, because the scapula prevents it. It usually goes toward the belly <note>anteriorly</note>. Since there are two heads at the inner side, it is not permitted to move because of the barrier of the shoulder's edge. Truly, if it is dislocated to the <term>domestic</term><note>inner or medial</note> side or the <term>wild</term><note>outer or lateral</note> side, it is separated by a small distance. But it most often goes out toward the lower side <note>inferiorly/into the armpit</note>, where it protrudes greatly. In these cases, the dislocation of the arm <note>original: "adiutorij," the humerus</note> occurs. Its restoration is generally easy. This is more common in fat people than in others. And when a dislocation occurs in adults, it is more difficult than in children or the elderly. Then, if they are not reduced quickly, the limb may be shortened in length, and the elbow remains weakened. How it may be verified: when it is not returned to its socket, but remains...

**The signs, therefore, of a true dislocation of the humerus.**
A cavity is seen at the head of the humerus, and that shoulder is not at all full; rather, it is hollowed near the head of the <term>scapula</term><note>original: "spatule"; the shoulder blade</note>. When this humerus is examined against the other, it appears sharper at this extremity, unless a swelling happens to occur there in the tissue or soft part of the head due to a blow or some other cause. And perhaps it is possible to see the unity of both heads of the humerus; then it is judged that the humerus is not well-attached to the side because of the inward curve of the hand. If one approaches it, the patient feels great pain. For certain, he is unable to lift his hand upward to touch his ear or the top of his head, and other movements are difficult for him. And these signs happen because of the dislocation, whether through an accident or through an injury.

**The treatment for a dislocation of the humerus.**
This must be done for those in whom it occurs. In bodies that are thin and have light blood, the method is to take the hand and place it under the armpit, near the head of the humerus, and try to bring it close. Then push it upward, while another hand extends the humerus downward. In infants, it is perhaps possible to reset the head of the humerus with the middle finger, then lead it back while the hand is held. But for more severe dislocations in strong bodies, the lighter way in this matter is for the <term>bone-setter</term><note>original: "restaurator"; the practitioner performing the reduction</note> to place his foot against the lower side, then place his heel against the head of the humerus. Or use a dry ball—or a moist one if it adheres closely—near the head of the humerus in the lower cavity. Then let him extend the arm with his hands in a straight line, as if he intends to pull it out from the shoulder blade. Then let him incline the hand slightly toward the injured side. And this is the most correct method of all for relieving the joint. Also, use a strong, long beam, longer than the patient. Then place his shoulder under the armpit of the patient, and lift him up so he is suspended under the shoulder. Then extend his hand toward his belly. If the patient is of light weight or thin body, let the practitioner grasp the hand firmly and let him be suspended by it until it turns. And when he is in the place of the foot, as if on a raised ladder, place a ball upon his head, and then from a standing position...

<column-break/>

...and let the bone-setter extend the arm widely with the other hand. If it does not fall from the neck with a small pull or suspension, and if the dislocation is small or difficult, or if much time has passed, then perhaps you will need all these actions and <term>maneuvers</term><note>original: "lulucināis"; likely referring to mechanical manipulations</note>. Let there be an instrument similar to the handle of a hoe, or a short rod, either the length of the humerus or a bit more or less, with a ball upon its head. This must be used with experience and reason, and it is pushed with that rod toward that lubricated space. The goal is that the instrument, being attached there, pushes it back toward the upper parts, or extends it upward. Or let two men resist the bone-setter as he extends the arm; let one man hold the other shoulder or the back, so it does not separate, or push against that shoulder. And let that bone-setter, while extending the arm, pull it as if his intention is to separate it from the shoulder blade by pulling it out. Then let it be moved toward the ear. When this is done, the joint falls back into its connection. Then let it be attached there immediately, so that the head of the humerus goes back into the upper cavity. And thus it will stay in its seat. Let it be así positioned over that which follows the humerus below, so the humerus is not broken; for it is not possible for the bone-setter to return it to its place through that which he attempted. And the physician, as if with a wedge, places the head of the humerus over the seat easily, while it is softened and managed according to the patient's will. And the man is suspended from the other side, the hand is extended, and the head of the humerus is guided into its place. Truly, the suspension should be done carefully near the head of the humerus so it does not break. And perhaps the foot is used in that place, and a round mass of spice or similar materials from that same place; then they are removed from it to another place, for fear of a fracture of the humerus. And it is treated by other methods derived from these. But the best of the methods is the first method. When the dislocation is reduced to its place, the best bandaging for it is to bind a ball into the shoulder. The bandage is made with woolen strips and should be kept separate from the part that was reduced. And it should be passed over the top of it, or near the other side of the cavity, up to the other shoulder. And when the <term>cross-bandage</term><note>original: "crue"; likely a crux or figure-eight bandage</note> falls over the injured shoulder, then the humerus is bound to the side toward the lower part. Then the elbow is bound, and the extremity of the hand is bound to the upper part of the neck. It is not undone until the seventh day, or according to the patient. And if an inflammation occurs during the reduction, it is necessary to use a poultice.

### Dislocation of the minor bone at the shoulder.

<margin>Note</margin>
This is the dislocation of the minor bone at the shoulder <note>original: "apud humerum"</note>. It occurs when the small bone that sits above the shoulder appears as if it has been separated from its neck. This is evident both to the touch and to the eye in such a dislocation. **Treatment.** It is necessary that it be extended with strong tension, but also compressed by the urging of the fingers so that it is tilted back into its proper place. Let it then be bound, and bound in this way with a small cord and padding. Thus they should watch carefully, for when the bone is made to return to its place, the patients suffer much pain. And if it is said of the one who pulls it out, for them the binding is preserved; thus he is instructed by it.

In the dislocation of the <term>elbow</term><note>original: "cubiti"</note>, there are three modes of dislocation... it becomes difficult, and likewise its reduction is difficult, because of the great strength of the ligaments and the "cords" <note>original: "canenū," referring to tendons</note> in that area, and because of their growth and the shape of their natural cavity. And since even a small separation occurs, a dislocation happens there immediately which never heals well. When it is dislocated, the dislocation is indicated by a bulging on the side and a narrowing on the opposite side. The worst kind is that which goes toward the back, because that tendon is very unyielding. And most often the dislocation happens in the lower <term>focile</term><note>original: "fodilii"; a medieval term for the bones of the forearm (radius or ulna)</note>; its restoration is easier because of what is said concerning the remedy.

The dislocation of the upper bone happens similarly, but the severity of the lower dislocation is greater because it is more forceful in its connection with the palm, and it is far from the arm to be moved. It is not possible for one of the two forearm bones to be dislocated or elongated from the second without some elongation occurring in the other. **Treatment.** One must hasten to its adjustment, because as long as fluid <note>original: "aqua"; likely referring to inflammatory swelling or joint effusion</note> collects there, it prevents the restoration.

When the surgeon pulls to equalize the head of the bone, he should bring it to the aforementioned position; this is done so that it is not impossible for it to be equalized while the head remains out of place. For a separation that was small, despite the difficulty, let him rather join the palm when he has returned the bone to its place. If the complete dislocation is toward the front, use one regimen. If it is toward the back, use another regimen.

The bone that is toward the front returns to its place when they open their palm toward the shoulder which is opposite to it through certain movements; let the hand be pushed in this manner. Then let him assist with the other hand, which is not extended. Regarding the tendon at the front, it is necessary to extend it with forceful tension. Then let it be pushed forward. If it does not return easily, let two strong men hold the upper arm and the forearm, and let the restorer lubricate his hand with oil; let him begin by entering and anointing with force until it enters. It is necessary that he bind it along the arm as if with a sling <note>original: "pensuloziū"</note>; leave the elbow bent and quiet, and then raise it. Afterward, let the procedure cease and let the sling be tightened gradually until the joint is fully bound.

### Dislocation of the wrist joint.

<column-break/>

Regarding the <term>wrist</term><note>original: "rachete"</note>, dislocations may occur and joinings may be difficult. For since it is extended with only a little protrusion, one of the two joints is opposed to the other; this is the case if the bulging is small. This happens because the substance that maintains the body's parts is pure and prevents the moisture necessary for union <note>A reference to the lack of "gluey" humors or perhaps synovial fluid in the small bones of the carpus</note>. The method for its extension is that it be stretched forward toward the front, and the restorer extends his palm toward the patient's... rather toward the front. Let him extend each finger, beginning from the thumb and reaching to the little finger. For it equalizes easily; reduce it and then let it be bound.

### Dislocation of the fingers, their signs, and their treatment.

When the fingers are dislocated, they tilt toward one side and a protrusion appears there in the joints, and a hollowness appears on the opposite side; it is similar to the bones of the wrist. **Treatment.** In returning the fingers to their proper state from a dislocation, there is some difficulty. It is not necessary that they be pulled with a straight extension; rather, it is necessary that you extend over them and raise the index finger from your hand under the base of the bone, and then touch upon it toward the upper parts as if you were pulling them out of their place; then you will see the dislocation now changing, and suddenly the force is achieved <note>The bone snaps back into place</note>.

### Concerning the setting and positioning of the joints of the wrist bones.

It is possible for it to be equalized, and the impulse of the whole... and the protrusion to its part, and the area should be splinted <note>original: "astellatū"</note>, with a bandage from above, and then it is left upon it. And as in the first place, let one take a piece of lead equal to the bone, smoothed to its place, to guide it. It is true that one may use a splint or lead as a plate, made strong, and it should not be moved.

### Concerning the dislocation of the vertebrae and their setting.

When the <term>vertebrae</term><note>original: "spondiles"</note> are dislocated in a complete dislocation, it is seen with little doubt. If it is not complete, it is seen when many other things are moved. It is considered a marvel that a complete dislocation is mortal, because without a doubt it compresses the <term>spinal cord</term><note>original: "nucha"</note> with a strong compression, and it cannot be restored. If the first vertebra of the neck is involved, the animal <note>the patient</note> loses its breath and cannot remain steady, because the nerves of breathing are compressed so that they cannot perform their operation. And if it is one of the vertebrae of the chest, and it is dislocated toward the lower part, it is not possible that the patient should live. These are things that happen quickly. And if he does not die, but his breath is hindered, he must be nourished and watched.

And if he does not die, and the spinal cord is not compressed with a forceful compression, he is left paralyzed, or the nerves of the voice that are below that place are affected, and it causes the "superfluities" <note>waste products like urine and feces</note> to exit involuntarily. But if the dislocation is toward the back, it is a wonder... for though he does not die, the compression of the nerves weakens the chest, the feet, and the sides. This does not happen except by a strong force, a forceful impulse, and great suffering which almost breaks the body's bounds until it is returned.

### **Dislocation of the hip**

**W**hen the hip lies in a way similar to one that lies for assistance, it is a dislocation toward the lower parts, and thus it is softened. And it is not possible, if the dislocation continues, for the part to expand. It is not just near the dislocation, but also at the knee; indeed, it is in that knee that the greatest problem lies. And for the one who has the dislocation, since it is in the lower part, it may be toward the exterior. Truly, the first kind of dislocation is toward the exterior, and the smaller dislocation is toward the interior. And it is dislocated internally toward the anterior, and superiorly, and toward the <term>calcaneus</term><note>original: "pullis calcã ciã"; referring to the heel bone.</note>. And when it lies in different parts, there is a bending above the bone where that foot is dislocated; then make that leg so it never deviates from the alignment of the body, which is weakened and not grasped.

**Signs.**
The signs between a dislocation toward the interior are that you see the dislocated foot appears longer than the other, and the knee is prominent. And the patient is not able to fold their foot at the groin without pain, since the head of the hip is in the lower part. And if it is dislocated toward the exterior, the foot is shortened, and a depth appears in the groin. And it falls in that which is opposite to it in the posterior parts with a prominence and a standing out. And the knee itself is situated as if turned toward the interior. And if it is dislocated toward the anterior, the foot is longer, and it is not possible for the sufferer to expand their leg, nor is it possible for them to maintain its natural color, and growth does not come to the <term>creciubula</term><note>original: "crecĩbula"; likely a corruption of a term for the joints or growth plates.</note>. And if they wish to walk, they walk upon the heel, and it happens to them many times from this that it appears in their groin, and their urine is retained. And if it is dislocated toward the posterior, their foot is shortened, and expansion upon it is difficult, and a softening appears in the groin, and the head of the hip is inclined at an angle.

**Treatment.** It is necessary that there be haste in the treatment, for if it is not returned quickly, perhaps it will pour out into a <term>deformity</term><note>original: "cãbũiditatẽ"; likely referring to a permanent swelling or hump-like protrusion of the joint.</note> and they will putrefy, and it will lead to the corruption of the whole <term>tibia</term><note>original: "tĩbiũ"; here used generally for the lower leg.</note>. And follow that out of fear of what you know. The rule for a dislocation of the hip toward the lower parts is that you should extend the foot, and finally make it return with vehemence after you have moved it right and left until it is opposite to that to which it returns. And place the foot that is in the <term>splint</term><note>original: "l̃astrĩge"; likely a corruption of "astringe" (bind) or "lastra" (a splint/board).</note> upon the leg, then bind it upon the chest and upon the knee that lifted it. Then let them be suspended from this suspension, lest it be possible for the joint to be over-extended. When it is dislocated toward the interior, it is commanded that the knees be reflected, and a strong man should hold him from the other side. ### **Dislocation of the Knee**

**A** dislocation of the knee happens quickly. Perhaps the dislocation occurs because of an injury, or from a sudden slip, or because the patient is slippery <note>prone to such injuries due to loose joints</note>; thus it is often dislocated in many ways. And the knee that is dislocated in any direction—except forward because of the <term>rotula</term> <note>the kneecap</note>—must be reset.

**Treatments.**
Let the patient sit upon his seat in a straight manner, and let his feet be raised a little bit. Then let a strong man extend his hand from above and from below with great force, and let the restorer bring the joint back into its proper distance according to the sight of the dislocation, and let it be bound so that the dislocation is arrested.

**W**hen a dislocation of the kneecap occurs, it is necessary that the foot be placed flat on the ground and the kneecap be reduced [pushed back into place]. Then fill the area with a healing compress; let cloths be added to the application, and let splints <note>original: "astelle"</note> be placed over it to resist the direction in which it tends to slip, and let it be bound. If the knee is bent with haste, let it be raised very gradually.

### **Dislocation of the Ankle at the Heel**

**L**et the heel be bound. It will need to be reset if it is dislocated toward the outside, using great tension and pushing with strength so that it returns. Then it is necessary that he refrain from walking for forty days, so that it is not dislocated a second time. If the dislocation is slight and minor, any simple extension is sufficient to reduce it. And when it is completely dislocated, then it must be reduced according to what we said previously.

In this case, it is necessary that the patient be extended along his whole length upon the ground. From the part that is in the hip at the <term>alhafege</term> <note>variant of alhahegi, the hip bone</note>, let it be placed parallel to the ground in its depth. If the hip joint is joined, it may move. Let his foot proceed toward the lower parts; indeed, it must be held for a little while and then the patient should be laid back. If there is a large piece of wood, in the middle of which we said another piece of wood is fixed, it will be necessary that the extension be made upon that wood. One assistant should hold the hip and pull it, and another assistant should extend the foot either with his hands or with a bandage, according to the extension the first assistant provides. And let the physician balance the limb with his hands to ensure it is level, so that it is held straight. Let another assistant hold the foot toward the inner parts. It must then be balanced and bound with strong bandages. And let the bandage go toward the <term>pecten</term> <note>the metatarsus or "comb" of the foot</note> and to the heel, and be bound there. And one should take care that the force exerted upon the ankle is not too great, nor should the bandages be too tight. Then the patient should be forbidden from walking for forty days. And if he tries to walk before then, he will not be fully healed, the limb will remain weak, and the treatment will be ruined.

**O**f the ankle bone <note>original: "scyp̄os tali"</note>, many times it is false [misdiagnosed], for that happens often; or it happens to this limb at the small cup <note>the socket of the ankle</note>. Observe that the limb should be treated with the patient lying on his face and extended.

### Second Treatise on Universal Rules for Fractures

### Universal Discourse on Fractures

A fracture is a breach of the continuity of the bones. It happens when they are scattered, or when they are in splinters. And it happens when it is an even break, and when it is a splintered break. And also when it happens in width <note>a transverse fracture</note>, and when it happens in length <note>a longitudinal fracture</note>, and those in width may be divided or not divided. And those in length involve the case where a piece falls away separately. Some have named these fractures with their own names, saying a large fracture proceeding in width is a *rasanale*, *rassale*, or *rasrudmale* <note>transliterated terms from Arabic medical traditions, likely referring to types of transverse or crushing breaks</note>. They say a fracture proceeding in length is a *lignecale* <note>a "wood-like" splintering</note>, and one proceeding in length with width is *lunare* <note>moon-shaped</note> or *mervale*. And there are those who suffer from a small... <note>the text lists various Arabic-derived names for fracture types like "alienuse" and "albulerien"</note>. When a fracture is complete, it is possible that two bones remain, but what is now between them regarding the opposition of the natural community <note>the healthy structure of the bone</note> is separated from its opposition. You shall see the appearance of the points I have noted, which are now covered by membranes and flesh, which happen when there is a separation. And when it is cut into pieces, it harms the limb with its sharpness. And it is better for the fracture to incline toward the outside rather than toward the inside, because the nerves that occur there are more numerous and it causes more pain. And when a fracture occurs near a joint, its restoration remains difficult to achieve unless there is a swelling that occurs and requires time until the condition is clear. And what happens in the vicinity of small bones is that the examination is more difficult, as in the joint of the ankle <term>cavilla</term>. And if there is a deformity from improper setting... that which is said, let the bandage be prolonged over it with a wonderful structure for a long time. And let it take from... and from that which sends blood to that part, as we have said. And the certainty regarding fractured bones is by the signs, as we have said, and regarding the nature of the marrow <term>medulla</term> which is inside, lest it be deprived of nourishment. For the marrow has a softness and viscosity that moistens the bone. And when 

<column-break/>

it happens that there is a fracture, there is also a wound, a flow of blood, and an abscess <term>aposema</term>, and whatever results from the flesh, which must be prevented from putrefaction <note>rotting</note> which happens from its corruption. The location of the fracture of large bones is known by the pain and the incision <note>break</note> with the fracture. In children or small ones, it appears through the pain of the break.

In these cases, many signs of restoration occur. And when these bones return to their proper places, it is possible for them to be healthy within a year, so that they are restored without any lasting damage in old age or youth. Rather, there is always a cartilaginous matter <term>cartillaginosi</term> joining the two bones together, from which those things that are seen to come out... and over the joint of those and others. And the bones most difficult to restore <margin>Note on the time of restoration</margin> are those of the jaw or the arm. Moreover, the collarbone <note>likely "furcula"</note>, since it breaks toward the internal parts, must be treated with specific care. And a fracture in the two fossils <note>the two bones of the forearm or lower leg</note> is like the fracture of the lower parts described in dislocation. The matter of their cure and healing is such that restoration is more common in them. And the limb which is divided in the space of restoration is found everywhere, when it is restored naturally as said in the medical art. The jaw in twenty days, the ulna <note>forearm</note> in that which approaches thirty up to forty days, and the same for others... long until it is restored around thirty or forty days, or what is beyond that. And so that the limb does not decline into a weakened state of restoration, it is better for it to incline towards the front than towards the back, as such a decline is more evident. And also in the restoration process, there is a need for a large amount of bathing with warm water <term>embrocatio</term>, and a large number of loosenings of the bandages and their re-binding. For haste in movement, or a lack of blood, or a lack of viscous blood in the body can hinder it. And because of this, the restoration of bone fractures is renewed; and among those things that signify restoration is the appearance of blood <note>bruising</note>, which is an excess expelled by nature that is busy at the site of the fracture.

### On the Methods of Restoration and Bandaging

The basis of restoration for a dislocation is the extension of the limb with the appropriate amount of force. For excessive extension harms the nature of the limb and causes injury, and from it comes fever and softening of the tissues. And that is harmful in bodies that are moist and soft because of their compliance with the extension. And a lack of extension prevents the solid union of the parts. Dislocation and fracture are treated similarly in this regard. And let it be certain according to the manner of the break, and let the concern be for the joining of the two bones according to their straightness, the protection of the new growth <note>the callus</note>, and the bandaging as is necessary. And place splints <term>astellas</term> over them, and place the bandages over the splints. And it is necessary that the limb be supported as much as possible, according to the proper measure.

In lifting a disruption <note>original: "disruptio," referring to a displaced fracture or break</note> of the bone, the surgeon must act with care so that the two bones may return to their proper place and reach a straight alignment. There must be no irregularity in the setting, for in irregularity lies the corruption of the bone. It is necessary for the surgeon to run his hand over the site of the fracture in a steady path, toward the upper and lower parts, with skill and care, until he senses a separation, a protrusion, or a fragment. restoration. For many times, bruising and numbness may be hidden. The positioning of the limb during restoration is done according to the amount of pain. ### On the squaring of bandages

It will also be possible to provide a clear explanation. Let the bandage begin from the location of the break, and from there it should decline toward the bone. And there let it be tightly bound. And that which does not appear to show signs in the bone itself, points to the marrow, and corrupts the marrow and the bone. This is done with **omphacine oil** <note>original: "oleo onfaa," oil made from unripe olives</note> rarely. And perhaps it is necessary to soothe the area with those things that contain **chamomile oil**, not with a styptic humor. So that the swelling itself is resolved and the limb is strengthened. And because the physician is fully aware, when the color begins to return, let the loosening and binding be done gently.

In the case of a diverse fracture, it is softened there. For this reason, the cerate should be extended, and it should not be used in an overly restrictive way; the pad should be long. This is therefore the first bandage. Then make a second bandage and wrap it over the fracture twice or thrice. Then make it descend to the lower parts to soften the area. Afterward, make a full third bandage, and bring it toward the upper parts. By making the bandages equal, you expel the superfluity of the humors and prevent them from returning to the lower part of the limb. And in these, it is superfluous to go too far in length, lest the limb be constricted or the veins blocked, through which the nourishment flows, and perhaps it might die. And when this is done correctly, first with the bandage going up, then following with the bandage going down, then beginning the binding at the swelling, the lower part of the bandage should move toward the upper part.

### On the Quality of Splints

Splints are made of wood, which adds tenacity and smoothness by its addition; such as alder <note>original: "alcone"</note>, and the wood of the oleander, and the wood of the pomegranate <note>original: "gnan"</note>, and the daughter of the reed <note>original: "reis filia," likely referring to thin ferula or reed strips</note>. ### Concerning a fracture with a wound

**A**nd when a fracture and a wound occur together, the restoration or correction must be handled differently. ### Signs of Poisoning
A watery spirit sometimes indicates poison solely through the onset of illnesses. For just as some things are biting and sharp, like medicines of a hot, stinging nature, such as **arsenic**, **alum**, and **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: liquid mercury, which was known to be toxic when processed or ingested</term> mixed with vinegar. And if there occur intense inflammation and a deep redness, along with swelling of the eyes and difficulty breathing, it signifies that the poison is of a hot nature, such as **euphorbia**. <note>original: "euforbiū," a caustic plant resin used in ancient medicine</note> And if there occurs a heaviness of sleep, stupor, and coldness, it signifies that the poison is of the class of **narcotics**. And if neither heat nor cold appears clearly, but there is paleness and coldness and fainting, then it is a poison that flows through the internal parts or the mouth of the stomach, and is visible on the outside.

### And when it is signified
by the odors of the body, such as a whistling or hissing <note>original: "seu sibilicas," possibly a description of the sound or smell of the breath</note> or an odor in what was drunk, or the odor of the limbs, as is the case with those who drink putrefying poisons, such as the **sea hare**, <term>sea hare: Aplysia, a marine mollusk believed in antiquity to be a deadly poison</term> **Spanish fly**, <note>original: "carandes" or "cantharides," toxic beetles used as a blistering agent</note> and **asafoetida**. And when it is signified by sight: for when poison is taken, it is not long before it falls into the body from what was given in the drink, so it may be recognized by the odor, or by a stone; just as visual signs appear upon **litharge** <term>litharge: lead oxide</term> and **gypsum**, and upon the melting of jelly and curdled milk. And the work of the poison may be recognized by the smell. The **sea hare** and others can be identified by their distinctive taste.

### Bad Signs
Watery poison is a bad sign if it leads to syncope <note>fainting or loss of consciousness</note> and the changing of the pupil, and if its darkness is hidden, then it is similar to death. Likewise, if the eyes turn red, or the tongue protrudes, or there is a falling of the senses, and a cold sweat, it is a bad sign. And in this, the life of the poisoned person departs.

### Rule for the relief of one who has drunk poison
so that they do not die. Indeed, when someone feels it, before it travels through the body to cause death, let them drink warm water and sesame oil, or just oil, and let them vomit. ## Quicksilver

**Q**uicksilver <term>quicksilver: liquid mercury</term>, which is called "the wine of lead," should not be drunk. It comes out through the various regions and is found in the mines. ## Cure

**H**ere, then, is the treatment. He should be given those medicines that are dry in weight, five drachms in wine, or given honey-water to drink. Its poisonous nature is well known. If it harms a man, it is said that it happens through the contact of their juices. The bite of this poison gnaws at the nerves and corrupts the flesh.

**The Cure.**
Enter into a regimen of almond oil, philonium <note>a famous medieval opiate electuary</note>, and butter that has been touched by sweet and fatty milk. This settles the gnawing and the moisture. Then give a drink of sour milk and cooling anacardium with nuts, oil in a mash, and cooled barley water or cooled fruit water. Let him sit in the water of unripe nuts and use a sharp syrup. There are many kinds of these, and the nut is the core of it, but the flesh is harmful. It is true that they kill by their sharpness.

**Ranunculus.**
<note>original: "Kebikegi," the Arabic name for *Ranunculus sceleratus* or Crowfoot</note>
It kills by its sharpness. **Its Cure.**
Treat it similarly to Anacardium. Use oils and things that are life-giving, but not his usual nourishment.

**Stavesacre.**
<note>original: "Staphisagria," a plant used to kill lice but toxic if swallowed</note>
The pains and symptoms are like those of anacardium. The cure is the same, or use the instructions given in its own chapter.

**Wild Rue.**
Anyone who drinks a decoction of this falls into a hatred of smells, then a burning sensation, then an inflammation or swelling.

**Its Cure.**
He must be made to vomit with warm water and oil. Then he should be treated with the cure for oleander.

**Thefi.**
This is the gum of mountain rue. It is very dry. It causes a collapse similar to taking too much garlic, and it makes the breath hot. It affects the water the person drinks and causes a retention of the bowels. It causes the tongue to swell, as well as a rumbling inflation of the belly, a burning in the throat, and a hatred of food.

The same as for the others. **Concerning Suffocation from Roasting and Corrupted Meat.**

Induce vomiting by drinking honey-water <note>original: "almelis"</note>.

### The Curdling of Milk in the Stomach

<margin>Obstruction</margin>
When milk curdles in the stomach because of some harmful cause, it congeals again either through the hardness of the milk or through an excess of food in the morning. And from this happens a cold sweat, and syncope <term>syncope: a sudden loss of consciousness or fainting</term>, and the shivers of fever. And if it was curdled with rennet, then it will be worse and more prone to causing suffocation. This congealing of milk in the stomach is similar to the genus of congealing blood. It happens from a disposition of the material, just as it happens from a wound or from poisons. For it happens that what is congealed in the stomach suffocates the body, and the pulse suffers, and there is suffocation and constriction in the belly.

### The Cure.

One must ensure that the milk does not turn into cheese <note>original: "caseet"</note> in the stomach. In this case, one adds to it [the remedy] that which was chosen, but it is best to give it with pure milk or mixed with water. And let him be given lime <note>original: "lumia"</note> according to the weight of 5 drachms, which is a wonderful thing for resolving the milk. And by its virtue, it prevents the person from being strangled or suffocated. And let there be given something of the rennets <note>original: "cauglis"</note> until it is resolved; for these themselves resolve it, or lead it out through vomiting or loosening the bowels. This should be given with a drink as a remedy for the congealing of blood in the stomach, and for that which was caused by chills and those things I have mentioned. Another medicine: clean frankincense <note>original: "toului'"; likely 'thous' or 'tus'</note>. Let it be given in a drink with water or dissolved in vinegar, which is effective against the "wood-poison" of dogs <note>original: "qanis ligni uenē"; possibly a reference to rabies or a specific toxic plant associated with dogs</note>, and let it be administered for the paths of the breath.

### Beginning of the Discourse on Bites and Punctures. First Treatise on the Universal Regimen of Bites, the Identification of Poisonous Creatures, and the Cure for Snake Bites and Their Species.

You should know that the greatest canon of help against poison is the strengthening of the universal heat and the excitation of the body to expel it. Thus do **Theriac** and the **Naples Antidote** <note>original: "nap' lauītanē"</note> work, so that they make the poison slippery and expel it to the exterior.

<column-break/>

The focus of strengthening is to remove the bite and the expulsion of the poison, and the destruction of the belief in its specific property, whether the snake is known or unknown according to what is said. And when these intentions are joined with another matter, which concerns the universal regimen of mothers <note>original: "matab'"; possibly 'materiae' (materials/substances)</note> when they move them or trample them. They enter in this way through the flow of humors and the wind of the breath and similar things. And it is more harmful when there is no flow [bleeding]; for it is enough that the poison has touched the spit, and not from those things that draw it out. And when these things are joined in this chapter, there is another thing. It is like the "bundres" bite <note>original: "moꝛq būdꝛes"; likely a specific local name for a viper or spider bite</note> on a part of the limb with small hair. And those things that are drunk against poison, such as Theriac and other universal saviors, are either for that specific poison or to mediate against the poison by completing the balance, just as garlic is to its own poison by its property. Or they lead the poison to the exterior by moving the humors outward, such as the famous remedies, or remedies that remove the humors from the presence of the poison. We have mentioned those that are proven, such as laxative, emetic, and reductive medicines. And the immediate remedies applied over the poisonous bites, like a plaster <note>original: "epydnmāte"</note>, are intended to be internal. The way is to prevent the penetration of the poison into the soul/vital breath <note>original: "in aī"; in animam</note>, either by a ligature or by constricting the extremities, and by prohibiting the swallowing, so that the heat is moved from the interior to the exterior and expels it. And as in this chapter, it is done by sucking the bite, or with medicines that are "anti-toxic" <note>original: "ātūuoꝛīs"; likely 'antidotis'</note>. And for those things taken [internally], it prevents the poison from penetrating deep within. In cases where the bite is heavy, cupping glasses <note>original: "uētūle"</note> are used. And perhaps an incision is needed, and it should be elongated. And the blood should be drawn out from it. This is a practice of the wise; for the blood that is pulled out carries the poison with it. And against the bite, the person sucking should have a good smell in his nose and wash his mouth, and have his teeth rubbed with oil. He should hold a little oil in his mouth, or soft oil <note>original: "oleū mol'"</note>. He takes it in his mouth and expels everything that he sucks. He must spit it out. Medicines are such as those drunk and those that cause redness <term>rubefacients: substances for external application that produce redness of the skin by causing dilation of the capillaries</term>. And they fight against the poison either through their heating power or by their ability to draw out, which is like a lizard used for the bite of a crocodile <note>original: "cocodallum ad moꝛsū cocodꝛillī"</note>. And it is used for the trembling of the extremities... these medicines are effective against many poisons. Some are more bile-like, and some act against the heart. ### A fumigation to drive out scorpions...

One should take storax <note>original: "stonea," likely styrax</note>, arsenic, and the dung of grey beasts <note>original: "ravoru'," possibly referring to wolves or grey birds</note> and ... in equal parts. And this is among the best fumigations for the scorpions themselves, as the smoke is made from their own kind <note>The text suggests a sympathetic magical or chemical repellent effect</note>. And likewise with arsenic.

### The driving away of fleas.

When the house is sprinkled with an infusion of colocynth <term>colocynth: a bitter, desert vine used as a powerful purgative and pesticide</term> and salt <note>original: "saliu'"</note>, the fleas flee. And likewise from a decoction of bramble. And they said that when the blood of a hyena <note>original: "hyraenae"</note> is placed in a pit in the house, the fleas gather toward it and even die. And similarly, they gather upon wood smeared with dog fat. And they are driven away by the odor of ... and the leaves of ... <note>original: "olemori"</note>. And there is a well-known herb in ... called pennyroyal <term>pennyroyal: a fragrant herb of the mint family, traditionally used to repel insects</term>; when it is placed in the bed, it intoxicates them, but does not overcome them, so that they no longer bite.

### The driving away and killing of mice.

For mice, an application of litharge <term>litharge: a lead-based mineral (lead oxide)</term> will destroy them, as will white hellebore <term>white hellebore: a highly toxic plant used in ancient and medieval times to kill pests</term>; and likewise the root of ... and similarly many other things for mice, such as the dross and slag of iron. ### The driving away of ants.

When milk is placed over their holes, they flee from it. And likewise from a magnet, and from the gall of a bull, and from pitch, and from alum. And they flee from the smoke of burned ants.

### The driving away and killing of flies.

Arsenic kills them when it is boiled with something in milk. And the flies flee, or the smoke of it kills them; also the smoke of incense, or a decoction of black hellebore.

### The driving away of beetles.

In comparison, the young of these creatures are held to be less dangerous than the old. <note>original: "In coplam sic hāre bntur iuuenes dñi oset sunt senibt," a comparison of the toxicity between young and old serpents.</note>

Rather, Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the primary medical authority in the Middle Ages.</note> says in his own work that they are distinguished by masculinity and femininity. And the males indeed have sharper teeth and more venom. Others say that the females are worse because of the multitude of their teeth. There is also a difference in age, because the old are more dangerous than the young. And regarding their bodies: for greater size makes them more dangerous than others when their species is the same. Or it is because of their locations: for those who inhabit a place in the north or in the deserts are worse than those who inhabit the shores and places with much water. Or it is because of their hunger; for those among them who are famished are worse in their venoms. Or because of their animal passions; for the bold and raging ones are more deadly. Or it is because of the seasons; for their venom is worse in summer. When serpents have fought, the venom is expelled from their teeth. And it is certain that the cold felt from their bite is because of the killing of the natural heat by the venom as it spreads. The innate heat is what makes the spirit disperse, causing inflammation. And when this heat is inflamed by a slight fire, it must be drawn out. Some venom attacks and reaches the blood of the heart and congeals it. And this is very dangerous, for it strongly dissolves the animal heat and kills it. This is reasoned because such a complexion occurs at the moment of death, and heat and burning happen. And whoever says otherwise should know that their reasoning is false; there is nothing seen in venom unless it be in the bodies of great animals. What signifies the corruption of this argument is that those of a very hot complexion are among those who are killed in winter, because then it moves.

### On the bite of the basilisk, which is the prince of serpents, and the barmene, whose nature is unknown.

Concerning the first kind, the species named Regulus <term>Regulus: Latin for "Little King," a common name for the Basilisk because of the crown-like crest on its head</term>, or others, which has a crown on its head. Its length is two palms, the head is very sharp, and its eyes are red. Its color inclines toward a golden redness, and it burns everything over which it walks. No bird falls near its habitat. No animal perceives it without fearing it; for if an animal is near, it is stupefied and cannot move. It kills with its hiss, which is its life-force. And he upon whom its sight falls dies even from a distance; it is said that its gaze falls upon and stays with the victim. The body of him whom it bites liquefies and rots. Everything that approaches the dead body is affected. Indeed, few escape who

<column-break/>

are present at its bite. It is possible at certain hours to touch it with a rod. But according to most, he who touches it with a rod dies through the medium of the rod. And because of this, they tell of a soldier who killed one with his lance; but because the venom touched the horse's lip, the horse and the man both died. And this kind of serpent is found in the deserts of Africa and Libya.

### Signs of its bite.

It seems to cause sudden death without an apparent cause appearing in the victim, especially in a place where no other animal is present, nor any other peril.

### Concerning the barmene.

We have heard of the *barmene* <note>An obscure or corrupted name for a legendary serpent, possibly related to the "burn-as" or similar desert snakes mentioned in medieval bestiaries</note> among the primary powers of the Regulus. It kills by its bite, and also by its sight and the hearing of its hiss. And that which dies a violent death by it dissolves, and anyone who approaches it among animals is affected. It shares the same nature and watery quality as the Regulus. Its venom is such that from the elbow to the [hand] it fails. And they say that a bite from it is like being struck by iron. If anyone were to be struck by it, he must be watched for seven days.

### Signs of the bite of the serpent called Ymi, which resembles the findis.

There is a loss of color, a stupor or numbing of the limbs, deep sleep, and the closing of the eyelids. The pulse of the <margin>heart</margin> is venomous because of the intensity of the color. And the breath of the victim is like the smell of sweat.

### Signs of the bite of the yellow asp, also called the "deaf one" that kills quickly.

Whoever it bites changes color and is stupefied; the color of the body is transformed, the limbs grow cold, the eyelids close, and the victim sleeps deeply. The breath is like the smell of sweat.

### Concerning the bite of the spitting serpent, the Fasilius.

When it bites, the sense remains until death, which happens because of the venom entering the home of the spirit. Beyond the things said in the previous chapter, the eyes are clouded and closed, the animal foams, and the pulse changes, though the color does not. And indeed it keeps to one color. Those who are bitten should put their fingers in their mouths to induce vomiting. And concerning what was mentioned about the *asityz* <note>Likely a corruption of "aspic" or a similar species</note>, it is told that it raises its head and spits venom. I have seen the venom; it is the color of death. The bite is small, but it produces blood that is purple or black. The result of its bite is darkness of the eyes, an unchanging color, and the closing of the eyes followed by deep sleep, and the wound lasts beyond one day. And they say it is of the nature of the deaf serpents.

### About the serpent called the water-snake and the chersydros.
The *Hydrus* is a water serpent. And it is called *chersydros* <note>a snake that lives both on land and in water</note> because in Greek, water is called *hydros*. And when it begins to live in the water, it is born as a *chersydros*. It is smaller than the "deaf asp" <note>original: "ala silan surda," likely the Seps or a similar small viper</note>, and wider of head, straighter, and more remarkable. And it happens from its bite that the wound takes on a leaden color and becomes inflamed. Then it becomes green and the flesh corrodes. And there occurs to the victim vertigo and the vomiting of a fetid-colored fluid, a heaviness in the stomach, and a weakness of the limbs.
<margin>Pliny</margin>
The victim may die unless a remedy is found. If he survives, because the venom is watery, and if the bite is strong, he may be consumed by "water-dropsy" <note>edema or swelling</note> that cannot be cured.

### Cure.
The cure for it is with wine, and that substance called *cyani* <note>possibly a blue mineral or plant extract</note>. And it is treated with cypress nuts ground with myrtle berries, or with grapes, or with honey-water or wine. And similarly, twelve weights of aristolochia <note>Birthwort, a plant used for snakebites due to its retort-shaped flowers resembling a snake</note> with wine, or with a mixture of vinegar. And similarly sweet leek; and fill the wound with lime and oil, and moving calamint. And from the roots of the oak with similar things, used individually or in combination. And among those things mixed in is barley flour.

### About the Hydra.
The *Hydra* is not spoken of in general, except when it is many-headed, though it is actually a single creature. Thus it is described in the sentences of the Greek speakers, or as another serpent. Truly, the place from which it comes makes the bite and its effects different. And they say that the bite is wide and spreads out, and its color is darkened. A black liquid flows from it, like a very thick plum juice. And the healing of it is prolonged and difficult, so that it is hardly cured at all. It is recognized and distinguished so that the treatment may be changed to a second order of remedies.

# General discourse on the bite of vipers, the rough and the "singing."
The outer characteristics of vipers and dragons are such that the males are safer, and the females are more dangerous. And the bite of the female is recognized by the number of tooth-marks: more than two teeth are fixed in the part she bit. And there comes out from the site of the two or three or more teeth, blood. Then it becomes hot and takes on a watery nature, then foamy, then like the rust of copper <note>original: "erugo eris," verdigris</note>. And it is known that these are the different stages of the poison. The color of the place becomes like bile, then it appears like a hot swelling, with a rough blistering as if from a fire burn. And as it spreads, the part around the bite becomes green and putrid. And there occurs a great inflammation, and redness joined with shivering. Then a cold sweat follows, and a corruption of the skin color, tending toward greenness, a movement of dizziness, and frequent sighing, nausea, and 
<margin>Note</margin>
hiccups. And then they vomit a bilious humor, and suffer difficulty in urinating, and the head shakes. And it brings on a flow of blood from the nostrils, and sometimes it appears in the back, along with a cold sweat, a trembling of the heart, and fainting. And it happens mostly that they die within three days, or it may linger until the seventh.

### Cure of the bite of vipers and of "dogs."
One should steep common roots in vinegar, then a stronger dose should be prepared with the animal itself <note>referring to the use of viper flesh in theriac</note> for the "Theriac of Vipers." And be cautious: it is possible that theriac should be offered many times, and it is possible it should not be. Note that when the poison is small, it is not so evil, because its nature is to be consumed within the human body; it is possible to survive them unless a different complication happens at the same time. And if possible, do not allow the victim much sleep, unless they are guarded against all increase of the poison's effect. And similarly, give leeks with wine, or garlic. And some observe that they eat roasted lizards <note>original: "gaaruu assata," likely a medicinal preparation of lizards or small reptiles</note> and take honey from those who offer medicine. And similarly mountain germander. And from the theriac of strong fish... with pepper, or four parts of round aristolochia, and one part of castoreum, if it be made with wine; or if it be crushed, one nut. And one part of castoreum, pepper, red arsenic, and two parts of dill seed, if it be made with wine. And this seed of *andacoka* <note>a botanical term, possibly of Arabic origin</note> and round aristolochia and mountain rue. And it is not *alharmel* <note>Peganum harmala, or Wild Rue</note> as some have thought; rather it is a species of mountain rue. And it should be given to drink frequently. And according to the ancients, he should sit in a pool of water, and his vigor should be judged. And let a bath be made, and he should stay in the bath until he produces a sweat. And let it be given with bread.

### On the types of scorpions and their likenesses

Some have said that the female scorpion is worse and larger than the male. The male is slender and smaller, and the female is fat and large. And the stinger of the female is [bal̄], and the stinger of the male is thick. And it happens that some scorpions have two stingers, but some estimate that they have two openings in their sting. And in coldness the sting is [cold], while the rest of the body heats up and is led into coldness. **A** scorpion with wings is large and many times it is prevented by being a flying creature, but it falls when it goes from region to region. And it is further said regarding the divisions of scorpions: among them are those that have six segments <note>original: "sfodiles"; referring to the tail segments</note>, because the malice becomes strong at the end of the tail, appearing like death to it. And there are those that have [multiple] stingers. And they estimated that there are nine colors: white, reddish, bright red, and saffron-yellow, and foul-smelling ones, and green ones, and among them are golden ones having black tails and tail-ends. And among them are wine-colored ones, from whose [pauſilā] is felt a sharp sting and harmful pain. And among them are smoky ones, and from their bite happens laughter and a loss of reason <note>likely referring to delirium or neurological symptoms</note>.

### On what happens from their stings...

**T**hese things regarding their stings, as it appears from its mouth: stings happen as it appears from its mouth, opening with a red color and previous pain, frequently inflating; and since it is chilled, he imagines that his heart is compressed with salty hairs. And sudden pains happen, and the sting is like the sting of a needle. And that place remains hard, and coldness [comes] to him, and expulsion with the vomiting of a viscous thing that gels over it, and shivering, and the hair standing on end, and trembling, and coldness of the extremities, and the wound is bitter.

# On the Mucilage of Boxwood. Concerning the Affliction <note>original: "fassione," likely a variant of "passione," meaning a disease or condition</note>
The cause is dryness—in some cases, a dryness of the hair—and for this, mild oils and <term>mucilages</term> <note>thick, gluey substances extracted from plants</note> are beneficial. Examples include the mucilage of marshmallow, the mucilage of psyllium <note>flea-wort</note>, and the mucilage of lily leaves. All of these are used to counteract the dryness.

## Concerning these substances
Borax, when applied to the actual substance of the hair, preserves half of the hair's [moisture or health].

## A Discourse on Youth and Graying...
I have already addressed its place elsewhere. Concerning the graying of youth: Grayness—which is called *iceni* <note>original: "iceni," likely a transliteration of a Greek or Arabic medical term for premature graying</note>—occurs while the blood remains fatty, thick, hot, and viscous, keeping the head dark. However, when the body begins to tend toward a watery state, the hair then declines into grayness.

### On those things that delay grayness through curative means. Grayness.
<margin>Regarding food</margin>
The royal remedy should be prepared later. Among those things that provide a royal regimen for the hair, one must first and at all times purge the <term>phlegmatic humors</term> <note>in medieval medicine, phlegm was a cold, moist humor; an excess was thought to cause graying</note>. This is done with knowledge, using enemas and by restoring the throat. Then, confections and medicines should be administered that create youthfulness—which is a restoration—along with the administration of an alchemical <note>original: "alvy," possibly referring to the belly or an elixery</note> mixture of high quality and balance. From these, one provides a favorable moisture. Such things include cereals and those items that are prepared with eggs and cooked in water; or roasted without juice, or nuts in juice. Let the patient eat in such a way that there is a proper quantity for digestion, which should be slow. For when digestion is interrupted, the blood is corrupted. And let all things in the diet be very moist, while administering hot seasonings such as mustard, pepper, Syrian herbs, <term>alkanna</term> <note>a root used for dyeing and medicine</note>, and chard with mustard. It is then sufficient to drink a little pure wine. Secondly, consume fruits, oil-enriched porridges, lettuce, and fish. Also, use <term>ptisans</term> <note>barley water or medicinal infusions</note> with water, or gruels and plenty of water. But take care: too much water can loosen the hair, as does excessive drunkenness. All these areas should be touched with those things that are [soothing], such as rose water, oil of quince <note>original: "cilunnū," likely *citonium*</note>, and bean-water for the hair. One should avoid staying in fresh water for too long, for if one does, it dries the hair out; extinguish the heat quickly. This washing of the hair preserves its integrity. Those who wish to use stronger washes use things like the pulp of <term>colocynth</term> <note>bitter apple, a strong purgative</note>, black cumin, lupins, and bull’s gall.

### Confections and spices which, without the hand of phlegm <note>i.e., without increasing phlegmatic humors</note>, delay grayness. These include Chebulic <term>myrobalans</term> <note>an astringent fruit used in many medieval tonics</note>; one of these should be taken every day, chewed and swallowed. This is a "fountain" that will preserve youth until the end of life. Likewise, prepare a syrup from both the minor and major myrobalans. Also, a confection of *scoru fem* <note>meaning unclear, possibly a floral or herbal extract</note>. The best version of this is if gold is included in it.

### And from this
Take black myrobalans and emblic myrobalans, one part of each. Better yet, add <term>anacardium</term> <note>cashew nut or marking nut</note>, using half the amount of the others. Mix this with cooked butter 

<column-break/>

and make it into an electuary <note>a medicinal paste</note> with honey, then administer it. This is very potent. Indeed, a small amount should be administered in a quantity that produces the appropriate effect. It is a strong cleanser and a powerful <term>theriac</term> <note>a "universal" antidote or cure-all</note>. Grayness and the loss of youth are prevented by the constant eating of these things.

### The method for making a good confection...
Take black myrobalans, <term>doronicum</term> <note>leopard's bane</note>, long pepper, and emblic myrobalans (which takes the place of the long pepper). Add *sora a feart* <note>meaning unclear</note> and nutmeg. Let a confection be made from these.

### Another, tested by itself: Take equal parts of Chebulic myrobalans, mace, and pepper, and administer.

### And likewise, take twenty weights of Chebulic myrobalans, four weights of *scone fcart*, five weights of agaric, and three weights each of amber, pepper, and cloves. Let them be made into an electuary with honey. One should take enough of this for an entire year to experience the "bitterness of youth" <note>likely referring to the pungent/bitter taste of the youth-preserving medicine</note> from such a confection, which should be tested until midday before eating food.

### To keep the hair clean
Because hot and strong oils—like those of lily or bitter almond—are harmful to the hair's structure and destroy the vital heat, they cause wrinkles and diminish the vessels of nourishment. Therefore, use <term>alkanna</term> and <unclear>aicorinū</unclear> for four hours before entering the bath. And let him enter with his head well-covered, warm and moist. Likewise, use oil of costus, for it is very strong, and oil of iris. Oil of black cumin is also very powerful for the scent. And a very strong oil can be made from mustard oil and black cumin; first, cook the black cumin in it, then cook colocynth pulp in it. <unclear>nira</unclear> <note>likely a instruction for pressing or straining</note> the oil from the highest quality olives. If this is used every day, it will prohibit grayness.

## Oil of Laurel <note>original: "lor.," likely *laurinum*</note>
Take clear omphacine oil <note>oil from unripe olives</note>, one weight of spikenard, and two weights each of <unclear>bclinae</unclear> and licorice flowers. Cook these over a medium heat until it remains clear, or in water until a hundred [units] have evaporated. Then decoct the oil in that water until the water is consumed. If the quantity of oil is reduced, it is sufficient. Then take <unclear>3</unclear> of acanthus, dissolve it with wine and <unclear>cāt' o pyme</unclear>, mix it together, and administer.

## Oil of Lentisk <note>original: "lyntu.," likely *lentiscinum* or mastic oil</note>
Take equal parts of oil of gems <note>or "gum-oil"</note>, oil of myrrh <note>original: "murini"</note>, and lily oil. Take one pound of the total mixture. Then take celery, cassia, spikenard, black cumin, cloves, colocynth pulp, costus, and others as heard <note>mentioned previously</note>, licorice flowers, and aromatic calamus in equal parts. Take 100 weights of this total mixture and decoct them in the juice of colocynth (if found) or in the juice of <unclear>armai nnao</unclear>, using four pounds. Let it sit in the water with the oil on top, and do not stop cooking until only the oil remains. This oil should then be administered.

...mine. I argue that there is no assimilation <note>the process of the body turning food into its own substance</note> regarding the humors. And since the matter of the humors is commonly united, and when this matter is united, it follows that the nature of the thing it reaches is not better structured. Thus, the complexion of this matter, which reaches a corrupted state, is not suitable for rectification. And just as farmers transplant from one planting to another, they turn bitterness <note>original: "auenēhositate," likely "avenenositate" or bitterness/toxicity</note> into usefulness, and harshness into sweetness. So it is with nature; as Galen says, a certain plant which nature made with poisonous fruit in one region <note>original: "im p̄ia," likely "in Persia"</note>, when planted in Egypt, produces fruit that is eaten. Thus the color of animals and plants follows the internal humors according to the members, which are to them as regions are to plants. 

And when the internal humor is phlegmatic, it rarely produces the flesh of shellfish <note>original: "caro ostracoy"</note>; it turns its blood toward its phlegmatic complexion and its color toward white. And there is a difference between the white types of morphea: one cause is melancholic matter and the other is phlegmatic matter. It is well known that one whitens blackness, and the first whitens the white itself. Hence the specific difference between black morphea and white morphea. Indeed, it is a diverse genus, not in the intention of being white, but in its nature. And this is because the white which is called "nigra" <note>referring to a dark, scaly condition</note> is that which arises in a peeling roughness; that is, a sharp scabiousness with vehement roughness. And it creates scales like those of a fish. The cause of this is melancholy turned into bile; however, it is said that the power of the humor is stronger than the color it holds. And this is among the precursors of leprosy, and it occurs in animals. Because of this matter, it is not easily healed. And there are those types of morphea that are safer than the pure white kind. 

The name for all of this is *albaras* <note>original: "albuas," referring to the Arabic term for vitiligo or white leprosy</note>. It follows certain marks and multiplies upon the tracks of dogs <note>likely a reference to a specific pattern of spreading or a folk name for the lesions</note> through that which is attracted with the blood from humidity. And the white does not occur with the blood but is saturated with wind, and remains in the veins. And because the skin is weakened, it is ulcerated by the completion of its own action.

### Signs.
Black morphea does not occur without some cause. It is a matter of doubt what the difference is between *al-guada* <note>original: "alguadū," an Arabic term for white morphea or pityriasis</note>, which is white morphea, and *albaras*, which is the "bad" white <note>vitiligo or leprosy</note>. The difference between them is that hair grows upon *al-guada*, and those hairs are black; however, on the "bad" white, the hair is white and not dark. Also, the skin is more depressed or even peeling in *al-guada* if it is very advanced. Furthermore, if the spot is pricked with a needle, blood comes out of *al-guada*, but from the "bad" white it is not blood, but rather a watery humidity. And it has no sensation. And when it is rubbed, it turns red; for this it is inclined toward healing. And if it appears like dust, it is morphea. And that which remains pale is bad.

### The difference between black morphea and the bad blackness.
It is characterized by excoriation, scaliness, and stiffness, which are not present in black morphea. Furthermore, among the white conditions, some are dark. Some are rough and some are smooth. <margin>Smooth is better.</margin>

<column-break/>

Of both white conditions, the rougher is worse. And of both black conditions, the smoother is better, because it is morphea. And from this comes the clemency of removing the color from the body. And because its onset is quicker, it is more easily saved. And in those cases where it follows the law of nature and is not just "dust," it is nourished by blood. And it is a sign of mercy when it spreads to a large place, for it is not then the "bad" species. And similarly, in every such humor, one should not despair of health, because the complexion of the furnace <note>metaphor for the body's heat or digestion</note> draws that which it reaches toward its own likeness. And because of this, it is very bad if it does not change.

**Concerning the condition of the sole of the foot.**
This is due to the evacuation [of humor] and the blockage of the pores, and the goodness of digestion, since they happen in the natural coldness of the feet, and roughness, and lengthy [pathology] which does not reach the soles of the feet. ### Treatment.

Because of this, it is necessary to reduce the blood and to evacuate the black bile <note>original: "melācoliā," one of the four humors thought to cause skin growths when in excess</note>; this is something that helps. And when the sickness multiplies, use phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> and a regimen of the four main foods, and other things which are often mentioned. Local treatment, however, involves medicines that have bitterness and astringency for the milder cases. Such is myrtle, or sun-dried figs used diligently, or a strained decoction of leaves mixed for several days, and leek water with sumac and oil of lily. One may also use caper leaves, cypress, and unripe olives, and the juice of tamarind. Use also wine, and moist myrtle leaves applied to the source. Also, moist nut barks with dry figs. These are placed with little harm to the patient; they are effective for those that are large and strong. Also use the bark of the roots of the carob tree <note>original: "algarab"</note> and its juice. And there are those things which are the most effective: take henna <note>original: "alcāna"</note> and <term>artellet</term> <note>possibly a local name for a specific plant or mineral</note> dissolved in cold water; indeed, this is an excellent source when applied to the roots. Likewise, use an ointment <note>original: "epȳthimū"</note> made from henna, arsenic, and alkali, and those things which are extinguished with vinegar, especially with oak ash and oil, and salt with expressed water, and the smoke of <term>bulbyrat</term> <note>likely a resin or aromatic</note>. Also use <term>camidis</term> with arsenic. And the use of the honey of the <term>anicardī</term> <note>the marking nut or cashew nut</note> is powerful in its potency. And the milk of the spurge <note>original: "tiamallū," referring to Tithymallus</note> when it is placed upon them, and the milk of the <unclear>mianus</unclear>. And the <term>alkebikegi</term> <note>possibly a Persian or Arabic medicinal term</note> magnificently destroys them. And black cumin prepared with urine; if these are applied, they are helpful and wonderful. And the "holy bitter" <note>original: "fel hyra," likely referring to Hiera Picra, a famous purgative</note> which is of a sharp composition, and when diluted, it is a composition of <term>anardis</term> <note>possibly marking nut oil</note>.

### Equal Composition.

Take of nut bark, tragacanth, and quicklime, of each an equal part. These shall be removed and placed on top so that they become like flowers. ### On Warts.

They are thick, nail-like additions born upon the skin during the course of nature, and for the relief of the mind <note>likely meaning for the patient's comfort</note>. And the cure for them is to resolve that which is painful. Then apply upon the residue a sharp medicine from the medicine of warts until they fall off, then follow with the powder.

### On fissures that appear on the skin and lips.

The cause of all fissures is dryness in that place. It occurs when the skin is dried out, either because of a specific complexion <note>the patient's natural temperament</note>, or the malice of humors, or the supply of sharp, dried-out matter. Or it may be dried by heat, or the velocity of drying winds. Or it may be thick moisture, as happens with fissures caused by the cold and the wind, or by heat moving strongly. And they occur because of "thick" waters, and those containing minerals or alum and the like, when they are used for washing. And things that are like the water of sulfur and asphalt. And we have experienced the difference between this water and that which is applied in an arched manner, and water in a <unclear>ūuclm̄</unclear>. ### Concerning the Generation of Lice and Nits.

The matter of humidity, in which there is heat, is sometimes expelled to the surface. Perhaps it is because of a resisting force and strength that it dissolves, but if it is preserved, the cause follows that which dissolves and it coagulates into nits. And the cause follows which is retained in the uppermost skin and is generated like <term>dandruff</term> <note>original: "fuzfures"</note> and sweatings, and those things which are similar. And the cause follows which is retained more deeply, which if it were bad, would cause <term>alopecia</term> <note>original: "alopuā," patchy hair loss</note> and similar things. And if it were very bad, the strength of the ointment [cannot reach it], and the putrefaction of the skin hastens toward it. And it is the material receiving the heat, which flows over it and pierces through its exterior, and lice are produced; they move and emerge. And how much the air affects them suddenly! And how figs help the generation of lice, moving them from within to the outside. And the movement of them toward that which appears, such as figs, and they gather toward that movement. And especially when the vapor of the generation of figs is associated with it. And it helps that cleansing and washing are neglected, and an ointment which opens the pores of the skin and moves the retained materials in the area toward resolution. And it makes an ointment for its [destruction] because of the conditions of putrefaction. And the uppermost lice flow to the vertex [of the head] where the human blood is, and it takes away the clear color, and they fall away if the body is thinned and its strength is dissolved.
