## Treatise on why [the body] wastes away and what hangs 
## from the body and extremities, and the completion of 
## the book of decoration. On the washing for thinning.

Thinning <note>original: "extenuatio," refers to bodily wasting or becoming lean</note> occurs either because of a deprivation of fatty food, or because of a great multitude of exercises which consume the substance of the body, because blood does not generate much in the body. It also happens from a dry regimen because of that which passes through it—the blood is signaled to be thin—or because of weakness of the power of appetite in the belly, or the digestive power, or from a fracture to the limbs because of a rupture of the <term>complexion</term> <note>the humoral balance</note> which is mostly cold. Or it happens because of excessive heat, as when one is exhausted by things that draw out [moisture]. For when the strength of the arteries is diminished, it does not attract nutrients as much as it should. Or it happens because the blood goes to the <term>colic</term> <note>referring to the colon or lower abdomen</note> limbs from watery moisture, while the spleen is nourished.

<column-break/>

When the liver <note>original: "epar"</note> is enlarged, it attracts more blood to itself and weakens the liver's usual function of nourishing the rest of the body. Or it happens because of things that inhabit the body <note>possibly parasites</note>, or because of the nature of certain washes which cause the body to turn cold or hot or moist, which one may recognize by their specific signs. It may also occur because of constant bandages upon the limb, because they block the passages so that nourishment cannot be drawn to it. It is also caused by eating vinegar, or by a multitude of resolutions <note>the "breaking down" of humors</note>, because the power that should direct nourishment to the limbs is instead separated. ### On Fattening Treatments
<margin>Concerning fattening</margin>
The principle of the cure for fatness and those seeking to be fattened includes the consumption of strong wine and white wine that produces light <term>chyme</term> <note>the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</note>. These are needed for those of a certain age, as is wheat, or boiled mashes, and other similar foods. Also, roasted meats are good, as they retain the quality of the cure and generate firm flesh. Broth made from meat, however, generates softness and extreme tenderness.

The cure for those wishing to fatten also includes chicken meat and the meat of the <note>original: "alai bugi," likely referring to the *al-habaj*, a type of nutritious forest bird or bustard mentioned in Arabic medical texts</note> with wine, and similarly various other meats. These are an excellent nourishment for fattening the body. However, one must beware of <term>oppilations</term> <note>obstructions or blockages</note> occurring in the liver. Refrain from fattening foods if such blocks exist. For in such cases, stones <note>calculi, like kidney or gallstones</note> multiply in anyone who seeks this treatment. Where people are prone to these, stones multiply by first causing obstructions, because the veins are naturally narrow. If the person feels a heaviness in the right side <note>the location of the liver</note>, they should take a drink of wild celery for liver obstructions. Let them take a drink before their food to purge the system with vinegar and honey (oxymel) and seeds until the heaviness is removed.

The best bath is one taken after the first digestion, when the food has already descended from the stomach. Here, one should eat after leaving the bath to prevent the loss of nutrients. This is the method of fattening. A long bath of many hours is good for fattening because it <term>rarefies</term> <note>makes the skin more porous and thin, allowing it to expand</note> the body. The bath should be taken after the first digestion, when the food has moved from the stomach into the bowels. It warms and helps; use milk, or a preparation made with vinegar.

<column-break/>

Another technique for fattening is the retention of blood in a specific limb. 
<margin>He describes the first way in the chapter on retention.</margin>
This is done by binding the limb on the opposite side of the body, as was said before. Bind the part below the limb so that the nourishment is directed toward the area where fatness is desired. For example, if the arm is thin but the <term>rasceta</term> <note>the palm or wrist area</note> is healthy and fat, bind it at the wrist. Or if the forearm is thin, bind it at the elbow on the upper part.

Among the fattening methods is that which depends on meat that is light and slow to digest. All this is made equal through fast rubbing, which acts upon both hardness and softness. Rubbing should continue until the skin turns red. Then the body should be moistened with a brief bath, followed by dry rubbing. This limits the fattening process. There is also anointing with "airy water." One must observe these things, for perhaps there is a specific cause for the wasting in the body.

Fattening can also be administered through liniments applied by moving them until the skin reddens, such as using <term>pitch</term> <note>original: "pix," a thick, resinous substance like tar</note> alone. It may be used as a liquid or dissolved in a quantity that allows it to be applied. When pitch alone is administered, it is warmed by the fire until it liquefies, then anointed on the skin, and washed off when it congeals. It draws nourishment to the limb and removes coldness if there was a weakness of power or blocked pores. Because of its viscosity and roughness, it binds the pores and excites the <term>attractive virtue</term> <note>the biological force believed to pull nutrients into a specific organ</note>. It remains there long enough to become part of the limb and is not easily dissipated.

In summer, this should be administered once a day by anointment; in winter, twice. The same applies to its removal from the limb. When it is administered, one must watch for the speed of reddening, the swelling it causes, and any distress to the heart. If the patient becomes distressed, the application should be ended and removed quickly. Perhaps it is enough to remove it with hot or cold water.

<margin>The second way.</margin>
It is beneficial to precede the treatment with a fast, hard, and rough rubbing. Then anoint it. Alternatively, one might strike the limb with a smooth, non-knotted rod <note>original: "virga boni equali non nodosa"</note> until it becomes red and swollen; then stop. Excessive rubbing or striking can actually dissolve the flesh rather than build it up. Then apply the pitch, warmed evenly by the fire. When it congeals and cools, remove it by pulling it off suddenly. 

It is even better to make the area sweat with water before applying the pitch, so that it warms and "bites" into the skin. 
<margin>Upon it.</margin>
Then apply the pitch. Sulfur waters and those from asphalt also serve to thin the nutrients for what is apparent...

### On the white spots <term>baras</term> that occur on the nails
Take an Aleppo nut <note>original: "nux apelli"; also known as an oak gall</note>, crushed, and mix it with vinegar and flour—specifically lupin flour—and apply it as a plaster, for it eradicates the whiteness <note>original: "albura"; likely referring to leukonychia or fungal spots</note>. ### On roughness and what erodes the nail
Take oak galls and alum with duck fat, or ox gall, or rocket seed <note>original: "semine eruce"</note>; let it be well mixed and applied with vinegar.

### On the friction between the flesh and the layers of the nails
Take the leaves of pomegranates, then apply soothing ointments. If it happens that the tips of the nerves are affected, administer the well-known fats and mild **croton** <note>original: "crotona lenia"; likely referring to oil from the croton plant or castor oil</note> to dilate them.

### Dark blood under the nail resulting from a crush or friction
Treat this with flour mixed with pitch and applied as a plaster. If this does not resolve it, then the nail must be handled carefully. See to it that the nail is easily slit with an oblique fissure using a sharp instrument, so that the blood contained there may flow out. If it happens that the nail is discolored by a bruise, make the blood exit. Then, place the nail over that which is... <unclear>per fb eiicl</unclear>... so that it remains firm and does not fester. Pour warm water and oil over the nail, and then apply the **royal ointment** <term>basilicon</term> <note>original: "basilicon"; a traditional ointment made of resin, wax, pitch, and oil</note> over it by dabbing.

# Here begins the book of Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine, and the anatomy of Avicenna.

<image-desc>Large historiated initial 'P' in blue with intricate red pen-flourishing patterns inside and around the letter. The flourishing extends down the entire left margin in a decorative border of red and blue filigree.</image-desc>

After we have set forth, in four books, the field of the science of medicine regarding universal principles and particular things for preserving health and curing sickness—whether in summary or detail—we arrive at this book with the help of God, whose glory is most high. In this book, I shall complete the work regarding universal compounded medicines, so that this may serve as the <term>Antidotary</term><note>A book of prepared medicines and antidotes, known as the *Antidotarium*.</note> of the work. And indeed, we have divided this book into treatises, focusing on the foundations of making compounds. The main chapters of the treatises are as follows:

The **first** is specifically on central compounded medicines and how they are handled; these include <term>theriac</term><note>original: "tiriaca"; a famous ancient polypharmaceutical "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients including viper flesh and opium.</note> and the "great electuary."
The **second** concerns <term>hiera picra</term><note>original: "penicerri" / "hiera picra"; a traditional bitter purgative medicine.</note> and laxative electuaries used for purging.
The **third** also concerns laxatives.
The **fourth** concerns <term>linctuses</term><note>original: "luffufet"; likely a corruption of the Arabic for a thick, lickable medicine.</note>, powders, myrrh, and infusions.
The **fifth** concerns <term>lohoc</term><note>original: "looch"; from the Arabic *la’uq*, a medicine to be licked, usually for chest or throat ailments.</note> and medicines for the spiritual organs <note>The lungs and heart.</note>.
The **sixth** is on syrups and <term>juleps</term><note>original: "iulububus"; rose-water based sweet drinks.</note>.
The **seventh** is on scents and aromatic powders.
The **eighth** is on inhalations.
The **ninth** is on the most reliable pills.
The **tenth** is on oils.
The **eleventh** is on ointments.
The **twelfth** is on <term>plasters</term><note>original: "blamasedum" / "emplastrum".</note> and compounded medicines for specific ailments, which consists of eight parts:
1. General medicines.
2. Medicines for the head. <margin>compounded</margin>
3. Medicines for the eyes.
4. Medicines for the color of the ears, nose, and mouth.
5. Medicines for the teeth and gums.
6. Medicines for the mouth and throat.
7. Medicines for the stomach and lower belly.
8. Medicines for nearby pains, the "sciatic vein," and <term>alopecia</term><note>hair loss</note>.

When I have brought these three modes together, we shall seal this book.
A treatise on the foundations of the composition and the necessity of compounded medicines.

<margin>to.</margin>
Sometimes we find that in every sickness, a compounded medicine is needed when single drugs are insufficient. Even if we found a single drug, we might not choose it over a compound. Indeed, perhaps if we examine the compounds, we find they are opposite to the disease's complexity. Or we find that in truth there is a need for a certain quality in one of the simples that we do not wish to be joined to another simple, or perhaps the strength of one is too great, so that it becomes as nothing. We find also that one may resolve more than another. How the strength of the virtue and the action of the medicine is increased by adding styptic <note>contracting/astringent</note> medicines to it. And when we find a single medicine that is heating, but we do not want its heating effect to be excessive, it is necessary for us to join it with cooling things, or more of them, which is

And since there are medicines which we add to help in the way we want—if it helps in another matter—it is natural that we mix with it those things that cool specifically so we do not lose the effect. And when there is an overflow of bile <note>original: "luvia bilis"</note> and the humors are such that they cause a blockage and do not expel it, we then join to it that which acts as a driver <note>original: "citonā" / "ducere".</note>. <margin>Not only... Not only... but...</margin> And since my intention is to act on the instrument of speech, I fear that it might be burned by the strength of the medicine, so I first say: I speak of the solute <note>the dissolved part</note>, so that by chance the composition reaches the patient. If it reaches the heart from the hearing of the two arguments, so that it arrives at the limb which one intends to cure; here, for example, we put opium into the medicine of <term>theriac</term>. And my intention is primary: if it is through its own power in its nature, until they are made to reach the heart. But when it arrives at the heart, it flows and is distributed through the heat from them; it destroys it. They resist in cooling and extinguishing the flame. Thus it causes the power of resolution and dissipation to be distributed, whether the medicine be made in its proper time, so that the resolutive medicine proceeds to it in a slow manner, which resolves the matter. And when we want a medicine that stays in the limbs and does its work there for a long time, then that medicine should be of swift penetration; for this reason, we first join it with something that delays it. Such was the medicine for the head. Its purpose is to be of swift penetration. And perhaps the nature of the compounded mass arrives more quickly, attributing the medicines to their specific parts, just as certain seeds are drawn to the mouth of the vessels. For which reason the medicine exists to quiet, so that it arrives with its help to the body that it must penetrate. And since there are medicines that we find are common, we lead them; the matter is necessary in a certain way. For which reason we mix with it that which leads it to the intended part, first curing in the median ducts as they are thinned and opened. And you should know that the first of medicines is influenced by <term>opium</term> and its duration. And since the intention of its operation is long-lasting, it requires a supporting matter. And those who intend its operation to be quick, it requires speed or delay. And you should know that what is experienced is better than what is not experienced. <margin>Note: concerning a medicine that is experienced/proven.</margin> And the parts of the medicines are better first in their intended strength... these chapters in the present book. And in these, that which is proven is better than the unproven, because every compounded medicine has a judgment.

# On the Quality of Composition

Regarding those things which occur by every nature of the time: the things you find for them are a middle point in nature and in artifice. ### The Antidote of Rufus.

**L**et them take vipers <note>original: "urre aut sinus neres," referring to the snakes required for the medicine.</note> as the winter turns toward the beginning of summer. And in that season, there are snakes having flat heads that are wide, and because of the fatness of the neck, they appear very small. Their tails are loud and make a sound as they move. And among those, do not choose the ones that are
<margin>Slavic females <note>The text likely refers to a specific variety or region, though "Slauis" is unusual here; it may refer to a physical descriptor like "tawny."</note></margin>
pale yellow; and the sign of them is that they have two teeth on each side. And choose the females over the
<margin>or of the forest</margin>
males. And you should change the variety and choose asps from the hills. They should be captured by those who drive them out from the reeds of rivers, waters, and seas in the early season, because in them there is a satiety <note>Likely referring to the potency of their venom or health.</note>. In no way should they be captured in a place far from water. And if you capture those that are weak in movement, it is better to choose those that have swift
<column-break/>
movements and lift their heads. And if it is possible, choose their life-force by cutting the head. And at the part of the head, four fingers' width, and at the tail, one finger's width, cut it. And if the blood that flows from it is swift and red, its movement in that dispensing is full; but if the blood is slow and dark, it is bad. And the sign of a good one is that its movement is swift and its appearance is bold. They should be drawn out from the end of the tail. When it is dead, remove the viscera and the gallbladder, and wash it with a very clean wash of water and salt. Then boil it in water and salt, where it is said dill should be added to this mixture while
<margin>or fennel</margin>
it boils. The collection of the meat is taken from the white bone. Clean the flesh from the bone and pound it well in a mortar. And let the one who makes this smell balsam oil and touch the mixture with the finger. When it is all gathered, mix it with the <term>troches</term> <note>Medicinal lozenges or tablets.</note> of squill described elsewhere, following the description of Andromachus <note>Andromachus was the physician to Emperor Nero and is credited with adding viper flesh to Theriac.</note>. Then let very fine tablets be made from it and dried in the shade. Place them in a storage vessel. And you must not let the rays of the rising sun fall upon them until they are dried. Only this described method
<margin>or it will take away the goodness</margin>
preserves their power to withstand the bites of vipers and all poisons that come from death.

### The Antidote of Squill.

**I**t is established that one should choose from the moist leaves those in which there is no greatness <note>i.e., not overly large or old bulbs.</note>. Nor should they be covered in mud, because that makes them thin and of little value. Rather, they should be cleaned and cooked in a new pot, or in an oven with a gentle heat, or in the hot ashes
<margin>bread</margin>
of a fire until they are cooked. Then they should be pounded in a mortar. Mix it with the flour of bitter vetch <note>original: "farnīā herbi," likely *ervum ervilia*.</note>. Andromachus softened one part of squill with two parts of flour. And others do it differently. When the squill is mixed with the vetch flour, then make from it fine troches. Grease your hands with rose oil, and
<margin>make them cut</margin>
dry them. And store them in a vessel just as you do with the vetch. In the middle of the time, they take two parts squill and one part vetch flour.

## Amisdarij
<note>Amisdarij is likely a corruption of an Arabic pharmaceutical name for a specific comforting electuary</note>

<margin>purified</margin>
A medicine indeed which softens and comforts the heart and the body, and makes the skin color lively, and removes worms, and makes the breath smell good, and is good for the liver. It is also taken in wine. It can be used before or after food. **Its Composition:** Take: red roses, 6 drachms; celery, 5 drachms; cloves and mastic; spikenard, of each 2 drachms; cinnamon, 1/2 drachm; carob, mace, cardamom, and nutmeg, 

<column-break/>

of each 2 drachms. Thus [take] these spices and grind them with sorrel; and mix the preparation by stirring it skillfully. Then take cleaned elderberries,

one pound, and boil them in one pound of sweet water until half remains. Then let it be strained. And again [boil] that water until it is soft, to which you should add 2 pounds of the sacred fruit <note>possibly referring to emblic myrobalans or similar</note> and boil it with a light flame until it reaches the thickness of an electuary. Then remove the pot from the fire, and add the powdered spices, and stir with a willow stick until everything is perfectly mixed. When it has cooled, store it in a clean vessel. The dose is one to two drachms taken while fasting.

## Confection named Al-Gere.
<note>Al-Gere likely refers to "Al-Jawari," an Arabic term for a class of aromatic electuaries</note>

It benefits the bile and provides relief; it strengthens a cold stomach and is useful for colic and roughness [of the throat]; it creates an appetite for food and strengthens the heart. **Its Composition:** Take: scammony <note>a strong laxative resin</note> and the pith of turbith <note>a root used as a purgative</note>, and long pepper, of each 6 drachms; seeds of celery and anise, 1/2 ounce; Indian calamus, 1 drachm; cloves and carob, of each 1/2 drachm; ginger, 1 aureus; peeled almonds, 1 drachm; sugar and tabasheer <note>a silica secretion from bamboo stalks</note>, of each 1 drachm. These medicines should be prepared carefully; especially the scammony and rhubarb, since they act quickly. Then mix the medicines together and compound them with clarified honey. The dose is from 3 drachms up to 3 and a half drachms.

### Confection of Halwa
<note>Halwa, or "allua," refers to a sweet medicinal paste, common in Arabic-influenced pharmacy.</note>

It is beneficial for bites and coldness, and for raw tumors <note>swelling that has not yet come to a head</note>, and for phlegm. It increases strength, clarifies the complexion, and aids libido <note>original: "uenerē"</note> such that it restores the appearance of youth. In the elderly, it celebrates the body by removing all sickness except for tumors; it alleviates the body’s burdens and arouses sexual desire. Its preparation: two ounces of cassia stems, infused in water. Then cleanse it, and cook it over a slow fire, covered with water until it darkens and is thoroughly worn down. Then cook the water until it becomes a paste. If you add one... <unclear>one part of each</unclear>, let them be cooked with it until they are boiled down into a halwa-like mass. Afterwards, take sweet cow's milk from above <note>perhaps the cream</note>... let it be thickened by five fingers. Then let it be cooked over a gentle fire; let a candle be held against it to see if the milk is dried out or how much remains. Then pour fresh cow's milk over it with honey, and again cook it over a slow fire; let a candle be held against it until it is dried out. Then place it all in a copper vessel until it becomes a mass. Now pour over it clarified white honey in a quantity that exceeds it by two fingers' breadth. Cook it until it thickens like a thread or as much as needed. Then add one pound of white sugar or gold-colored honey... and it should be beaten in a thin glass vessel with eight portions of white pepper. Take for the stewards <note>original: "uiliciꝛ," possibly referring to the keepers of the pharmacy</note> an ounce of amomum <note>an aromatic spice</note>, an ounce of gold-colored galangal with cinnamon. Grind these medicines and sprinkle them over the top, mix them, and store in a clean vessel. From this, let a dose of five coins be given.

### Great Athanasia, for the Liver
<note>"Athanasia" means "immortality" in Greek; it was a famous compound medicine intended to preserve health.</note>

It treats pains of the liver and spleen, and flatulence <note>original: "uētrofittaꝛbꝰ" from uentrositas</note>, and dysentery, and chronic coughs. It is for those who vomit blood and for those with acute pain; it is as effective as the Philonium <note>a famous opiate-based electuary</note>. It stops a cold or flowing phlegm and a flux of the belly. It heals discharges from the tongue and the color of the kidneys... it cleanses the body. This is used for hemorrhoids. Its dose is from a quarter of a gold coin <note>aureus</note> up to a half. Its preparation: Take camphor, opium, castor <note>a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note>, and half a portion of white juice, costus <note>an aromatic root</note>, cardamom, poppy, spikenard, and copper-water <note>original: "cupurogi," likely a corruption of chalcanthum</note>, and epithyme for the liver, and all the "horns" <note>likely tips or sprouts</note> of Cappadocia; all in equal parts. Grind those that are to be ground, and dissolve them in fragrant wine. Mix with clarified honey and use for six months.

### Lesser Athanasia

It has the same life-giving property as the previous one. Its preparation: Take storax, saffron, costus, spikenard, opium, and carpobalsamum; of each 4 drachms. Take 1 drachm of copper-water, 12 drachms of lily roots, and as much honey as suffices. A dose should be the size of a hazelnut with the liquid that comes from the pots. And therein, let two other medicines be added: myrrh and xylobalsamum <note>wood of the balsam tree</note>, of each 4 drachms as provided.

### Lesser Dialacca
<note>"Dialacca" is a medicine whose primary ingredient is "lac," a resinous secretion of the lac insect.</note>

It treats the weakness of the liver and spleen, and the stomach, and their hardness, and

<column-break/>

the beginnings of dropsy <note>original: "dꛝoꝑisio," swelling caused by excess fluid</note> which they have... and it makes the complexion very good. It is offered for long-standing ancient illnesses. Its preparation: Take spikenard, mace, myrrh, cassia, costus, flowers of schoenanthus <note>camel grass</note>, and cinnamon. Take equal parts of all, amounting to... <unclear>drachms</unclear>. Let it be infused, mixed day and night in a folded cloth, and let everything be brought together and clarified with skimmed honey. Store it in a vessel and use it for a year. It is also called *mezanon* in another place.

### Greater Art of Cumin, according to the Art of Galen

## Dia sulphur.

This is a drinkable medicine and it is mild; it is

## Confection of Asa <note>Asafoetida</note>.

It is beneficial for the periods of fevers and takes away quartan fever after digestion. Its dose should be 1 drachma by weight in wine for the sting of scorpions, and in oxymel <term>oxymel: a mixture of honey and vinegar</term> for fever.

**The art of the medicine which is called the Gift of God.**
And these were found in the royal treasury. And they said it is offered for gout and hemorrhoids, and corruption of the womb, and hiccups. And it makes [one] desire food... and it should be drunk in the spring time. It is golden for those with monthly fevers in all events. Its mixture is made with black, belliric, and chebulic myrobalans <term>myrobalan: a dried plum-like fruit from India, highly prized in medieval medicine for balancing the humors</term>, and birthwort, roses, fennel, cardamom, cloves, chamomile, celery seeds, and unpeeled cinnamon; 108 drachms of each. And 7 drachms of the root of celery; and... these [should be taken] for weeks.

<column-break/>

[Take it] for a week with sugar, and a week with water and honey, and a week with vinegar. Then, for one day... let it be made in the morning... See that you do this for ten weeks according to this manner. Then make it with [the honey] and grind it until it becomes like a fine powder <note>original: "alchvhol"; in this period, the word referred to any substance ground into an impalpable powder, like eye kohl</note>. And grind the remaining medicines, and powder them, and sift them. Then take three parts of the medicines and one part of the dross. Then wrap them in cow’s butter... and mix with honey. Then melt it... until it becomes like thick honey. Then place it in a clean, new glass vessel and tie the top of it. And bury it in the earth in a similar way. Let the dose be the size of a gallnut <note>original: "galla"; a growth on an oak tree, used as a common size reference for pills</note> in the morning while fasting; and let him not eat anything until three hours of the day have passed; then let him eat. And let him be governed by a calm regimen, so that he may avoid nausea and distress.

**The remainder, from which harm is feared.**
Certain of the doctors have affirmed that this medicine drives away the malice of deadly poison and causes [the patient] to possess health.

**A finished medicine.**
Which is beneficial for weakness of the liver, and erosion, and the spitting of blood. Take myrobalans, dragon's blood <term>dragon's blood: a bright red resin obtained from certain plants, used to stop bleeding</term>, and leaves of *alafik*, and alum; an equal weight of each. Grind them and powder them, and boil them in water. Give it to them to drink warm during the [full] moon.

**The "Rucene" confection of mine, made for the corruption of the complexion of the liver, and it strengthens the stomach and clears the complexion.**
Its mixture: Take yellow myrobalans, 25 drachms of each. Celery, cinnamon; 10 drachms of each. White pepper; 23 drachms. *Altalasfar*; 3 drachms. Galangal; 5 drachms. *Neremik*; 6 drachms. Juice of wormwood; 15 drachms... Grind the medicines and powder them, and mix them with honey, and make from them pills the size of peppercorns. And let the dose be 2 drachms with warm water.

**The Imperial confection, which is beneficial for the difficulty of passing urine, and pain of the back, and weakness of the kidneys, and it breaks stones.**
Its mixture: Take seeds of white poppy; seeds of *porti*; seeds of oats; seeds of celery; seeds of lily; seeds of lettuce; seeds of endive; seeds of purslane; red and white *bc*; bird's tongue <note>original: "lingue auis"; usually refers to the seeds of the ash tree</note>; seeds of *alkem_a*; 1 drachm of *kesile*; seeds of *lteha*; pepper; anise; watercress seeds; and seeds of mustard.

### Hiera Logodion

This is the true and blessed "living" medicine of Pliny <note>referring to Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note>, cleansing the body from its outermost extremities. It alone suffices for the labor of all humors and superfluities, and it is beneficial for ailments of the head, for pain, for <unclear>canuanue</unclear>, <margin>According to Galen.</margin> cephalea <term>cephalea: a chronic, severe headache</term>, for dizziness, and for madness, mania, epilepsy, <unclear>amote</unclear>, palsy, and the softening of the nerves. When taken, it drives away all these things. Thus it is said in those books that there is no better thing than this medicine of Pliny. It also benefits pains of the ear and eye, and strengthens them. It opens obstructions of the liver and provokes menstruation, removes difficulty of breathing, and is beneficial for quartan fevers <term>quartan: a fever that recurs every third day, traditionally associated with "black bile"</term>, all ailments caused by crude phlegm, and long-standing fevers. It is effective for pains of the belly, for gout, for the sciatic nerve <note>sciatica</note>, and is useful for <unclear>adari</unclear>, for alopecia, for ulcers in the head, and for <unclear>albuio</unclear>, morphew <term>morphew: a skin disease causing scurfy eruptions</term>, impetigo, and leprosy, and for scrofula <term>scrofula: a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck</term>. In another version, I find it also aids against cold and bitter humors.

### Electuary Alkasru, called the Electuary of Amber.

<margin>the lesser</margin>
This electuary was used by the kings of Greece. It is effective for cold ailments and for the kidneys, and it increases the desire for coitus <note>The Latin 'addit indefidio coit' refers to increasing sexual libido</note>. **## Quince Electuary**
<note>original: "Electuarium diacetoniton"</note>
Which is made to stimulate the appetite. It also strengthens the stomach. Let it be kept [in a vessel] with 2 pounds <term>pound: (libra) a unit of weight, roughly 327 grams</term> of [quince] juice, 3 pounds of honey, and 3 pounds of [vinegar?]. It is taken over coals to remove the froth. Take 5 [measures]... 8 drachms of white pepper, and mace. Of all these, [take] equal parts <term>ana: a medical shorthand meaning "of each"</term>, 4 drachms. **## Indian Electuary**
<note>original: "Electuarium indicum"</note>
Effective for colic and pain in the joints, for gout <term>podagra: a historical term for gout, specifically in the foot</term>, and for back pain. **Its mixture is as follows:** Scammony... 5 drachms; cinnamon, half a drachm; [more] cinnamon, and [sweet] cinnamon; and [nerefinc?], and cloves, and pepper. Of all these, 5 [measures]. Let them be ground... Grind this medicine and mix it with honey.

**## Electuary of Kings**
<note>original: "Electuarium regum"</note>
This is a medicine that is taken whole every day. Once taken, it rectifies the suspicion of [illness] until the end of life without harm. He who uses it regularly will not find sickness in his body... it is the medicine of kings, which is strong and does not burn the heart... It is valuable for black, white, and red fistulas <term>fistula: an abnormal passage or sore in the body</term>, and for the relief of colic, and for [fingoza?], and for pain of the heart and joints. It wipes away [burnt humors] and pain... and there is no malice in it, nor does it obstruct the womb. **Its mixture is as follows:** Black, belleric, and emblic myrobalans <term>myrobalan: a dried fruit used as a laxative and tonic</term>, of all these, 27 [measures]. With 24 [measures] of honey. White pepper, and [amorca], and mace... of all these, 5 [measures]. # Syrup of Aristotle

Then let strong wine vinegar be sprinkled over it many times. Then let it be gathered again and mixed with the oil of four roasted nuts for a little while, and sumac cleaned of its seeds in the same amount as the salt, and roasted wood-food [liques], and emollient seeds. Mix them and administer it.

# Fifth Treatise on Linctuses
<note>original: "de allolvcat"; This is a Latinization of the Arabic term "al-la'uq," meaning a linctus or electuary—a medicine meant to be licked and swallowed slowly.</note>

This discourse concerns these [remedies]. I have set the manner of this discourse in the chapters that come before it. And a linctus <note>original: "alohoc"</note> is that which is not swallowed quickly, but rather is held in the mouth for a long time. They take it so that some of it may pass to the lungs, and some may be pushed toward the stomach. For the breath of those [taking it] is prolonged from the stomach to the lungs.

<margin>Suddenly.</margin>
A linctus for a dry cough: Take whole linseed, crushed, and as much honey as needed. Store it in a vessel and administer it when night falls.

<margin>Castor seed, but cleaned first.</margin>
Another linctus for a cough caused by heat and dryness: Take 5 drachms <term>drachm: a unit of weight, approx. 3.9 grams</term> of hulled <note>original: "atitoli" likely a corruption of "amygdali"</note> kernels; 6 drachms of sweet peeled almonds; 5 drachms each of marshmallow seed and mallow seed; 3 drachms of gum tragacanth; 3 drachms of starch; 3 drachms each of hulled seeds of various types; 3 drachms of licorice juice and peeled aloe; licorice root [steeped] in another liquid and reserved. Let these medicines be ground and sifted, then cooked with water until they thicken. Afterward, let them be washed with a fruit rob <term>rob: a thickened, boiled-down fruit juice or syrup</term> and let the medicinal waters be thickened with it. Then, in a little while, make a thick paste <note>original: "pultab̄"</note> with bran water, bean flour, sugar candy <note>original: "p̄midus/penidior"</note>, and sweet almond oil, and let it be carried by the rice water.

<margin>Clean oils are suitable.</margin>
A linctus for a cough caused by heat: Take 3 handfuls of large grapes with the seeds removed; 30 drachms of licorice root; 40 drachms of sweet cleaned kernels; 15 drachms of cassia fistula. Let them be cooked in 6 pounds of water until 1 pound remains. Then let it be strained and let fruit rob be poured over it.
<margin>Let it be cooked with honey.</margin>
Add half a pound of sugar candy and 1 pound of licorice root. Let it be cooked until it thickens like honey. Then let it be mixed with as much bean flour as suffices, and let it be made into lozenges with sugar.

Poppy linctus: Prepared for the expulsion of blood <note>original: "expluonē sanguinis"; likely hemoptysis or coughing up blood</note>, and for high fever, coughs, chest pain, and pleurisy <term>pleurisy: inflammation of the lungs' lining causing sharp chest pain</term>. Take half a drachm each of red roses and gum arabic; 2 drachms each of starch, tragacanth, and poppy seeds; half a drachm each of spodium <term>spodium: a medicinal powder made from burnt minerals or ivory, used to cool and dry</term> and [missing ingredient]. Add 2 drachms of licorice. Grind and sift these medicines. Let them be mixed with ivy juice and stored in a vessel. Then, when it is night, let it be dissolved and taken with a decoction of hyssop.

<margin>Weight of poppy seeds: 2 drachms.</margin>
Spodium linctus: Prepared for coughs, vomiting of blood, excessive phlegm, chest pain, and ulcers of the lungs. Take 4 drachms weight of cardamom; 8 drachms of gum; 10 drachms each of wheat starch, white poppy seeds, and [missing]; 4 drachms of spodium; 40 drachms of refined white sugar <note>original: "tabuzed"</note>; 8 drachms each of peeled kernels and almonds and pine nuts; 5 drachms each of bitter almonds (peeled of both skins), licorice juice, and tragacanth; 2 drachms of fennel seed. Let these be ground and sifted.

<column-break/>

And let them be prepared with skimmed honey and cow's butter, processed gently, and stored in a vessel to be administered when night falls.

Another spodium linctus: Prepared for phthisic <note>original: "ptisicas"; relating to consumption or tuberculosis</note> fevers and lung ulcers. Take 5 drachms each of bishop's weed <note>original: "ammi"</note>, cardamom, and aloe; 12 drachms each of starch and wheat starch; 4 drachms of spodium; 60 drachms of sugar; 8 drachms each of peeled kernels and pine nuts. Let it be licked, and let it be drunk with warm water or with asses' milk <note>original: "lacte asine"; commonly prescribed in antiquity for lung ailments</note>.

Squill linctus: Effective for a cough caused by phlegm; it cleanses the chest and digests bronchial humors. Take 1 pound of [cleansed] squill <term>squill: a sea onion used as an expectorant</term> and let it be cooked with 1 pound of butter until they are dissolved in the decoction. Let it be strained. Then take 2 pounds of fresh skimmed honey. Let it be cooked over a slow fire until it thickens, then remove it from the fire.

Another linctus: Take 5 drachms each of hulled kernels and psyllium <note>original: "psyllij"; flea-seed, used for its mucilage</note>; half a drachm of pepper; 3 drachms each of licorice root and [missing]. ## Galen’s Method for Oxymel
<note>original: "Modus sirupi acetosi galieni"; Oxymel (vinegar and honey) was one of the most famous remedies attributed to the Greek physician Galen.</note>

Take good honey, place it over a gentle fire and remove its foam. After this, add the vinegar to it, so that the acidity is not [too] apparent in the mixture. Let it boil over the fire gradually until they are well combined and the "raw" quality of the vinegar is gone. Then let it be removed from the fire and allowed to rest. If you wish to use it, mix it with as much water as there is syrup. And if he who drinks it finds it repulsive because of its acidity or its sweetness, then let him use it steadily [in small amounts]. And if he wishes to drink it so that the acidity is manifest, then let more vinegar be added. And that which is said to be "praiseworthy" is what is made according to the quantity of wine, which seems to be suitable for those who drink wine, so that it may be mixed with water first... it is said that those who are accustomed to bile should have this. When they drink it, let them remain standing. And for those who have said their bile is disturbed when they drink it, a very thorough mixing prevents nausea. The cause of this action is that it constricts the stomach <note>original: "patriis"; likely a corruption of "stomachus"</note> and it is of "oxysaccharum" <note>original: "oxusuchuchen"; a syrup of vinegar and sugar</note> which dilutes the bile the most. They should not use more oxymel than is necessary. It is our custom that those who drink wine should drink this... And the three types are formed as was said before, according to the person who drinks it. I prefer that you do what you find most delightful for the one using it, and for this reason, it is more beneficial; and he who is harmed by it is the one who finds it unpleasant. The balance of these types is that it should be made according to what is most suitable for those who drink wine.

<margin>
Note: he who is harmed by wine should drink the syrup that harms wine.
</margin>

<column-break/>

According to every dispensation. If I prepare one part vinegar, let two parts of clarified honey be mixed with it, and let them be cooked over a light fire until their flavors are combined. Similarly, for the [syrup] of vinegar, if there remains in it... let it be made in honey. It becomes a syrup that is more acidic; that is, place one part honey to seven parts water. Then let them be cooked over a slow fire

And mostly what remains is the first part, which makes it half the quantity. And the decoction is repeated for it until it is well mixed and remains thickened. 

And there is an oxymel <note>original: "syrupus acetosus"</note> which mixes three species of celery <note>original: "apii"</note>; namely, take one part of the species of vinegar, three parts of honey, and four parts of water, and let it be cooked until a fourth remains, and its foam is removed. When you wish to make it, take as much vinegar as honey, and it is drunk like mixed wine. Let it be drunk steadily for one or two days, because the species there are directed against vice <note>original: "vitium"; likely referring to a morbid condition or "vice" of the humors</note>, and it draws out the humor from the infected intestines and resolves the "grossness" <note>original: "pinguetudinem"</note> of the body. And concerning the fluids which are upon the water when it is oxymel, it is drunk thus: 1 [part] to 1 [part]. And for the one who wants to have his illness [expelled], let the humidity exit from the mouth of the stomach and let the corruption be drawn out of him. And he who drinks it should wait until the middle of the day before he eats chicken and drinks.

## Solar Oxymel for Drawing Out Bile
Take clarified honey or sugar, and a similar amount of sharp vinegar. Cook over a slow fire. And take of asarum <term>asarum: wild ginger, used as an emetic or purgative</term> and scammony <term>scammony: a harsh herbal purgative resin</term> and aloe, 1 drachm each, or more or less according to the physician’s judgment. When it is thickened, remove it from the fire. And some add to the place of the scammony—as I say—scammony with celery seed and fennel root at the beginning of the decoction.

# Method of making a julep.
<margin>Book 2, Question 6</margin>
Take one part of sugar and pour over it 3 parts of water. Cook over a slow fire. When it has boiled down, add 1 or 2 parts of rosewater and remove from the fire and strain. Let it be kept in a clean place.

# Water of honey and sugar.
It is useful for those with cold conditions and pain of the stomach and... Take 1 part of pure honey and an equal part of water; cook over a slow fire and skim off its foam. Let it boil until it remains [thickened], then remove from the fire and strain. Sugar water is made in the same way. When we wish to make it more warming and produce heat, add to it (after the foam is removed) mastic, cloves, and other spices like cinnamon, galangal, and similar things.

# Another description of honey water.
<margin>Afterward</margin>
This is used for fever, inflammation, excessive thirst in the stomach, and especially for heat and pleurisy. Take: 7 pounds of cleaned red roses and place them in a glass vessel; pour over them 10 pounds of hot water.
<margin>Day and night</margin>
Seal the vessel well and let it sit for a day and a night. Then squeeze it out thoroughly and strain it. Add 10 pounds of sugar to it and cook over a slow fire until it thickens; then strain and use.

# Julep with rose water.
Take sugar... and rose water in a clear glass vessel and cook over a slow fire until it thickens, removing the foam. Some put [the spices] in a cloth while it cooks so the foam is cleared... Others do not put them in until it is removed from the fire... [let it] cool in a clean vessel.

# Syrup of quince and endive.
Because it strengthens the stomach, settles the belly, and is useful for pain of the liver, coughs, nausea, and hiccups. Take: 30 pounds of sour quinces <note>original: "citonıoy acetōsoy"</note>... 15 pounds of water. Cook over a slow fire until half remains. Then skim the foam and strain it. Finally, add 1 ounce of musk and mix it with wine.

**A seasoned wine for a cold stomach.** For defects of digestion and weakness of the liver caused by cold, and for quartan fevers <note>A fever that reoccurs every fourth day, traditionally associated with malaria and an excess of "black bile"</note>. **Syrup of Mint.** This is made for vomiting and the discomfort of those suffering from nausea, as well as for hiccups and the flux of the belly. It is made thus: Grind the mint with juice and vinegar with their pulp, and decoct over a slow fire to half. Then take two pounds of it... add honey or sugar, and decoct until reduced. Then strain.

**Syrup of Pears.** For those thirsty and for the flux of the belly, and it comforts the stomach. Take mature pears and decoct them until they are soft. Strain them and return the liquid to a clean vessel; decoct until reduced and administer.

**Syrup of Apples.** This is made for a weak stomach, for heart palpitations and "heat" <note>inflammation or feverishness</note>, and it stops vomiting and colic.
<margin>the source/fountain of the stomach</margin>
Take mountain apples. In another way, take musk... Grind them and express the juice. Decoct to half and strain; let it sit overnight. Return it to the vessel and decoct over a slow fire until reduced. Strain and place in a glass vessel. If it is summer, let it sit in the sun for several days until the liquid becomes clear. Then administer. If you wish to sweeten it, add one pound of sugar to the juice and cook it as before.

**Syrup of Verjuice.** <note>original: "agsta" for *agresta*; the tart juice of unripe grapes</note> This is made for heat of the stomach and eases the colic of the belly, hot tumors, and poisons. It stops thirst and takes away bad humors. Take the juice of unripe grapes and decoct it until half remains. Strain and let it sit overnight. Then return it to the vessel and add two drams of cloves. Cook until the scent is gone and it has reduced. Strain and administer. If you wish to sweeten it, add sugar... over a slow fire until reduced... and it will be a sub-acid syrup.

**Syrup of Fruits.** This comforts the stomach and the belly, stops vomiting, and eases the flux... It is made from the juice of pomegranates <note>original: "maloy puni..."</note> and wine... and decoct over a slow fire until reduced. If you wish to sweeten it, add as much sugar as you like and boil it.
<margin>item</margin>

**Syrup of Refreshing Things.** <note>original: "lactabilib"; possibly referring to *lactuca* (lettuce) or other "milky" cooling plants</note> This comforts the stomach. It is made from the juice of aromatics and apples. Take one pound of fresh red coral and decoct it with water until it remains... strain it and add honey. Decoct over a slow fire until reduced, and use it like a julep.

### Syrup of Poppy.

Syrup of Poppy. It is necessary that the poppies be gathered <note>original: "fuanet' cōtū"; likely *sumantur centum*, meaning take one hundred</note> in the middle of their growth so that they are dried out upon their own height. Do not gather them when they are too mature. And if you press from them when they are not yet dry, and they are gathered while still green, the power of the herb will desire a solution <note>referring to the extraction of the opium-rich sap</note>, which is sent to the superfluity. From these, let there be poured over them five measures of rain water—if it can be found—to prevent putrefaction; otherwise, use fountain water. And let it be infused in it for a day and a night until it is clarified. If it has been thinned, let it be diminished more. Then boil it until the poppies are dissolved with their quality. Then let them be squeezed out. Then let it be thickened with half its mixture of clarified honey. Which, if it be for cleansing the chest and for sharpening the sight, is always better than a fruit juice concentrate <term>rob: a thick, boiled-down fruit juice or syrup</term> of wine. And it is a great help for the lungs.

### Recipe for Syrup of Poppy.

It is beneficial for those who suffer from a wasting consumption <note>likely tuberculosis or a chronic cough</note> and it prevents those who vomit blood. Take of cleaned poppies, half a dram; and of rain water, 15 pounds. Let them be infused for half a day, and boil them until they are dissolved. Let it be reduced to half, and let the poppies be squeezed out and filtered, and let the water be well strained. And take of that strained water, one pound; and of honey, one and a half pounds. Boil it until it reaches a proper thickness. Then add red acacia, and gum arabic, and myrtle, and pomegranate flowers <note>original: "balaustie"</note>, and each of these things in equal parts. Of each, 1 dram. Let it be well thickened and put in a vessel, and let it be administered.

### Another Syrup.

It is offered for those with pleurisy, and it strengthens the stomach. Take of sweet pomegranate juice, 3 pounds; and of apple juice, 1 pound; of cane juice <note>original: "canam' mcania'"; likely *canamellis*</note>, 1 pound; or of sugar candy <note>original: "penedio'y"; *penidium* is a pulled sugar twisted into sticks, used for coughs</note>, 1 pound. Boil it until it has a proper thickness and let it be administered.

### Syrup of Honeycombs.

<margin>for itself</margin>
Syrup of Honeycombs. ¶ The opinion of Galen. And it is drunk just as one drinks cooling things, because it destroys thirst when it is mixed with cold water. And also, when it is mixed with digestive herbs, it digests and purges the sharp humors. And this is because it is often read that those who are burdened by a multitude of humors are cured by it. It should be made with any kind of water, but it is better with rain water, just as syrup of honey is made. And this is the method for it: take good honey from the combs, then pour it into a pan in which there is clear, sweet water. Boil it together until all the watery parts have evaporated. Then let it be taken back from the water and cooled, and administered.

### Another Syrup of Honeycombs.

Another Syrup of Honeycombs. Pour over one part of very fresh honey some rain water and prepare it in the sun. And some pour over it fountain water and boil it until it remains pure.

### Syrup of Wormwood, profitable for restoring the appetite and for weakness of the stomach.

Syrup of Wormwood, profitable for restoring the appetite and for weakness of the stomach. Take of strong wine, 2 measures; of honey, 4 measures; let it be skimmed of impurities. Pour over it mastic, 4 drams; lemongrass <note>original: "sq'na'i"; *squinanthi* or camel grass</note>, and Indian leaf <note>original: "foliy indi"; likely *malabathrum*, an aromatic leaf used like cinnamon</note>, and spikenard, and oil of rose <note>original: "i'oli ri"</note> in a dry state; and of silver-colored aloes, of each 2 drams; 14 parts of Roman wormwood <note>original: "bet'e ablad'n r'u'm"</note>,

<column-break/>

8 drams; agaric <note>a medicinal fungus used as a purgative</note>, 2 drams; and gum arabic, 1 dram. Take the middle parts of the herbs and tie them in a clean cloth; let it be infused for six days in the sun during the summer. And let the cloth be squeezed out with many pressings. Then let the syrup be used.

### Syrup of Sour Wormwood from our own composition.

Syrup of Sour Wormwood from our own composition. And the juice of it is squeezed out, and it is made more than the other. Take of Roman wormwood, the weight of 100 drams; and boil it in half a measure of water. Measure it with clean cloths until it retains a fourth part of its volume over a slow fire. And let it be cooled by hand. And take of its juice to make that water, and take a fourth part of honey, or a half part of it. Boil them together until they thicken.

### Syrup for Quenching Thirst.

It is beneficial for fevers. Take of the juice of sour pomegranates, 1 pound; and of the juice of sour lemons <note>original: "acerofitat' is am'ti"; literally 'bitter sourness'</note>, half a pound; and of juice of small herbs, 1 pound. Boil it over a slow fire until it is clarified. This should be taken as a drink with cold water <margin>water of tamarinds</margin> or with other waters.

### Syrup of Fruits.

Syrup of Fruits. It is beneficial for those who suffer from an excess of bile <note>original: "coli' aria"</note> and it makes the appetite warm for food and strengthens the stomach.

### Instructions.

Take sweet and sour apples, and pears, and quinces <note>original: "ag'sta"</note>. Squeeze out the juice of all of them, and infuse in it some sumac and barberry <note>original: "zare"; likely *zarzero*</note>. In another version, add myrtle, and Syrian sumac <note>original: "anabac"</note>, and myrtle berries, and silver-colored aloes. Let it sit for a day and a night, then squeeze and strain it. Pour honey over it and boil it until it reaches a proper thickness, and let it be administered.

### Syrup of Prunes...

It is beneficial for fevers. It gently softens the nature <note>a polite way of saying it acts as a laxative</note>. Take sweet prunes that are old, and remove their pits. Place them in a clean stone vessel and pour water over them until they are covered. Boil them until they are resolved. Then strain it and bring it to a slow fire. Pour over them sugar <note>original: "ryuan' tab'"</note> and boil it until it thickens to the consistency of honey.

### Syrup of Myrrh <note>or "Mocra"</note>.

This gently helps against all infirmities of its nature. It is helpful for weakness of the stomach and spleen, and for those of a broken constitution. **The Ingredients are:** ginger, and cumin, and white pepper, of each the weight of 1 dram; and 3 drams of dried figs; and myrtle, and wormwood flowers, and gallnuts, of each 3 drams. Let them be taken and placed in a glazed vessel, and pour white wine over them until it submerses them to the depth of four fingers. Let it be covered at the top and let it sit for three nights. Afterward, let it be drunk for its medicinal virtues.

### Rose Water for the Lungs. <note>original: "Rosat. a poves" — "poves" is likely an abbreviation for *pulmones* (lungs).</note>

**R**ose water. Take roses semi-cooked in winter. Let them be prepared and distinguished in this way: add 4 pounds and cook over a slow fire until the foam is removed. Then let there be poured over it one pound of thick honey for every 4 pounds of liquid. Let it boil over a slow fire until the foam is removed again and it is reduced to half. Then let there be added <term>cloves: "ganofilorum" (caryophyllorum)</term>, pepper, and <term>long pepper: "macropipis"</term>, one and a third eighth-parts of each, finely ground. Place these in a linen cloth and let them be infused for eleven days after the foam has been washed away and the decoction is complete. It is possible to cook this in water first and then let it sit... <note>The text here describes a process of sun-steeping</note> it is better if it is placed in the sun, then collected from it; and the older it is, the better.

### Syrup of Wormwood which is called "Compound."

**I**t dissolves obstructions of the <term>Agrimony: "Eupatorii"</term> and purges bile. Take 8 dram-weights of <term>agaric: a medicinal fungus</term>, 4 drams of aloes, 2 drams of mastic, and a half-measure of celery seed, and <term>squinancy: a medicinal grass</term>, and anise, 1 dram of each. Add 2 drams of <term>calamint: a mint-like herb</term>, 2 drams of lily roots, and 5 drams of <term>wormwood: "abfanthij"</term>. Let it be prepared in 2 drams of wine and as much of <term>spikenard: "spice"</term>, and 1 dram of various leaves. Boil this in 8 pounds of wine until half remains, then let it be strained and thickened with 1.5 pounds of honey.

### Preserved Quince.

It is beneficial for weakness of the stomach and helps to digest food. Take ripe ones <note>quinces</note> and cut them lengthwise into four parts. Clean the inside of the core and place them in a new small vessel. Let them sit in clear sweet water with salt... until they soften. Then for seven days in water without salt, so the color changes and that white flesh, called the *niffa*, appears. Rinse the water until no saltiness remains. Take one part of honey and two parts of water, in a quantity that covers the quince. Put it in a vessel and cook over a slow fire for two hours. Then remove from the water and honey. In the morning, boil the honey again, remove its foam, and put the quince back in. Let it boil... and sprinkle over it half an ounce of [spices]... 12 drams of cardamom... cloves and cinnamon... half a sextary <note>A Roman measure of volume, roughly a pint.</note>... spread these spices over the quince on both sides, pour the honey over it, and administer.

### Preserved Quinces.

Which is beneficial for strengthening the stomach and balancing the nature and bad humors of the stomach. As for the remedy made for a weak stomach, take only the following. Regarding the nature of the amomum <note>original: "amonis" — a spice similar to cardamom</note>, cut it into pieces and clean the interior of the body from any gums. Wipe it with a linen cloth and pour over it one part pure honey and three parts water, along with a quantity of aromatic spices. Let it boil for two or three boilings. Then let them be strained and spread out upon a flat surface, such as a board, and leave them until they are dried of their moisture <note>original: "hydrositate"</note>. Let them boil for one boiling and sprinkle over them the spices I mentioned for those in need of others. Place this in a clean earthen vessel and seal it well. This medicine is given for consumption <note>original: "phthisi" — a wasting disease like tuberculosis</note>, for fainting <note>original: "supca lipsi"</note>, for nerve pains <note>original: "neurdmon"</note>, and it contains cloves <note>original: "ganofilos"</note> and aloe <note>original: "auai"</note>.

## Preserved Balm...

This remedy is used for chills, for weakness of the kidneys, for back pain, and it assists the desire for coitus <note>as an aphrodisiac</note>. There are two types of balm: the clear colored ones and the clean ones. Remove the two ends from them. Then spread over them either a little juice or three parts sugar. Pour over them enough water to cover them and cook over a gentle fire until they soften. Remove them from the fire and spread them on a flat surface like a board until they dry. Wipe away any spoilage that appears on them and return them to a vessel. Pour over them enough clarified honey to cover them by three finger-widths. Cook over a gentle fire until the honey is seen to penetrate all their parts. Remove them from the fire and place the vessel inside another earthen vessel. Sprinkle the spices over them and keep them well-sealed until they are finished.

## Preserved Myrobalans...

<note>Myrobalans are astringent plum-like fruits from India, highly prized in medieval medicine for balancing the "humors."</note>
These are made from fresh ones found in India. Those brought from there are very beneficial to men. They are prepared by us in this manner: Take *kebuli* myrobalans <note>Chebulic myrobalans, the black variety</note> and make a hole in the moist sand. Place the myrobalans inside, with a layer of moist sand above them and a layer of moist sand below. Sprinkle water over them. After two days, take the myrobalans and spread them in fresh sand, or reuse the first. Leave them for two days while they are moistened. Let this continue for ten days until the myrobalans swell, as if they had been soaked in a bath. Then wash them with sweet water four or five times. Take dates and wild celery <note>original: "apiū"</note> and cook them with rainwater. Throw the myrobalans into that cooked water and cook them slowly over a gentle fire. When they are cooked, wash them with a clean wash. Then take honey, boil it, and remove the scum. Cook them

<column-break/>

with the honey. Take the medicines <note>spices</note> I mentioned for the mature ones and place them in a clean, fine linen cloth and hang it in the vessel. Leave it in the wash until the scent of the spices infuses the myrobalans. When they are cooked, spread them in a glazed bowl and leave them for two or three days until the myrobalans absorb the essence of the medicines. Then spread them in an earthen vessel and pour clarified honey over them. Add musk <note>original: "musa"</note> over them,

<margin>seal it firmly.</margin>
and a small quantity of ambergris <note>original: "ambe"</note>. Tighten the mouth of the vessel. The older they are, the better they become.

## Another preparation of myrobalans in two ways.

Take large *kebuli* myrobalans, a certain number, and soak them in water <note>unclear: "u-chely"</note>. Then extract them from the water and place them in moist dung for five days, turning them every day. Wash them with a clean wash. Return them to this dung for seven weeks, until the earth becomes moist. Then extract them and wash them with a clean wash. Soak them in rose water <note>original: "aqua r-zi"</note> in another vessel with galingale <note>original: "galie"</note> and ginger <note>original: "zi[n]ceci"</note>. In another, add a tenth part of <term>lalk<gloss>possibly a local name for a specific resin or seed</gloss></term> and a quantity of aloes to cover them. Cook over a gentle fire until the water is consumed. Remove them and wipe them with a linen cloth. Prick them with a needle and pour clean honey over them in such quantity that it covers them by four finger-widths. Cook them until they are finished, and then administer them.

## Another kind of species...

Take *kebuli* myrobalans and other myrobalans and wash them with a clean wash. Let them stay overnight until they are slightly dried. Pour water or rose water over them in a quantity that covers them by three finger-widths. Cook over a gentle fire until the water is gone. Place them in dung, and every morning extract them and spread them on a flat surface like a board. Wipe them with linen and prick them with a small needle. Then pour <term>rob<gloss>a thick medicinal fruit syrup</gloss></term> over them. Cook until they soften and remove from the fire. Sprinkle spices over them, store them, and let them be administered.

Then cook it with water and honey in which it was moistened; let there be two parts water and one part honey. Then pour on honey alone and boil it for one boiling. Spread it in an earthen vessel.

### Preserved Wood of Balsam.
**I**t is made from fresh balsam woods, which I have mentioned, using two hands [as a measure], and spices are provided over them as we said. **Emblic Myrobalans and such.**

All these are prepared as [above].

# Pills for Lunacy

<margin>In another [source]: 1 gold weight.</margin>
The head being weakened in many ways, these pills are beneficial for those suffering from epilepsy <note>original: "apīra"; likely referring to 'epilepsia'</note>. Let them be administered especially during the last hours of the morning. **Their first composition is:** 60 parts of washed aloes and the pulp of colocynth <note>bitter apple</note>. 6 gold weights of each aloe. Saffron, spikenard, cinnamon, and balsamic oils, as well as mastic, wormwood rue, and [sermōce]. 2 gold weights each of turbith <note>a purgative root</note> and cassia. Let these be made into a mass with lukewarm water. Form the pills and moisten your hand with sweet almond oil. Take them according to the quantity of the illness. 3 pills, or up to 6 pills. The full dose is 3 drachms, taken when going to bed.

# Pills of the Son of Al-Lanj

<note>Likely referring to Mesue the Younger, a celebrated but semi-legendary apothecary.</note>
These are beneficial for foul skin eruptions <note>original: "morfeā fētīdā"; morphea or skin discolorations associated with leprosy</note>, removing it within a few days. They also benefit quartan fever <note>a fever that recurs every four days, associated with "black bile"</note> and pains of the joints. They are the king of pills for lunacy and melancholy. **Take:** Black and citrine myrobalans <note>astringent plum-like fruits</note>, washed aloes, [lūrecolle], red bdellium <note>a semi-transparent resin</note>, [tarapīu de spulūm], and the pulp of colocynth. Of all these, 5 parts. White [asktīrtī], rue, [psīa], [mīselle], and cumin. Also rock salt and [rūs a rūm]. Of all these, equal parts. Take these half-weights and mix them. Infuse the gums in rue-water in a glass vessel until the medicines are refined. Place in the sun until the gums dissolve. Then add the remaining medicines and let them stand. Form into pills the size of peppercorns and dry in the shade. The dose is 1 gold weight with lukewarm water. Abstain for two days from all things, especially meat and [azmaleīs].

# Pills of the Son of Huieure

<margin>and [m̄gy]</margin>
These provide manifest help for many conditions: for clearing the vision <note>original: "u e lōsītātībʒ enīcz oy darū"</note>, for hearing, for skin eruptions, and for pleurisy. They are to be taken in the morning during winter and summer. **Their first composition is:** Citrine and [bellīlīcoz] myrobalans, and [ablans īuelas]. 4 gold weights of each. 5 gold weights of [cblīcoz]. Indian cassia and [māapīpīs]. 5 gold weights of each aloe. 2 gold weights of rock salt. Turbith and aloes. 6 gold weights of each. [tē 7 astella]. And

<column-break/>

make the preparation with violet oil. Form into small pills and dry in the shade. The dose is 7 gold weights, taken at midnight with hot water. It works wonders and gives life to the spirit.

# Aggregate Pills of the Son of Al-Ga

<note>Likely referring to Haly Abbas (Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi), a famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note>
These are suitable for drying up superfluities <note>excess humors</note> of the womb and for strengthening the body. They also resolve sharp obstructions. They benefit the stomach and are used for chronic fevers. They purify the humors, clear the blood, and heal types of ulcers and pustules. For those who have hemorrhoids, this medicine is powerful. Let the patient touch their finger with a little sweet almond oil, then touch the pills so they are coated with oil, then swallow them. This will prevent them from causing any harm. **Their first composition is:** 28 drachms of Hierapigra. 6 drachms each of black myrobalans and aloes. 4 drachms of mastic. 5 drachms each of eupatorium <note>the herb agrimony or hemp-agrimony</note> and wormwood juice. 4 drachms of [ī uolūnī] of rue. Let them be ground, sifted, and prepared with water. Form into pills the size of peppercorns. The dose is 1 to 2 drachms. It does no harm to take them with a little celery water before sleeping. Then let the patient rise and take [astellū] until the morning.

# Pills Made with Euphorbium

These benefit "internal water" <note>dropsy or edema</note>, eye pain, and podagra <note>gout of the foot</note>. They soften the [cl' ī nū bzoy]. **Their first composition is:** 2 drachms of Euphorbium <note>a potent, irritating resin from the spurge plant used as a drastic purgative</note>. 4 drachms each of mastic and aloes. 5 drachms each of [ser mōce], [sagaīa], and aloes. 4 drachms of colocynth pulp. 5 drachms of aloe and epithymum. 15 units of wormwood juice. [r̄] weight of Indian salt. 2 drachms of [mātropīpīs]. 5 drachms of spikenard. Grind the medicine and prepare with [caū f'] water. Form into pills the size of peppercorns. The dose of this medicine is 17 pills, up to half a drachm. Drink hot water after taking them.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of medicinal pills, transitioning into a comprehensive section on medicinal oils (olea). These oils are primarily "inunctions" (rubbing medicines) intended for joint pain, kidney issues, and various systemic ailments, reflecting a strong influence of Arabic pharmacology (using terms like "kist" for measurements and Arabic plant names).</meta>

**Inunctions** <note>medicinal oils or ointments rubbed into the skin</note> for the joints to which matter has flowed. It clears out secretions and cold humors from the head, and it warms the kidneys and the bladder from the effects of coldness. **Take** sesame oil, and 3 ounces of dry storax <note>a fragrant resin from the Styrax tree</note>; let it be cooked over a slow fire until the oil reflects the virtues of the storax.

### Oil of Chamomile

<margin>And application by hand</margin>
**Take** sesame oil, one kist <note>original: "kist"; an Arabic measure roughly equal to a liter</note>; fenugreek; and flowers of chamomile, washed and dried in the shade; 2 ounces of each. Let it be placed in a glass vessel and left in the sun for 40 days, then administered.

### Oil of Mastic

**Inunctions** for the same purpose, and for weakness of the stomach and to open it, and it softens hardness. **Take** one kist of sesame oil and 6 ounces of mastic <note>resin from the lentisk tree</note>. Let the mastic be crushed and placed over the oil in a double-walled vessel <note>a bain-marie or double boiler</note>.

### Oil of [Ablacino] made in the sun

It alleviates and strengthens cold limbs. **Take** sesame oil and [dauit ecā]. Place 2 ounces in a glass vessel and hide it in the sun for 40 days.

### Oil of Dill

**Take** one kist of sesame oil and 1 ounce of dill seeds, dried in the shade. Place them in a vessel and let it sit in the sun for 40 days, then it may be administered.

### Oil of Lily

Which is beneficial for cold matters and for colic, and it warms the kidneys and the bladder. **Take** 1 ounce of wood of aloes; 1 ounce of costus <note>a root used in ancient perfumes and medicine</note>; 1 ounce of cloves; and 1 ounce of mastic. **Also**, half an ounce each of cloves and cassia <note>a spice similar to cinnamon</note>. Grind them and place them in a vessel with 1 pound of lily oil and 4 pounds of sesame oil. [The text describes a process of steeping the roots and petals]. Keep the oil where it can retain its virtue, and administer it.

### Oil of Halsech

<margin>1 ounce of each</margin>
Which is beneficial for difficulty of urine. **Take** 1 kist of sesame oil and 1 pound of water; 1 ounce of [rā]; 3 ounces of [plens]; and 10 ounces of halsech <note>likely *al-shih*, a type of wormwood or aromatic herb used in Arabic medicine</note>. Boil these together in a vessel with the water and sesame oil until all the water has evaporated and only the oil remains. It is distilled into the opening of the penis <note>original: "forāi uirgre"; the urethra</note>.

### Another Oil of Halsech

It is effective for the joints, makes the skin color healthy, and induces the desire for coitus <note>sexual intercourse</note>, and it rectifies the kidneys, bladder, and back. It can be drunk in a quantity of 1 ounce every day, or taken with wine, and administered to the joints.

### Its mixture contains:

Sesame oil, sweet cow's milk, and fresh halsech: 10 pounds of each. 5 pounds of [peridion]. 2 pounds of [zilētis]. Let it be purified and placed in an earthen vessel over a gentle fire until the water of the halsech and the milk evaporates, leaving only the oil. Drink it as we have said; it is powerful for weakness of the kidneys and induces desire and vigor.

### Oil of Daseh

<margin>all</margin>
**Inunctions** for difficulty of urine, and for pain of the iliac <note>the lower abdomen or flanks</note>, the kidneys, and the bladder.

### Its mixture contains:

15 ounces of [laciati] sweet water...

<column-break/>

...3 ounces in weight. 10 ounces of halsech. 1 kist of sesame oil. Boil in a clean vessel over a gentle fire until all the water is gone and only the oil remains. Remove it and administer it to the joints and for skin color; likewise, it may be used by pouring it into the opening of the penis <note>the urethra</note>.

### Oil of [Ontēis] for Impetigo and Serpents

It softens the stomach. **Take** 4 kists of sesame oil and place it in an earthen vessel. Put into it up to 10 black serpents <note>possibly literal vipers or a name for a specific herb; "serpillum" or wild thyme is often confused in OCR</note>. Seal the head of the vessel and cook over a slow fire until they are dissolved in the decoction. Remove from the fire and let it cool. Open the lid, drain the water, and let it cool until it settles. Administer for impetigo <note>a contagious skin infection</note> by applying it with a feather.

### Oil of King David

Which is of great virtue for paralysis, tremors, gout <note>podagra</note>, joint swelling, and for the distress of joint pain; also for fistulas, hemorrhoids, colic, and elephantiasis <note>a term used for severe skin diseases or leprosy in this period</note>.

### Its mixture contains:

Half an ounce of bdellium <note>a semi-transparent resin</note>; ammoniacum; and [sum p m̄]; [oppo p nna]; and carpobalsamum <note>the fruit of the balsam tree</note>. **Take** [topij], polypody <note>a type of fern</note>, white and red hellebore, [felaulū], cassia, and blanched bitter almonds; 6 ounces of each. **Also** cloves and nutmeg: 2 ounces each. Galangal, cinnamon, ladanum <note>a sticky resin from Cistus shrubs</note>, and castoreum <note>a secretion from beaver sacs</note>: 2 ounces of each. **Also** [kefie], half a portion of white [uisgani], [ste cos], [silkani], mastic, and rocket seeds: 5 ounces of each. **Also** anise and seeds of harmel <note>wild rue</note>: [m m] quantity. Seeds of [uiedū], seeds of [alkeuā], and [linsua]: 3 ounces of each. Cypress leaves and usnea <note>a type of lichen/moss</note>: 5 ounces of each. Grind these and strain them. Place them in a vessel and pour over them 6 pounds of [sua culī]. Boil over a slow fire until reduced to 2 pounds, then remove and strain. 
<margin>Specifically of fir/pine tree.</margin> 
If any of the strength of these medicines remains, return it to the vessel. Pour over it 6 pounds of olive oil, cow's butter, [arazaki] oil, [kerua] oil, and [teemese] oil (which is a decoction of laurel and is brought from Egypt): 10 ounces of each. **Also** 2 ounces of bitter almond flour; 6 ounces of laurel berries; 5 ounces of lily oil and oil of [iuct']; 5 ounces of [uiedū] seeds; 3 ounces of sesame oil or [arazaki] cooked with rue; 2 ounces of usnea; 5 ounces of alkanet oil; and 3 ounces of cashew honey <note>original: "mell auacardi"</note>. Add all these into the vessel and dissolve them with 10 ounces of [lac z’ uea].
<margin>slow</margin>
Cook over a very slow fire until the water is consumed. Remove from the fire and strain through a clean cloth.
