## Ointment of White Lead
Which is beneficial for burns from fire. Take 1 ounce <note>original: "3. j."; the symbol 3 denotes an uncia or ounce</note> each of lard and litharge <note>lead monoxide</note>, 6 ounces of white lead, and 7 ounces of white wax <note>original: "alle."; likely 'cerae albae'</note>, and 2 ounces of rose oil. Let the wax be melted and the oil poured over it; let the white lead and litharge be mixed in a mortar and combined before it cools. Add the white of one egg and administer it.

## Another Ointment
10 ounces of white lead, 5 ounces of litharge, 1 gold-weight <note>original: "aūr. j."; referring to an aureus or solidus weight</note> of mustard seed, and 1 ounce of tragacanth <note>a natural gum</note>. Let them be ground and sifted with gold-solder <note>original: "orali"; possibly 'chrysocolla'</note> and made with egg white; let it be melted with 2 ounces of rose oil and poured over these ingredients in a mortar and mixed.

## Great Basilicon Ointment
<margin>pitch, black pitch <note>original: "zimar. p̄nauo"</note>, liquid pitch</margin>
Effective for ulcers and for those in old places <note>long-standing sores</note> and wounds where there is heat. 1 pound of wax, 7 ounces of pitch, 3 ounces each of myrrh, resin, and frankincense <note>original: "oū."; likely 'olibanum'</note>, 2 ounces of white glue, and 10 pounds of oil.

## Lesser Basilicon Ointment
Take equal portions of resin, pitch, and wax; let them be mixed with olive oil.

## Ointment of White Lead with Vinegar
<margin>pitch, black pitch, liquid pitch</margin>
Take as much litharge as you wish and sift it; put the white lead in a hand-pot and pour vinegar and oil over it; mix well by hand and use.

## Ointment of Flower of Copper for Old Ulcers
2 ounces of flower of copper <note>original: "flore eris"; verdigris or copper acetate</note>, 5 ounces each of resin and white wax. Grind the flower of copper; melt the other medicines with oil—the best that can be found—and pour over the flower of copper; let it be stirred until even and administered.

## Ointment of Chalcitis
<margin>1 amina <note>a Greek measure</note>, in another [version] bull's fat</margin>
Which Galen called "the generous one" <note>original: "mūtikā"; likely 'munifica'</note>, effective for pestilential abscesses; it heals wounds that are difficult to close and those that bleed. It is beneficial for the hardness of the bladder and difficulty of the kidneys. It is prepared first with <insert>oil</insert> and the fat of a mountain goat <note>original: "zurbi"; possibly referring to a wild goat or ibex</note>, 2 pounds of each; 4 pounds of oil; 4 ounces of Chalcitis <note>original: "calceadis"; a copper-bearing mineral</note>. Melt the fat... mix with 1 pound of oil, 2 pounds of resin, and litharge mixed with them... clean out the fistulas which have been cut from the skin with a blade until even, and administer it.

## Black Ointment
1 ounce of litharge, 2 ounces of strong [pitch?], 2 ounces of oil. <margin>1 [portion] administered</margin> <margin>the best</margin> Prepare all with care so they do not burn; stir until thickened.

## Diachylon Ointment
Effective for nodules, fistulas, and abscesses. Its composition is: fenugreek, linseed, and marshmallow root, one *keleria* <note>a specific measure</note> of each. Infuse each by itself for a day and night. Then take 1 and a quarter pounds of the mucilage <note>the gummy extract</note> of each; 1.5 pounds of litharge, 2 pounds of oil. Let them boil together in one boiling. Then remove from the fire; first boil the oil with the litharge until it thickens... then add the mucilages one after another; let them thicken over a gentle fire.

**Here begins the second [book] of the Antidotary.**
In this SUMMARY we shall bring forth those compound medicines which are of great power for every illness, through which we shall be restored; and a memory of those things which were spoken of in the first summary, so that for the one who reads this book, there may be a comprehension of all operations, or at least many of them. And this is why, for example, when one understands the operations for the itch <note>scabies</note>, let him go to the second book and into the book of written medicines. And he shall know in one hour the comprehension of all the medicines aforementioned. And when he first turns to the chapter of the second book, let him seek the chapter on the itch, and he will understand the aforementioned operations. Likewise, when he arrives at the "meditarium," <note>likely the dispensary or a specific section of the text</note> he will understand the remaining compound operations. For it will be easy to understand all specific operations, or many of them. ## Another Head-Cleanser

<margin>Alachar <note>likely a Latinized Arabic name for the recipe</note></margin>
Take juice of ivy leaves <note>original: "lubleb"; Arabic 'lablab' for ivy</note> 1 aureus; stonecrop <note>original: "sedunū"</note> one sixth, that is 1 aureus; juice of squirting cucumber <note>original: "cucumeri asininū"; a potent purgative used to clear the head</note> one sixth, that is 1 aureus. ## Another Head-Cleanser

Bone oil <note>original: "oleū oseū"</note> for the restoration of hair, and the softening of the limbs and tremors, and for all cold and moist pains, and obstructions that arise from coldness and moisture in the joints and nerves.

## With the Blessed Mixture

Take the juice of colocynth roots <note>original: "radicū colloqn̄itid"; Bitter Apple, a drastic laxative</note> and let it flow... <note>The text is abbreviated here regarding the collection process</note> and let the roots of all these be prepared: nigella <note>original: "codearū"</note>, and harmel <note>Syrian Rue</note>, and others elsewhere. Then grind them with these liquids so they are well-mixed; then grind it again. When you have need of it, take from it the weight of a grain of earth <note>a tiny amount</note> and dissolve the head-cleanser with the milk of a woman nursing a girl; apply it to the interior of the nose. It opens obstructions and warms the brain and the head, drawing out those superfluities that are within it.

## Another Head-Cleanser

Effective for wandering head pains. ℞. Minium <note>Red lead, commonly used in ancient medicine despite its toxicity</note>, nutmeg, amber, camphor, and musk; take 1 drachma <note>unit of weight indicated by the symbol .z.</note> of each. Let each be ground by itself, then let them be mixed and prepared with *Sabuan* oil and a little balsam oil. Let there be a weight of six grains, and let it be dissolved with some water, and use it as a head-cleanser.

## The True Confection for Cleansing the Head

Which cleanses the head and expels the superfluities and bad ailments within it. ℞. Pulp of colocynth cleaned of its seeds and its roots, 10 aurei; frankincense and white pepper, 8 drachmas; mace and [long] pepper, 3 or 5 aurei of each; cloves, 1 aureus; aloes, myrrh, ammoniacum, and salt, 1 aureus of each; *samac* <note>sumac</note>, 8 aurei; and cleaned *ablaenj* <note>possibly a corruption of a plant name like bdellium or an Arabic ingredient</note>, 5 aurei. Let them be made and refined; 2 aurei of these should be used.

## The True Related Confection

Take colocynth pulp... and see that it is cleaned of its skin and its seeds; frankincense and aloes, 20 drachmas of each; birthwort root, celery, white pepper, 5 drachmas of each; opopanax and aloes, 8 drachmas of each; *sualco* 2; spikenard and camphor; "bird’s tongue" <note>ash tree seeds</note>, *cauamā*, cassia, ginger, and polypody, 3 drachmas of each. Let them be ground, mixed, and refined.

## Safe Pills for Cleansing the Head

Rhubarb <note>original: "Rubrit."</note> and aloes, 10 drachmas of each; cleaned colocynth 3 drachmas; and myrrh 3 drachmas; of each. If it fails, add 2 drachmas of aloes. The strong dose is 5 drachmas, or it ought to be 5 aurei.

## Pills for Head Pain other than Melancholy

Take epithyme <note>dodder of thyme</note> and agaric, 3 drachmas of each; and 7 or 8 drachmas of aloes; and polypody 3 drachmas; and 7 drachmas of aloes; 5 drachmas of salt; 5 drachmas of black myrobalans <note>an astringent fruit from India</note>; 2 drachmas of lapis lazuli; 5.5 drachmas of all.

## Pills for Head Pain from Wind, that is, Melancholy

Take chebulic, belleric, and emblic myrobalans, the weight of 3 drachmas of each; salt 4 drachmas; lavender <note>stoechas</note> 4 drachmas; Hiera Pigra <note>the "Sacred Bitter," a classic aloe-based purgative</note> 8 drachmas; colocynth pulp 3 drachmas; *ablaenj* 5 drachmas; agaric 8 drachmas; *tut bich* [?]; epithyme and aloes, 25 drachmas of each; black hellebore 5 drachmas; cassia fistula 5 or 50 drachmas.

## Decoction of Water for the Same

With which water a compress should be made for several days. ## Concerning the True Solace... Decoction of Myrobalans

<margin>Myrobalans.</margin>
Which cleanses for migraines... chebulic myrobalans, 10 drachmas of each; manna 20 drachmas; tamarinds 15 drachmas;... 7 drachmas; *ablat̄rj* 3 drachmas. ## Concerning the Errhines <note>original: "emictmea"</note>

Rose-scented remedies which are effective for the itch, and produce an excellent result with linen applied two or three times.

# The art of the Indian electuary <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term> which increases semen and strengthens the appetite.

### Preparation of troches <term>troche: a small medicated lozenge or tablet</term> of coral. 
From the book of Ahmed, son of Isaac <note>original: "Amete filij ysaach," likely referring to the 10th-century physician Isaac Judaeus</note>. These stop the mixing of blood, are useful for hemorrhoids <note>original: "remozoydariū," a corruption of "haemorrhoidarum"</note>, and help against the spitting of blood. Take coral, troches of gall <note>original: "tr̄ozalli," likely gallnuts</note>, hemorrhoid treatment, and acacia, tragacanth <term>tragacanth: a natural gum obtained from the dried sap of Middle Eastern legumes</term>, and gum arabic, and "lucit" and "lulinke" <note>unidentified botanical terms, possibly phonetic transcriptions of Arabic names</note>, and their own iris; of each 6 drachms. Mastic and poppy seeds, and "ayan"; of each 3 drachms. Opium, 4 drachms. Let them all be ground and prepared with mucilage of psyllium <term>psyllium: seeds used for their mucilaginous, soothing properties</term>, and let troches be made. The dose of each should be 2 drachms. It should be drunk with grape syrup or with syrups effective for that purpose.

### Preparation of "molatum" troches, from the book of Ahmed, son of Isaac.
Take the flowers of "molatum" <note>unclear, perhaps a specific flower preparation</note>, 1 part; turbith <term>turbith: the root of *Operculina turpethum*, used as a purgative</term>, 1 part; clean licorice, 1 part; "diagdy" <note>likely *diapenydeon*, a sugar-based medicine</note>, 1/4 part. Let them be wrapped in rose oil and prepared with syrup of "molatum," and let the weight of the dose be 2 drachms.

### The Diachylon plaster <term>diachylon: a classic lead-based plaster used to soften tumors and heal wounds</term> which is fortified for the abdomen <note>original: "ziraum," possibly from the Arabic *zir*, referring to the lower abdomen</note>.
Take golden litharge <term>litharge: lead monoxide, used as a drying agent in ointments</term> in which there is no blackness nor lead, as much as you wish, with thick oil in proportion. Put them in a vessel and add 4 parts of oil for each part of litharge in summer, and [a different amount] in winter. Let them boil until the litharge coagulates. Then remove from the fire and add to each part of litharge the mucilage of fenugreek, the mucilage of linseed, and an equal amount of mucilage of anise or its root. Let it be stirred in a mortar and stretched until it reaches the thickness of an ointment. This is one of the secrets of this ointment. Add 1 part of iris root when it is pounded in the mortar, because it is extremely effective in resolving and maturing [abscesses].

### Ointment of palm, which is refined in the book of Abulcasis <note>original: "azalauau," referring to Al-Zahrawi, the great medieval surgeon</note>.
Take calf fat cleaned of its skins, exactly 1 pound. Let it be melted with fire, and add to it old oil, litharge, and aloe; of each half a pound; and tragacanth, 2 drachms. Let each of the two—namely the tragacanth and the clean litharge—be pounded for a long time in a mortar. Then lift the whole mixture over the fire and stir it with a spatula of dry palm wood whose end has been burnt; this is done to remove impurities. And if it appears [needed], stir it again and let it be discarded. And let

<column-break/>

the spatula be wet and cut into small pieces and added over the ointment before the decoction is added to it. Let it be cooked until it becomes like liquid wax with water and oil.

### Preparation of the "alakar" eye salve, from the antidotary of Ahmed, son of Isaac.
<margin>For when the nipple [of the eye] is opened too much <note>referring to a perforated ulcer or extreme dilation</note></margin>
This is helpful for "musaragi" <note>original: "muſara gi," likely *myocephalon*, a protrusion of the iris through a corneal ulcer</note> and all ulcers of the eye, and for excessive heat. Take golden calamine <term>calamine: a mineral used to treat skin and eye irritation</term>, white lead <note>original: "ceruse"</note>, burnt copper, starch, gum arabic, and tragacanth; of each 8 drachms. Lead burnt with sulfur, 4 drachms. Antimony, 20 drachms. Frankincense, 2 drachms. Opium, 9 drachms. Aloe, 1 drachm. Let these be ground and sifted and prepared with rainwater, and make eye salves <term>collyrium: a medicinal lotion or salve for the eyes</term> and use them.

### Preparation of the white eye salve, from the aforementioned book.
Made for the pain of ophthalmia <note>original: "obitalme," a corruption of *ophthalmia*</note> and its side. Take white lead, 20 drachms. Gum arabic and starch; of each 10 drachms. White tragacanth, 1 drachm. Sarcocolla <term>sarcocolla: "flesh-glue," a Persian tree resin used to heal wounds</term> nourished with donkey milk or breast milk, 20 drachms. Opium, 1 drachm. Let them be ground and sifted, and prepared with water, and let eye salves be made.

### Preparation of the sharp powder, from the aforementioned book.
Which cleanses at the end of ophthalmia, and removes the remaining redness of the eye, and is shown to be effective in ophthalmia of much moisture, and for "lentice" <note>likely *lentigo*, or spots</note>, and for "guardmigi" <note>unclear ocular term</note>, and for all difficult ophthalmia in the blurring <note>original: "lentia"</note> of the eye. Take sarcocolla, 10 drachms. Saffron, spikenard, and aloe; of each 1 drachm. Let them be ground, sifted, and applied.

### Pure Spices...
Take mastic, wood of balsam, fruit of balsam, cassia, and cinnamon; of each 6 drachms. Good "calois" <note>unclear, perhaps *calamus*</note>, 5 drachms. Yellow, Indian, and Chebulic myrobalans <term>myrobalan: an astringent fruit used in medieval medicine</term>, and belliric and emblic myrobalans; of each 5 drachms. Let them be powdered and anointed with almond oil and prepared with honey. It is useful for headache and odors, and for ringing in the ears.

# Definition of weights and measures according to Mesue, son of Lampior.

Italian kist: 1 and a half pounds.

He said: This is excerpted from the chapter where it was gathered, because those who use the Arabic language in their chapters do not yet recognize the measure I have brought here. But because necessity compelled me to show it. Therefore, before there is anything else concerning it, let one *amiai* <note>possibly a corruption of an Arabic measure</note> be made into a small pill from this book. The "kist" <term>kist: derived from the Greek 'xestes,' a unit of volume roughly equal to a pint</term> is known among the people who speak the Greek language as a measure used for all things. And this is because some of them use one version, while others use another. The "kist" among the Romans contains one and a half pounds plus a sixth, which makes 20 [ounces]. And the pound is seven. The Roman *cemum* is 20. And the Italian and Egyptian *muna* <note>original: "muna," likely the 'mina'</note> is 16. And the *muna* is a *sextarius* <term>sextarius: a Roman measure of volume, about half a liter</term> of 40. And the pound is a *sextarius* of 90. And the *sextarius* is six and a half. Or the gold "y" is five. The grain of laurel is one gold [unit]. And the Italian *dorac* is eight *lotem*. And the *lotem* is six Roman *acitc*. And the *coala* is eight. The *kimu* is a quarter and one unit, up to half a drachma... or a drachma is a half... and each one of these is six gold [units]. The *adur* is one and a half. ### The book being finished, I return thanks to Christ.

Medicinal weights and signs are taken up against names <note>meaning: defined against their common names to avoid confusion</note>, because errors often happen to readers through ignorance. These are represented by their forms and characters as seals of invention, because people of different nations have established these measures and weights, and those who are ignorant or malicious disparage them. One ought to know the methods of weights and measures as they have been established. Nature added weight to all bodily things, but she also gave weight to the heart. Moses, who preceded the time of the pagan philosophers, first described the distinct varieties of measures and weights. Later, the sharp-witted Phydo established the nature of narrating weights. And other ancients instituted them. If one were more experienced in this art. A "weight" <note>original: "pondus"</note> is so called because it is weighed on a balance <note>original: "statera"</note> in pounds. A pound <note>original: "libra"</note> is a weight, as seen in these examples: The *modius* <term>modius: a dry measure, often translated as a 'bushel'</term> is a measure of 22 *sextarii* established among the Hebrews. A *modius* of 48 pounds is another conversion. The authors said the *modius* is a certain type of measure according to the custom of the province of Palestine, containing one and a half *modii*, whose name is taken from the Hebrew; for among the Hebrews it is called a "fustensio" or "elevation" <note>likely referring to the 'heave offering' or 'terumah'</note>. And there is another high measure among the Egyptians containing 15 or 5 *sextarii*. The *calc* is the smallest part of a weight, similar to two grains of lentils. The drachma <note>original: "dragma"</note> is a small weight, the silver *denarius* of victory. A drachma is the eighth part of an ounce. A drachma has 7 obols. A drachma has 23 *siliquae* <term>siliqua: a very small unit of weight, originally the seed of the carob tree; the ancestor of the 'carat'</term>. A drachma is the weight of 3 *denarii*. A drachma weighs 60 grains of barley. A scruple <note>original: "scropulus"</note> has two obols. A scruple has 12 *siliquae*. A scruple is the weight of half a *denarius*. A scruple is the weight of 20 grains of barley. An obol <note>original: "obulus"</note> has two or six *siliquae*. An obol has half a scruple. An obol weighs half a *denarius*. An obol weighs 5 grains of barley. A *siliqua* weighs 4 grains of barley. And a *cyathus* <note>original: "ciat"</note> has 10 drachmas. A *cyathus* has 30 scruples. A *cyathus* has 60 obols. A *cyathus* has 340 *siliquae*. A *statera* is half an ounce, equaling 3 gold units. It is called a *statera* because it consists of three *solidi*. It is said that Abraham first had this form in the borders of Canaan; among the Latins it was called by another name, the *sextula*, because it is completed by six of these. However, the common people call this number a *solidus*. The *cogius* <note>congius</note> has 6 [sextarii]. A *sextarius* weighs 8 ounces.

# The Secrets of Hippocrates

It is related to us that when Hippocrates <note>original: "ypaas"</note> was approaching
death, he commanded that these virtues [medical secrets] written in a book should be placed in an ivory box, and placed with him in
his tomb, lest anyone should discover them. When Caesar
wished to see them, the disciples of Hippocrates
prayed to him, for they were very distressed that he was in a tomb.
By his command, they were removed
and his body was found entirely whole, but he left [the box] for himself. When they dug up the tomb,
the ivory box was found inside. And
in it were these "virtues." From that place, Caesar, looking upon my soul, handed them to his faithful friend.
Here begins Hippocrates, and he said:

When a sick person is at their lowest, and is found [in this state]: if his left hand is
placed upon his chest, know that he will move [towards death]
within 20 days, and especially when in that
sickness he frequently touches his nose.
Likewise he said: And when there was a swelling in the knees
of the sick person of great intensity, know that
he will move [towards death] within 8 days. And especially
when in the height of sickness he has sweated
much sweat.

When there is a small pustule upon the vein in the [place]
which is [near the knee], and if in that
place there should be dust <note>possibly a dry, powdery discharge</note>, then know that the
sick person will move [towards death] on the 3rd day, the day I have indicated.

<meta>The previous page concluded a detailed discussion of weights and measures before transitioning into a legendary account of Hippocrates and medical secrets. So be it.

The sign of it is that, just as it was in the beginning of his illness, it remains severe.

When there was a pustule on the tongue like a <note>original: "naris," possibly meaning a berry or a small polyp</note> berry, and the tongue is clean as if in a mass of flesh; to this person, the signs are clearly known. Then you should know that the person will die on his day—that is, on no day <note>This likely implies sudden death or that no day remains for recovery</note>. And the sign of this is that at the beginning of the end of his illness, he desires hot things upon his buttocks.

When there was a small black pustule on any finger, and like others it hurts, then the patient will die on the second day of his illness. And the sign of this is that his body will be more swollen during his judgment <note>original: "iudie sue," likely referring to the crisis or 'judicium' of the disease</note>.

When there was a small pustule on the thumb of the left hand, like a dry, darkened, or pale color that does not hurt, then you should know that the infirm person will die in the coming days <note>original: "fer' dieb'," possibly the fourth or sixth day</note> from the start of his illness. And the sign of this is that in the beginning of his illness, he will suffer many delusions <note>original: "afellanoia," likely a corruption of a term for delirium or melancholy</note>.

When there was a pustule on the middle finger of the left hand <note>original: "pect'," likely referring to the metacarpus or "comb" of the hand</note>, of a golden color or reddish or dark, then you should know that the patient will die on the twelfth day from the beginning of his illness. And the sign of this is that in the beginning of his illness, he settles upon things having sharpness <note>pungent or acidic flavors</note> with a vehement desire.

When the fingernails are darkened or of a pale color, and on the forehead there is a bloody pustule, then you should know that this man will die on the seventh day from the start of his illness. And the sign of this is that there are many fluctuations at the start of his illness, with many expectorations.

And when there was a vehement itching on the soles of both feet, and the color of the flesh was very pale, then you should know that this man will pass away on the fifth day of his illness, or at sunset. And the sign of this is that at the start of his illness, he urinates much but without relief.

When there were three pustules upon the eyelid of the infirm, of which one is black, another darkened or of a pale color, and the third inclining toward whiteness, then you should know that this man will die on the twenty-seventh day from the beginning of his illness. And the sign of this is that in the beginning of his illness, there is much spitting.

When there was a pustule upon the eyelid of one eye like a smooth hazelnut, of a darkened color, then you should know that the man having it will die on the second day of his illness. And the sign of this is that in the beginning of his illness, he finds his body to be very heavy.

When, before dinner, his teeth turn to a whiteness or a redness, and there appears on his right hand a white pustule that does not hurt, then you should know that the man having it will die on the fourth day from the beginning of his illness. The sign of it is that he does not desire anything at all.

<column-break/>

When there appears on the left hip <note>original: "cor'a," likely 'coxa'</note> of the infirm a vehement redness that does not hurt, then you should know that the man having it will die on the eleventh day of his illness. And the sign of it is that in the beginning of his illness, he finds a vehement itching and desires to eat vegetables.

When a black pustule occurs behind the left ear, then you should know that the man having it will die on the thirty-third day of his illness. And the sign of it is that in the beginning of his illness, he desires to drink cold water with a vehement desire.

When there occurs behind or at the back of the left ear a pustule or a white grain like wheat, then you should know that the man having it will die on the twentieth day from the beginning of his illness, in that very place where the pustule appeared. And the sign of it is that he passes much urine at the beginning of his illness.

When a red, hot pustule occurs behind the right ear, similar to a fire burn, know then that the man having it will die on the seventh day from the beginning of his illness with much vomiting.

When a red pustule occurs under the chin, the size of an Egyptian bean <term>Egyptian bean: the seed of the Nelumbo nucifera, used as a standard for size in medical texts</term>, then you should know that the patient having it will die on the fifty-fourth day from the start of his illness. And the sign of that illness is that the head, in the beginning of the illness, produces much spitting.

<margin>Note what the "sputus" <note>spittle or dregs</note> is.</margin>
It happened once that a man had a pain in the <note>original: "i'puctio' i. maure," perhaps referring to the membrane of the ear or temple</note> that covers the <note>unclear</note>. When this happens to anyone, and then a darkened pustule appears in the white of the eye, then you should know that he will die on the fifth day of his illness. And the sign of this is that at the beginning of his illness, he desires to drink wine.

When there was a darkened pustule on the right side that does not hurt, then you should know that the man having it will die on the ninth day of his illness or at sunset. And the sign of it is that there will be many obstructions during his illness.

<margin>Note what the "nucleus" <note>a kernel or swollen gland</note> is.</margin>
When there was a darkened pustule in the *tatilico*—that is, the left armpit—the size of a tick <note>original: "gtonis," likely 'crotonis'</note>, then you should know that the man having it will die on the fifteenth day of his illness. And the sign of it is that it happens to him in the beginning of his illness that a heavy kernel <note>swelling</note> appears.

But if there were many black pustules upon the flesh, then you should know that the infirm person will pass away on the third day at the latest from the beginning of his illness. And the sign of it is that he desired cold air and <note>unclear</note> with a vehement desire.

<meta>This page continues the "Secreta Hippocratis" (also known as the *Capsula Eburnea* or Ivory Casket), a series of fatalistic medical signs. The previous page detailed omens involving the tongue and fingers; this page concludes the work with signs found on the head, neck, and eyes.</meta>

...[When there was a] whitish pustule <note>original: "pustula subalbida"</note>, then you should know that the person will die on the fourth day of his illness. And the sign of this is that it happened to him at the beginning of his illness, or very specifically in his eyes, such that it was not enough for him to scratch them <note>This likely describes a persistent, deep-seated itch or irritation in the eyes as a secondary symptom</note>.

When there was a pustule in the middle of the head like a smooth black nut that does not hurt, then you should know that the person will die forty days from the start of his illness. And the sign of this is that at the beginning of his illness, he experienced a craving for melon <note>original: "desiderium melonis"</note> and a change in his urine.

When there was a pustule under the neck and a white pustule on the lower eyelid of the left eye, then you should know that the patient will die from it on the eleventh day of his illness. And the sign of this is that at the start of his illness, he felt a vehement craving for sweets <note>original: "desiderium dulcium, desiderio uehementi"</note>.

**Pomer**: That is, arsenic; and Indian stone, that is, pumice. <note>original: "P omer. i. senic... pomica"; *senic* is likely an abbreviation for *arsenicum*.</note>
**Stone-parsley**: That is, mountain celery seed. <note>original: "P etroselinum. i. sem̃ apy mõtanu."</note>

<column-break/>

**Roba**: It is the Indian hazelnut. <note>original: "R oba. ẽ auelana inda"; usually refers to the nutmeg.</note>
**Raatiungi**: It is colophony. <note>original: "R aatiungi. ẽ colofonia"; from the Arabic *ratinaj*, a distilled pine resin.</note>
**Reielen**: It is a stone that is like a magnet. <note>original: "R eielen. ẽ lapis q̃ ẽ sic̃ cmetr"; *cmetr* is likely a corruption of *calamita* (lodestone).</note>
**Ratuba**: It is aloe. <note>original: "R atuba. ẽ aloe."</note>
**Raib**: That is, *agog*; it is sour milk. <note>original: "R aib... lac acetolũ"; from the Arabic *rayb*, referring to fermented or curdled milk.</note>
**Al-luffah root**: That is, *sebifech* root; it is mandrake or *yab*. <note>original: "R adix alletcheza. i. radix sebifech. ẽ mãdragora ul' yab"; *yab* is from the Arabic *yabruh*, a common name for the mandrake plant.</note>
**Rob**: It is juice. <note>original: "R ob. ẽ sucus"; from the Arabic *rubb*.</note>
**Rubub**: It is juice thickened by itself. <note>original: "R rubub. ẽ sucus inspissatꝫ ꝑ se"; the plural of *rob*, referring to thick fruit concentrates or medicinal syrups.</note>
**Rusne**: Which is *leregi*, that is, called a syrup, which is clarified; also called *alkergi seneic*; all these are from India. <note>original: "R usne... dĩ rurub... t̃ alkergi seneic. oĩs sũt inde"; refers to various imported medicinal preserves.</note>
**Robulir**: It is a legume which is called bitter vetch. <note>original: "R obulir. ẽ legum̃... acerole"; *acerole* often identifies *ervum ervilia*.</note>
**Raursent**: That is, *nulasurum*. <note>original: "R aurſent. i. nulaſurũ."</note>
**Racatiam**: That is, fumitory. <note>original: "R acatiam. i. ſumus terre"; *fumus terrae* (smoke of the earth) is the Latin name for the plant *Fumaria officinalis*.</note>
**Rihes**: That is, the flower of sage. <note>original: "R ihes. i. flos ſalias"; *rih* is Arabic for fragrance or wind, often applied to aromatic flowers.</note>
**Rabam**: That is, myrtle. <note>original: "R abam. i. murtus"; from the Arabic *rayhan*.</note>
**Rimegi**: Which is a stone similar to coral. <note>original: "R imegi. qđ ẽ lapis ſilis c̃iar"; *c̃iar* likely a corruption of *coralius*.</note>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical synonymary of medical and botanical terms, specifically focusing on the letters S and T. It follows the previous sections which covered the letters O through R, maintaining the same format of providing transliterated Arabic or Greek terms followed by their more common Latin equivalents or descriptive definitions.</meta>

**Clean Spikenard**: A clean herb, also called spikenard. <note>original: "Spice. adlue. e. herba uel celia. i. e. spica munda." *Spica* usually refers to Nard (*Nardus*), a valued aromatic and medicinal root.</note>
**Senis**: Arabic anise. <note>original: "Senis. arthautir. e. adrach"; likely a corruption of the Arabic *anisun*.</note>
**Senis Arthadilon**: A species of mountain laserwort. <note>original: "Senis arthadilon. e. spes sile leos"; referring to *Seseli silaus* or a similar species used in herbal remedies.</note>
**Myrtle**: The myrtle plant. <note>original: "Siueblogu. e. mirtus"; *Myrtus communis*, known for its fragrant oil and berries.</note>
**Scordion**: Wild garlic. <note>original: "Scordion. e. alea agreste"; *Teucrium scordium*, often called water germander, known for its garlic-like smell.</note>
**Suaiduū**: Alum. <note>original: "Suaiduū. i. e. alūū. i. e. ade"; alum was a common mineral astringent.</note>
**Suauu**: A type of soap. <note>original: "Suauu. e. sep unu"; *sep* likely refers to *sapo*, the Latin word for soap.</note>
**Siela**: It is a beet. <note>original: "Siela. est bleta"; referring to the garden beet (*Beta vulgaris*).</note>
**Semunion**: Wild celery. <note>original: "Semunion. e. apus silue"; *Apium sylvestre*.</note>
**Red Poppy**: That is, the flower of the red poppy. <note>original: "Sachukna hūme. i. e. olu'ru leatulem. i. e. floru pipue ris russi"; *Papaver rhoeas*.</note>
**Saffinū**: Anise, which acts like a stone in the stomach. <note>original: "Saffinū. e. anis q d' agit la pide"; likely refers to the carminative properties of aniseed.</note>
**Sular**: It is hay. <note>original: "Sular. est fenu"; possibly referring to fenugreek (*foenum-graecum*).</note>
**Sassaf**: Sage. <note>original: "Sassaf. e. salus"; likely a variant of *Salvia*, named for its "saving" or healing properties.</note>
**Sebedenegu**: Mustard. <note>original: "Sebedenegu. e. seu cinapis"; from the Arabic *sinap*.</note>
**Selea**: Known in Latin as manna or French lavender. <note>original: "Selea. e. ablatine mannū. uel sticados"; *Lavandula stoechas*.</note>
**Secacul**: Sea holly. <note>original: "Secacul. e. yrengi"; Arabic *shaqaqul*, identifying the *Eryngium* plant.</note>
**Seglem**: A turnip. <note>original: "Seglem. e. napus"; the edible root *Brassica napus*.</note>
**Seerbm**: Pine resin. <note>original: "Seerbm. e. aluū altanaru i. e. de gūe pini"; gum or resin collected from pine trees.</note>
**Sechamiabi**: Spindle tree. <note>original: "Sechamiabi. e. fusa a cool"; *Euonymus europaeus*, used for making spindles.</note>
**Satulen**: Oregano. <note>original: "Satulen. e. organum"; the common culinary and medicinal herb.</note>
**Sedue**: Hemp seed. <note>original: "Sedue. e. sem enabis"; *Cannabis sativa* seeds.</note>
**Selabra**: Called laureola in Latin. <note>original: "Selabra. uocat' latine lautrola"; *Daphne laureola*, or spurge laurel.</note>
**Selabra**: A Greek name for the king's purple. <note>original: "Selabra. e. nom' greū. qm eptat' mur' regis"; refers to the *murex* sea snail used for dye. It has leaves at the top and long stems where flowers grow, the color of which is like mulberry.</note>
**Suen**: Dragon's blood. <note>original: "Suen. e. sanguis dravis"; a bright red resin used as a pigment and medicine.</note>
**Sullet**: Suet or watercress. <note>original: "Sullet. e. seue. i. e. berlu"; *seuum* is animal fat, while *berlu* might refer to *berula* (watercress).</note>
**Suuedegii**: A stone for sharpening. <note>original: "Suuedegii. e. lapis q d' fine nillo. cu q' ali' lapides p ferantur"; a whetstone used to work other stones.</note>
**Saaulifuderion**: It is hart’s-tongue fern. <note>original: "Saaulifuderion. est scolopendria"; *Asplenium scolopendrium*.</note>
**Setuagi**: Earth of Taphos. <note>original: "Setuagi. e. tapha"; a type of medicinal earth.</note>
**Salguifora**: Aloe wood. <note>original: "Salguifora. e. aluoranu"; likely *Aquilaria* or fragrant wood.</note>
**Selineahur**: Unknown substance. <note>original: "Selineahur. e. bel".</note>
**Siserū**: Skirret or parsnip. <note>original: "Siserū. i. e. arxunes"; *Sium sisarum*.</note>
**Spici Alab**: Clean spikenard. <note>original: "Spici alab. e. pete mda"; another variation for clean nard.</note>
**Suc**: Wild bedstraw. <note>original: "Suc. e. galie reufestr"; *Galium silvestre*.</note>
**Senis Alsueni**: A species of boxthorn. <note>original: "Senis alsueni. est aluar cad"; from the Arabic *al-gharqad*.</note>
**Senetberegi**: Barley. <note>original: "Senetberegi. i. e. ordei"; *Hordeum vulgare*.</note>
**Siyeur**: Boxwood. <note>original: "Siyeur. e. bux"; *Buxus sempervirens*.</note>
**Sede Vegi**: A type of stone. <note>original: "Sede uegi. i. e. al[...]antes. i. e. est lapis".</note>
**Siraki Fagi**: Lesser centaury. <note>original: "Siraki fagi. i. e. xu cau rea minor"; *Centaurium erythraea*.</note>

<column-break/>

**Sunesser**: Unknown substance. <note>original: "Sunesser. i. e. bel".</note>
**Stehigū**: A type of poison. <note>original: "Stehigū. i. e. gen' uenerant' i. e. de obstiaca"; likely a toxic plant preparation.</note>
**Sadussa**: A poisonous vapor. <note>original: "Sadussa. id e' q' de uene ne. qd' sūi alco uapl asportatur"; a poison carried through the air, having a pearly internal color.</note>
**Senen**: Columbine or water lily. <note>original: "Senen. i. pro colūbin' cu q tingit' arundi'e. test ra dix nifea"; *Nymphaea* root.</note>
**Sel**: Elder. <note>original: "Sel. i. sambucus"; the elderberry tree.</note>

<column-break/>

**Talc**: That is, a star. <note>original: "Talk. e. qn. stella"; referring to the mineral talc or a star-like mineral substance.</note>
**Tuseni**: A star measured by the modius. <note>original: "Tuseni. e. stella q' e' modio".</note>
**Tarmon**: Resin of a pear tree. <note>original: "Tarmon. i. de gūe pirem"; *gummi pyri*.</note>
**Turafas**: A species of cucumber. <note>original: "Turafas. e. spes cucuure"; a type of gourd or cucumber.</note>
**Teramiabi**: Dew or manna. <note>original: "Teramiabi. i. ros. i. e. manna"; Arabic *taranjubin*, a sweet substance gathered from plants.</note>
**Tstiracost**: Storax. <note>original: "Tstiracost uo' e'"; *Styrax officinalis*, a fragrant resin.</note>
**Tuiear**: Borax or dragon's head. <note>original: "Tuiear. e. borac. i. e. capt' trū"; borax was used both as a flux and in medicine.</note>
**Tefisile**: Nut gum. <note>original: "Tefisile. e. gūma nuce. igita"; resin from a nut tree, perhaps walnut.</note>
**Tutiamnenus**: Wild pennyroyal. <note>original: "Tutiamnenus. e. pulegiū dūmū"; *Mentha pulegium*.</note>
**Tri or Nusne**: Finely ground wheat. <note>original: "Tri. ul' nusne. e. minutu facti de tritico. ul' i' fariuatina"; fine flour or semolina.</note>
**Telisafar**: A mass. <note>original: "Telisafar. e. maas".</note>
**Taw**: Mastic tree. <note>original: "Tāw. i. lentiscus"; *Pistacia lentiscus*.</note>
**Tenagat**: Spurge-laurel. <note>original: "Tenagat. i. latuula"; *Daphne laureola*.</note>
**Terra Aloau**: Furnace earth. <note>original: "Tera aloau. e. tia furn' in quo decoquitur"; earth or clay from a furnace used in medicinal preparations.</note>
**Terra Quadnuu**: Substitute earth. <note>original: "Tere quadnuu. loco ei' pōit' i: mox ativlos. q nō: sani".</note>
**Tylea**: Dodder of thyme or wild vine. <note>original: "Tylea. e. pythuma. Cuapio dicit' q d' lapa i. uuuū actū"; *Epithymum* or a wild grape vine.</note>
**Tulub**: A herb that grows in rivers. <note>original: "Tulub. i. herba q' in flumine nascit'".</note>
**Tuden**: Grows on roofs, called houseleek. <note>original: "Tuden. nascit' in tectis. q uo catur elipsem"; *Sempervivum tectorum*.</note>
**Til**: A type of gum. <note>original: "Til. i. uueline".</note>
**Tasca**: A medicinal drink in two forms. <note>original: "Tasca. tascada e' duplex. una q' e' alba. alta uindis"; White is made from rainwater alone; Green is made from meat, water, coriander, and green herbs.</note>
**Taw**: Mastic tree. <note>original: "Taw. u. lentisais"; repetition of the entry for the mastic tree.</note>
**Taur**: A bird having teeth in its crop. <note>original: "Taur. i. auis. h'ns dentes i puluo"; a reference to the grit or "teeth" found in a bird's gizzard.</note>
**Tortelle**: A type of bread or cake. <note>original: "Tortelle. i. pmi' bitatus".</note>
**Terathir**: Hypocistis. <note>original: "Terathir. i. ypqthidis"; *Cytinus hypocistis*, a parasitic plant used for its astringent properties.</note>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of botanical and medicinal terms, transitioning from the end of the letter S through U/V, X, and Y. It then shifts to a new section or supplementary list beginning with the letter C. The text provides synonymies between what appear to be Arabic or transliterated Eastern terms and their Latin or Greek equivalents, common in medieval pharmaceutical "synonymaries."</meta>

**Senarum alessind** is **basilur**, which is **white honey**. <note>original: "basilur mel albu." *Mel album* or white honey was considered the purest grade of honey in medieval medicine.</note>
**Senarum undirum**, when dry, is **almeus**. <note>original: "Senarū undirū siccarū. est almeus." This likely refers to a specific dried resin or gum.</note>
**Vefcestre gin** is **starch**. <note>original: "amulū." *Amylum* is starch, usually derived from wheat, used as a thickening agent or to soothe skin.</note>
**Uva manticanca** is **stasiliaga** and **habitus**. <note>original: "stasiliaga." Likely a corruption of *staphisagria* (stavesacre), a plant used to treat skin parasites.</note>
**Ungula anitias** is **blacte bi**. <note>original: "blacte bi." Referring to *Blatta byzantia*, the operculum (lid) of a certain sea shell used in perfumes and medicines for its musky odor when burned.</note>
**Sene atic** is the **root of celandine**. <note>original: "radix celidonie." Celandine (*Chelidonium majus*) was traditionally used to treat jaundice and eye problems.</note>
**Sneca** is the **downy fuzz** found on **willow trees and stones**. <note>original: "lanugo qē in. alvonib. 7 lapid." *Alvonib* likely refers to *alnus* (alder) or *salicibus* (willows). *Lapid* refers to stone-growing mosses or lichens.</note>
**Afur**, that is, **hemp**; it is... <note>original: "canabū." *Cannabis sativa*, used for fiber and medicinal seeds.</note>
**Senarum tiaro**, that is, **madder root**. <note>original: "radix rubee." Madder (*Rubia tinctorum*) was a primary source of red dye and was used medicinally as a diuretic.</note>
**Varae indi**, that is, the **leaf of the grain**. <note>original: "foliū. grni." Likely *folium granum*, possibly referring to Malabathrum (Indian leaf).</note>
**Veneru**, that is, **obsica**, which carries...
**Sne**, that is, **triki**, which is **one palm** [high]. This stone with **vinegar**... and treats **cancerous** [sores] in white... <note>This entry describes a mineral treatment for ulcers or "cancers," a common topic in medieval wound-care texts.</note>
**Varices**, that is, **twisted veins** which are in the **legs** or elsewhere. <note>original: "uene tortuose q̄ sūt in crurib." A precise anatomical description of varicose veins.</note>

**Xilailas** and **lud** are both **aloeswood**. <note>original: "lignūū aloes." Aloeswood (Agarwood) was a precious fragrant wood imported from the East.</note>
**Xiruxet**, that is, a **syrup made from fruit juice**, namely of the... <note>original: "rob de suco fructuū." *Rob* is an Arabic term (*rubb*) for a thickened, boiled-down fruit juice or syrup.</note>

<column-break/>

**Yabzo** is the **root of mandrake**. <note>original: "radix mādragore." Mandrake was one of the most famous plants of the Middle Ages, used as an anesthetic and in folk magic.</note>
**Humid esypum** is the **greasy filth** collected from the **wool of sheep** in... <note>original: "Ylop' hūida. ē sordities... suꝑ lanā." This refers to *oesypum*, or crude lanolin, harvested from unwashed sheep's wool for use in ointments.</note>
**Ypopsidios** is the **wild pomegranate juice**. <note>original: "huba yiana." Likely *hypocistis*, a parasitic plant found on rockroses, often confused with or used similarly to pomegranate flowers (*cytinus*).</note>

---

**Caror** or **zarur** is **sotir**.
**Bucari albusar** is **manna**. <note>original: "manna." Manna is the sweet, dried sap of the flowering ash, used as a gentle laxative.</note>
**Cumar** is a species from which...
**Curukted** is **redcuria**.
**Cereske** is **tartar**. <note>original: "tartaris." Tartar is the potassium bitartrate deposit found in wine casks, used in various chemical and medicinal recipes.</note>
**Carnech** is **orpiment** or **arsenic**; they are the same. <note>original: "auripimentū. ul' arsenia." Orpiment is a bright yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and for skin conditions.</note>
**Cufferab** is the **root of mandrake** and **yabo**; they are the same. <note>original: "radix mādragore 7 yabo." Reiteration of the mandrake entry, showing the synonymy between Arabic and Latin terms.</note>
**Cegi**, that is, **vitriol** or **ink**. <note>original: "atramentu." *Atramentum* refers to any black substance, specifically iron gall ink or copperas (vitriol).</note>
**Carabum** or **masmacoza**, that is, **long birthwort**. <note>original: "aristologia longa." *Aristolochia* was named for its supposed aid in "best childbirth" and was used to treat wounds and snakebites.</note>
**Colvic**, that is, **zipi**.
**Cusekese**, that is, **juvenile**.
**Fizabil**, that is, **sizziler**.
